title: System Design
subtitle: HLD, LLD, distributed systems and 20 case studies

modules.title: System Design Fundamentals
modules.summary: Clients and servers, API styles, latency, throughput, availability, scaling up and out.

lessons.title: Speed, capacity, uptime and scaling: the vocabulary of system design

blocks.text: Latency vs throughput, bandwidth, availability vs reliability, the nines, vertical vs horizontal scaling and why stateless services scale easily.
In simple words

A system can be judged on four simple questions. How fast does one answer come back? How many answers can it give per second? How often is it up? And when more people arrive, can we add more machines instead of buying one giant one? These ideas are the vocabulary used in every design discussion.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Picture a toll road. Latency is how long one car takes to drive through. Throughput is how many cars pass per hour. Bandwidth is how many lanes the road has. Availability is how often the road is open. If traffic grows you can build a wider road (vertical) or add more roads side by side (horizontal), and side-by-side only works if any road can take any car.

diagram.title: Horizontal scaling with stateless servers (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: A browser or app. It sends requests and does not care which server answers.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.detail: Spreads requests across the servers and stops sending traffic to a server that fails its health check.

nodes.label: App server A
nodes.detail: Stateless copy of the application. Keeps nothing between requests, so it can be added or removed at any time.

nodes.label: App server B
nodes.detail: An identical copy. Two or more copies give both more capacity and protection from a single server failing.

nodes.label: Session store
nodes.detail: A shared in-memory store that holds login sessions. Because it is shared, any app server can read any session.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.detail: Durable shared state. This is usually the hardest tier to scale because it holds the data of record.

steps.text: The client sends a request. It only knows the load balancer address, never an individual server.
The load balancer picks App server A, a healthy instance.
Server A looks up the session in the shared store instead of its own memory.
Server A reads the data it needs from the database.
Server A returns the response to the load balancer.
The response goes back to the client.
The next request from the same user arrives. Nothing ties it to Server A.
This time Server B is chosen. It is equally able to answer.
Server B finds the same session in the shared store, so the user stays logged in.

blocks.text: How it works

**Latency and throughput.** Latency is the time one request takes from send to response, measured in milliseconds. Throughput is how many requests the system completes per unit time, for example 2,000 requests per second. They are related but not the same: a pipeline can have high latency and high throughput, like a cargo ship. Always report latency as percentiles. The average hides slow requests, so p50, p95 and p99 are used. A p99 of 800 ms means 1 in 100 requests took at least that long.

**Bandwidth.** Bandwidth is the maximum data a link can carry per second, for example 1 Gbps. It limits throughput when responses are large, such as images or video. Low bandwidth hurts large transfers, but for small API calls latency (round trips) matters far more than bandwidth.

**Availability and reliability.** Availability is the fraction of time a system is able to serve requests. Reliability is the probability that it behaves correctly over a period. A service that is always up but returns wrong data is available and unreliable. Availability is quoted in nines: 99.9% allows about 8.8 hours of downtime a year (0.001 x 8,760 h), 99.99% allows about 53 minutes, 99.999% about 5 minutes. Each extra nine usually costs much more, so choose the target from business need, not from habit.

**Availability of chains.** If a request needs service A and service B in series, availabilities multiply: 99.9% x 99.9% is about 99.8%. Redundancy in parallel works the other way: two independent copies each at 99% give 1 - (0.01 x 0.01) = 99.99%, assuming failures are independent. This is why removing single points of failure matters more than making one machine perfect.

**Vertical vs horizontal scaling.** Vertical scaling (scale up) means a bigger machine: more CPU, memory, faster disk. It is simple and needs no code change, but it has a ceiling, gets expensive and leaves one point of failure. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means more machines behind a load balancer. It has no hard ceiling and tolerates failures, but the software must cope with many copies.

**Stateless vs stateful.** A stateless service keeps nothing between requests: everything it needs arrives with the request or is read from a shared store. Any instance can answer any request, so scaling out is just adding instances. A stateful service holds data in its own memory or disk, so requests must reach the right instance and failures lose data unless it is replicated. The usual pattern is to make the application tier stateless and push state into databases, caches and queues, which are scaled with their own techniques such as replication and partitioning.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Fast answers, many answers per second, rarely down, and the ability to add more machines when more people show up. Those are the four things to ask about any system.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Latency is time per request, throughput is requests per second, availability is uptime measured in nines. Scale up means a bigger server, scale out means more servers, and scale out needs stateless application servers.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Percentile latencies, not averages, drive user experience. Availability multiplies across serial dependencies and improves with independent redundancy. Statelessness moves the scaling problem into the data tier, where replication and partitioning take over.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Define SLIs and SLOs per user journey, derive an error budget, and design redundancy against correlated failures such as shared deploys, shared zones and shared dependencies, which break the independence assumption behind the parallel-availability formula.
Trade-offs

rows: Vertical scaling
No code change, no distribution problems, simple operations.
Hard ceiling, cost rises faster than capacity, single point of failure, restarts mean downtime.
Early stage, databases that are hard to shard, quick relief while a better design is built.
Horizontal scaling
Near-linear capacity growth, survives instance failure, rolling deploys.
Needs stateless design, load balancing, more moving parts to monitor.
Any tier expected to grow or that must stay up during failures.
Higher availability target (more nines)
Fewer outages for users, stronger trust.
Multiplies cost and complexity: multi-zone, multi-region, more testing and on-call.
Payments, ordering and other journeys where downtime directly loses money or trust.
Sticky state in the app server
Fast local reads, no network hop for session data.
Breaks scale-out, a crash loses sessions, uneven load.
Rarely. Prefer a shared session store or signed tokens.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: One app server crashes while holding user sessions in its memory
Those users are logged out and carts may be lost.
Keep sessions in a shared store or in signed tokens so any instance can continue the session.
Load grows 5x on a single large server
CPU saturates, latency climbs for everyone, then requests time out.
Scale out behind a load balancer, add autoscaling on CPU or request rate, and set limits to shed excess load.
Two services in series each promise 99.9%
The user-facing availability is only about 99.8%, so the promised target is missed.
Compute availability across the whole chain, add redundancy, and make non-critical calls optional with timeouts and fallbacks.
The team watches average latency only
A slow 1% of requests goes unnoticed while real users complain.
Alert on p95 and p99 per endpoint and track them against an SLO.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What is the difference between latency and throughput, and why use percentiles?
blocks.text: Latency is time per request, throughput is requests completed per second. Percentiles (p95, p99) expose the slow tail that averages hide, and the tail is what users notice. Mention that tail latency compounds when a request fans out to many services.

blocks.title: Availability vs reliability?
blocks.text: Availability is the share of time the system can serve requests, quoted in nines. Reliability is correct behaviour over time. A system can be available but wrong. Design targets need both: SLOs for uptime and for correctness such as error rate.

blocks.title: Vertical or horizontal scaling, and what do you need for horizontal?
blocks.text: Start vertical for simplicity, move horizontal for headroom and fault tolerance. Horizontal needs a load balancer, health checks, stateless services with shared state in a database, cache or token, and a plan for scaling the data tier by replication and partitioning.
Takeaways

items: Latency is time per request; throughput is requests per second; report latency as percentiles.
Availability is quoted in nines; each nine costs more and serial dependencies multiply downward.
Redundancy in parallel raises availability only if failures are independent.
Scale up is simple but capped; scale out is flexible but needs stateless services.
Keep application servers stateless and move state to shared stores that scale in their own way.

quiz.q: A system handles 5,000 requests per second but each request takes 2 seconds. Which statement is true?
options: Throughput is high and latency is high
Throughput is low because latency is high
quiz.why: Many requests can be in flight at once, so throughput and latency are independent measures.

quiz.q: About how much downtime per year does 99.9% availability allow?
quiz.why: 0.1% of 8,760 hours is about 8.8 hours. 99.99% allows about 53 minutes.

quiz.q: Why must application servers be stateless to scale out easily?
options: So each server can be bigger
So any instance can serve any request and instances can be added or removed freely
quiz.why: If state lives in a shared store, the load balancer is free to send any request to any instance.

quiz.q: Two independent copies of a service each have 99% availability. Running them in parallel gives about:
quiz.why: Both must fail together: 0.01 x 0.01 = 0.0001, so availability is 99.99%, if the failures are truly independent.

lessons.title: REST, GraphQL, gRPC and real-time: choosing how systems talk

blocks.text: Compare REST, GraphQL and gRPC, then WebSockets, Server-Sent Events and polling, and synchronous vs asynchronous communication.
In simple words

Programs need an agreed way to ask each other for things. Some ways are like filling in a standard form, some are like asking a custom question, and some are like a fast private phone line. You also choose whether to wait on the line for the answer or leave a note and get called back later.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: REST is a restaurant menu with fixed dishes at fixed numbers. GraphQL is a build-your-own bowl where you say exactly which ingredients you want. gRPC is the kitchen staff shouting short coded orders to each other. Polling is asking the waiter every minute whether your food is ready, SSE is the waiter bringing updates to your table, and WebSockets is a walkie-talkie both sides can press at any time.

diagram.title: Mixed API styles behind one gateway (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client app
nodes.detail: A mobile or web app that reads data, places commands and wants live updates.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Single entry point. Authenticates, rate limits and routes to the style that fits each use case.

nodes.label: REST orders API
nodes.detail: Resource-oriented HTTP endpoints for commands such as creating an order. Easy to cache and easy to call from anywhere.

nodes.label: GraphQL server
nodes.detail: Lets the client ask for exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, assembling data from several backends.

nodes.label: Realtime channel
nodes.detail: A WebSocket or SSE endpoint that keeps a connection open and pushes updates to the client.

nodes.label: gRPC inventory service
nodes.detail: Internal service called with compact binary messages over HTTP/2. Fast and strongly typed between services.

nodes.label: Message queue
nodes.detail: Holds events so the producer does not wait for slow consumers.

nodes.label: Async worker
nodes.detail: Consumes events later: sends emails, updates search, triggers fulfilment.

steps.text: The product page needs name, price and stock. The app sends one GraphQL query naming exactly those fields.
The gateway authenticates the call and forwards it to the GraphQL server.
The GraphQL server calls the inventory service over gRPC, a fast typed internal call, to fetch stock.
The inventory service answers in a few milliseconds with a compact binary response.
The GraphQL server merges the pieces into one JSON response.
The user places an order. The app sends POST /orders, a simple command that fits REST well.
The gateway routes the command to the REST orders API, which validates and stores it.
The API publishes an OrderPlaced event and returns immediately without waiting for emails or fulfilment.
A worker picks up the event later and does the slow follow-up work asynchronously.
The app keeps one open connection. Status changes are pushed to it instead of the app asking repeatedly.

blocks.text: How it works

**REST.** Resources are named by URLs (`/orders/42`) and manipulated with HTTP verbs: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Responses are usually JSON. REST is simple, works everywhere, and gets HTTP caching, status codes and tooling for free. Its weaknesses are over-fetching (you get fields you do not need) and under-fetching (you need several calls to build one screen).

**GraphQL.** The client sends a query describing the exact shape of data it wants and the server returns exactly that, usually through one endpoint. This reduces round trips for screens that combine many resources and lets frontends evolve without new endpoints. The costs are harder HTTP caching, the need to guard against expensive queries with depth and cost limits, and the N+1 problem inside resolvers, which batching tools such as data loaders address.

**gRPC.** Contracts are defined in Protocol Buffers and calls travel as compact binary messages over HTTP/2, which multiplexes many calls on one connection and supports streaming in both directions. It gives strong typing, generated clients and low overhead, so it suits service-to-service traffic. It is harder to call directly from browsers and harder to debug by eye than JSON.

**Polling, SSE and WebSockets.** Short polling asks repeatedly on a timer: simple but wasteful and always a little late. Long polling holds the request open until there is news. Server-Sent Events keep one HTTP response open and let the server push text events one way, with automatic reconnect. WebSockets upgrade the connection to a two-way channel, ideal for chat or live collaboration. Persistent connections cost memory per client and need care when load balancing and deploying.

**Synchronous vs asynchronous.** In synchronous communication the caller waits for the answer, so latency and failures of the callee become the caller latency and failures. It is easy to reason about and right when the user needs the result now. In asynchronous communication the caller sends a message or event and carries on. It decouples services in time, absorbs spikes in a queue and improves resilience, but results arrive later, ordering and duplicates must be handled, and debugging a flow is harder.

**Picking a style.** A common layout is REST or GraphQL at the edge for clients, gRPC between internal services, queues for work that can wait, and SSE or WebSockets only where live updates have real value. Mixing is normal. The deciding questions are who the caller is, how big the payloads are, whether the user must wait, and whether the server needs to push.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Different ways of asking a server for things, each with a different strength: simple and universal, exactly what you need, very fast, or live updates. You can also wait for the answer or get notified later.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: REST for resources over HTTP, GraphQL for client-shaped queries, gRPC for fast internal calls. Polling, SSE and WebSockets differ in who can send and how long the connection stays open. Use async messaging when the caller does not need the result immediately.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Choose by caller and payload: public clients get REST or GraphQL, internal hops get gRPC over HTTP/2, slow side effects go to queues. Handle idempotency on retries, version contracts carefully, and limit GraphQL query cost.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Treat each protocol as a failure-mode choice: sync chains add availability products and tail latency, long-lived connections shift load balancing to connection counts and make deploys need draining, and async flows need idempotent consumers, schema evolution rules and dead-letter handling.
Trade-offs

rows: REST
Simple, universal, cache-friendly, easy to debug.
Over-fetching and under-fetching, many round trips for rich screens.
Public APIs, simple CRUD, commands, anything that benefits from HTTP caching.
GraphQL
Client picks fields, one round trip for composite screens, typed schema.
Complex caching, risk of expensive queries, resolver N+1 issues.
Many clients with different data needs, screens that combine several backends.
gRPC
Compact, fast, strongly typed, streaming support.
Awkward from browsers, harder to inspect, needs shared schemas.
Internal service-to-service calls with high volume or tight latency.
WebSocket / SSE vs polling
Instant updates and less wasted traffic than frequent polling.
Long-lived connections cost memory and complicate scaling and deploys.
Live tracking, chat, dashboards. Use plain polling when updates are rare or latency is relaxed.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: A client sends a deeply nested GraphQL query
One request triggers thousands of backend calls and exhausts the database.
Enforce depth and cost limits, use batching and persisted queries, set timeouts.
A synchronous chain of four services has one slow link
Latency adds up and threads pile up in every caller, causing a cascading outage.
Set timeouts and budgets, use circuit breakers, call in parallel where possible, move non-essential work to async.
A deploy restarts servers holding 200,000 WebSocket connections
All clients reconnect at once and overload the system.
Drain connections gradually, use jittered exponential backoff in clients, keep connection state out of the server.
A queue consumer receives the same event twice
The customer is emailed or charged twice.
Make consumers idempotent using an event id and a processed-events check.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC: how do you choose?
blocks.text: REST for simple, cacheable, public resource APIs. GraphQL when many clients need different shapes of data and screens combine several resources. gRPC for internal service calls where speed and typed contracts matter. Mention that one system often uses all three at different layers.

blocks.title: Polling, SSE or WebSocket for live order tracking?
blocks.text: Start from the need: one-way status updates fit SSE well and work over plain HTTP. Use WebSocket if the client also sends frequent messages. Use polling with a sensible interval if updates are rare. Discuss connection cost, reconnect backoff and load balancer support.

blocks.title: When should a call be asynchronous?
blocks.text: When the user does not need the result to continue, when the work is slow or can fail and be retried, or to absorb spikes. Use a queue, keep consumers idempotent, and give the user a way to see the eventual status.
Takeaways

items: REST is the simple default; GraphQL shapes data per client; gRPC is for fast internal calls.
Polling is simple but wasteful; SSE is one-way push; WebSockets are two-way.
Synchronous chains add latency and failure risk; asynchronous messaging decouples at the price of complexity.
Mixing styles by layer is normal and usually the right answer.
Retries and queues need idempotency to be safe.

quiz.q: A mobile screen needs data from five resources and the network is slow. Which style cuts round trips most directly?
quiz.why: GraphQL lets the client request all needed fields from several resources in one call.

quiz.q: Which is the best fit for high-volume calls between internal services?
quiz.why: gRPC uses compact binary messages over multiplexed HTTP/2 connections with typed contracts.

quiz.q: The server must push live delivery updates one way to a web page. Simplest fit?
quiz.why: SSE is one-way server push over plain HTTP with built-in reconnect. WebSockets are only needed for two-way traffic.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of asynchronous communication?
options: Results arrive later and duplicates or reordering must be handled
quiz.why: You trade immediate answers for decoupling, so consumers must be idempotent and flows are harder to trace.

modules.title: Networking and Request Lifecycle
modules.summary: DNS, TCP, TLS, CDN, load balancer, gateway, service, database. One request, end to end.

lessons.title: How one request travels from a phone to a database and back

blocks.text: Follow a single "open home page" tap through DNS, TLS, CDN, load balancer, API gateway, service, cache and database.
In simple words

When you tap a button in an app, the phone sends a small message over the internet to a computer owned by the company. That computer finds the data you asked for and sends a message back. Between the phone and the data there are several helpers, and each one does exactly one job.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of ordering at a large restaurant. You look up the address (DNS), walk through a guarded door (TLS), a host seats you at a free table (load balancer), a waiter checks you are allowed to order and takes the order (API gateway), the kitchen cooks it (service), using ingredients already on the counter if possible (cache) or fetched from the storeroom if not (database).

diagram.title: Request lifecycle (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Mobile app
nodes.detail: Builds an HTTPS request: method, path, headers (auth token, app version) and an optional JSON body.

nodes.label: DNS
nodes.detail: Turns a host name into an IP address. The answer is cached on the phone for its TTL, so most requests skip this hop.

nodes.label: CDN / edge
nodes.detail: Servers close to the user. Terminates TLS, serves cacheable content directly, blocks abusive traffic, forwards the rest.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.detail: Spreads requests over healthy servers. Stops sending traffic to an instance that fails health checks.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: One front door for all APIs: authentication, rate limiting, routing by path to the right service.

nodes.label: Home service
nodes.detail: Business logic. Stateless: any instance can serve any request because state lives in the cache and database.

nodes.label: Cache (Redis)
nodes.detail: In-memory key-value store. Answers in about a millisecond. Holds copies of data that is read often.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.detail: The source of truth on disk. Slower than the cache but durable and consistent.

steps.text: The app asks DNS for the IP address of api.example.com (skipped when the answer is still cached on the device).
TCP handshake, then TLS handshake with the nearest edge server. Now the connection is encrypted. The app sends GET /home.
The response is personalised, so the edge cannot serve it from its own cache. It forwards the request to the origin.
The load balancer picks a healthy gateway instance (round robin or least connections).
The gateway validates the token, checks the rate limit, and routes /home to the Home service.
The service looks up home:{userId} in the cache. This time it is a miss.
On a miss the service queries the database through a pooled connection.
It stores the result in the cache with a TTL so the next request is a hit.
The service returns JSON to the gateway, which adds response headers.
The response travels back over the same encrypted connection. The app parses the JSON and draws the screen.

blocks.text: How it works

**Name to address.** The client resolves the host name through DNS. Resolvers cache the answer for the record TTL, so DNS costs time only on the first request or after expiry. Low TTLs allow fast failover but increase lookup volume.

**Connection setup.** HTTPS needs a TCP handshake (1 round trip) and a TLS 1.3 handshake (1 more round trip). On a 100 ms mobile network that is about 200 ms before the first byte of the request is sent. Clients keep connections alive and reuse them (HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests on one connection), so the cost is paid once.

**Edge.** A CDN terminates TLS close to the user and serves static or cacheable responses without touching the origin. It also absorbs traffic spikes and attacks. Dynamic, per-user responses pass through to the origin.

**Load balancer and gateway.** A layer 4 balancer forwards TCP connections. A layer 7 balancer or API gateway understands HTTP, so it can route by path, authenticate, rate limit and retry. Both rely on health checks to remove bad instances.

**Service, cache, database.** The service is stateless so it can be scaled horizontally. It reads the cache first (cache-aside) and falls back to the database through a **connection pool**. Opening a database connection costs several round trips, so a pool keeps a fixed number open and lends them to requests.

**Latency budget.** Total time is the sum of every hop. If the service calls three downstream services one after another, their latencies add up. Calling them in parallel makes the total equal to the slowest one. This is why aggregation endpoints fan out in parallel.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The phone asks, a server answers. Helpers in the middle find the server, keep the conversation private, share the work across many servers and remember recent answers.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: DNS resolves the host, TCP and TLS set up an encrypted connection, a load balancer spreads requests, a gateway authenticates and routes, and the service reads a cache before the database.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Each hop adds latency and a failure mode. Connection reuse, HTTP/2 multiplexing, edge TLS termination, connection pooling and parallel fan-out are the main tools for keeping p99 latency inside the budget.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Design the path by budget: allocate p99 per hop, set timeouts shorter than the caller timeout at every layer, cap retries with budgets to avoid retry storms, and decide per endpoint which layer may serve stale data when a dependency is down.
Trade-offs

rows: Terminate TLS at the edge
Fewer round trips for far-away users, origin CPU saved.
The edge provider sees plaintext; traffic from edge to origin needs its own encryption.
Almost always for public consumer APIs.
API gateway in front of every service
Auth, rate limiting and routing in one place.
One more hop and a critical shared component.
As soon as there is more than one backend service.
Cache in front of the database
Much lower latency and database load.
Stale data and invalidation complexity.
Read-heavy data that tolerates seconds of staleness.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: One service instance hangs
Requests routed to it time out.
Health checks remove it; clients use timeouts and a single retry to another instance.
Cache is down
Every request hits the database, which may overload.
Rate limit, serve stale responses from the edge, size the database for a partial cache loss.
Connection pool exhausted
Requests queue inside the service and latency explodes.
Bound the queue, fail fast, fix slow queries, add read replicas.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: What happens when you type a URL or tap a button that calls an API?
blocks.text: DNS resolution, TCP and TLS handshakes, HTTP request to the edge, load balancing, gateway auth and routing, service logic with cache then database, and the response back on the same connection. Mention connection reuse and where caching happens at each layer.

blocks.title: Layer 4 vs layer 7 load balancer?
blocks.text: L4 forwards TCP or UDP by IP and port: fast, protocol-agnostic. L7 parses HTTP: can route by path or header, terminate TLS, retry and rate limit, at a higher CPU cost.

blocks.title: Why use a connection pool?
blocks.text: Opening a database connection needs TCP, TLS and auth round trips and server memory. A pool reuses a bounded set, which lowers latency and protects the database from too many connections.
Takeaways

items: Every hop has one job, a latency cost and a failure mode.
Connection setup is expensive, so connections are reused.
Caches exist at several layers: device, edge, service.
Stateless services plus shared state stores make horizontal scaling possible.
Total latency is the sum of sequential hops, or the maximum of parallel ones.

quiz.q: Why is the first request after app launch usually slower than the second?
options: The server is cold every time
DNS lookup plus TCP and TLS handshakes happen once, then the connection is reused
quiz.why: Connection setup costs round trips. Keep-alive and HTTP/2 reuse the connection afterwards.

quiz.q: A service calls three downstream APIs taking 40, 60 and 80 ms. Called in parallel, the total is about:
quiz.why: Parallel calls finish when the slowest one finishes.

quiz.q: Why keep services stateless?
options: So any instance can serve any request and instances can be added or removed freely
quiz.why: State in shared stores is what makes horizontal scaling and failover simple.

lessons.title: Designing for unreliable mobile networks

blocks.text: A phone loses its connection many times a day. This lesson covers timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, idempotency keys, deduplication, connectivity changes, payload size, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, request priority and what happens when the app is backgrounded mid-request.
In simple words

A phone is not a computer on a desk with a cable. It moves between Wi-Fi and mobile data, enters lifts and tunnels, and the operating system can pause the app at any moment. So every request the app sends might be slow, might never arrive, or might arrive while the answer gets lost on the way back. A well designed app expects this: it waits a sensible amount of time, tries again carefully, and makes sure that trying again never does the same thing twice.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Imagine ordering by post from a town where letters are sometimes lost. You write an order number on every letter. If no reply comes in a week you send the same letter again with the same order number. The shop keeps a book of order numbers, so when the second letter arrives it does not ship a second parcel, it just posts the original receipt again. You also wait a bit longer before each new attempt, so the shop is not buried in letters after a postal strike.

diagram.title: One order request surviving a lost response (generic grocery app)

nodes.label: Checkout screen
nodes.detail: Starts the user action. Shows progress, a retrying state or an offline state based on what the network layer reports, never a raw socket error.

nodes.label: Connectivity monitor
nodes.detail: Listens to OS path updates (Wi-Fi, cellular, none, constrained). It is a hint for when to retry, not proof that a request will succeed.

nodes.label: Network layer
nodes.detail: One shared component that owns timeouts, retry policy, idempotency keys, in-flight deduplication, priority and cancellation for every feature.

nodes.label: Pending request store
nodes.detail: A small durable table on the device. A write that must not be lost is saved here with its idempotency key before it is sent.

nodes.label: OS background transfer
nodes.detail: A system service (background URL session on iOS, a work scheduler on Android) that can finish or reschedule a transfer after the app is suspended.

nodes.label: CDN / edge
nodes.detail: Terminates TLS and HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 close to the user, compresses responses and keeps warm connections to the origin.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates, rate limits and routes. Can return `Retry-After` to tell clients when to come back.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.detail: Executes the write exactly once per idempotency key, even when the same request arrives several times.

nodes.label: Idempotency store
nodes.detail: Maps idempotency key to status and stored response for a retention window, for example 24 hours.

nodes.label: Orders database
nodes.detail: Source of truth. A unique constraint on the idempotency key or client order id is the last line of defence against duplicates.

steps.text: The user taps Place order. The network layer generates one idempotency key (a UUID) for this user action, not for this attempt.
The request body and its key are saved on the device before anything is sent, so the intent survives an app kill.
The connectivity monitor reports a cellular path. The layer picks the timeout and retry profile for a critical write.
POST /orders is sent with the header `Idempotency-Key`, on an existing HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection if one is open.
The edge forwards the request to the origin over a warm connection.
The gateway validates the token and rate limit, then routes to the order service.
The key has not been seen. The service records it as in progress so a concurrent duplicate will wait or be rejected.
The order is inserted and committed.
The final status code and response body are stored against the key.
The phone enters a lift. The response never arrives and the client timeout fires. The client cannot know whether the order was created.
The layer waits for a usable path, then waits a further randomised backoff delay before retrying.
Attempt two sends the identical body with the same idempotency key.
The key is found as completed. The service returns the stored response without creating a second order.
The client receives 201 with the order id, deletes the pending entry and the screen shows the confirmation.

blocks.text: How it works

**The failure model.** On mobile a request has three outcomes, not two: success, known failure, and **unknown**. Unknown means the client timed out or the connection dropped after the bytes left the device. The server may have done the work. Every design decision in this lesson follows from treating unknown as a normal case. The second fact is that the network changes under you: Wi-Fi to cellular handover, captive portals that return HTML with status 200, and paths the OS marks as expensive or constrained (low data mode).

**Timeouts.** Use separate budgets: a connect timeout (short, a few seconds, because a dead path should be detected fast), a read or idle timeout between bytes, and a total deadline for the whole user action including retries. One global 60 second timeout is the usual mistake: the user stares at a spinner for a minute on a dead connection. Pick budgets per request class: interactive reads short, uploads long with progress. The client deadline should be longer than the server processing timeout, otherwise the client gives up on work the server is about to finish.

**Retry with backoff and jitter.** Retry only what is safe and likely to help: connection errors, timeouts, `502`, `503`, `504` and `429`. Do not retry `400`, `401`, `403`, `404` or `422`; they will fail the same way. Wait `min(cap, base * 2^attempt)` and then randomise it (full jitter picks a random value between 0 and that number). Without jitter every phone that failed in the same second retries in the same second, and a recovering server is knocked over again. Cap attempts (2 to 3 for interactive requests), respect `Retry-After`, and use a **retry budget** so retries are a bounded fraction of traffic.

**Idempotency keys.** `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE` are idempotent by definition. `POST` that creates or charges is not, so the client attaches a unique key generated once per user intent and reused across every retry. The server stores key to result. A repeat with the same key returns the stored result. A repeat while the first is still running returns `409` or waits. The same key with a different body is rejected. The key must be persisted on the device before the first send; a key held only in memory is lost with the process, and the relaunched app would create a new key and a duplicate order.

**Request deduplication and coalescing.** Separate from server idempotency, the client should not send the same request twice concurrently. Two screens asking for the same profile share one in-flight request and both receive its result. A double tap on a button maps to one operation. Searches as the user types cancel the previous request instead of letting six responses race. This saves radio time and removes a class of out-of-order response bugs.

**Connectivity changes.** A reachability API tells you an interface exists, not that the server is reachable, so do not block requests on it. Just try, and use path updates as a trigger: when a path returns, flush the retry queue (with jitter, since every app on the phone gets the same signal). Prefer the OS option that waits for connectivity over failing instantly. Respect constrained and expensive path flags by deferring prefetch, large downloads and analytics uploads.

**Payload size and protocol.** On a slow link, bytes are latency. Enable gzip or Brotli, paginate, request only the fields a screen needs, use delta responses with `ETag` and `If-None-Match` (a `304` has no body), and resize images on the server for the device. **HTTP/2** multiplexes many requests on one TCP connection, which removes per-request handshakes, but one lost packet stalls every stream on that connection (TCP head-of-line blocking). **HTTP/3** runs on QUIC over UDP: streams are independent under loss, setup needs fewer round trips, and a connection can survive a change of IP address (connection migration) because it is identified by a connection id, not by the address pair. Clients must fall back to HTTP/2 when UDP is blocked.

**Prioritisation.** Not all requests are equal. Classify them: user-blocking (the screen the user is looking at), user-visible (images below the fold), and background (analytics, prefetch, log upload). Limit concurrency for the lower classes, let the top class jump the queue, and cancel work for screens the user left. Batch background traffic, because each radio wake-up has a battery cost well beyond the transfer itself.

**Backgrounded mid-request.** When the user switches apps, the OS gives the process a short grace period and then suspends it; in-flight sockets in the app process stall and later fail. Exact limits vary by OS version. The design answer has three parts. Critical small writes: request the short background grace period to finish, and rely on the persisted intent plus idempotency key to retry on next launch. Large uploads and downloads: hand them to the OS background transfer service, which runs outside the app process and relaunches the app on completion. Deferred work: schedule it with the platform job scheduler with a network-required constraint. In all three, the server must treat a repeated request as the same operation.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Phone connections drop often. The app should wait a reasonable time, try again a few times with growing pauses, and tag each action with a unique number so the server never performs it twice.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Split timeouts into connect, read and total deadline. Retry only transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter. Attach an idempotency key to every non-idempotent write, persist it before sending, and coalesce identical in-flight requests on the client.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Treat timeouts as an unknown outcome and make every write replayable. Classify requests by priority with separate concurrency limits, use HTTP/3 where available for loss tolerance and connection migration, and move long transfers to OS-managed background sessions. Retry budgets and `Retry-After` keep a fleet of clients from amplifying an outage.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Own the policy end to end as a contract between client and server: per-endpoint retry classes published in the API spec, server-driven backoff and load shedding signals, idempotency retention sized to the maximum offline replay window, and client telemetry that reports attempts, not just final outcomes, so the real error rate is visible. Model the fleet as a thundering herd: after an outage or a push campaign, millions of devices reconnect on the same signal, so jitter, staged reconnection and edge-level admission control are capacity requirements, not polish. Decide per feature what the client is allowed to do without the server and for how long.
Trade-offs

rows: Aggressive retries (many attempts, short delays)
Hides brief blips from the user; high eventual success rate.
Multiplies load exactly when the backend is unhealthy; drains battery; risk of duplicates without idempotency.
Only for cheap idempotent reads, with a cap and jitter.
Short timeouts
Fast feedback, quick switch to cached or offline state.
More requests end in the unknown state; slow but working networks look broken.
Interactive reads with a cache to fall back on. Use longer deadlines for payments and uploads.
Server-side idempotency store
Makes retries of writes safe; allows the client to be simple and persistent.
Extra storage and a lookup on every write; needs a retention policy and careful handling of in-progress keys.
Every create, charge, send or submit endpoint a mobile client calls.
HTTP/3 (QUIC)
No TCP head-of-line blocking, faster setup, connection migration across network switches.
UDP is blocked or throttled on some networks; more CPU; needs fallback and extra observability.
Consumer apps on lossy cellular networks, with automatic fallback to HTTP/2.
One coarse aggregated request per screen
Fewer round trips and radio wake-ups; one loading state.
Larger payload; one slow dependency delays everything unless the server returns partial results.
Screen-level loads on high latency networks. Keep independent, slow parts as separate requests.
OS background transfer for uploads
Survives app suspension and termination; system picks good network and power conditions.
Timing is at the discretion of the OS; less control over headers, progress and retries; harder to debug.
Media uploads, large downloads and anything that takes longer than the background grace period.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Response lost after the server committed a payment
The client times out, the user taps Pay again, and without protection is charged twice.
Idempotency key generated per intent, persisted before send, enforced by the server and a unique database constraint. On relaunch, query the status of the pending intent before offering a retry.
Backend recovers from an outage and all clients retry at once
A synchronised wave of retries overloads the service again (retry storm).
Exponential backoff with full jitter, capped attempts, retry budgets, `Retry-After` and load shedding at the gateway.
Captive portal or proxy returns HTML with status 200
The app tries to parse a login page as JSON and crashes or shows empty content.
Validate content type and schema, treat parse failure as a network-class error, and use TLS so the interception fails visibly.
App suspended in the middle of a multipart upload
The socket dies, the upload restarts from zero on every attempt and never completes on slow links.
Resumable chunked upload with an upload session id and server-reported offset, run through the OS background transfer service.
Slow search responses arrive out of order
Results for an older query overwrite results for the latest query.
Cancel superseded requests and tag each response with a request sequence number; drop any response older than the latest issued.
Single long timeout on a dead connection after Wi-Fi to cellular handover
Requests hang on the stale connection until the full timeout expires.
Short connect and idle timeouts, connection health checks (HTTP/2 PING), drop pooled connections on path change, or use QUIC migration.
Idempotency key retention shorter than the offline replay window
A queued request replayed two days later is treated as new and duplicates the action.
Align retention with the maximum time a client may hold a pending write, expire stale intents on the client, and keep a natural-key uniqueness check in the database.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you make a "place order" call safe on a flaky network?
blocks.text: Generate an idempotency key per user intent, persist the request and key locally before sending, send with a bounded deadline, and retry transient failures with backoff and jitter using the same key. The server stores key to result with an in-progress state, returns the stored result on replay, and a unique constraint in the database backs it up. On relaunch the client reconciles pending intents by asking the server for their status.

blocks.title: What retry policy would you put in a shared mobile network layer?
blocks.text: Policy per request class. Idempotent reads: up to 2 or 3 retries on connection errors, timeouts, 502, 503, 504 and 429, with exponential backoff, full jitter, a cap and respect for Retry-After. Writes: retried only when they carry an idempotency key. Never retry 4xx validation or auth errors, except one retry after a successful token refresh on 401. Add a total deadline and a retry budget, and report attempt counts in telemetry.

blocks.title: The user backgrounds the app while a 50 MB video is uploading. What happens and how do you design for it?
blocks.text: An in-process upload is suspended and later fails. Design it as a resumable upload: create an upload session on the server, send chunks with offsets, and let the OS background transfer service run the transfer outside the app process. On completion or relaunch the app asks the server for the committed offset and continues. The final "attach media to post" call is a small idempotent write. Exact background time limits vary by OS version, so the design must not depend on them.

blocks.title: Should the app check reachability before making a request?
blocks.text: No, not as a gate. Reachability says an interface exists, not that the server can be reached, and it produces both false positives (captive portal) and false negatives. Attempt the request, classify the error, and use path change notifications as a trigger to retry queued work and to drop stale pooled connections. Do use the constrained and expensive flags to defer optional traffic.

blocks.title: How do you reduce latency for a home screen on a slow 3G-class network?
blocks.text: Cut round trips and bytes. Reuse one multiplexed connection, show cached content first and revalidate with ETag, aggregate the first screen into one request, compress, paginate and trim fields, serve device-sized images from a CDN, prioritise above-the-fold requests and defer analytics. Measure with real-user metrics split by network type, because lab numbers on Wi-Fi hide the problem.
Takeaways

items: A timeout means unknown, not failed. Design every write so it can be replayed safely.
Idempotency keys are created per user intent, persisted before sending and enforced on the server.
Retry only transient errors, with exponential backoff, jitter, a cap and a total deadline.
Coalesce and cancel on the client: one in-flight request per resource, no stale responses winning races.
Bytes and round trips are latency on mobile: compress, paginate, revalidate, and prefer HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 with fallback.
Prioritise user-blocking requests and batch background traffic to protect battery and data.
The OS can suspend the app at any time: persist intent, use background transfer for large payloads, and reconcile on relaunch.

quiz.q: A POST /orders request times out on the client. What does the client know?
options: Nothing about whether the order was created
quiz.why: A timeout is an unknown outcome. The request may have been processed and only the response lost, which is why writes need idempotency keys.

quiz.q: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
options: To stop many clients retrying at the same instants and overloading a recovering server
To save battery on the device
quiz.why: Clients that failed together would otherwise retry together. Randomising the delay spreads the load.

quiz.q: When must the idempotency key for a write be generated?
options: Once per attempt, so each retry has a fresh key
Once per user intent, persisted before the first send and reused on every retry
By the server when it receives the request
quiz.why: The key identifies the action, not the attempt. A new key per retry would defeat the purpose, and a key only in memory is lost if the app is killed.

quiz.q: What does HTTP/3 improve over HTTP/2 on a lossy cellular link?
options: It removes the need for TLS
A lost packet delays only its own stream, and the connection can survive a network switch
It guarantees delivery while the app is suspended
quiz.why: QUIC streams are independent under loss and connections are identified by a connection id, so they can migrate between networks.

quiz.q: Which status code should a client NOT retry automatically?
options: 429 Too Many Requests, after the Retry-After delay
quiz.why: A validation error will fail identically every time. Retries are for transient conditions.

lessons.title: Real-time updates on mobile: polling, SSE, WebSocket and push

blocks.text: How a phone learns that something changed on the server: polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events, WebSocket and push notifications, with their battery, cost and lifecycle consequences, and how to reconnect and resume with a cursor.
In simple words

Sometimes the app needs to know about new things without the user pulling to refresh: a new chat message, a driver moving on a map, an order changing status. The app can keep asking the server "anything new?", or it can keep a line open so the server can speak whenever it wants, or the server can ask Apple or Google to wake the phone with a notification. Each way costs a different amount of battery and server money, and only one of them works when the app is closed.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: You are waiting for a parcel. Polling is walking to the door every five minutes to look. Long polling is standing at the door until the courier arrives, then going back inside and returning to the door straight away. A WebSocket is a phone call you keep open with the courier, where either of you can speak at any time. A push notification is the doorbell: it works even when you are asleep, but it only tells you someone is there, and it is the building manager, not you, who decides whether the bell rings.

diagram.title: Chat app: live socket in the foreground, push in the background

nodes.label: Chat app
nodes.detail: Renders messages from its local store. Knows the last message sequence it has applied (the cursor).

nodes.label: Connection manager
nodes.detail: Owns the socket lifecycle: connect on foreground, heartbeat, reconnect with backoff and jitter, close on background.

nodes.label: OS push client
nodes.detail: One system-owned connection to the push provider shared by every app on the phone. Works when the app is not running.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.detail: Routes normal HTTP to the API and long-lived upgraded connections to the realtime gateway. Needs idle timeouts tuned for long connections.

nodes.label: REST API
nodes.detail: Request/response endpoints, including catch-up: messages after a given cursor.

nodes.label: Realtime gateway
nodes.detail: Holds hundreds of thousands of open connections per node. Stateful in connections, stateless in data: it only forwards events.

nodes.label: Pub/sub bus
nodes.detail: Fans events out to whichever gateway node holds the connection for a given user or channel.

nodes.label: Chat service
nodes.detail: Validates and stores messages, assigns a per-conversation sequence number, publishes events.

nodes.label: Message store
nodes.detail: Durable ordered log of messages per conversation. The source of truth that makes resume possible.

nodes.label: Push service
nodes.detail: Decides whether a user needs a push (no live connection), builds the payload and calls the platform providers.

nodes.label: APNs / FCM
nodes.detail: Platform push providers. Delivery is best effort, may be delayed, collapsed or dropped, and is rate limited for silent pushes.

steps.text: The app comes to the foreground. The connection manager reads the stored cursor: last applied sequence 1041 in this conversation.
It first calls GET /messages?after=1041 to catch up on anything missed while it was not connected.
The load balancer routes the plain HTTP request to the REST API.
The API asks the chat service for messages after sequence 1041.
The store returns messages 1042 to 1045 in order. The app applies them and moves its cursor to 1045.
Now the manager opens a WebSocket, sending its auth token and cursor 1045 in the first frame.
The connection is upgraded and pinned to one realtime gateway node, which registers the user and subscribes to their channels.
Another user sends a message. The chat service stores it as sequence 1046 and publishes an event.
The gateway node holding this connection receives the event and writes it to the socket.
The app applies 1046 because it is exactly cursor plus one, persists the new cursor and sends an acknowledgement.
The user switches to another app. The manager closes the socket cleanly instead of waiting for the OS to kill it.
Message 1047 arrives. The recipient has no live connection, so the chat service asks the push service to notify them.
The push service sends a small payload (conversation id, preview, collapse key) to the platform provider using the stored device token.
The OS shows the notification. When the user taps it the app opens and resumes from cursor 1046, so nothing depends on the push having carried the data.

blocks.text: How it works

**Short polling.** The client calls an endpoint on a timer. It is plain HTTP, works through every proxy, scales on the normal stateless stack and is trivial to cache at the edge. The cost is wasted requests when nothing changed and a delay of up to one interval. Make it cheap with conditional requests (`ETag`, a `since` cursor) so the empty answer is a tiny `304` or an empty list. Polling is the right answer more often than interviewers expect: order status that changes every few minutes does not need a socket.

**Server-controlled polling interval.** Do not hard-code the interval in the binary. Let each response carry the next delay (a `next_poll_ms` field or a `Retry-After` style header). The server can then poll fast while an order is out for delivery, slow when it is days away, and back the whole fleet off during an incident without an app release. Add jitter on the client so devices do not align, and stop polling when the screen is not visible.

**Long polling.** The client sends a request and the server holds it open until there is an event or a timeout (commonly tens of seconds), then the client immediately asks again. Latency is near real time and it still looks like ordinary HTTP. Each event costs a full request cycle, the server must hold an open request per client, and ordering across reconnects needs a cursor. It is a good fallback when WebSocket is blocked.

**Server-Sent Events (SSE).** One long-lived HTTP response over which the server streams text events. It is one-directional (server to client), runs over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 as a normal stream, and the protocol has resume built in: each event has an id, and on reconnect the client sends `Last-Event-ID`. Client to server traffic uses normal requests. For feeds, live scores, price tickers and order tracking, SSE gives most of the benefit of a socket with far less protocol surface.

**WebSocket.** A full-duplex, message-framed connection created by an HTTP upgrade. Use it when both sides send frequently and latency matters: chat with typing indicators, collaborative editing, live location from driver to rider. It brings real costs: stateful gateway nodes, sticky routing, a pub/sub layer to reach the node that owns a connection, heartbeats, your own protocol for acks, ordering and resume, and deploys that must drain connections gradually so a restart does not trigger a reconnect storm.

**Push notifications.** APNs and FCM are the only way to reach an app that is not running. The OS keeps a single shared connection for all apps, which is why push is battery efficient. Treat it as a **signal, not a data channel**: delivery is best effort, payload size is small, notifications can be delayed or collapsed (only the latest per collapse key is kept while the device is offline), and background or silent pushes are throttled by the OS and are not guaranteed to wake the app. Device tokens change and expire, so the backend must handle token refresh and prune tokens the provider reports as invalid. On receipt, the app fetches the truth from the server using its cursor.

**Lifecycle on a phone.** In the foreground an open socket is fine. In the background the OS suspends the process shortly after the app leaves the screen, and the socket silently dies; exact limits vary by OS version. So the standard design is hybrid: live connection in the foreground, close it on background, push for anything the user must know about while away, and catch-up on return. Keeping a radio awake with frequent heartbeats is expensive, so heartbeat intervals should be as long as the intermediaries allow (NATs and load balancers drop idle connections, often after tens of seconds to a few minutes).

**Reconnect and resume.** Connections on mobile break constantly, so resume is the core of the design, not an edge case. Every event carries a monotonic sequence number or opaque cursor per stream. The client persists the last applied cursor and on reconnect asks for everything after it. The server keeps a replay window (a durable log or a bounded buffer); if the cursor is older than the window it replies "reset" and the client does a full refetch. The client applies events idempotently and ignores any sequence it has already seen, so at-least-once delivery becomes effectively exactly-once. Reconnect uses exponential backoff with jitter, and the server can send a "reconnect after N seconds" hint during deploys.

**Cost model.** Polling cost is requests per second: `users x (1 / interval)`. With 1,000,000 active users and a 10 second interval that is 1,000,000 / 10 = 100,000 requests per second, almost all returning nothing. Persistent connections flip the cost from CPU to memory and file descriptors: 1,000,000 connections at an assumed 20 KB each is about 20 GB of memory across the gateway tier, with little CPU while idle. The choice is therefore about event frequency: rare events favour polling or push, frequent events favour a held connection.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The app can ask the server again and again, keep one line open so the server can talk at any time, or rely on a notification to wake it. Asking repeatedly is simple, an open line is fast, and notifications are the only thing that works when the app is closed.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Polling and long polling are plain HTTP and scale statelessly. SSE streams server to client with built-in resume. WebSocket is bidirectional but needs stateful gateways and your own protocol. Push is best effort and should only signal that the app must fetch. Most apps use a socket or SSE in the foreground plus push in the background.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Design around a durable, sequenced event log per stream. Any transport then becomes a delivery optimisation: the client holds a cursor, resumes after any gap, and applies events idempotently. Make the polling interval and reconnect delay server-controlled, drain connections during deploys, and size gateways by memory per connection and by reconnect rate, not by steady-state throughput.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Treat the realtime tier as a capacity and blast-radius problem. The worst case is not peak messages but mass reconnect: a gateway deploy, a regional network flap or an OS-wide push wave brings millions of clients back at once, each wanting catch-up reads. Budget for it with jittered and server-hinted reconnect, admission control at the edge, cheap resume (cursor compare before any database read) and catch-up served from a cache or log rather than the primary store. Choose per feature the weakest transport that meets the latency target, and keep the transport swappable behind one client abstraction so a blocked protocol or a cost change does not require a rewrite.
Trade-offs

rows: Short polling with server-controlled interval
Simplest to build and operate; stateless; cacheable; interval tunable without a release.
Latency up to one interval; wasted requests and radio wake-ups when nothing changes.
Low-frequency state such as order status, wallet balance, config. Also as the universal fallback.
Long polling
Near real-time over plain HTTP; works where upgrades are blocked.
One request cycle per event; server holds a request per client; header overhead.
Moderate event rates, restrictive networks, or as a WebSocket fallback.
Server-Sent Events
Simple one-way stream; standard resume with Last-Event-ID; rides on HTTP/2 or HTTP/3; ordinary auth and load balancing.
Server to client only; text framing; native mobile clients need a small library or custom parser.
Live tracking, feeds, tickers, progress updates where the client rarely sends.
WebSocket
Lowest latency in both directions; small per-message overhead; binary frames.
Stateful gateway tier, sticky routing, custom ack and resume protocol, harder deploys and debugging.
Chat, collaboration, multiplayer, high-frequency location: both sides send often.
Push notification (APNs / FCM)
Reaches a closed app; battery efficient because the OS owns one shared connection.
Best effort, delayable, collapsible, throttled when silent; needs user permission for visible alerts; small payload.
Anything the user must learn while the app is not in the foreground. Never as the only source of data.
Hybrid: socket in foreground, push in background, cursor catch-up
Good latency when it matters, low battery cost otherwise, correct after any gap.
Three delivery paths to build, test and keep consistent; duplicate suppression needed.
The default for messaging and live-order style products.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Gateway deploy drops every connection at once
All clients reconnect in the same second and each runs a catch-up query; the API and database are overloaded.
Drain nodes gradually, send a server reconnect hint with a randomised delay, client backoff with jitter, rate limit new connections at the edge.
Half-open connection after a network switch
The app believes it is connected but receives nothing; messages appear only after a manual refresh.
Application-level heartbeat with a deadline, reconnect on OS path change, and always resume from the cursor after reconnecting.
Push notification is delayed or never delivered
A design that carries data only in the push loses the message.
Push is a hint. Persist events server side and let the app fetch after the cursor on next open or on a background wake.
Client cursor is older than the server replay window
The server cannot send the missing events; the client would silently skip a gap.
Server returns an explicit reset signal; the client discards its local state for that stream and performs a full paginated refetch.
Same event arrives over the socket and through a push-triggered fetch
Duplicate message bubbles or double-counted unread badges.
Apply events idempotently by event id or sequence; the local store rejects anything at or below the cursor.
Fixed 5 second polling interval shipped in the binary
Backend cannot reduce load during an incident; old app versions keep polling at that rate for years.
Server-controlled interval with a client-side minimum, jitter, and pausing when the screen is hidden.
Stale device tokens after reinstall or restore
Pushes go to tokens that no longer exist; users report missing notifications and send success metrics look fine.
Re-register the token on every launch, store it with a last-seen time, delete tokens the provider rejects, and measure delivery by client acknowledgement.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you choose between polling, SSE and WebSocket for a ride app showing the driver on a map?
blocks.text: Start from the requirement: update every 1 to 3 seconds while the screen is visible, server to client only. That rules out slow polling and does not need duplex, so SSE or a WebSocket subscription both fit; I would pick SSE for simplicity unless the app already has a socket for other features. In the background close the stream and send pushes for state changes (driver arrived). On return, fetch the current trip state first, then resubscribe. Location updates are latest-wins, so no replay is needed, only the newest sample.

blocks.title: How does a client resume a stream after being offline for an hour?
blocks.text: Each stream has ordered events with a sequence or cursor. The client persists the last applied cursor and on reconnect requests events after it, either in the socket handshake or with a REST catch-up call. The server replays from a durable log within a retention window; beyond it, it tells the client to reset and refetch a snapshot. Apply is idempotent, so overlap between catch-up and live events is harmless. Subscribe before or atomically with the catch-up read to avoid missing events in between.

blocks.title: What limits apply to background delivery on mobile?
blocks.text: The app process is suspended soon after backgrounding, so its sockets stop. Visible pushes need user permission. Silent or background pushes are rate limited and delivered at the discretion of the OS, and are affected by battery saver and by the user force-quitting the app. High-priority pushes are intended for user-visible content. Exact limits vary by OS version, so the design must work when a push never arrives: the next foreground fetch repairs state.

blocks.title: How do you scale WebSocket connections to millions of users?
blocks.text: A tier of connection gateway nodes that only hold sockets and forward events, sized by memory per connection. A pub/sub or routing layer maps user or channel to the node holding the connection. Business logic stays in stateless services that publish events. Add presence with TTL heartbeats, connection draining for deploys, backoff with jitter on clients, and edge admission control. Keep per-connection state minimal so a node loss means reconnect and resume, not data loss.

blocks.title: Why make the polling interval server-controlled?
blocks.text: Because app binaries live for years and cannot be changed quickly. A server-supplied next-poll delay lets you speed up when an entity is in a fast-changing state, slow down when it is idle, and shed load across the whole fleet during an incident. The client enforces a floor and adds jitter. It also allows different intervals per user segment or network type without a release.
Takeaways

items: Pick the weakest transport that meets the latency need: polling, then SSE, then WebSocket.
Push is the only channel to a closed app, and it is a best-effort signal, never the source of truth.
Foreground socket, background push, cursor catch-up on return is the standard mobile pattern.
Sequenced events, a persisted cursor and idempotent apply make every transport correct across disconnects.
Polling cost is users divided by interval; connection cost is memory per open socket. Event frequency decides which is cheaper.
Keep intervals, heartbeats and reconnect delays server-controlled and jittered.
Plan capacity for mass reconnect, not for the steady state.

quiz.q: Which mechanism can inform the user of an event when the app process is not running?
options: Push notification through APNs or FCM
quiz.why: Only the OS-owned push channel is alive when the app is suspended or terminated. Sockets held by the app die with the process.

quiz.q: 2,000,000 active users poll every 20 seconds. What is the average request rate?
quiz.why: 2,000,000 / 20 = 100,000 requests per second, regardless of whether anything changed.

quiz.q: Why should a push notification be treated as a signal instead of the data itself?
options: Delivery is best effort and can be delayed, collapsed or throttled, so the app must fetch the truth from the server
quiz.why: The platform providers do not guarantee delivery or ordering. A cursor-based fetch makes the app correct whether or not the push arrived.

quiz.q: What makes resume after a dropped connection correct?
options: Events with monotonic sequence numbers, a persisted client cursor and idempotent apply
quiz.why: The client asks for everything after its cursor and ignores anything it already applied, so gaps and duplicates are both handled.

quiz.q: A live scoreboard only sends data from server to client. Which is the simplest fitting choice?
quiz.why: SSE is a one-way stream over normal HTTP with built-in event ids and reconnection. Silent pushes are throttled and unsuitable for streams.

modules.title: High-Level Design (HLD)
modules.summary: A repeatable method: requirements, estimates, APIs, data, boxes and arrows, bottlenecks.

lessons.title: A repeatable method for high-level design, using a grocery ordering system

blocks.text: Walk through requirements, estimation, APIs, services, data, caching, messaging, reliability, security and monitoring on a generic grocery-delivery ordering system.
In simple words

High-level design is deciding the big boxes of a system and how they talk, before writing any code. A good method keeps you from jumping to tools too early: first understand what must be built, then how big it will get, then draw the boxes and check what happens when something breaks.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Planning a new supermarket works the same way. You first ask what it must sell and to how many people, work out how many tills and storerooms you need, then draw the floor plan, and finally plan for power cuts, theft and busy Saturdays. You would never start by choosing the colour of the shelves.

diagram.title: Grocery ordering system, high-level design (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Customer app
nodes.detail: Browses products, builds a cart and places orders over HTTPS.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authentication, rate limiting and routing to services. The single public entry point.

nodes.label: Catalog service
nodes.detail: Read-heavy product and price data. Optimised for fast reads and cached aggressively.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.detail: Owns the order lifecycle. Write path where correctness matters most.

nodes.label: Inventory service
nodes.detail: Tracks stock per store and reserves items so two customers cannot buy the last unit.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.detail: In-memory copy of hot catalog data. Cuts database load and latency for browsing.

nodes.label: Orders database
nodes.detail: Relational store with transactions for orders and payments records, the source of truth.

nodes.label: Payment provider
nodes.detail: External payment service called with an idempotency key so retries never double charge.

nodes.label: Event queue
nodes.detail: Carries OrderPlaced events so follow-up work does not slow down the customer request.

nodes.label: Fulfilment worker
nodes.detail: Consumes events to assign a picker, schedule delivery and send notifications.

steps.text: The customer opens a category. The app calls GET /products through the gateway.
The gateway authenticates the request and routes it to the catalog service.
The catalog reads hot product data from the cache. Most browsing never reaches a database.
The customer taps Place order. The app sends POST /orders with an idempotency key.
The gateway rate limits and forwards to the order service.
The order service asks inventory to reserve the items for a short time.
It charges the payment provider, sending the idempotency key so a retry cannot charge twice.
In one database transaction it saves the order and its items as CONFIRMED.
It publishes an OrderPlaced event and replies to the customer right away.
The fulfilment worker handles picking, delivery slots and notifications asynchronously.

blocks.text: How it works

**Step 1: requirements.** Split into functional requirements (what the system does: browse catalog, add to cart, place order, track delivery) and non-functional requirements (how well: p99 browse latency under 300 ms, order placement 99.95% available, no double charges, orders never lost). Write the out-of-scope list too, for example substitutions and driver routing. Ask about scale, regions and consistency needs before drawing anything.

**Step 2: estimate.** All numbers below are labelled assumptions. Assume 1M daily active users, 30 catalog reads per user per day and 0.3 orders per user per day. Reads: 1M x 30 = 30M per day, divided by 86,400 s is about 350 rps on average. Evening traffic is concentrated, so assume a 5x peak: about 1,750 rps. Orders: 1M x 0.3 = 300,000 per day, divided by 86,400 is about 3.5 orders per second, with a 10x peak of about 35 per second. Storage: 300,000 orders x 2 KB = 600 MB per day, or about 220 GB per year (600 MB x 365). The conclusion: reads dominate by 100x, so cache the catalog; order writes are small, so one primary database with replicas is enough at first, and correctness matters more than raw speed.

**Step 3: API design.** Define a small set of resource APIs before any internals: `GET /products?category=`, `POST /orders` (with an `Idempotency-Key` header), `GET /orders/{id}`, `POST /orders/{id}/cancel`. Use pagination for lists, version the API, and return the order state so clients can show progress. Idempotency on the write path makes client retries safe on flaky mobile networks.

**Step 4: decompose and choose data stores.** Split by business capability and write pattern: catalog (read-heavy, cached, can use a document store or search index), orders and payments (relational database with transactions), inventory (strongly consistent counters per store), notifications (async). Each service owns its data. Choose the database from the access pattern and consistency need, not from fashion: money and stock need transactions; browsing needs fast reads and tolerates seconds of staleness.

**Step 5: caching and messaging.** Cache the catalog with cache-aside and short TTLs so a price change appears within seconds. Use a queue for work the customer does not wait for: confirmation messages, picker assignment, analytics. Events let new consumers be added without touching the order service. Use consumer idempotency, because delivery is at least once.

**Step 6: reliability, security and monitoring.** Reliability: multiple instances per service behind a load balancer, health checks, timeouts, bounded retries with backoff, circuit breakers around the payment call, and a plan for degraded mode such as showing cached catalog data when a dependency is down. Security: TLS everywhere, authentication at the gateway, authorization per resource so users read only their own orders, input validation, secrets in a vault, and never storing raw card data. Monitoring: the four golden signals (latency, traffic, errors, saturation) per service, business metrics such as orders per minute and payment failure rate, distributed tracing with a request id, and alerts tied to SLOs.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Understand what to build, estimate how big it gets, draw the main parts, then think about what breaks. Do it in that order every time.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Separate functional and non-functional requirements, estimate reads and writes per second with stated assumptions, define the APIs, split services by capability, and pick each store from its access pattern.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Let the numbers drive the design: a 100:1 read to write ratio argues for caching and read replicas, while a small write rate with strict correctness argues for one transactional store with idempotent APIs and an outbox for events.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Design for the failure budget: define SLOs per journey, put timeouts and retry budgets on every call, use sagas or an outbox for cross-service consistency, plan capacity for peak and for the loss of a zone, and keep degraded modes explicit and tested.
Trade-offs

rows: Synchronous order placement (reserve, charge, save in one request)
Simple to reason about, customer gets a definite answer.
Latency and availability depend on every downstream call.
Core steps where the answer is needed now: stock reservation and payment.
Asynchronous follow-up work through a queue
Fast response, isolates slow consumers, easy to add new consumers.
Eventual consistency, duplicates, harder tracing.
Notifications, fulfilment, analytics, search indexing.
Single relational database for orders
ACID transactions, simple model, enough for tens of writes per second.
Vertical limit on writes, one failure domain unless replicated.
Early and mid scale. Shard by customer or region only when numbers demand it.
Aggressive catalog caching
Huge drop in latency and database load.
Stale prices or stock for a few seconds, invalidation complexity.
Read-heavy data. Do not trust the cache for the final price check at order time.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: The payment provider times out after charging
The customer may be charged but the order looks failed, and a retry could double charge.
Send an idempotency key, record a pending payment state, and reconcile with the provider by polling or webhook.
Two customers buy the last unit at the same moment
Stock goes negative and one order cannot be fulfilled.
Reserve with an atomic conditional update on stock, expire reservations after a timeout, and show out-of-stock immediately.
The cache cluster fails during the evening peak
About 1,750 rps of reads hit the catalog database at once.
Keep database headroom, use request coalescing, serve stale data from a local fallback, and rate limit.
The event queue is down
Orders are saved but no fulfilment starts.
Write events to an outbox table in the same transaction and publish from it, so events are sent when the queue recovers.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Walk me through how you would start a high-level design interview question.
