blocks.text: Clarify scope, split functional and non-functional requirements, state assumptions and estimate traffic and storage with arithmetic, define the core APIs, sketch services and data stores, then deep dive on the hardest part and cover failure, security and monitoring. Keep the user journey as the thread.

blocks.title: How do you prevent overselling the last item?
blocks.text: Make the stock decrement atomic and conditional (update where available >= quantity) or use a reservation with expiry. Never read-then-write without a lock or version check. Reconcile reservations that expire and expose out-of-stock quickly.

blocks.title: How do you keep an order and its event consistent?
blocks.text: Use the transactional outbox: save the order and an outbox row in one database transaction, then a relay publishes the event. Consumers are idempotent because delivery is at least once.
Takeaways

items: Follow the order: requirements, estimation, API, services, data, caching and messaging, reliability, security, monitoring.
Always state assumptions and show the arithmetic behind capacity numbers.
Let the read to write ratio and consistency needs choose caches, replicas and stores.
Keep decisions synchronous only where the user needs the answer now; use queues for the rest.
Make writes idempotent and think through each dependency failing.

quiz.q: With 1M daily active users making 30 reads each, what is the average read rate?
quiz.why: 30M reads divided by 86,400 seconds is about 350 per second. Peak is then a multiple of that.

quiz.q: Why add an idempotency key to POST /orders?
options: So a retried request does not create or charge a second order
quiz.why: Mobile clients retry on timeouts. The key lets the server recognise the repeat and return the original result.

quiz.q: Which step belongs on the asynchronous path?
quiz.why: The customer does not need to wait for the notification. Stock and payment decide the order outcome so they stay synchronous.

quiz.q: Reads outnumber writes about 100 to 1. What is the first design response?
options: Cache the read-heavy catalog and add read replicas
quiz.why: The ratio shows where load is. Caching and replicas relieve read load cheaply.

lessons.title: A repeatable method for mobile system design interviews

blocks.text: A step-by-step method for designing a mobile feature end to end: requirements, client layers, API contract, local data model, sync and conflicts, pagination, images, offline and error states, performance budgets, testing, observability and rollout.
In simple words

A mobile system design question such as "design the product list of a grocery app" is not about drawing screens. It asks how data gets from the server to the phone, where it is kept on the phone, what the user sees when the network is slow or gone, and how the app stays fast and safe to release. If you answer the same ordered list of questions every time, you will not forget an important part and the interviewer can follow your thinking.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a small corner shop supplied by a distant warehouse. The shelf is what customers see. The stockroom at the back holds what was delivered earlier, so customers are served even when the delivery van is late. The shopkeeper keeps an order book of things to send back or request, and hands it to the driver whenever the van turns up. Designing a mobile feature is deciding what goes on the shelf, what the stockroom holds, how the order book works and what to tell customers when the van is stuck.

diagram.title: Mobile client architecture and its backend (generic grocery app)

nodes.label: UI layer
nodes.detail: Renders state and forwards user intents. Holds no business rules and never talks to the network directly.

nodes.label: Domain layer
nodes.detail: Use cases and business rules in plain language of the product: load product page, add to basket, validate quantity.

nodes.label: Repository
nodes.detail: The single entry point to data. Decides whether to answer from the local store, the network or both, and hides that choice from callers.

nodes.label: Local database
nodes.detail: Persistent store on the device and the source of truth for what the screen shows. Observable, so changes flow to the UI.

nodes.label: API client
nodes.detail: Shared networking: auth headers, timeouts, retries, idempotency keys, serialization, request priority.

nodes.label: Sync engine / outbox
nodes.detail: Durable queue of pending writes plus the logic that pulls changes. Runs when connectivity returns and from background tasks.

nodes.label: Image pipeline
nodes.detail: Memory cache, disk cache, decode and downsample off the main thread, request cancellation when a cell scrolls away.

nodes.label: Image CDN
nodes.detail: Serves images resized and encoded for the requesting device from edge locations.

nodes.label: API gateway / BFF
nodes.detail: Auth, rate limiting and a mobile-shaped API that aggregates backend services into screen-level responses.

nodes.label: Backend services
nodes.detail: Catalog, basket, pricing and so on. Own the authoritative data and business rules.

steps.text: The user opens the Fruits category. The UI layer asks the domain layer for the product list state.
The use case subscribes to the repository for products in this category.
The repository immediately returns the rows saved from the last visit, with their saved-at time.
The screen renders cached products within the startup budget, before any network response.
In parallel the repository revalidates: GET /categories/fruits/products?limit=20 with the stored ETag.
The API client adds auth, app version and locale headers, with a short timeout for an interactive read.
The BFF fetches catalog, price and stock in parallel and returns one page plus a next cursor.
The repository upserts the page into the local database in one transaction. Observers fire and the list updates itself.
Visible cells request thumbnails at the size they will be drawn. Memory and disk caches are checked first.
Misses are fetched from the CDN with a size parameter; requests for cells that scroll away are cancelled.
The user taps Add on a product. The domain layer validates the quantity rule.
The use case calls the repository to add the item to the basket.
The repository writes the basket row locally (optimistic) and appends a mutation with an idempotency key to the outbox, in the same transaction.
The sync engine sends the mutation. On success it marks it done; on a business rejection it restores the server value and the UI shows why.

blocks.text: How it works

**Step 1: requirements and scope.** Spend the first minutes on questions, then state assumptions out loud. Functional: which screens and actions are in scope (list, detail, search, add to basket), is there real-time data, is it read-only. Non-functional: must it work offline and for which actions, how fresh must data be, expected data size (hundreds of items or millions), target devices and networks, platforms, accessibility and localisation. Also ask about the team: one app or many teams contributing modules. Write down what is explicitly out of scope (login, payments) so the interviewer can redirect you.

**Step 2: client architecture layers.** Draw three layers with one-way dependencies. **UI layer**: renders state and emits intents. **Domain layer**: use cases and business rules, independent of frameworks. **Data layer**: a repository per data type that fronts a local store and a remote API client. Name the cross-cutting pieces: sync engine, image pipeline, analytics, feature flags, navigation. The point is not a naming convention; it is that every decision has a home. Caching policy lives in the repository, retry policy in the API client, and neither leaks into screens. Keep library names out unless asked.

**Step 3: API contract.** Define the endpoints the screen needs before any internals. For each: method, path, request parameters, response fields, pagination style, error format. Prefer screen-shaped responses from a BFF so first paint needs one round trip. State the protocol choice (REST with JSON by default; GraphQL when many screens need different shapes; a streaming channel only if a requirement demands it). Include the headers every call carries: auth token, app version, platform, locale, idempotency key on writes. Say how the contract evolves: additive changes only, unknown fields ignored, old versions supported for a defined window.

**Step 4: data model and local persistence.** List the entities and their keys, then decide what is stored where. A relational local database for structured, queryable data that feeds lists. A key-value store for small preferences. The platform secure store (Keychain or Keystore) for tokens. Files plus a metadata table for media. In-memory only for derived view state. Add the fields sync needs: server version or `updated_at`, a local `pending` flag, a soft-delete marker. Mention schema versioning and migration, because users upgrade across many versions at once.

**Step 5: sync and conflict strategy.** Decide the read policy per data type: cache-then-network (stale-while-revalidate) for catalog, network-only for payment status, cache-only with periodic refresh for static config. For writes, choose online-only (disable the button offline) or an outbox with optimistic updates. Then say who wins a conflict: the server for money and stock, last-write-wins for simple preferences, field-level merge for editable records. State how the client learns of server changes: pull on open, delta sync with a cursor, or a push hint that triggers a fetch.

**Step 6: pagination, images and lists.** Use cursor pagination for anything that changes while the user scrolls; store the next cursor with the cached page. Prefetch the next page before the user reaches the end, cap pages kept in memory and rely on the database for the rest. For images: request the display size from the CDN, two cache tiers (memory bounded by cost, disk bounded by bytes with LRU eviction), decode off the main thread, cancel on reuse, low-quality placeholder first. These two topics decide scroll performance and data usage more than anything else on a list screen.

**Step 7: error, empty and offline states.** For every screen, name the states: loading with no cache, content, content with stale banner, empty, partial failure, full failure with retry, and offline. Classify errors into retryable (network, 5xx), user-fixable (validation), auth (refresh then retry once) and fatal (forced upgrade). Decide which actions are allowed offline and how pending work is shown. An answer that only covers the happy path reads as junior.

**Step 8: performance budgets.** State budgets as numbers you would track, noting they are targets you chose, not universal facts: cold start to first useful content, scroll frame time, memory ceiling on low-end devices, data per session, background battery impact, app download size. Then name the lever for each: defer non-critical initialisation and serve cached content for startup; pagination and image downsampling for memory; batching and server-controlled polling for battery; compression and field selection for data.

**Step 9: testing, observability and rollout.** Testing: unit tests for domain rules, contract tests against the API schema, repository tests with a fake server and real local database, a few end-to-end flows, plus tests for migration and for offline to online transitions. Observability: crash-free rate, startup and screen load times, API error and latency by app version and network type, sync queue depth and age, cache hit rate. Rollout: ship behind a feature flag, staged store rollout, a kill switch, and a backend that tolerates old app versions. Finish by naming the two or three biggest risks and what you would cut if time were short.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Answer the same questions in the same order: what must the feature do, where does the data come from, where is it kept on the phone, what does the user see when the network fails, and how do we release it safely.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Draw UI, domain and data layers with a repository in front of a local store and an API client. Define the API contract, the local schema and a cache policy per data type. Cover pagination, images and each error state explicitly.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Make the local database the source of truth for the UI, with reads that revalidate and writes that go through an outbox with idempotency keys. Choose a conflict rule per entity, quantify performance budgets, and tie each budget to a concrete mechanism and a metric segmented by app version and network.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: At Staff level the answer is about boundaries and change over time. Define ownership of modules and the contracts between them so many teams can ship independently; make the client tolerant of server evolution and the server tolerant of N old clients; push volatile decisions (layout, thresholds, intervals) to the server; and design for operability with flags, kill switches and telemetry that can explain a regression by version, device class and region. Call out the irreversible decisions (local schema, sync protocol, id formats) and spend the design effort there, while keeping the rest cheap to change.
Trade-offs

rows: Local database as source of truth for the UI
Instant render, offline reading, one data flow for cached and fresh data.
Schema migrations, storage growth, staleness to manage, more upfront design.
Lists and detail screens users revisit. Skip for one-shot flows such as checkout confirmation.
Network-only screens
Always fresh; trivial to reason about; no persistence code.
Blank screen on bad networks; every visit pays full latency.
Sensitive or rapidly changing data such as payment status or live inventory at the point of purchase.
Screen-shaped BFF endpoint
One round trip per screen; server can change composition without a release.
Backend work per screen; risk of a BFF that accumulates business logic.
High-latency networks and screens that combine several services.
Optimistic writes with an outbox
Feels instant and works offline.
Rollback UX, conflict handling, ordering and duplicate protection needed.
Low-risk, high-frequency actions: like, add to basket, mark as read. Avoid for payments.
Thin client with server-driven layout
Change screens without store review; consistent across platforms.
Harder offline support, limited by the component set already shipped, more complex tooling.
Merchandising and home screens that change weekly.
Strict layering with modules per feature
Testable, parallel team work, faster incremental builds.
Boilerplate and indirection for small apps.
Apps with several teams or a multi-year lifetime.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Design starts from screens and widgets
The interview time is spent on UI detail and data flow, offline and scale are never covered.
Follow the method order. Mention the UI layer in one sentence and move to data and contracts.
No local persistence on a list screen
Every app open shows a spinner and a blank screen on weak networks.
Cache-then-network through a repository with an observable local store.
Offset pagination on a changing feed
Items are duplicated or skipped as new content is inserted while the user scrolls.
Cursor pagination with a stable sort key and client-side de-duplication by id.
Full-resolution images in list cells
High memory use, dropped frames, out-of-memory terminations on low-end devices and wasted data.
Server-resized images per display size, downsampled decode, bounded caches, cancellation.
Local schema changed without a migration path
App crashes on launch for users upgrading from older versions.
Versioned migrations tested from every supported version, with a safe fallback of dropping and refetching cache-only tables.
Client breaks when the server adds an enum value or field
Old app versions crash or hide content after a backend deploy.
Tolerant parsing: ignore unknown fields, map unknown enum values to a default, contract tests against old client versions.
No telemetry by app version
A regression in one release is invisible in aggregate metrics until reviews drop.
Tag every metric and API call with app version, OS and network type; alert per version during rollout.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Walk me through how you would structure a 45 minute mobile design answer.
blocks.text: About 5 minutes on requirements and scope; 5 on the high-level picture of client layers and backend; 10 on API contract and data model including local storage; 10 on the hard part of this specific problem (sync, real-time, pagination or media); 5 on error and offline states; 5 on performance, testing, observability and rollout; and the rest for trade-offs and questions. I say the plan at the start so the interviewer can steer.

blocks.title: Design the product listing of a grocery app. What are the key decisions?
blocks.text: Read-heavy, must feel instant, prices and stock change. Repository with a local database as UI source of truth and stale-while-revalidate; cursor pagination with prefetch; a BFF endpoint returning product, price and stock per page; image CDN with sized thumbnails and two-tier cache. Price and stock are server-authoritative and revalidated at add-to-basket and checkout. Offline: browse cached pages with a stale indicator; add-to-basket through an outbox. Metrics: time to first content, scroll frame drops, cache hit rate, by app version.

blocks.title: How is mobile system design different from backend system design?
blocks.text: The client is a constrained, unreliable, long-lived node you do not control: limited memory and battery, a network that disappears, an OS that suspends you, and binaries that cannot be rolled back and stay in use for years. So the emphasis moves to local state, sync, API compatibility, performance budgets and release safety, where backend design emphasises throughput, partitioning and availability. A good answer still shows the backend at box level and the contract in detail.

blocks.title: How do you decide what to store on the device?
blocks.text: By four questions per data type: is it needed for first paint or offline, how stale may it be, how large can it grow, and how sensitive is it. Needed and tolerant of staleness goes into the local database with an eviction rule. Sensitive secrets go into the secure store, and sensitive content is either not persisted or encrypted and cleared on logout. Large media goes to a size-bounded disk cache. Everything persisted needs a migration and invalidation story.

blocks.title: What would you monitor after launching the feature?
blocks.text: Crash-free users and sessions per version; cold start and screen time-to-content percentiles; API latency and error rate split by endpoint, version and network type; sync outbox depth, age of oldest item and rejection rate; cache hit rate and image load time; data and battery impact from OS-level reports; and product funnels to catch silent functional breaks. Alerts are compared against the previous version during staged rollout.
Takeaways

items: Use a fixed order: requirements, layers, API, data model, sync, lists and images, failure states, budgets, quality and rollout.
Every decision needs a home: cache policy in the repository, retries in the API client, rules in the domain layer.
Define the API contract and the local schema explicitly; they are the hardest things to change later.
Choose read policy, write policy and conflict rule per data type, not once for the whole app.
Name every screen state, including offline and partial failure.
State performance budgets as numbers and attach a mechanism and a metric to each.
Close with rollout safety: flags, staged release, kill switch, compatibility with old versions.

quiz.q: What should you do first in a mobile system design interview?
options: Clarify functional and non-functional requirements and state assumptions
quiz.why: Scope, offline needs, freshness and data size drive every later decision. Without them the design has no basis.

quiz.q: Where does the decision "serve from cache or from network" belong?
options: In the repository of the data layer
quiz.why: The repository hides data sources from the rest of the app, so the policy can change without touching UI or domain code.

quiz.q: Which data should go in the Keychain or Keystore?
quiz.why: Secrets belong in the hardware-backed secure store. Bulk data belongs in a database or file cache.

quiz.q: Why is cursor pagination preferred for a feed that updates often?
options: It allows jumping to page 50 directly
It stays stable when items are inserted or removed during scrolling
It needs no index on the server
quiz.why: A cursor says "after this item", so inserts at the top do not shift the window the way an offset does.

quiz.q: Which is the best lever for cold start time?
options: Initialising every SDK before first frame
Rendering cached content first and deferring non-critical initialisation
quiz.why: Startup improves by doing less before first content: show persisted data and move analytics, flags refresh and prefetch after first render.

modules.title: Low-Level Design (LLD)
modules.summary: Turning a box on the HLD into tables, state machines, interfaces and failure handling.

lessons.title: From boxes to classes: turning a high-level design into a low-level design

blocks.text: SOLID, aggregates, an Order state machine, Repository, Factory, Strategy and Observer, dependency injection, optimistic locking and transaction boundaries.
In simple words

A high-level design shows boxes such as "order service". A low-level design opens one box and decides which classes live inside, what each one is responsible for, and how they depend on each other. The goal is code that is easy to change, test and keep correct when many requests arrive at once.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: High-level design is the floor plan of a house. Low-level design is the wiring, plumbing and the rules for each room: the kitchen handles cooking, the bathroom handles water, and a fuse box protects everything. If one room needs a change, you want to touch only that room and not rewire the whole house.

diagram.title: Order service internals (generic reference design)

nodes.label: OrderController
nodes.detail: HTTP layer. Parses the request, calls the application service and maps results to status codes. No business rules here.

nodes.label: OrderApplicationService
nodes.detail: Use-case layer. Defines the transaction boundary and orchestrates repository, aggregate, payment and events.

nodes.label: Order aggregate
nodes.detail: Domain object that owns the rules and the state machine. It is the only way to change an order and its items.

nodes.label: PaymentStrategy
nodes.detail: Interface with implementations such as card, wallet and cash on delivery. The service depends on the interface, not a concrete type.

nodes.label: OrderRepository
nodes.detail: Interface that loads and saves whole aggregates, hiding SQL from the domain. Applies the version check.

nodes.label: EventPublisher
nodes.detail: Observer-style publisher that announces domain events such as OrderConfirmed to any interested listener.

nodes.label: Payment provider
nodes.detail: External system reached through the strategy. Called with an idempotency key.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.detail: Stores the order row with a version column used for optimistic locking.

steps.text: POST /orders/42/confirm arrives. The controller validates input shape and calls confirmOrder(42).
The application service starts a transaction and loads the Order aggregate, including its current version.
The repository reads the order and items in one query and rebuilds the aggregate.
The service calls order.confirm(). The aggregate checks the state machine: only PLACED can become CONFIRMED.
The service picks the PaymentStrategy for this order and asks it to charge the amount.
The chosen strategy calls the provider with an idempotency key, so a retry cannot charge twice.
The service saves the aggregate. The repository updates the row where version equals the loaded version.
If another request changed the order first, zero rows match and a concurrency error is raised. Otherwise version increments.
After the commit, the service publishes OrderConfirmed so listeners such as notifications can react.
The service returns the result and the controller replies 200 with the new state.

blocks.text: How it works

**SOLID in practice.** Single responsibility: the controller handles HTTP, the application service handles the use case, the aggregate handles rules. Open/closed: add a new payment method by adding a class, not editing a long if-else. Liskov: every `PaymentStrategy` must honour the same contract. Interface segregation: small interfaces such as `OrderRepository` rather than one huge data access class. Dependency inversion: high-level code depends on interfaces, and concrete classes are supplied from outside.

**Entities and aggregates.** In domain-driven design an entity has an identity (order id) that persists while its data changes. An aggregate is a cluster of objects treated as one consistency unit with a single root. The Order root owns its OrderItems, and outside code never edits an item directly. This keeps invariants such as "total equals the sum of items" true after every change, and it defines what is loaded and saved together.

**State machine.** An order moves through states: CREATED, PLACED, CONFIRMED, PACKED, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, plus CANCELLED. The aggregate holds a table of allowed transitions and rejects the rest, so a delivered order can never become cancelled by a bug in a caller. Each transition can raise a domain event. Keeping the rules inside the aggregate means every caller gets the same behaviour.

**Patterns that fit.** Repository hides persistence behind a collection-like interface and makes the domain testable with an in-memory fake. Factory builds a valid aggregate from a request, for example `Order.create(customer, items)`, enforcing invariants at birth. Strategy swaps behaviour behind one interface: payment method, delivery fee rules or discount rules. Observer lets the order publish events to many listeners without knowing them, which is the in-process form of event-driven design.

**Dependency injection and interfaces.** Classes receive their collaborators through the constructor instead of creating them. The application service takes an `OrderRepository`, a `PaymentStrategyResolver` and an `EventPublisher`. In tests you pass fakes; in production a container wires the real ones. Design interfaces around what the caller needs (`confirm(orderId)`), not around how the implementation works, and keep them small and stable.

**Concurrency and transactions.** Two requests can load the same order at once. Optimistic locking adds a `version` column: the update runs `WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`, and if no row changes the request fails and may retry. It avoids holding locks and works well when conflicts are rare. Pessimistic locks (`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`) suit hot rows with frequent conflicts. Keep the transaction boundary in the application service, make it as short as possible, never hold it open across a network call to a slow provider, and publish events only after commit, ideally through an outbox row written in the same transaction.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Break one big box into small classes where each has one job, and let the important object protect its own rules so nobody can put an order into a nonsense state.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Layer the service: controller, application service, domain aggregate, repository. Use interfaces for things that vary, such as payment methods, and pass dependencies in through constructors.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: The aggregate enforces invariants and the state machine, the repository loads and saves whole aggregates with a version check, and the application service owns the transaction and publishes events after commit.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Choose aggregate boundaries by consistency needs, not by tables: one transaction should change one aggregate. Cross-aggregate and cross-service effects go through events and outbox with idempotent consumers, and conflicts are handled by optimistic locking with bounded retries.
Trade-offs

rows: Optimistic locking (version column)
No locks held, scales well, simple to implement.
Conflicting requests fail and need retry logic.
Conflicts are rare, such as one customer editing their own order.
Pessimistic locking (SELECT FOR UPDATE)
Prevents conflicts up front, no retries.
Blocks other requests, risks deadlocks and lower throughput.
Hot rows with frequent contention, for example a stock counter for a popular item.
Rich domain model (rules in the aggregate)
Rules in one place, easy to unit test, invalid states impossible.
More upfront modelling, needs discipline about boundaries.
Non-trivial business rules such as order lifecycle.
Anemic model with logic in services
Quick to start, familiar.
Rules scatter across services, invariants get broken by some callers.
Simple CRUD with almost no rules.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Two requests confirm and cancel the same order at once
Without protection the last write wins and the order ends in a wrong state.
Version check on save, reject the loser with a conflict error, retry by reloading and re-applying the rule.
The payment call is made inside an open database transaction
A slow provider holds locks and connections, exhausting the pool.
Keep transactions short: reserve and record intent first, call the provider outside the transaction, then record the result.
The event is published before the transaction commits and the commit then fails
Listeners act on an order change that never happened.
Publish after commit, or write the event to an outbox in the same transaction.
A new payment method is added by editing a large if-else block
Existing methods break and tests grow brittle.
Use the Strategy pattern with one class per method behind a shared interface.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you model an order and its lifecycle?
blocks.text: An Order aggregate root with items and a status enum, a transition table enforced inside the aggregate, domain events on transitions, a factory for creation, and a repository that loads and saves the whole aggregate with a version for optimistic locking.

blocks.title: How do you handle two concurrent updates to the same order?
blocks.text: Optimistic locking with a version column and a bounded retry for conflicts that are safe to repeat. If contention is high on one row, use a pessimistic lock or an atomic conditional update. Return a clear conflict error otherwise.

blocks.title: Where do you draw the transaction boundary?
blocks.text: In the application service, one transaction per use case that changes one aggregate. Keep it short, do not call slow external systems inside it, and publish events after commit or through an outbox.
Takeaways

items: Layer the code: controller, application service, aggregate, repository, with rules in the aggregate.
An aggregate is a consistency boundary: one transaction changes one aggregate.
Encode the lifecycle as a state machine so illegal transitions are impossible.
Use Strategy for interchangeable behaviour, Repository for persistence, Observer for events, and inject dependencies through interfaces.
Use optimistic locking for rare conflicts, keep transactions short and publish events after commit.

quiz.q: Where should the rule "a delivered order cannot be cancelled" live?
options: In the Order aggregate state machine
quiz.why: The aggregate is the single place every caller goes through, so the rule holds regardless of who calls it.

quiz.q: What does optimistic locking add to the UPDATE statement?
options: A version condition in the WHERE clause
quiz.why: If the version no longer matches, no row is updated, which signals that someone else changed the data.

quiz.q: Which pattern lets you add a wallet payment without editing existing payment code?
quiz.why: Strategy puts each payment method behind one interface so new ones are added as new classes.

quiz.q: Why inject an OrderRepository interface instead of creating a database class inside the service?
options: The service can be tested with a fake and the storage can change without touching it
It removes the need for transactions
quiz.why: Dependency inversion keeps the use case independent of the storage technology and easy to test.

modules.title: Monolith vs Microservices
modules.summary: What you gain and what you pay when you split a system, and when not to.

lessons.title: Monolith, modular monolith or microservices: choosing the shape of a system

blocks.text: Compare monoliths, modular monoliths, SOA and microservices, with service discovery, BFF, service-to-service communication, shared configuration, database per service, ownership and fault isolation.
In simple words

A system can be built as one big program or as many small programs that cooperate. One big program is easier to build and run at first. Many small programs let separate teams work and fail independently, but they add the hard work of making all the pieces talk to each other reliably.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A monolith is a single shop where one team runs the counter, the kitchen and the delivery. It is easy to coordinate. Microservices are a food court: each stall has its own owner, equipment and queue, so one stall closing does not close the others, but you now need signs, a shared cashier system and rules for how stalls work together.

diagram.title: Microservices with discovery, config and database per service (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client app
nodes.detail: A mobile or web app. It talks to one entry point and knows nothing about the services behind it.

nodes.label: Gateway / BFF
nodes.detail: A backend-for-frontend shaped for this client. It routes, authenticates and combines responses from several services.

nodes.label: Service discovery
nodes.detail: A registry of live service instances and their addresses. Callers look up where a service is running right now.

nodes.label: Orders service
nodes.detail: Owns order logic and order data. One team owns it end to end, including its deployment.

nodes.label: Catalog service
nodes.detail: Owns product data. Other services read it only through its API, never through its database.

nodes.label: Config service
nodes.detail: Central store for settings and feature flags, so values can change without rebuilding services.

nodes.label: Orders DB
nodes.detail: Private database of the orders service. Not accessible to other services.

nodes.label: Catalog DB
nodes.detail: Private database of the catalog service, chosen to fit catalog reads.

nodes.label: Event bus
nodes.detail: Carries events such as OrderPlaced so other services can react without being called directly.

steps.text: The app sends one request, for example "place this order and show the summary".
The BFF asks service discovery for healthy addresses of the orders service instead of using a fixed address.
It calls one of the returned instances with a timeout.
The orders service reads feature flags and limits from central config, loaded at startup and refreshed periodically.
It asks the catalog service for current prices through its API. It cannot read the catalog database directly.
The catalog service reads from its own private database.
The orders service saves the order in its own private database.
It publishes OrderPlaced. Other services subscribe, so orders does not need to know about them.
The orders service returns the result to the BFF.
The BFF shapes the response for this client and returns it. If catalog were down, the BFF could still answer with limited data.

blocks.text: How it works

**Monolith.** One deployable unit holds all features and usually one database. Calls between features are plain function calls, transactions span everything, and there is one thing to deploy, test and debug. It breaks down when many teams collide in the same code, a small change needs a full release, one hot feature forces scaling everything, or one memory leak takes the whole app down.

**Modular monolith.** Still one deployable unit, but the code is split into modules with clear public interfaces and no reaching into each other internals. Each module owns its tables. This gives most of the organisational benefit of services at a fraction of the operational cost and is the safest starting point, because a well-bounded module can later be extracted into a service.

**SOA and microservices.** Service-oriented architecture split systems into larger business services, often sharing a central bus and sometimes a database. Microservices push further: small services around a business capability, each independently deployable with its own database and owner team, and communication through lightweight APIs or events. The goal is independent change and scaling, not small size for its own sake.

**Talking to each other.** Services find each other through service discovery (a registry or the platform DNS) so addresses can change as instances come and go. Synchronous calls (REST or gRPC) are simple but couple availability; every call needs a timeout, bounded retries and a circuit breaker. Asynchronous events decouple services in time but give eventual consistency. A backend-for-frontend (BFF) sits per client type, such as mobile or web, and shapes data so clients make one call instead of many. Shared configuration and feature flags come from a config service so behaviour changes without redeploys.

**Data and ownership.** Database per service is the core rule: only the owning service touches its tables, and others use its API or events. This allows each team to choose the store and change the schema freely, but it removes cross-service joins and ACID transactions. Consistency across services uses sagas, outbox events and idempotent consumers. Clear ownership means one team owns each service, its on-call and its SLO.

**Fault isolation and cost.** A failure in one service should not take down the rest: use bulkheads (separate pools), timeouts, circuit breakers and fallbacks, and deploy services independently so a bad release has a small blast radius. The price is operational: more deployments, network failures between components, distributed tracing, versioned contracts and a platform team. Choose microservices when team count and scaling differences justify that price.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: One big program is simple. Many small programs let teams work separately but need extra machinery so the pieces can find and trust each other.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Start with a monolith or a modular monolith. Split into services when teams, scaling needs or release speed demand it. Each service owns its data, and services talk through APIs and events.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Split along business capabilities with stable boundaries. Use discovery, timeouts, retries with budgets and circuit breakers for sync calls, events for decoupling, and sagas for multi-service workflows.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: The real cost of microservices is distributed failure and organisational coordination. Make boundaries match team ownership, keep contracts backward compatible, invest in tracing, standard platform tooling and consumer-driven contract tests, and avoid a distributed monolith where services must deploy together.
Trade-offs

rows: Monolith
Simplest to build, test, deploy and debug; local calls and ACID transactions.
Team contention, whole-app deploys and scaling, shared failure domain.
Small team, early product, unclear domain boundaries.
Modular monolith
Clear boundaries and ownership with one deployment; easy path to extraction.
Needs discipline to keep modules separate; still scales and fails as one unit.
Growing team that wants structure without distributed-system cost.
Microservices
Independent deploys and scaling, fault isolation, team autonomy.
Network failures, eventual consistency, heavy operational and tooling overhead.
Many teams, parts of the system with very different scale or release cadence.
SOA with shared database or bus
Reuse of coarse business services, central governance.
Shared database couples teams; central bus can become a bottleneck.
Integrating large existing systems where full independence is not feasible.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: A downstream service becomes slow
Callers wait, threads pile up, and the slowness cascades upward until the front door fails.
Timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks; shed load instead of queueing forever.
Services share one database
A schema change in one service breaks others, and teams cannot deploy independently.
Database per service; share data through APIs and events.
Service discovery returns a dead instance
Some calls fail until the registry notices.
Health checks with short intervals, client-side retry to another instance, and removal of failing instances.
Services must be released together because of tight coupling
All the cost of microservices with none of the independence, a distributed monolith.
Version APIs, keep changes backward compatible, and redraw boundaries around real capabilities.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: When would you move from a monolith to microservices?
blocks.text: When team size and release conflicts slow delivery, when parts of the system need very different scaling or availability, and when boundaries are well understood. Do it incrementally, extracting one capability at a time, with the data and ownership moving along with it. Do not do it only because it is fashionable.

blocks.title: How do services find and call each other safely?
blocks.text: Service discovery via a registry or platform DNS, with health checks. Calls use timeouts, bounded retries with backoff, circuit breakers and idempotent operations. Prefer events where the caller does not need an immediate answer.

blocks.title: How do you keep data consistent without cross-service transactions?
blocks.text: Each service owns its data and uses sagas with compensating actions, outbox events written in the same transaction as the state change, and idempotent consumers. Accept eventual consistency and design the user experience around it.
Takeaways

items: Start simple: a monolith or modular monolith is often the right first shape.
Microservices buy independent deploys, scaling and fault isolation at a high operational price.
Database per service and clear team ownership are the heart of the model.
Use discovery, timeouts, circuit breakers and events to make service-to-service calls safe.
A BFF and central config simplify clients and operations.
Beware the distributed monolith: split by capability, not by technical layer.

quiz.q: Which is the usual best starting point for a new product with a small team?
quiz.why: Boundaries are unclear early on, and a modular monolith keeps cost low while allowing later extraction.

quiz.q: What does database per service imply?
options: Other services read its tables directly
Only the owning service touches its data; others use its API or events
quiz.why: Private data lets teams change schemas freely but removes cross-service joins and transactions.

quiz.q: What is the job of a BFF?
options: Shape and combine backend responses for one type of client
quiz.why: A BFF is a backend tailored to a client such as mobile, reducing round trips and exposing the right fields.

quiz.q: Services that must always be deployed together are best described as:
quiz.why: They have network overhead but no independence, the worst of both styles.

modules.title: API Gateway and Load Balancing
modules.summary: L4 and L7 balancing, health checks, routing, rate limits, auth at the edge.

lessons.title: Reverse proxies, load balancers and API gateways: the front door of a system

blocks.text: Reverse proxy vs L4 and L7 load balancers vs API gateway, balancing algorithms, health checks, TLS termination, rate limiting, edge authentication, and why sticky sessions are best avoided.
In simple words

When many people use a service, their requests should not all hit one computer. A front-door component receives every request and hands each one to a healthy server. Some front doors only pass traffic along quickly, and some also check who you are and how often you are asking.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of an airport check-in area. A greeter at the entrance sends each traveller to a desk with a short queue (load balancer). The desks check ID and tickets and turn away people who ask too often or lack a pass (gateway). If a desk is closed, the greeter stops sending people to it.

diagram.title: Front door: L4 balancer, API gateway and backends (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: A browser or app sending HTTPS requests to one public address.

nodes.label: L4 load balancer
nodes.detail: Forwards TCP connections by IP and port without reading HTTP. Very fast, and spreads load across several gateway instances.

nodes.label: API gateway (L7)
nodes.detail: Understands HTTP. Terminates TLS, checks authentication, applies rate limits, routes by path and balances across backends.

nodes.label: Identity provider
nodes.detail: Issues tokens. The gateway validates token signatures locally and only calls here for keys or revocation checks.

nodes.label: Rate-limit store
nodes.detail: Shared counters in memory so all gateway instances enforce the same per-client limit.

nodes.label: Backend A
nodes.detail: A stateless instance of the service. Reports health to the gateway.

nodes.label: Backend B
nodes.detail: A second identical instance. Receives its share of requests.

nodes.label: Backend C
nodes.detail: A third instance. Removed from rotation if its health check fails.

steps.text: The client opens a connection to the public address. The L4 balancer picks a gateway instance by connection.
The connection reaches a gateway instance, which terminates TLS and reads the HTTP request.
The gateway validates the access token against the identity provider keys. Invalid or expired tokens get 401.
It increments this client counter in the shared store. Over the limit means 429 Too Many Requests.
The route matches /orders. Using least connections, the gateway picks Backend A.
Backend A answers. The gateway adds headers and returns the response.
The next request goes to Backend B because it currently has the fewest active connections.
Backend C fails its health check, so the gateway stops sending it traffic until it recovers.
The response goes back through the balancer on the same connection.
The client receives the response over the encrypted connection.

blocks.text: How it works

**Reverse proxy, load balancer, gateway.** A reverse proxy sits in front of servers and forwards client requests to them, hiding the servers. A load balancer is a reverse proxy whose main job is to distribute requests across several servers. An API gateway is a layer 7 reverse proxy with API-specific features: authentication, rate limiting, request routing and transformation, versioning, and observability. In practice one product can play several roles.

**Layer 4 vs layer 7.** An L4 balancer works on TCP or UDP connections using IP addresses and ports. It does not read HTTP, so it is very fast and works for any protocol, but it cannot route by path or header. An L7 balancer parses HTTP, so it can route `/orders` and `/products` to different pools, terminate TLS, retry, rewrite headers and make smarter decisions, at higher CPU cost. Large systems often chain them: L4 in front for raw scale, L7 behind for routing.

**Balancing algorithms.** Round robin sends requests to servers in turn: simple and fine when requests cost about the same. Weighted round robin gives bigger machines more traffic. Least connections sends each request to the server with the fewest active ones, which adapts to slow requests. Consistent hashing maps a key, such as a user id or cache key, to a server on a hash ring, so the same key keeps landing on the same server and adding or removing a server moves only about 1/N of the keys. It suits caches and sharded backends.

**Health checks.** Active checks probe each backend on a timer, for example `GET /health` every 5 seconds, and remove it after 3 failures. Passive checks watch real traffic and eject servers that return errors or time out. A good health endpoint reflects whether the instance can serve traffic, not only whether the process is running. Slow start and connection draining let instances warm up and finish in-flight requests when added or removed.

**Edge responsibilities.** TLS termination at the edge saves backends the encryption work and centralises certificates; traffic to backends should still be encrypted inside the network where policy requires it. Authentication at the edge validates tokens once so backends receive a verified identity header, but each backend must still authorise actions, because the edge cannot know every business rule. Rate limiting protects backends from abuse and bugs: common algorithms are fixed window, sliding window and token bucket, keyed by client, user or IP, with counters in a shared store.

**Sticky sessions and why to avoid them.** Sticky sessions pin a user to one backend using a cookie or IP hash. They exist because the backend keeps session state in memory. The problems: load becomes uneven, a failed server loses its users sessions, scale-out and scale-in do not rebalance existing users, and deploys disturb users. The better design is stateless backends with session data in a shared store or in signed tokens, so any backend can serve any request. Use stickiness only for a narrow need, such as a long-lived WebSocket connection or a locality-sensitive cache, and keep it a preference, not a requirement.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: A front door receives all requests and sends each to a working server. Better front doors also check who you are and stop anyone asking too fast.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: L4 balancers forward connections quickly, L7 balancers and gateways read HTTP to route, terminate TLS, authenticate and rate limit. Health checks remove broken servers, and algorithms like least connections spread load.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Chain an L4 tier for scale with an L7 gateway tier for policy. Use least connections for uneven request cost, consistent hashing for cache locality, shared counters for rate limits, and keep backends stateless to avoid sticky sessions.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: The edge is itself a critical dependency: run it redundantly across zones, keep policy data cached locally so identity or limiter outages degrade gracefully, tune health-check thresholds against flapping, use outlier ejection and retry budgets to avoid retry storms, and rotate certificates and keys automatically.
Trade-offs

rows: L4 load balancing
Very fast, protocol agnostic, low CPU.
No awareness of HTTP paths, headers or errors.
Raw scale in front of gateways, non-HTTP protocols.
L7 load balancing / API gateway
Path routing, auth, rate limiting, retries, rich metrics.
More CPU, another hop, a critical shared component that needs high availability.
Public APIs and any system with more than one backend service.
Consistent hashing
Stable key to server mapping, minimal movement when servers change, great for caches.
Can create hot spots; needs virtual nodes for balance.
Cache clusters and sharded stateful backends.
Sticky sessions
Works with legacy servers that keep state in memory.
Uneven load, lost sessions on failure, hard scale-out.
Only for long-lived connections or legacy constraints; prefer stateless backends.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: A single gateway instance serves all traffic and fails
Every client sees an outage even though backends are healthy.
Run several gateway instances across zones behind an L4 balancer, with automated health checks.
Health checks are too aggressive or too shallow
Healthy servers flap in and out, or a server with a broken dependency stays in rotation.
Use thresholds (for example 3 failures to eject, 2 successes to return) and health endpoints that check key dependencies cheaply.
The rate-limit store becomes unavailable
Either all traffic is blocked or limits stop applying and backends get flooded.
Decide fail-open or fail-closed per route, keep a local fallback limiter, and monitor the store.
A sticky backend crashes
All users pinned to it lose their sessions and must log in again.
Keep sessions in a shared store or signed tokens so any backend can take over.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain the difference between a load balancer and an API gateway.
blocks.text: A load balancer distributes traffic across identical servers, at L4 or L7. An API gateway is an L7 front door that adds API concerns: authentication, rate limiting, routing between different services, transformation and metrics. Often both exist: an L4 tier for scale, a gateway tier for policy.

blocks.title: How would you design rate limiting for a public API?
blocks.text: Choose a key (API key, user or IP) and an algorithm such as token bucket for bursts. Keep counters in a shared store like Redis so all instances agree, return 429 with a Retry-After header, and decide fail-open or fail-closed if the store is unavailable. Layer coarse limits at the edge and finer limits per service.

blocks.title: How do you remove the need for sticky sessions?
blocks.text: Make backends stateless. Store session data in a shared cache or database, or use signed tokens that carry the state. Then any instance can serve any request, and load balancing, scaling and failover become simple.
Takeaways

items: A load balancer spreads traffic; an API gateway adds authentication, rate limiting and routing on top.
L4 is fast and generic, L7 is smart and costlier; large systems often use both in sequence.
Pick the algorithm to match the workload: round robin, least connections, or consistent hashing for key affinity.
Health checks with sensible thresholds keep broken servers out of rotation.
Terminate TLS and authenticate at the edge, but still authorise in each service.
Avoid sticky sessions by keeping backends stateless.

quiz.q: What can an L7 load balancer do that an L4 balancer cannot?
options: Route by URL path or header
quiz.why: L7 parses HTTP, so it can make routing and policy decisions based on the request content.

quiz.q: Which algorithm best keeps the same cache key on the same server while servers come and go?
quiz.why: Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of keys when the server set changes.

quiz.q: Why are sticky sessions discouraged?
options: They cause uneven load and lose sessions when a server fails
quiz.why: Pinning users ties state to one server. Stateless backends with shared session data avoid this.

quiz.q: Rate limiting across several gateway instances needs:
options: A counter in each instance only
A shared counter store or a coordinated scheme
quiz.why: Per-instance counters let a client exceed the intended limit by spreading requests across instances.

lessons.title: API design for mobile clients: BFF, versioning and contracts

blocks.text: How to design APIs that serve mobile apps well: Backend-for-Frontend, living with old app versions, backward-compatible changes, cursor vs offset pagination, partial responses, batching, server-driven UI, and forced-upgrade and kill-switch contracts.
In simple words

A website can be changed for everyone in a minute. A phone app cannot: people keep the version they installed for months or years. So the server has to keep understanding old apps while also serving new ones. On top of that, a phone on a slow network wants one small, ready-made answer per screen, not twenty separate answers to stitch together. A mobile API is designed around these two facts.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A hotel has a concierge desk. Guests do not phone the kitchen, the laundry and the taxi company themselves; they ask the concierge once and get one combined answer. Guests carry brochures printed in different years, and the concierge still honours the old brochure, or politely explains that a service printed there has ended and hands over a new brochure. The concierge is the Backend-for-Frontend, and the brochures are app versions.

diagram.title: Mobile BFF serving a new and an old app version (generic grocery app)

nodes.label: App v5 (old)
nodes.detail: Installed two years ago. Knows only the fields and component types that existed when it was built.

nodes.label: App v9 (new)
nodes.detail: Current release. Understands newer fields and components and sends its version on every request.

nodes.label: CDN / edge
nodes.detail: TLS termination, compression and caching of responses that are not personalised.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authentication, rate limiting, routing by path and client type to the right BFF.

nodes.label: Version policy / flags
nodes.detail: Minimum supported version, recommended version and kill-switch flags, keyed by platform and app version.

nodes.label: Mobile BFF
nodes.detail: Aggregates downstream services into screen-shaped responses and adapts them to the capabilities of the calling app version. No core business rules.

nodes.label: Web BFF
nodes.detail: A separate aggregation layer for the web client, which has different screens, payload needs and release cadence.

nodes.label: Catalog service
nodes.detail: Owns products. Exposes a general-purpose internal API that does not know about screens.

nodes.label: Cart service
nodes.detail: Owns the basket and its rules.

nodes.label: Promo service
nodes.detail: Owns offers. Slower and less critical than catalog and cart, so the BFF treats it as optional.

steps.text: App v9 calls GET /mobile/v2/home with headers for app version 9.0, platform and locale.
The response is personalised, so the edge forwards it. The gateway validates the token and rate limit.
The gateway routes the mobile path to the mobile BFF.
The BFF reads the version policy: v9 is above the minimum, no upgrade needed. It also reads which features are switched on for this version.
It requests featured products. The three downstream calls are sent in parallel, each with its own timeout.
It requests the basket summary for the header badge.
It requests offers. The promo service is slow and the call hits its timeout.
The BFF returns a partial response: products and basket filled, the offers section marked unavailable. The screen still loads.
App v9 receives one compressed payload containing only the fields the home screen draws, plus a cursor for the next page.
App v5 calls the same endpoint with app version 5.2 in its header.
The request takes the same path through the edge and gateway.
The same BFF handles it. There is no separate deployment per app version.
Policy says v5 is below the recommended version but above the minimum. The BFF leaves out component types v5 cannot draw and adds a soft upgrade hint.
App v5 gets a response it fully understands, ignores any field it does not know, and shows an optional "update available" banner.

blocks.text: How it works

**Why a Backend-for-Frontend.** Internal services expose general, fine-grained APIs. A phone on a 200 ms network cannot afford to call six of them and join the results, and you do not want join logic shipped in a binary you cannot change. A **BFF** is a thin server-side layer owned by the client team that exposes screen-shaped endpoints: it fans out in parallel, trims fields, applies client-specific formatting and returns one payload. Web and mobile get separate BFFs because their screens, payload budgets and release cadences differ. The rule that keeps a BFF healthy: aggregation and presentation shaping only. Pricing, eligibility and other business rules stay in the owning services, otherwise each BFF becomes a divergent copy of the business.

**Old versions never go away.** After any release a long tail of users stays on earlier versions: auto-update is off, the device OS is too old for the new build, or storage is full. So at any time the API serves many client versions at once. Every request should identify the client (`app version`, `platform`, `OS version`, optionally a capabilities list) so the server can adapt and so metrics can be split by version. The usage distribution by version is an operational input: it tells you when an old contract can be retired.

**Versioning strategy.** Prefer one evolving API with additive changes over a new version per release. Reserve a new major version (a path such as `/v2/` or a versioned media type) for real breaking changes, and when you create one, keep the old one running until the apps that call it are below your support threshold. Within a version, vary behaviour by the client version header or by declared capabilities rather than by forking endpoints. Capabilities ("I can render component `carousel_v2`") age better than version comparisons scattered through server code.

**Backward-compatible changes.** Safe: adding an optional field, adding an endpoint, adding an optional request parameter with a default, relaxing validation. Breaking: removing or renaming a field, changing a type or unit, making an optional request field required, changing the meaning of an existing value, changing default sort order, and adding a new enum value when clients parse enums strictly. The client side of the contract matters equally: ignore unknown fields, map unknown enum values to a safe default, never depend on field order, and treat missing optional fields as normal. To change a field, use expand and contract: add the new field, serve both, migrate clients, and remove the old one only when usage data shows it is safe.

**Pagination.** **Offset** pagination (`?offset=40&limit=20`) is simple and allows jumping to a page, but the database must skip all earlier rows, and inserts or deletes during scrolling shift the window, producing duplicates or gaps. **Cursor** pagination returns an opaque token that encodes the position in a stable sort order (for example the last item sort key plus id); the next request says "after this". It is stable under change and efficient with an index. For infinite scroll on mobile, cursors are the default. Keep cursors opaque so the server can change their encoding, include a `has_more` or null cursor to signal the end, enforce a maximum page size, and let the client de-duplicate by id.

**Partial responses, field selection and batching.** Three tools reduce bytes and round trips. Partial success: a screen-level response should mark a failed section as unavailable instead of failing the whole request, with per-section status the client can render. Field selection: a `fields` parameter or GraphQL selection lets a list screen ask for five fields instead of fifty. Batching: accept several ids in one call (`GET /products?ids=...`) or several operations in one request, with a per-item result so one failure does not hide the others. Batch writes need per-item idempotency. Aggregation can go too far: one slow dependency in a giant endpoint delays everything, so split above-the-fold from below-the-fold content.

**Server-driven UI.** Instead of returning only data, the server returns a description of the screen: an ordered list of components from a registry the app already contains (`banner`, `product_grid`, `carousel`) with their data and actions. Layout, ordering and experiments can then change without a store release, and all platforms stay consistent. The contract is the component schema: each component is versioned, the client declares which ones it supports, and the server never sends a component the client cannot draw, or supplies a fallback. Costs: weaker offline behaviour, harder debugging, a design system that must be disciplined, and new native capabilities still need a release.

**Forced upgrade and kill switch.** Build these into the first version you ship, because they cannot be added to binaries already in the field. The contract: the app sends its version; the server holds `min_supported_version` and `recommended_version` per platform. Below minimum, the API responds with a dedicated signal (commonly HTTP `426` or a specific error code in a standard envelope) and the app shows a blocking screen linking to the store. Below recommended, the app shows a dismissible prompt. A **kill switch** is a remotely controlled flag per feature that the client checks before entering a flow and the server enforces too, so a broken feature in a shipped version can be disabled in minutes. The app must behave sensibly when the config cannot be fetched: use the last known values, then safe built-in defaults.

**Error envelope.** Standardise one error shape for every endpoint: a stable machine-readable `code`, a human-readable localised `message`, optional field-level details, a `retryable` hint and a request id for support. Clients branch on the code, never on message text. A stable envelope is what lets a two-year-old app show a sensible message for an error type invented last week.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The server gives the app one ready-made answer per screen, and it keeps understanding old copies of the app because people do not update. New things are added without taking old things away.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: A BFF aggregates internal services into screen-shaped responses. Changes are additive, clients ignore unknown fields, lists use cursor pagination, and every request carries the app version so the server can adapt and can ask very old versions to upgrade.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Treat the API as a long-lived contract with many simultaneous client versions. Use capability negotiation over version checks, expand-and-contract migrations driven by usage data, partial responses with per-section status, and server-driven UI for surfaces that change often. Forced-upgrade and kill-switch signals are part of the base protocol.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: The design problem is governance of change across independently deployed parties with very different release speeds. Define a compatibility policy (supported version window, deprecation process, contract tests replaying recorded traffic from old clients in CI), give the BFF clear ownership boundaries so it does not become a shadow monolith, and decide deliberately which logic lives where: anything that must change faster than the store allows belongs on the server, anything needed offline belongs on the client. Measure the cost of the long tail (extra code paths, security exposure of old binaries) against the users lost by raising the minimum version, and make that an explicit business decision.
Trade-offs

rows: BFF per client type
Screen-shaped payloads, fewer round trips, client team can evolve it at its own pace.
Another service to run; duplicated aggregation across BFFs; risk of business logic creeping in.
Mobile and web have different screens or payload budgets, and there are several backend services.
Single general-purpose API for all clients
One contract, less code, consistent behaviour.
Chatty for mobile, over-fetching, every change negotiated between all client teams.
Small product, one backend team, similar clients.
GraphQL for field selection
Clients fetch exactly what a screen needs in one request; typed schema with deprecation support.
Harder HTTP caching, query cost control needed, resolver fan-out problems, more client tooling.
Many screens with varied data shapes and a team ready to operate it.
Cursor pagination
Stable under inserts and deletes; efficient at any depth.
No jump to arbitrary page; needs a stable unique sort key.
Feeds, search results and any infinite scroll.
Server-driven UI
Change layout and run experiments without a release; cross-platform consistency.
Complex contract and tooling; limited to shipped components; weaker offline; harder to test.
Home, merchandising and campaign surfaces. Not for core flows that need rich native interaction.
High minimum supported version
Fewer code paths, faster backend evolution, old security bugs retired.
Locks out users on old devices or OS versions; forced upgrades cause churn.
When old-version usage is small or a security or legal issue demands it.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Backend adds a new enum value to an existing field
Old apps with strict parsing fail to decode the whole response and show an error screen.
Clients map unknown values to a default; server only sends new values to versions that declare support; contract tests with old client parsers.
A field is renamed in place
Every installed version that reads the old name breaks at the moment of the backend deploy.
Expand and contract: add the new name, serve both, remove the old one only after usage by version drops below the threshold.
One slow dependency inside an aggregated endpoint
The whole home screen waits for the slowest service or fails entirely.
Per-dependency timeouts, parallel fan-out, partial responses with section status, cached fallback for optional sections.
No forced-upgrade path in early versions
A version with a serious bug or security flaw can never be retired; the backend must support it indefinitely.
Ship the minimum-version check and blocking screen in the very first release, and test it regularly.
Server-driven UI sends a component an old app does not know
Blank gaps or a crash on old versions.
Client declares supported components; server filters or substitutes a fallback; client skips unknown components safely.
Offset pagination on a feed with frequent inserts
Users see repeated items or miss items while scrolling.
Cursor pagination on a stable key plus client-side de-duplication by id.
BFF accumulates pricing and eligibility rules
Web and mobile show different prices; fixes must be made in several places.
Keep rules in domain services; review BFF changes for business logic; BFF owns composition and formatting only.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you evolve an API when app versions from two years ago are still in use?
blocks.text: Additive changes by default, tolerant clients, and expand-and-contract for anything else. Every request carries app version and platform, so I can see usage per version and adapt responses by capability. Real breaking changes get a new major version run in parallel. A published support window plus a minimum-version check lets me retire very old clients with a forced upgrade. Contract tests replay fixtures from old versions in CI before each backend deploy.

blocks.title: When would you introduce a BFF and what should not go into it?
blocks.text: When the mobile screens need data from several services and the generic APIs make the client chatty or over-fetch, or when web and mobile needs diverge. The BFF does parallel fan-out, field trimming, pagination shaping, partial failure handling and version adaptation. It should not own business rules, data or long-running workflows. It is owned by the client-facing team and deployed independently.

blocks.title: Cursor or offset pagination for a product search screen?
blocks.text: Cursor for the infinite scroll list, because results and ranking can change between pages and deep offsets are slow. The cursor is opaque and encodes the sort key and a tie-breaker id, or a server-side search context with an expiry. If the product needs "jump to page N" or a total count, offset or a hybrid can be justified, with a cap on depth. The client de-duplicates by id in both cases.

blocks.title: Design the contract for forced upgrade and kill switches.
blocks.text: Client sends version and platform on every call and fetches a small config at launch and periodically. Server keeps minimum and recommended versions per platform and a set of feature flags. Below minimum: a specific status and error code on any API call, which a global interceptor turns into a blocking upgrade screen. Below recommended: a field in config for a dismissible prompt. Kill switches: flags checked on the client before entering a feature and enforced by the server. Config is cached with safe defaults so a config outage never blocks a healthy app.

blocks.title: What are the risks of one aggregated endpoint per screen?
blocks.text: Latency is bound to the slowest dependency, a failure in one section can fail everything, payloads grow, caching is harder because parts have different freshness, and the endpoint changes whenever the screen does. Mitigate with per-dependency timeouts, partial responses, splitting critical and deferred sections into separate calls, and caching stable fragments. Aggregate to remove round trips, not to make one endpoint do everything.
Takeaways

items: Mobile APIs serve many app versions at once; identify the client on every request.
A BFF gives one screen-shaped response per round trip and keeps composition off the device, but must stay free of business rules.
Add, never rename or remove in place. Clients ignore unknown fields and tolerate unknown enum values.
Use opaque cursors for infinite scroll; offsets shift under change and slow down with depth.
Return partial results with per-section status instead of failing a whole screen.
Server-driven UI moves change from the store to the server, bounded by the components already shipped.
Forced upgrade, soft upgrade and kill switches belong in the very first release.

quiz.q: Which change is backward compatible for existing app versions?
options: Adding a new optional response field
Changing a price field from a number to a string
Making an optional request parameter required
quiz.why: Clients that ignore unknown fields are unaffected by additions. The others break parsers or reject requests from old versions.

quiz.q: What is the main job of a mobile BFF?
options: Aggregate and shape downstream data into screen-level responses for the mobile client
Replace the API gateway for authentication
quiz.why: It reduces round trips and moves composition off the device. Business rules and data ownership stay in the domain services.

quiz.q: Why does offset pagination produce duplicates in a live feed?
options: New items inserted at the top shift every later item, so the next offset window overlaps the previous one
quiz.why: Offset counts from the start of a moving list. A cursor anchors to a specific item instead.

quiz.q: When must the forced-upgrade mechanism be built?
options: When the first breaking change is planned
In the first released version, because it cannot be added to binaries already installed
quiz.why: A version without the check can never be told to upgrade. The mechanism only helps for versions that already contain it.

quiz.q: With server-driven UI, how do you avoid breaking old app versions?
options: The client declares supported components and the server sends only those or a fallback
Use a different domain per version
quiz.why: Capability negotiation keeps the response within what the installed binary can render.

modules.title: SQL and NoSQL Databases
modules.summary: Choosing a store, transactions and isolation, replication, sharding.

lessons.title: Choosing a database: SQL, document, key-value, cache and search

blocks.text: Compare PostgreSQL/MySQL, MongoDB, DynamoDB, Redis and Elasticsearch by data model, query pattern, consistency and scaling, then pick one per use case for carts, orders, payments, inventory and users.
In simple words

A database is a place where an app keeps its information safe. Different databases are good at different jobs: some are great at keeping money records exact, some at finding a word in millions of items, and some at answering in a blink. A good design uses the right one for each job instead of one for everything.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a shop. The accounts ledger is a strict bound book where every line must add up (relational database). The shopping basket on the counter is a quick tray that holds whatever the customer put in (key-value or document store). The sticky notes by the till are for things you need in a second and can throw away (cache). The catalogue index at the back lets you find any item by any word (search engine).

diagram.title: One checkout, several stores (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client app
nodes.detail: Sends the checkout request with an idempotency key, so a retry after a timeout cannot create a second order.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.detail: Stateless business logic. It picks the right store for each kind of data instead of forcing everything into one.

nodes.label: Relational DB (orders, payments, stock)
nodes.detail: PostgreSQL or MySQL. Multi-row transactions, constraints and joins. The source of truth for money and stock.

nodes.label: Key-value store (carts)
nodes.detail: DynamoDB or a document store. One cart is read and written by its key, so it scales by spreading keys across partitions.

nodes.label: Redis (sessions, hot counters)
nodes.detail: In-memory store with expiry. Holds login sessions, rate limit counters and short-lived data. Not the only copy of anything important.

nodes.label: Change event stream
nodes.detail: Committed changes in the relational DB are published as events, so other stores update without slowing the checkout.

nodes.label: Indexer
nodes.detail: Consumes events and writes documents into the search index. Safe to replay because writes are keyed by product id.

nodes.label: Search index
nodes.detail: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. Inverted index for text search, filters and facets. A derived copy that can be rebuilt.

steps.text: The user taps Pay. The request carries a session token and an idempotency key.
The service validates the session and checks the rate limit counter in Redis. Both are fast, expiring data.
It reads the cart by key. One lookup, no joins, a single-digit millisecond answer.
One transaction creates the order and its lines, records the payment intent and decrements stock. Either all of it commits or none of it.
After commit, a change event for the new stock level is published asynchronously.
The indexer reads the event. If it is down, events wait in the stream.
The product document is updated in the search index, so the "in stock" filter becomes correct within seconds.
The service returns the order id. Later the user searches the catalogue and the service answers from the search index.

blocks.text: How it works

**Start from the access pattern, not the brand.** Write down the queries first: lookup by key, range scan, join across entities, full-text search, atomic counter. Then ask what must never be wrong (money, stock) and what may be a few seconds late (search results, counts). The answers pick the store.

**Relational (PostgreSQL, MySQL).** Rows in tables with a fixed schema, joins, constraints, and multi-row ACID transactions. Strong choice for orders, payments, inventory and users because correctness rules (unique email, stock never below zero, order total equals sum of lines) can be enforced by the database itself. Scaling is vertical first, then read replicas, then sharding when one primary cannot take the writes. A single well-tuned node handles thousands of writes per second, which is more than most products need.
