**Document and key-value (MongoDB, DynamoDB).** A document store keeps a nested JSON-like record that is read and written as a whole, which fits carts and profiles. DynamoDB goes further: every item is found by a partition key, and capacity is spread across partitions automatically, so it scales almost without limit if the key spreads load evenly. The price is that you design tables around the queries, joins are your job, and cross-item transactions are limited and costlier. Consistency is tunable: eventually consistent reads are cheaper, strongly consistent reads cost more and read from the leader.

**Redis and search.** Redis keeps data in memory with expiry and atomic operations (increment, set if absent), so it suits sessions, rate limits, leaderboards and short locks. Treat it as a cache unless persistence is configured and the loss window is acceptable. Elasticsearch and OpenSearch build an inverted index so you can search text, filter and aggregate fast. They are not transactional and they are fed from a primary store, so a search index is a derived copy that can be rebuilt.

**Polyglot persistence has a cost.** Every extra store adds operations, backups, monitoring and a consistency gap to reason about. Keep one source of truth per fact and make everything else a derived copy fed by events or change data capture. A reasonable default for a new product is one relational database, plus Redis once the load needs it, plus search when text queries appear. Add a key-value store when a single access pattern outgrows the relational primary.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Pick the tool for the job. Use a strict database for money and stock, a fast tray for baskets, a short-term memory for things that expire and a search engine for finding words.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Relational stores give transactions and constraints. Key-value and document stores give easy horizontal scaling for access by key. Redis gives microsecond reads for expiring data. Search engines give text queries. Choose from the query pattern and the correctness need.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Model the access patterns first. Keep one source of truth per fact, feed derived stores through change events, and make consumers idempotent. Decide per read whether stale data is acceptable and choose consistency levels accordingly.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Evaluate on partition key cardinality, write amplification, transaction scope, failover time and operational cost, not on feature lists. Plan the migration path early: relational with read replicas covers most workloads, and moving one hot access pattern to a key-value store later is cheaper than starting distributed.
Trade-offs

rows: Relational database as the default
ACID transactions, constraints, joins, mature tooling, flexible ad hoc queries.
Write scaling needs sharding eventually, and schema changes need care.
Orders, payments, inventory, users: anything where wrong data costs money.
Key-value or document store (DynamoDB, MongoDB)
Predictable latency at huge scale, simple access by key, flexible item shape.
Query patterns must be designed up front, weaker multi-item transactions, joins in application code.
Carts, sessions, profiles, event logs: access is by key and the data is self-contained.
Redis as a store
Sub-millisecond latency, atomic counters, expiry, simple data structures.
Memory is costly, durability depends on configuration, data must fit in RAM.
Rate limits, sessions, caches, short locks, leaderboards.
Search engine (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch)
Full-text search, relevance ranking, filters and facets over large catalogues.
Not transactional, eventually consistent with the source, extra cluster to run.
Product search and log search, always fed from a primary store.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Search index falls behind the primary
Users see items as in stock that are sold out, or new items are missing from search.
Monitor event lag, treat the primary as truth at checkout, rebuild the index from the primary when it drifts.
Hot partition key in a key-value store
One partition is throttled while the rest are idle, so requests fail even though total capacity looks fine.
Choose a high-cardinality key, add a random suffix to spread a hot key, and cache hot reads.
Cart kept only in Redis and the node restarts
Customers lose their carts.
Keep carts in a durable store, or enable persistence and replicas and accept the stated loss window.
Payment write goes to a store without transactions
A crash between two writes leaves a charge with no order, or an order with no charge.
Write money records in one relational transaction and use idempotency keys for retries.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you choose the databases for an e-commerce platform?
blocks.text: List the access patterns and correctness needs. Orders, payments, inventory and users go in a relational database for transactions and constraints. Carts and sessions go in a key-value store or Redis. Product search goes in a search index fed by change events. Keep one source of truth per fact.

blocks.title: SQL vs NoSQL: what is the real difference?
blocks.text: It is a trade between flexible queries with strong transactions (relational) and predictable scaling by key with simpler models (most NoSQL). The decision follows the query pattern and consistency need, not fashion. Many systems use both.

blocks.title: Where would you keep inventory counts and why?
blocks.text: In the relational primary, updated with a guarded statement such as UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty >= 1, so concurrent buyers cannot oversell. A cached or indexed copy is used only for display and is verified at checkout.
Takeaways

items: Choose from the access pattern and the correctness requirement, not from the product name.
Money and stock belong in a transactional relational store.
Key-value and document stores scale by key, but you design the tables around the queries.
Redis and search indexes are fast helpers and derived copies, not the source of truth.
Each extra store adds operations and a consistency gap, so add one only for a clear reason.

quiz.q: Which store is the best fit for the order and payment records?
quiz.why: Money needs atomic multi-row writes and constraints. A cache can lose data and a search index is a derived copy.

quiz.q: A shopping cart is always read and written by cart id and rarely joined with other data. A good fit is:
options: A key-value or document store keyed by cart id
A table with ten foreign keys
quiz.why: Single-key access on self-contained data is what key-value stores scale best at.

quiz.q: Inventory must never go below zero under concurrent buyers. Where does that rule belong?
options: In the relational database as a constraint plus a guarded update
quiz.why: Only the database sees all concurrent writers, so it must enforce the rule. Clients and derived copies cannot.

quiz.q: Why should the search index never be the source of truth?
options: It is eventually consistent and can be rebuilt from the primary
It is always slower than SQL
quiz.why: A derived copy lags the primary and has no transactions. Keep the truth where writes are atomic.

lessons.title: Transactions, isolation, locks and indexes: stopping a double sell

blocks.text: Use the "last item in stock" and double-spend problems to learn ACID, isolation levels and their anomalies, row locks, optimistic vs pessimistic locking, deadlocks, indexes and connection pooling.
In simple words

Two people tap Buy on the last item at the same moment. If the system is careless, both purchases succeed and one customer gets nothing. A database can make sure the two requests are handled one after the other for that item, and that each purchase either fully happens or does not happen at all.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of one last concert ticket and two buyers at two counters. A good box office puts a "being sold" sign on that ticket while one clerk finishes the sale. The second clerk waits, then sees the ticket is gone. The index is the seating chart that lets the clerk find the ticket without walking every row.

diagram.title: Two buyers, one row (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Buyers
nodes.detail: Two clients send "buy the last unit" at nearly the same time. Retries are possible, so each request carries an idempotency key.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.detail: Runs the purchase as one short transaction. It never reads stock, thinks, and writes later without protection.

nodes.label: Connection pool
nodes.detail: A bounded set of open database connections lent to requests. Protects the database from thousands of simultaneous connections.

nodes.label: Query planner
nodes.detail: Chooses how to run the statement: use an index or scan the whole table. Good plans depend on good indexes and fresh statistics.

nodes.label: B-tree index on sku
nodes.detail: A sorted tree that finds one row in a few page reads instead of scanning millions of rows.

nodes.label: Stock row (row lock)
nodes.detail: The row for the item. An update takes a row lock that other writers of the same row must wait for until commit or rollback.

nodes.label: Write-ahead log
nodes.detail: Changes are written to a sequential log and flushed to disk before commit is acknowledged. This gives durability after a crash.

steps.text: Buyer A and buyer B both request the last unit of one SKU within the same millisecond.
Each request borrows a connection from the pool. If the pool is empty the request waits briefly, then fails fast.
Each runs: BEGIN; UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty >= 1; then checks the affected row count.
The planner uses the B-tree index on sku to find the row in a few page reads.
A gets the row lock first and writes qty = 0. B reaches the same row and waits on the lock.
A commits. The change is flushed to the write-ahead log, then the lock is released.
B resumes, re-checks qty >= 1, finds 0, updates zero rows, and rolls back with "sold out".
A receives an order id. B receives a clear out-of-stock response and nothing was charged.

blocks.text: How it works

**ACID.** Atomicity: all statements in a transaction commit or none do. Consistency: constraints hold before and after. Isolation: concurrent transactions do not see each other half done. Durability: once commit returns, the data survives a crash because it was written to a log on disk. Atomicity and durability come from the write-ahead log; isolation comes from locks or multi-version snapshots.

**Isolation levels and anomalies.** Read uncommitted allows dirty reads (seeing uncommitted data). Read committed, the default in PostgreSQL, stops dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads (the same row changes between two reads) and phantoms (new rows appear in a repeated range query). Repeatable read in MySQL InnoDB fixes those for a snapshot, while PostgreSQL repeatable read also stops phantoms but can abort with a serialization error. Serializable behaves as if transactions ran one at a time, at the cost of aborts you must retry. The classic bug is **lost update**: two requests read qty = 1, both compute 0, both write 0, and two items are sold.

**Fixing the double sell.** The simplest fix is a guarded atomic update: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty >= 1, then check that one row changed. The database serializes writers on that row, so no read-then-write gap exists. When you must read first, use **pessimistic locking**: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the row until commit, which is safe but makes concurrent requests queue. **Optimistic locking** keeps a version column: UPDATE ... SET qty = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If zero rows change, someone else won and you retry. Optimistic is cheap when conflicts are rare; pessimistic is better for a hot row where retries would pile up. For double-spend on a wallet, the same guarded update (balance >= amount) plus a unique idempotency key on the payment makes a retried request harmless.

**Deadlocks and lock waits.** A deadlock happens when transaction 1 holds row A and wants row B while transaction 2 holds B and wants A. The database detects the cycle and aborts one, so the application must retry. Prevent them by locking rows in one fixed order (for example sorted by sku), keeping transactions short, and never calling a payment gateway or another service while holding a lock. Set a lock timeout so waits fail fast instead of piling up.

**Indexes and query plans.** A B-tree index keeps keys sorted, so equality and range lookups cost a few page reads (log N) instead of a full scan. A composite index on (user_id, created_at) serves queries that filter by user_id, or by user_id plus a created_at range, but not by created_at alone: put equality columns first, then the range or sort column. A covering index contains every column the query needs, so the database answers from the index without touching the table. Each index speeds reads but slows writes and uses space, so index for real queries and check them with EXPLAIN. Beware functions on indexed columns (WHERE lower(email) = ...) and leading wildcards (LIKE %abc), which prevent index use.

**Connection pooling.** Opening a database connection costs round trips and server memory, and a database serves best with a limited number of active connections, often tens to a few hundred. A pool such as PgBouncer or the application driver pool keeps connections open and lends them. Size it from the database capacity divided by the number of app instances, not from request volume. If every instance opens its own large pool, a scale-out can exhaust the database. Long transactions hold connections and cause queueing, which is one more reason to keep them short.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: When two people want the same last item, the database lets one finish first and tells the other it is gone. A transaction makes a purchase all-or-nothing. An index lets the database find an item quickly.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Use one transaction per purchase and a guarded update such as qty >= 1 so concurrent buyers cannot oversell. Isolation levels control which anomalies are possible. Indexes make lookups fast, and a connection pool limits how many connections hit the database.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Lost updates come from read-modify-write gaps. Remove the gap with an atomic update, FOR UPDATE, or a version check with retry. Avoid deadlocks with consistent lock order and short transactions. Design composite indexes with equality columns first and use covering indexes for hot queries.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Choose the lightest correct mechanism per hot path: atomic guarded updates for counters, optimistic versions for low-conflict aggregates, queued single-writer processing for extremely hot rows, and serializable only where write skew is a real risk. Keep transactions free of network calls, size pools from database limits, and watch lock wait time, deadlock rate and plan changes as first-class metrics.
Trade-offs

rows: Atomic guarded update (qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty >= 1)
One statement, no explicit lock code, correct under concurrency.
Only covers simple invariants that fit in one statement.
Stock decrement, wallet debit, any counter with a floor.
Pessimistic lock (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE)
Simple to reason about, no retries needed.
Requests queue on hot rows, risk of deadlocks and long waits.
Conflicts are frequent and the read-then-write logic is complex.
Optimistic lock (version column)
No locks held while thinking, scales well when conflicts are rare.
Needs retry logic, wasted work under heavy contention.
Profile or cart edits where two writers rarely collide.
Higher isolation (serializable)
Strongest guarantees, removes whole classes of anomalies.
More aborts and lower throughput, retries are mandatory.
Invariants span several rows and cannot be expressed as one guarded update.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Read stock, check in code, then write
Two buyers both see qty = 1 and both succeed, so stock goes negative (lost update).
Use a guarded atomic update or FOR UPDATE, and add a CHECK (qty >= 0) constraint as a last line of defence.
Two transactions lock the same rows in opposite order
Deadlock: the database aborts one transaction and the user sees an error.
Lock in a fixed order, keep transactions short, and retry the aborted one automatically.
Slow query holds connections
The pool runs dry and unrelated requests time out.
Add the missing index, set statement and lock timeouts, cap the pool and fail fast.
Client retries a payment after a timeout
The customer is charged twice (double spend).
Store a unique idempotency key with the payment so the second attempt returns the first result.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you prevent overselling the last item under high concurrency?
blocks.text: Make the decrement a single atomic guarded update (UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty >= 1) and check the affected rows. Add a CHECK constraint, an idempotency key for retries, and keep the transaction short. For a very hot SKU, queue the requests so one writer processes them in order.

blocks.title: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?
blocks.text: Pessimistic locks the row up front and makes others wait: safe, simple, but can queue and deadlock. Optimistic reads a version, writes only if it is unchanged and retries on conflict: cheap when conflicts are rare, wasteful when they are common. Pick by conflict rate.

blocks.title: A query that should be fast is slow. What do you check?
blocks.text: Run EXPLAIN to see whether it uses an index or scans the table. Check column order in composite indexes, functions on indexed columns, stale statistics and whether a covering index would avoid table reads. Then confirm with the slow query log and watch the effect on write cost.
Takeaways

items: Lost updates come from a read-then-write gap. Close it with one guarded atomic statement.
Isolation levels trade anomalies against throughput. Know what read committed does not stop.
Optimistic locking suits rare conflicts, pessimistic suits hot rows, and both need a plan for retries and waits.
Prevent deadlocks with consistent lock order and short transactions, and never hold locks across network calls.
Composite index order is equality columns first, then range or sort. Covering indexes avoid table reads.
Size connection pools from database capacity, not from traffic.

quiz.q: Two requests read qty = 1, each writes qty = 0, and two items are sold. This anomaly is called:
quiz.why: Both wrote based on a stale read, so one decrement was lost. A guarded atomic update removes the gap.

quiz.q: Which index serves WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC best?
quiz.why: Equality column first, then the sort column, so rows come out already ordered.

quiz.q: Transaction 1 locks row A then B. Transaction 2 locks B then A. The best prevention is:
options: Lock rows in one consistent order
quiz.why: A consistent order cannot form a cycle, so no deadlock appears.

quiz.q: Why call a payment gateway after the transaction commits rather than inside it?
options: A slow call inside holds locks and a connection for too long
quiz.why: Long lock holds block other buyers and drain the pool. Use an outbox or an idempotent follow-up step.

lessons.title: Replication, sharding, backups and safe schema changes

blocks.text: Learn how databases survive failures and grow beyond one machine: sync vs async replication, lag, failover, sharding and shard keys, rebalancing with consistent hashing, RPO and RTO, and expand-contract migrations.
In simple words

One database machine can break, and one machine can only hold so much. So we keep extra copies on other machines in case one fails, and we split very large data across several machines so no single one is overloaded. We also keep backups and change the table layout in small safe steps so the app never stops.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a library. Photocopies of popular books on a second shelf mean readers do not crowd one copy, and a fire in one room does not destroy everything (replication). When the library grows too big for one building, A to F goes in building one and G to Z in building two (sharding). Off-site storage of the whole catalogue is the backup.

diagram.title: Replicated shards with a router and backups (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Application
nodes.detail: Sends reads and writes through a shard-aware router or driver. It should retry safely because failover can drop a connection.

nodes.label: Shard router
nodes.detail: Computes the shard from the shard key (for example a hash of customer id) and sends writes to that shard primary. Sends tolerant reads to a replica.

nodes.label: Shard A primary
nodes.detail: Accepts all writes for the keys in shard A. Streams its write-ahead log to its replicas.

nodes.label: Sync standby (other zone)
nodes.detail: Must acknowledge each commit before the client gets success, so no acknowledged write is lost on failover. Becomes the new primary if the primary dies.

nodes.label: Async read replica
nodes.detail: Receives the log without blocking commits, so it can lag by milliseconds to seconds. Serves reads that tolerate a little staleness.

nodes.label: Shard B primary
nodes.detail: Owns a different range or hash slice of the keys. Has its own replicas, not shown. Writes to A and B run in parallel.

nodes.label: Object storage backups
nodes.detail: Periodic base backups plus the continuous log archive. Together they allow point-in-time recovery to any second.

steps.text: The app sends an update for customer 4821.
The router hashes the shard key 4821 and finds the owner is shard A, so the write goes to the shard A primary.
The primary writes to its log and waits for the standby in another zone to confirm before it acknowledges the commit.
The log also streams to the read replica without waiting. For a short time the replica still shows the old row.
A product page read goes to the replica. A read right after a write by the same user is sent to the primary instead (read your writes).
The log is archived continuously and a base backup runs nightly, which defines the recovery point.
If the primary dies, the standby is promoted, the router updates its map, and writes resume. This is failover.
Customer 9033 hashes to shard B, so its write runs on a different machine in parallel with shard A.

blocks.text: How it works

**Replication.** A primary applies writes and ships its log to replicas. **Synchronous** replication waits for at least one replica to confirm before commit returns: no acknowledged write is lost on failover, but each write pays a network round trip and a slow replica slows writes. **Asynchronous** replication does not wait: commits are faster and the primary is not blocked by a replica, but the replica **lags**, and if the primary dies before shipping the log, recent commits are lost. Many systems use one sync standby plus async read replicas. Reads from replicas can be stale, so route "read your own write" cases to the primary or wait for the replica to pass a known log position.

**Failover.** Detecting a dead primary takes seconds (heartbeats and timeouts), promoting a standby takes more, and clients must reconnect to the new primary. The dangerous case is **split brain**, two nodes both believing they are primary, which a consensus-based coordinator or fencing prevents. Tune detection so a short network blip does not trigger a needless failover, and test failover regularly because an untested failover rarely works the first time.

**Partitioning vs sharding.** Partitioning splits a large table into pieces inside one database (for example by month) to make scans, deletes and maintenance cheaper. Sharding spreads data across several database servers, each owning a slice, so write throughput and storage grow by adding machines. Sharding is costly: cross-shard joins and transactions become hard, and operations multiply. Exhaust the cheaper steps first: indexes, query fixes, caching, read replicas and a bigger machine.

**Shard key and hot shards.** The key decides everything. A good key has high cardinality, spreads writes evenly and keeps data that is queried together on one shard (customer id for an order system). Range sharding on a timestamp sends all new writes to the latest shard, a hot shard. Hashing the key spreads load evenly but loses range scans. A celebrity customer or one huge tenant can still make one shard hot, which may need that key split further or isolated on its own shard. The key is very hard to change later, so choose it from the main query patterns.

**Rebalancing and consistent hashing.** Plain hash(key) mod N moves almost every key when N changes. **Consistent hashing** places shards and keys on a ring so adding or removing a shard moves only about 1/N of the keys. Using many virtual nodes per server evens out the load. Many systems pre-split into a fixed, larger number of logical shards (for example 256) and move whole logical shards between machines, which makes rebalancing a copy-and-switch job instead of a rehash of everything.

**Backup, RPO, RTO and migrations.** **RPO** (recovery point objective) is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time: with a nightly backup only it is up to 24 hours, with continuous log archiving it is seconds. **RTO** (recovery time objective) is how long recovery may take: restoring a large backup can take hours, a hot standby takes a minute. A backup that was never restored is not a backup, so rehearse restores. For schema changes use **expand-contract**: first expand (add the new nullable column or table, deploy code that writes both and reads old), then backfill in small batches, then switch reads to the new column, then contract (stop writing old, drop it in a later release). Each step is backward compatible so a rollback is always possible, and long locks (a full table rewrite) never block production.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Keep several copies of the data on different machines so one failure does not lose it, and split a huge table across machines so no one machine does all the work. Keep backups and change the table design in small safe steps.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: A primary ships its log to replicas. Sync replicas lose nothing but slow writes, async replicas are fast but lag. Sharding splits data by a shard key across servers. Backups plus a log archive allow recovery, and expand-contract changes the schema without downtime.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Choose the shard key from the access patterns: high cardinality, even writes, co-located related data. Use consistent hashing or fixed logical shards so adding capacity moves little data. Set RPO and RTO as numbers and pick sync or async replication and backup frequency to meet them.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Reason about failure explicitly: quorum or fencing to prevent split brain, lag-aware routing for read-your-writes, per-tenant isolation for hot keys, online resharding with dual writes and verification, and schema migrations as a sequence of independently deployable and reversible steps backed by tested restores.
Trade-offs

rows: Synchronous replication
No acknowledged write is lost on failover.
Higher write latency, and a stuck replica can block writes.
Money and orders where RPO must be zero, with the standby in a nearby zone.
Asynchronous replication and read replicas
Fast commits and easy read scaling.
Replica lag gives stale reads, and recent writes can be lost on failover.
Catalogues, feeds and reports that tolerate seconds of staleness.
Hash sharding
Even load and simple routing.
No efficient range queries, and resharding needs a plan.
Large key-based workloads such as customers, carts and orders.
Range sharding
Range scans stay on few shards.
Sequential keys cause hot shards, and ranges need manual splitting.
Data accessed by ordered ranges and written with well-spread keys.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Primary fails with async replicas only
The promoted replica is missing the last few committed writes.
Use a sync standby for critical data, measure lag, and reconcile from logs or upstream events after failover.
Hot shard from a skewed key
One shard is saturated while others are idle, so latency and errors rise for those customers.
Pick a high-cardinality key, split or isolate heavy tenants, and add caching in front.
Reads served by a lagging replica
A user saves a change and the next page shows old data.
Route recent writers to the primary, or compare log positions before reading from a replica.
Schema change takes a long table lock
Writes block, the pool fills and the service times out.
Use expand-contract with small backfill batches, online DDL tools and lock timeouts.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you scale a relational database that is write-bound?
blocks.text: First remove cheap bottlenecks: indexes, slow queries, batching, a bigger machine and caching. Offload reads to replicas. If one primary still cannot take the writes, shard by a high-cardinality key that matches the main queries, use consistent hashing or logical shards, and accept the cost of cross-shard queries.

blocks.title: Sync vs async replication, and what are RPO and RTO?
blocks.text: Sync waits for a replica, so RPO is zero but commits are slower. Async is faster but can lose the last writes and serves stale reads. RPO is acceptable data loss in time, RTO is acceptable recovery time. Pick replication and backup strategy from those two numbers.

blocks.title: How do you rename a column without downtime?
blocks.text: Expand-contract. Add the new column, deploy code that writes both, backfill old rows in small batches, switch reads to the new column, then stop writing the old one and drop it in a later release. Every step can be rolled back.
Takeaways

items: Replication protects against failure and scales reads. Sharding scales writes and storage.
Sync replication trades latency for no data loss. Async trades possible loss and lag for speed.
The shard key is the hardest decision to undo. Choose from query patterns, cardinality and even load.
Consistent hashing or fixed logical shards keep rebalancing cheap.
Set RPO and RTO as numbers, and rehearse restores and failovers.
Change schemas with expand-contract so every step is reversible.

quiz.q: The business can lose at most 5 seconds of data. Which setup meets this RPO?
options: Continuous log archiving or a sync standby
quiz.why: RPO is limited by how recently data was copied elsewhere. Nightly or weekly backups are far too coarse.

quiz.q: Why does hash(key) mod N cause trouble when you add a shard?
options: Almost every key maps to a different shard and must move
quiz.why: Changing N changes the result for most keys. Consistent hashing or fixed logical shards moves only a small share.

quiz.q: Sharding orders by created_at ranges and everyone writes new orders. What happens?
options: The newest shard becomes a hot shard
quiz.why: All new writes land in the latest range, so one shard takes all the write load.

quiz.q: In expand-contract, when is the old column dropped?
options: Last, after all code reads and writes the new column
quiz.why: Dropping last keeps every earlier step backward compatible and reversible.

modules.title: Redis and Distributed Caching
modules.summary: Cache-aside, TTLs, stampedes, eviction, Redis Cluster, locks and rate limiting.

lessons.title: Caching patterns: cache-aside, write-through, write-behind and stampedes

blocks.text: How applications use a cache in front of a database, how entries are invalidated and evicted, and how to survive a cache stampede.
In simple words

A cache is a small, very fast shelf that keeps copies of answers you have already worked out. Instead of asking the slow database again, the app first looks on the shelf. The hard part is keeping the copies fresh and not letting everyone rush to the database at the same moment when a copy disappears.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a teacher who gets the same question from thirty students. The first time, she walks to the library and looks up the answer. Then she writes it on the whiteboard so the next twenty-nine students just read it. When the whiteboard is full she erases the least useful answer. If the facts change, she must erase the old answer or students will copy a wrong one.

diagram.title: Caching patterns around one service (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: Sends reads and writes to the service. It never talks to the cache or database directly.

nodes.label: App service
nodes.detail: Contains the caching logic: look in the cache first, fall back to the database, and decide how writes reach the cache.

nodes.label: Cache (Redis)
nodes.detail: In-memory key-value store with a TTL on every entry and an eviction policy such as LRU when memory is full.

nodes.label: Rebuild lock key
nodes.detail: A short-lived key in the same cache. Only the request that creates it may rebuild an expired hot entry, which stops a stampede.

nodes.label: Write-behind buffer
nodes.detail: Holds recent writes in memory or a log so they can be saved to the database in batches. Risk: data not yet flushed can be lost.

nodes.label: Flush worker
nodes.detail: Reads buffered writes and applies them to the database in batches, merging repeated updates to the same key.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.detail: The source of truth. Slower than the cache and the first thing to overload if the cache stops absorbing reads.

steps.text: A read arrives for product:42. The service runs the cache-aside pattern: look in the cache first.
GET product:42 returns nothing. This is a miss, either because the key was never loaded or its TTL expired.
To avoid a stampede the service tries SET lock:product:42 NX PX 5000. Only one request wins. Losers wait a few milliseconds or serve a slightly stale copy.
The winner reads the row from the database.
It stores the value with a TTL of 300 s plus a random 0 to 60 s of jitter, so many keys do not expire at the same instant.
Later a write arrives: the price of product:42 changes.
Write-through style: commit to the database first, because it is the source of truth.
Then delete product:42 (or overwrite it) so the next read loads the new value. Deleting is safer than updating when several writers race.
For a high-volume counter such as view counts the service uses write-behind instead: it appends the increment to a buffer and returns at once.
A worker drains the buffer every second and merges 1,000 increments of the same counter into one.
The worker writes one batched update. The database sees 1 write per second per counter instead of 1,000.

blocks.text: How it works

**Cache-aside (lazy loading).** The application owns the logic: on a read, check the cache; on a miss, read the database and put the value in the cache. On a write, update the database and then delete the cache key. It is the most common pattern because the cache can be empty or lost at any time and the system still works. The cost is that the first read after a miss is slow.

**Write-through and write-behind.** With write-through every write goes to the cache and the database together, so reads are always fresh but each write pays both latencies. With write-behind (write-back) the write lands in the cache or a buffer and is saved to the database later in batches. Writes become very fast and batching reduces database load, but anything not yet flushed is lost if the buffer node crashes. Use it only for data you can afford to lose or rebuild, such as counters.

**Invalidation and TTL.** Deleting the key on every write is the precise approach, but it fails if the delete is lost or races with a concurrent read that repopulates old data. A **TTL** (time to live) is the safety net: even a wrongly stale entry disappears after, say, 5 minutes. A common rule is to do both: explicit delete for correctness in the normal case, and a TTL to bound the damage when something goes wrong.

**Eviction.** A cache has fixed memory. When it is full it must remove something. **LRU** (least recently used) drops the entry not touched for the longest time and works well for recency-driven traffic. **LFU** (least frequently used) drops the entry used least often and protects long-term popular keys from being pushed out by a one-time scan. Some stores approximate both by sampling a few keys, which is cheaper than tracking exact order.

**Cache stampede.** A hot key with 5,000 reads per second expires. For the next 50 ms about 250 requests all miss and all query the database for the same row, and the database may fall over. Fixes: a **lock or single-flight** so only one request rebuilds while others wait or serve stale; **jittered TTL** so related keys do not expire together; and **stale-while-revalidate**, where the cache keeps serving the old value for a short grace period while one background request refreshes it.

**Consistency.** Cache and database are two stores, so they can disagree. The classic race: reader A misses and reads old row X; writer B updates the row and deletes the key; reader A then writes old X into the cache. Stale data now lives until the TTL ends. Mitigations are short TTLs, versioned values (store a version and refuse older writes), or accepting eventual consistency for data like product descriptions while bypassing the cache for money or stock counts.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: A cache keeps copies of popular answers in fast memory so the app does not keep asking the slow database. Copies must be refreshed or removed when the real data changes.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Cache-aside checks the cache first, loads from the database on a miss and deletes the key on write. TTLs bound staleness and LRU or LFU decide what to evict when memory is full.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Write-through gives fresh reads at the price of slower writes; write-behind gives fast writes at the risk of loss. Stampedes are prevented with single-flight locks, jittered TTLs and stale-while-revalidate, and the read-then-write race is reduced with versioned values.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Treat the cache as a latency tool, not a source of truth: size the database to survive a cold cache, set per-key-class TTL and staleness budgets, monitor hit ratio and eviction rate, and decide per data type whether a stale answer or a slow answer is the lesser evil during an outage.
Trade-offs

rows: Cache-aside
Simple, resilient to cache loss, only caches what is actually read.
First read after a miss is slow; stale data possible; every service must implement the logic correctly.
Default choice for read-heavy data that tolerates seconds of staleness.
Write-through
Cache is always fresh after a write; reads rarely miss.
Higher write latency; caches data that may never be read.
Read-after-write freshness matters and write volume is moderate.
Write-behind
Very fast writes and fewer database writes through batching.
Data loss if the buffer fails before flushing; harder to reason about ordering.
Counters, analytics and other loss-tolerant, high-volume writes.
LRU vs LFU eviction
LRU adapts quickly to changing traffic; LFU keeps long-term popular keys.
LRU lets a big scan flush the cache; LFU is slow to forget keys that were popular once.
LRU for recency-driven data, LFU when a stable set of hot keys dominates.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Hot key expires under heavy load (stampede)
Hundreds of identical database queries at once, latency spikes, possible database outage.
Single-flight lock, jittered TTL, stale-while-revalidate, and pre-warm known hot keys before expiry.
Write to database succeeds but the cache delete fails
Readers see old data until the TTL ends.
Keep a TTL as a safety net, retry the delete, or publish invalidation events that are retried until acknowledged.
Cache node restarts empty (cold cache)
All reads go to the database at once and may overload it.
Rate limit, warm the cache gradually, and size the database for a partial cache loss.
Write-behind buffer node crashes
Buffered writes that were not flushed are lost.
Back the buffer with a durable log, flush frequently, and use write-behind only for loss-tolerant data.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you design caching for a read-heavy product catalogue?
blocks.text: Use cache-aside with a TTL of a few minutes per product, delete the key on update, add jitter to TTLs, protect hot keys with single-flight locking, and size the database to survive a cold cache. Keep price and stock reads on a shorter TTL or bypass the cache.

blocks.title: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
blocks.text: Many requests miss the same expired hot key and all hit the database. Prevent it with a lock so only one request rebuilds, jittered TTLs, stale-while-revalidate to serve the old value during refresh, and proactive refresh of known hot keys.

blocks.title: How do you keep cache and database consistent?
blocks.text: You cannot get strict consistency cheaply. Write the database first, then delete the cache key, keep a TTL as a bound, version values to reject older writes, and decide per data type whether eventual consistency is acceptable. For money or stock, read from the database.
Takeaways

items: Cache-aside is the default: read cache, fall back to database, delete the key on write.
Always pair explicit invalidation with a TTL as a safety net.
LRU favours recency, LFU favours long-term popularity.
A stampede is fixed with a lock, jittered TTLs and stale-while-revalidate.
Write-behind trades durability for speed; use it only for loss-tolerant data.
The cache and the database can disagree, so decide the allowed staleness per data type.

quiz.q: In cache-aside, what should the service do after updating a row in the database?
options: Nothing, the TTL will fix it
quiz.why: Deleting the key makes the next read load fresh data. The TTL is only a safety net.

quiz.q: A key read 5,000 times per second expires and the database gets hit by hundreds of identical queries. What is this?
quiz.why: Many requests miss the same key at once. Locks, jittered TTL and stale-while-revalidate prevent it.

quiz.q: Which pattern risks losing acknowledged writes if the cache or buffer node crashes?
quiz.why: Write-behind acknowledges before the database has the data, so unflushed writes can be lost.

quiz.q: Why add random jitter to TTLs?
options: So many keys do not all expire at the same instant
quiz.why: Spreading expiry times avoids synchronized misses that overload the database.

lessons.title: Redis in depth: data structures, Cluster, distributed locks and rate limiting

blocks.text: What Redis offers beyond plain keys, how Redis Cluster splits data into hash slots, and how to build locks, sessions and rate limiters safely.
In simple words

Redis is a very fast store that keeps data in memory and understands more than plain text: lists, sets, sorted scoreboards and counters. When one machine is not enough, many Redis machines share the data between them. People also use it as a shared notice board for things like login sessions, "who holds this lock" and "how many requests has this user made".

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Imagine a large office with many filing cabinets. Each cabinet owns a fixed range of drawer numbers, and a directory at the front tells you which cabinet holds drawer 9,000. Each cabinet has a twin in another room that copies everything. A sign on a drawer saying "in use by Priya for 5 minutes" is a lock, and a tally sheet per visitor limits how often they may enter.

diagram.title: Redis Cluster behind an application (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: Sends requests that carry a session id and an API key or user id.

nodes.label: App service
nodes.detail: Uses a cluster-aware Redis client for sessions, rate limiting and locks.

nodes.label: Cluster client (slot map)
nodes.detail: Keeps a map of hash slot to node. It computes CRC16(key) mod 16384 and sends each command straight to the owning node.

nodes.label: Primary A (slots 0-8191)
nodes.detail: Owns half of the 16,384 hash slots in this small example and serves all reads and writes for them.

nodes.label: Primary B (slots 8192-16383)
nodes.detail: Owns the other half. Real clusters usually have at least three primaries so a majority can agree on failover.

nodes.label: Replica of A
nodes.detail: Copies A asynchronously. Promoted to primary if A fails. Because copying is asynchronous, a few latest writes can be lost on failover.

nodes.label: Replica of B
nodes.detail: Copies B asynchronously and takes over if B fails.

steps.text: A request arrives with a session cookie and an API key.
The service needs session data for key sess:abc. The client computes CRC16("sess:abc") mod 16384 to find the hash slot.
The slot belongs to Primary A, so GET sess:abc goes directly there. Sessions are stored with a TTL so abandoned ones expire by themselves.
Next the service rate-limits the caller. The key rate:user:7 hashes to a different slot.
A small Lua script on Primary B runs the token bucket check and update atomically, so two concurrent requests cannot both spend the last token.
For a critical job it takes a lock: SET lock:order:42 <random-token> NX PX 10000, and increments a counter to get a fencing token.
The owning primary accepts the lock only if the key does not exist. The service gets the lock and the fencing token 107.
Primary A copies the writes to its replica asynchronously. A crash right now could lose the lock key, which is why the storage layer must also check fencing tokens.
Primary B replicates the bucket state the same way.
After a reshard moves a slot, the old owner replies MOVED. The client updates its slot map and retries on the new node.

blocks.text: How it works

**Data structures.** A plain string holds a value or a counter (`INCR` is atomic). A hash stores fields of one object. A list works as a simple queue. A set stores unique members and supports union and intersection. A **sorted set** keeps members ordered by a score, which fits leaderboards and time-ordered windows. Bitmaps and HyperLogLog give compact flags and approximate unique counts. Choosing the right structure often removes the need for application-side logic.

**Redis Cluster.** Data is split into **16,384 hash slots**. A key goes to the slot `CRC16(key) mod 16384`, and each primary node owns a range of slots. Each primary has one or more replicas. Clients cache the slot map and talk to the right node directly; if a slot has moved the node answers `MOVED` and the client updates its map. Multi-key commands only work when all keys share a slot, which you force with **hash tags** such as `{user:7}:cart` and `{user:7}:session`.

**Failover and its limit.** If a primary stops answering, its replica is promoted after a majority of primaries agree. Replication is asynchronous, so writes acknowledged by the old primary but not yet copied are lost. Redis is therefore great for data that can be rebuilt or that tolerates small loss, and a poor choice as the only copy of data you cannot lose.

**Distributed locks.** The single-node recipe is `SET lock:x <random-token> NX PX 10000`: set only if absent, with an expiry so a crashed holder cannot block forever. Release with a script that deletes the key only when the stored token matches yours, otherwise you may delete someone else lock. Expiry creates a hazard: a paused holder (a long garbage collection, say) wakes up after the lock expired and writes anyway. A **fencing token** fixes this: every lock grant returns an increasing number, and the protected resource rejects any request with a number lower than one it already saw. **Redlock** (acquiring locks on several independent nodes) tries to survive node failure but depends on timing assumptions, so use a consensus system or fencing when correctness, not just efficiency, depends on the lock.

**Sessions.** Store the session as a hash under a random id with a TTL, and refresh the TTL on activity. It is fast and shared by all service instances, so any instance can serve any request. Plan for the session store being lost: users are asked to log in again, which is acceptable for most products.

**Rate limiting and hot keys.** A **fixed window** counter (`INCR` with expiry) is simple but allows a burst of 2x the limit across a window edge. A **sliding window** uses a sorted set of timestamps or weights two adjacent windows, and is smoother but costs more memory. A **token bucket** refills at a steady rate and allows controlled bursts; it needs an atomic read-modify-write, usually a Lua script. A **hot key**, one key receiving a disproportionate load such as 100,000 reads per second, overloads its single owning node whatever the cluster size. Fix it with a local in-process cache, by splitting the key into several copies (`key#0` to `key#9`), or by using replicas for reads.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Redis keeps data in memory with handy shapes like counters, lists and sorted scoreboards. Many Redis machines can share the work, and a copy machine takes over if one breaks.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Cluster splits keys into 16,384 hash slots across primaries with replicas. Locks use SET NX PX with an expiry and a unique token; rate limiting uses counters, sliding windows or token buckets; sessions use hashes with TTLs.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Replication is asynchronous, so failover can lose recent writes and a lock can be granted twice. Fencing tokens checked by the protected resource make locks safe, and Lua scripts make read-modify-write rate limiting atomic.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Design around the hot key and the failure model: use hash tags only where multi-key atomicity is required, spread hot keys across slots, keep Redis a rebuildable layer, and use a consensus-backed lock service or database constraint when a lock protects correctness rather than efficiency.
Trade-offs

rows: Fixed window rate limit
Very cheap: one counter per window.
A client can send twice the limit around a window boundary.
Coarse protection where small bursts are fine.
Sliding window rate limit
Smooth and accurate limit with no boundary burst.
More memory per user (a log of timestamps) or approximate weighting.
Public APIs where fairness matters.
Token bucket
Allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate; easy to explain.
Needs atomic update, usually a script, and per-key state.
Most API gateways and per-user limits.
Redis lock with expiry (single node or Redlock)
Fast and simple for avoiding duplicate work.
Not safe alone for correctness: expiry plus pauses plus failover can give two holders.
Efficiency locks. For correctness add fencing tokens or use a consensus store.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Primary fails before its replica copied the latest writes
Recently written keys, sessions or lock entries are lost after failover.
Treat Redis as rebuildable, keep sessions short-lived, and never store the only copy of important data.
Lock holder pauses past the lock expiry
Two clients believe they hold the lock and both write.
Use fencing tokens checked by the resource, keep critical sections short, and renew only with care.
One hot key receives most of the traffic
Its owning node is saturated while other nodes are idle; adding nodes does not help.
Cache in the application process, split the key into several copies, or serve reads from replicas.
Rate limiter Redis is unreachable
Either all requests are blocked or the limit disappears.
Decide fail-open or fail-closed per endpoint, and keep a coarse in-process fallback limit.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How does Redis Cluster scale and what happens when a node fails?
blocks.text: Keys hash to 16,384 slots spread over primaries; each primary has replicas. Clients route directly using a cached slot map and follow MOVED redirects. On failure a replica is promoted after a majority of primaries agree, and because replication is asynchronous the last few writes can be lost.

blocks.title: Design a distributed lock with Redis. Is it safe?
blocks.text: SET key token NX PX ttl to acquire, a compare-and-delete script to release, and a fencing token that the protected resource validates. It is fine for efficiency locks. For correctness, expiry, pauses and failover can produce two holders, so rely on fencing or a consensus system, not Redlock alone.

blocks.title: Implement rate limiting for 100 requests per minute per user.
blocks.text: A token bucket in a Lua script keyed by user id: refill by elapsed time, spend one token, return allowed or denied atomically. Fixed window is cheaper but bursts at the edge; sliding window is smoother but costs more memory. Decide fail-open or fail-closed if Redis is down.
Takeaways

items: Redis offers structures (strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets) that replace application logic.
Cluster splits keys over 16,384 hash slots; hash tags keep related keys on one node.
Replication is asynchronous, so failover can lose recent writes.
A lock needs a unique token, an expiry and, for correctness, a fencing token.
Token bucket allows bursts at a steady average; fixed window can double at the edge.
A hot key limits one node no matter how large the cluster is.

quiz.q: How does Redis Cluster decide which node stores a key?
options: CRC16(key) mod 16384 gives a hash slot owned by one primary
The oldest node always stores it
quiz.why: Keys map deterministically to one of 16,384 hash slots and each slot has one owning primary.

quiz.q: Why must lock release check a stored random token?
options: So a client never deletes a lock that expired and was taken by someone else
quiz.why: Without the check, a slow client could release another client lock after its own had expired.

quiz.q: What does a fencing token protect against?
options: A paused lock holder acting after its lock expired
quiz.why: The resource rejects any request whose token is lower than one it has already seen, so stale holders are ignored.

quiz.q: A fixed-window limit of 100 per minute is used. What is the worst-case burst around a window edge?
quiz.why: 100 requests at the end of one window plus 100 at the start of the next: up to 200 in a short time.

lessons.title: Client-side caching and offline-first sync

blocks.text: How an app keeps working without a network: the local database as the source of truth for the UI, cache policies, an on-device outbox, optimistic updates and rollback, delta sync with cursors, conflict resolution, image caching, invalidation and schema migration.
In simple words

An offline-first app keeps its own copy of the data on the phone and always shows that copy. When you change something, the app saves the change on the phone first and remembers that it still has to tell the server. When the network is available, it sends the saved changes and collects whatever changed on the server. The hard part is deciding what to do when the phone and the server both changed the same thing.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A travelling salesperson carries a notebook with a copy of the customer list. On the road they read from the notebook and write new orders into it, with no need to call the office. Each evening they phone the office, read out the new orders one by one, and write down what changed at the office during the day. If the office says "that product was discontinued this morning", the salesperson crosses out that order and tells the customer. The notebook is the local database, the list of orders to read out is the outbox, and the evening call is sync.

diagram.title: Offline edit, replay and delta sync (generic shared shopping list app)

nodes.label: List screen
nodes.detail: Observes the local database and redraws when rows change. Never waits for the network to show data.

nodes.label: Repository
nodes.detail: Applies reads and writes to the local store and enqueues mutations. The only component the UI layers talk to for data.

nodes.label: Local database
nodes.detail: Source of truth for the UI. Rows carry a server version, a pending flag and a tombstone marker.

nodes.label: Outbox
nodes.detail: Ordered, durable table of pending mutations, each with a client-generated mutation id. Written in the same transaction as the data row.

nodes.label: Sync engine
nodes.detail: Pushes the outbox and pulls server changes. Triggered by connectivity, app foreground, push hints and OS background scheduling.

nodes.label: Image cache
nodes.detail: Memory tier for decoded images and a size-bounded disk tier with LRU eviction, keyed by URL and size.

nodes.label: Image CDN
nodes.detail: Serves immutable, versioned image URLs so the client can cache them for a long time.

nodes.label: Sync API
nodes.detail: Two operations: accept a batch of mutations, and return changes after a cursor.

nodes.label: List service
nodes.detail: Validates each mutation, de-duplicates by mutation id, detects conflicts by version and applies the conflict rule.

nodes.label: Change log
nodes.detail: Ordered record of every change per user or list, including deletions. The basis for delta sync.

nodes.label: Server database
nodes.detail: Authoritative state shared by all devices and users.

steps.text: With no network, the user ticks off "milk" and renames "bread" to "brown bread".
The repository updates both rows locally and marks them pending.
In the same transaction it appends two mutations to the outbox, each with a unique mutation id and the row version it was based on.
The database change notifies the screen, which shows the new state immediately with a small "not synced" mark.
Connectivity returns. The sync engine wakes and reads pending mutations in order.
It sends POST /sync/mutations with both mutations in one batch.
The service checks each mutation id for duplicates, then compares the base version with the current server version.
The tick on "milk" applies cleanly. "bread" was deleted by another family member, so the rename is rejected with a conflict code.
The accepted change is appended to the change log with the next sequence number.
The response returns a result per mutation: one applied with its new version, one rejected with the reason.
The engine clears the pending flag on "milk", removes the local "bread" row (rollback to server state), deletes both outbox entries and records a message for the user.
Then it pulls: GET /sync/changes?since=cursor_812.
The service reads the change log after that cursor and returns upserts, tombstones and a new cursor.
Changes and the new cursor are written in one local transaction, so a crash can never leave the cursor ahead of the data.

blocks.text: How it works

**Single source of truth on the device.** In an offline-first design the UI reads only from the local database. The network never updates the screen directly; it updates the database, and the screen observes the database. This gives one data path for cached, fresh and locally modified data, removes the "which copy is right" bugs of screens holding their own network results, and makes the app usable at launch with no connectivity. The cost is that you now operate a small database product: schema, migrations, storage limits and correctness under concurrent writers (UI, sync engine, push handler).

**Cache policies for reads.** Choose per data type. **Cache-first with revalidation (stale-while-revalidate)**: return local data immediately, fetch in the background, update the store; the default for catalog-like data. **Network-first with cache fallback**: for data where freshness matters but something is better than nothing. **Network-only**: balances, payment state, one-time codes. **Cache-only**: static reference data refreshed on a schedule. Attach metadata to cached data (fetched-at time, ETag, max age) so the repository can decide when to revalidate and the UI can show staleness honestly. Use conditional requests so an unchanged resource costs a `304` and no body.

**The outbox.** Local writes follow the same pattern as the transactional outbox on a backend. In one local transaction, apply the change to the data table and append a mutation record to an outbox table: mutation id (doubles as the idempotency key), entity id, operation, payload, base version, created-at, attempt count. A sync worker drains it in order when a network is available. Because the intent is durable, it survives app kills and reboots. Ordering matters per entity (create before update before delete), so either process strictly in sequence or serialise per entity and parallelise across entities. Entities created offline need **client-generated ids** (UUIDs) so later queued mutations can reference them before the server has seen them.

**Optimistic updates and rollback.** The UI shows the result of a write before the server confirms it. That requires a plan for the three outcomes. Applied: clear the pending flag and store the server version. Transient failure: keep it queued and retry with backoff. Permanent rejection (validation, permission, conflict): undo the local change and tell the user what happened. Rollback is simplest when you refetch or apply the authoritative server row instead of trying to reverse the operation locally. Reserve optimism for actions that are likely to succeed and cheap to undo. For payments and bookings, wait for the server and show progress.

**Delta sync with cursors.** Downloading everything on every sync does not scale. The server keeps an ordered change feed per sync scope (user, list, workspace) and the client stores a **cursor**: an opaque token meaning "I have applied everything up to here". A pull returns changes after the cursor plus a new cursor. Deletions are sent as **tombstones**; without them a deleted row lives forever on other devices. Prefer server-assigned sequence numbers to timestamps, because device clocks are wrong and two changes can share a millisecond. If the cursor is older than the retention of the feed, the server answers "full resync required" and the client rebuilds from a paginated snapshot. Apply the page of changes and the new cursor in one local transaction.

**Conflict resolution.** A conflict exists when a mutation was based on a version that is no longer current. Options, from simple to complex. **Server-authoritative**: reject the stale write and let the client refetch; right for stock, prices, money. **Last-write-wins**: the later write replaces the earlier; simple but silently loses data, and "later" must be decided by the server, not by device clocks. **Field-level merge**: changes to different fields both survive; conflicts only when the same field changed. **Domain-specific merge**: for example counters merge by adding deltas, sets by union. **CRDTs** (conflict-free replicated data types) are data structures designed so that replicas can apply operations in any order and converge to the same state without a central decision, at the cost of extra metadata and complexity; they suit collaborative text and shared documents. **Ask the user** only when the data is valuable and automatic merge would be wrong.

**Image caching.** Images dominate bytes and memory. Use two tiers: a memory cache of decoded bitmaps bounded by total cost and cleared on memory warnings, and a disk cache of encoded files bounded by size with least-recently-used eviction. Key by URL including the requested size. Make image URLs immutable (a content hash or version in the URL) so they can be cached for a long time and a changed image is simply a new URL. Request the size you will draw, decode and downsample away from the main thread, and cancel loads for views that left the screen. For true offline use, explicitly prefetch the images the offline dataset references; a lazy cache only contains what the user happened to view.

**Invalidation and expiry.** Cached data becomes wrong in three ways: time passes, the server changes it, or the user context changes. Handle each: TTL or max-age for time; delta sync, push hints or revalidation for server changes; and a hard wipe on logout or account switch so one user never sees data cached for another. Scope caches by user id, and include locale or region in keys when responses depend on them. Bound total storage with eviction, since the OS may purge cache directories and users uninstall apps that take too much space. Keep the outbox out of any evictable location: pending user writes are not cache.

**Schema migration.** The local schema ships inside the binary and users upgrade from any older version directly to the newest. Every schema change needs a versioned migration that runs at open, and migrations must be tested from each supported starting version with realistic data sizes, since a slow migration on the main thread looks like a frozen launch. Separate tables by recoverability: pure cache tables may be dropped and refetched as the safe fallback; tables with unsynced user data (outbox, drafts) must be migrated carefully and never dropped. Also version the sync protocol itself, so the server can tell an old client to resync or upgrade.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The app keeps its own copy of the data and always shows that copy, so it works without a network. Changes are saved on the phone first and sent later. When the phone and server disagree, a rule decides which change is kept.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: The UI observes a local database. Reads use stale-while-revalidate. Writes update the local row and add a mutation to an outbox in one transaction; a sync engine replays the outbox with idempotency keys and pulls server changes with a cursor. Conflicts are settled by server authority, last-write-wins or merge, chosen per entity.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Sync is a replication protocol. It needs client-generated ids, per-entity ordering, version-based conflict detection, tombstones, a server change feed with bounded retention and a full-resync path, atomic cursor advancement, and idempotent apply on both sides. Rollback is implemented as convergence to server state plus user-visible explanation, not as inverse operations.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: The Staff-level questions are about scope and guarantees. Define sync scopes so a user downloads only what they can see and permission changes revoke local data; define the consistency model per entity (what can be stale, for how long, and what must be confirmed online); and bound every unbounded thing: outbox age, tombstone retention, device storage, resync cost after long offline periods. Protocol evolution is the trap: the wire format and conflict semantics live in old binaries for years, so version the protocol, make the server tolerant of old mutation shapes, and build telemetry for divergence (checksums or periodic reconciliation) because silent drift between replicas is the failure you will not otherwise see. CRDTs remove the coordinator but move cost into metadata growth, garbage collection and intent preservation, so adopt them per data type, not as a platform default.
Trade-offs

rows: Offline-first (local database as source of truth)
Instant UI, works without network, resilient to backend incidents for reads.
Sync, conflicts, migrations and storage management are substantial engineering; harder to test.
Apps used on the move or for long sessions: notes, lists, field work, messaging, browsing a catalog.
Online-only with a short-lived response cache
Simple, always fresh, small local footprint.
Unusable offline, slow on weak networks.
Transactional flows where stale data is harmful: payments, live inventory at checkout.
Last-write-wins
Trivial to implement and explain; always converges.
Silently discards the earlier concurrent edit; depends on a trustworthy ordering.
Single-user data across devices and low-value fields such as preferences.
Server-authoritative rejection
Invariants are always enforced in one place; no bad merges.
User work can be rejected after the fact; needs clear rollback UX.
Stock, pricing, balances, bookings, anything with business invariants.
Field-level or domain merge
Preserves both edits in most real conflicts.
Per-entity logic, more metadata per field, harder to test exhaustively.
Shared records edited by several people where edits usually touch different fields.
CRDT-based data model
Automatic convergence without a coordinator; good for real-time collaboration and long offline periods.
Metadata overhead, garbage collection, hard to enforce global invariants, steep learning curve.
Collaborative text, drawings and documents. Rarely worth it for forms and simple lists.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Response to an outbox push is lost and the mutation is replayed
Without protection the item is created or the counter incremented twice.
Mutation id as idempotency key, stored server side for at least the maximum offline window; client-generated entity ids.
A permanently failing mutation at the head of the outbox
Every later mutation is blocked forever and the user thinks changes are saved.
Classify errors: retry transient ones with backoff, move permanent failures to a dead-letter state, roll back the local change and notify the user.
Cursor saved but the change page was not fully applied
The skipped changes are never fetched again; the device silently diverges.
Write changes and the new cursor in one local transaction; periodic checksum or full reconciliation to detect drift.
Deletes are not propagated as tombstones
Items deleted on one device reappear or remain on others.
Soft deletes in the change feed with a retention longer than the supported offline period, and forced full resync beyond it.
Cached data survives logout
The next user on the device sees the previous user data: a privacy incident.
Scope storage by user id, wipe database, caches and secure-store entries on logout, and block logout or warn when the outbox still holds unsynced writes.
Schema migration fails or runs for a long time at launch
Crash loop or frozen first screen after an update.
Test migrations from every supported version with large datasets, run them off the main thread with progress UI, and allow dropping cache-only tables as a fallback.
Conflict resolved by device timestamp
A phone with a wrong clock always wins or always loses; edits vanish.
Server-assigned versions or sequence numbers for ordering; treat client time as display metadata only.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Design offline support for a shared shopping list.
blocks.text: Local database as UI source of truth; rows with id, fields, server version, pending flag, deleted flag. Writes go to the row and an outbox in one transaction with a mutation id; ids for new items are generated on the client. Sync engine pushes the outbox in order with idempotency, then pulls changes since a cursor from a per-list change feed with tombstones. Conflicts: field-level merge for name and quantity, checked state last-write-wins by server order, delete wins over edit. Triggers: foreground, connectivity change, push hint. Show unsynced marks and explain rejected changes.

blocks.title: How do optimistic updates work and when would you avoid them?
blocks.text: Apply the change locally and render it at once, queue the mutation, then reconcile with the server result: confirm, retry or roll back to server state with a message. Avoid them when the action is irreversible or expensive to be wrong about (payment, booking, sending money), when success depends on scarce shared state (last item in stock), or when a rollback would confuse the user more than a short wait.

blocks.title: Explain delta sync. Why a cursor instead of "updated since timestamp"?
blocks.text: The server exposes changes in a total order per scope and the client stores a position. A cursor based on a server sequence is immune to clock skew, never misses rows committed with the same timestamp, and can encode shard or snapshot information because it is opaque. Timestamps from long-running transactions can commit out of order and be skipped. The feed includes tombstones, has bounded retention, and the protocol has an explicit full-resync response.

blocks.title: How do you choose a conflict resolution strategy?
blocks.text: Per entity, by asking what is lost if one side is discarded and whether an invariant spans users. Invariants and money: server-authoritative. Single-user settings: last-write-wins by server order. Multi-field records: field-level merge. Counters and sets: operation-based merge. Rich collaborative content: CRDT or operational transform. I prefer the simplest rule the product can accept and make conflicts rarer through finer-grained mutations ("set quantity to 3" rather than "replace the whole item").

blocks.title: What goes wrong with local caching at scale and how do you guard against it?
blocks.text: Stale data shown as current, storage growth, cross-user leakage, corrupted or unmigratable databases, and silent divergence from the server. Guards: freshness metadata and visible staleness, size-bounded caches with eviction, user-scoped storage wiped on logout, tested migrations with a drop-and-refetch fallback for cache tables, atomic cursor updates, periodic reconciliation, and metrics for cache hit rate, outbox age and resync frequency by app version.
Takeaways

items: The UI reads from the local database only; the network and the user both write to it.
Pick a cache policy per data type and store freshness metadata with the data.
Local writes go to the data table and an outbox in one transaction, with client-generated ids and mutation ids.
Optimistic UI needs a defined outcome for applied, retry and rejected, and rollback means converging to server state.
Delta sync needs server-ordered cursors, tombstones, bounded retention and a full-resync path.
Choose conflict rules per entity: server-authoritative for invariants, merge where both edits matter, CRDTs only for true collaboration.
Treat invalidation, logout wipe and schema migration as first-class design items.

quiz.q: In an offline-first app, what does the screen read from?
options: The latest network response held in memory
The local database, which network and user writes both update
quiz.why: A single observable local store gives one data path and lets the UI work with or without connectivity.

quiz.q: Why must the data change and the outbox entry be written in one transaction?
options: So a crash cannot leave a local change that will never be synced, or a queued mutation with no local change
quiz.why: Atomicity guarantees that what the user sees and what will be sent to the server stay consistent.

quiz.q: What is a tombstone in delta sync?
options: A cache entry past its TTL
A record in the change feed saying an entity was deleted
quiz.why: Other devices can only remove a row if the deletion is delivered to them as a change.

quiz.q: Which conflict strategy fits "stock quantity of a product"?
options: Server-authoritative: the server decides and the client refetches
quiz.why: Stock is a business invariant owned by the server. Client copies are hints that must be revalidated.

quiz.q: The client cursor is older than the server change-log retention. What should happen?
options: Server signals a full resync and the client rebuilds from a snapshot
Server replays from the oldest entry it has and says nothing
quiz.why: Replaying from a later point would silently skip changes. An explicit reset is the only correct answer.

modules.title: Kafka and Message Queues
modules.summary: Topics, partitions, consumer groups, lag, outbox, saga and CQRS.

lessons.title: Kafka core: partitions, consumer groups, offsets and delivery guarantees

blocks.text: How a replicated, partitioned log works, how consumers share it, and how to get safe processing with retries, idempotency and a dead letter queue.
In simple words

Kafka is like a very long notebook where programs write down events in order, and other programs read them at their own speed. The notebook is split into several parts so many readers can work at once, and copies are kept on other machines so nothing is lost if one machine breaks.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Picture a post office with several numbered conveyor belts. Letters for the same customer always go on the same belt, so they stay in order. Each team of clerks is assigned some belts and keeps a bookmark of the last letter it handled. If a clerk is away, belts are handed to a colleague, who continues from the bookmark.

diagram.title: One Kafka partition and its consumer (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Producer
nodes.detail: Sends events with a key such as the order id. The key decides the partition, so all events for one order stay in order.

nodes.label: Broker A: partition 0 leader
nodes.detail: The leader appends events to the partition log and serves reads. Each event gets an increasing offset.

nodes.label: Broker B: follower
nodes.detail: Copies the leader log. A follower that keeps up is part of the in-sync replica set (ISR).

nodes.label: Broker C: follower
nodes.detail: A second copy on a different machine, ideally a different rack or zone, so one failure never removes all copies.

nodes.label: Consumer (in a group)
nodes.detail: Reads events in offset order. Within a group each partition is read by exactly one consumer at a time.

nodes.label: Processed-ids store
nodes.detail: Records event ids already handled, so a redelivered event is detected and skipped. This makes processing idempotent.

nodes.label: Retry topic
nodes.detail: Failed events wait here with a delay and are tried again. It keeps one bad event from blocking the main partition.

nodes.label: Dead letter queue
nodes.detail: Events that keep failing are parked here for inspection and replay by a human or a repair job.

steps.text: The producer sends event OrderPaid with key order-42 and acks=all. The key hashes to partition 0, whose leader is Broker A.
The leader appends the event at offset 1,057 and Broker B fetches and copies it.
Broker C copies it too. Both followers are in the in-sync replica set.
With acks=all the leader acknowledges only after every in-sync replica has the event. If the leader dies now, the event survives on a follower.
The consumer polls partition 0 and receives events starting from its last committed offset.
Before applying the event it checks the processed-ids store. If the id exists this is a duplicate and it is skipped; otherwise it is applied and recorded in one database transaction.
Only after processing succeeds does it commit offset 1,058. Commit after processing gives at-least-once delivery.
A different event fails because a downstream service is down. It is published to the retry topic so the partition keeps moving.
After 5 delayed attempts the event moves to the dead letter queue, where it is kept for investigation and replay.

blocks.text: How it works

**Log, topics and partitions.** A topic is a named stream. It is split into **partitions**, each an append-only log where every event has a sequential **offset**. Partitions are the unit of parallelism and of ordering: Kafka guarantees order only inside one partition. A producer picks the partition from the event key (`hash(key) mod partitions`), so using the order id as the key keeps all events of one order in order.
