**Consumer groups and offsets.** A consumer group shares a topic: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, so a group of 6 consumers reading 12 partitions gives 2 partitions each. Adding a 13th consumer to 12 partitions gives no extra speed because one would sit idle. Each group stores its own committed offset per partition, so many groups (billing, analytics, search) can read the same topic independently. **Rebalancing** reassigns partitions when consumers join, leave or are too slow; during a rebalance consumption pauses briefly, so avoid long processing between polls.

**Replication and durability.** Every partition has a leader and followers on other brokers. Followers that keep up form the **ISR** (in-sync replicas). With `acks=0` the producer does not wait, `acks=1` waits for the leader only, and `acks=all` waits for every in-sync replica. With replication factor 3, `acks=all` and `min.insync.replicas=2`, a write is acknowledged only if at least two copies hold it, so one broker failure loses nothing. If fewer than 2 replicas are in sync the write is rejected, which chooses consistency over availability.

**Retention and lag.** Kafka keeps events for a configured time or size (for example 7 days), not until they are read. Consumers can rewind and replay. **Consumer lag** is the distance between the newest offset and the committed offset. Steadily growing lag means consumers are slower than producers: add consumers (up to the partition count), speed up processing, or add partitions. Lag measured in time (how old is the oldest unprocessed event) is the number users feel.

**Delivery guarantees.** **At-most-once**: commit the offset before processing; a crash loses the event. **At-least-once**: commit after processing; a crash causes redelivery, so duplicates happen. **Exactly-once** inside Kafka uses idempotent producers and transactions to write results and offsets atomically, but once you touch an outside system (a database, an email) you only get effectively-once by making the consumer **idempotent**: record the event id with the side effect in one transaction, or use a natural unique key so a repeat has no further effect.

**Retry topics and DLQ.** Never let one poison event block a partition by retrying it forever. On failure publish it to a retry topic with a delay (for example 1 min, 10 min, 1 hour); after a set number of attempts move it to a **dead letter queue** with the error attached. Retried events lose partition order, so consumers must tolerate out-of-order events, for example by comparing a version or timestamp before applying.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Kafka is a shared notebook of events. Writers add lines at the end, readers keep a bookmark, and copies of the notebook live on other machines.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Topics are split into partitions; order holds only within a partition. Consumers in a group split partitions between them and commit offsets. Replication with acks=all keeps data safe if a broker dies.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Choose keys to preserve per-entity order and spread load, size partitions for the target consumer parallelism, and watch lag and ISR. Commit offsets after processing and make handlers idempotent to turn at-least-once into effectively-once.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Partition count is hard to change without breaking key ordering, so plan for growth. Use replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas=2, tune max poll interval to avoid rebalance storms, handle hot keys, and design retry tiers so out-of-order redelivery cannot corrupt state.
Trade-offs

rows: Kafka (partitioned log)
High throughput, durable, replayable, many independent consumer groups, ordered per key.
Operationally heavier; ordering only per partition; no per-message routing or priorities.
Event streams, analytics feeds, integration between many services, anything needing replay.
RabbitMQ (broker with queues)
Flexible routing, per-message acknowledgement, priorities and TTLs; simple task queue semantics.
Messages are removed once consumed, so no replay; lower peak throughput for huge streams.
Background job queues and work distribution with rich routing.
REST / RPC (synchronous call)
Simple, immediate response, easy to debug.
Caller waits and fails when the callee is down; tight coupling in time.
The caller needs the answer now, such as reading a price.
WebSockets (live connection)
Low-latency two-way push to clients such as chat or live prices.
Stateful connections are harder to scale and are not durable if the client is offline.
Real-time updates to browsers and apps, usually fed by a broker behind the scenes.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Consumer crashes after processing but before committing the offset
The event is redelivered and applied twice.
Make the handler idempotent with a processed-ids table or a unique business key.
A poison event always throws an error
The partition is stuck and lag grows without bound.
Retry a limited number of times via a retry topic, then move it to a DLQ with the error and keep going.
Leader broker fails
Writes pause briefly until a follower becomes leader; with acks=1 acknowledged events can be lost.
Use acks=all, replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2, and spread replicas across zones.
Slow processing triggers repeated rebalances
Consumers keep losing partitions and throughput collapses.
Keep work between polls short, tune session and poll timeouts, and move slow work to a separate worker pool.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you guarantee ordering of events for one order in Kafka?
blocks.text: Use the order id as the message key so all its events go to the same partition, which is an ordered log, and process each partition with one consumer. Ordering is not guaranteed across partitions, and retries or reprocessing can disturb it, so handlers should also check versions.

blocks.title: Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once.
blocks.text: At-most-once commits before processing and may lose events. At-least-once commits after processing and may duplicate. Exactly-once within Kafka uses idempotent producers and transactions; for external side effects you aim for effectively-once with idempotent consumers keyed by event id.

blocks.title: When would you choose Kafka over RabbitMQ or a REST call?
blocks.text: Choose Kafka for high-volume event streams, replay and multiple independent consumers. Choose RabbitMQ for job queues needing rich routing and per-message handling. Choose REST when the caller needs an immediate answer. Often they combine: REST for commands, Kafka for events.
Takeaways

items: A topic is split into partitions; order exists only inside a partition, so choose the key carefully.
Within a consumer group each partition has one consumer, so partitions cap parallelism.
acks=all with replication factor 3 and min.insync.replicas=2 survives one broker loss.
Commit offsets after processing and make consumers idempotent to handle duplicates.
Use retry topics and a DLQ so one bad event never blocks a partition.
Pick Kafka, a queue, REST or WebSockets by the need: replay and streams, jobs, an answer now, or live push.

quiz.q: Where does Kafka guarantee event order?
quiz.why: Only a partition is an ordered log. Use the entity id as the key so its events share a partition.

quiz.q: A topic has 6 partitions and a consumer group has 10 consumers. How many consumers do useful work?
quiz.why: Each partition goes to at most one consumer in a group, so 4 consumers sit idle.

quiz.q: You commit the offset after processing and the app crashes between the two steps. What happens?
options: The event is redelivered, so the handler must be idempotent
quiz.why: Commit-after-processing gives at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible.

quiz.q: Which setting combination gives the strongest durability for a producer?
options: acks=all with min.insync.replicas of 2 and replication factor 3
quiz.why: The write is acknowledged only once at least two replicas hold it, so one broker failure cannot lose it.

lessons.title: Outbox, Saga, event sourcing and CQRS: consistency across services

blocks.text: How to update a database and publish an event reliably, run a multi-service workflow with compensations, and separate reads from writes, using an order, payment and inventory flow.
In simple words

When one action, like placing an order, needs several teams to do their part (charge the card, reserve the stock), there is no single switch that makes all of them succeed or fail together. So we do it in small steps, write down every step, and have a clear plan for undoing earlier steps if a later one fails.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of booking a holiday: flight, hotel and car. You book the flight, then the hotel, then the car. If the car is unavailable you do not pretend nothing happened; you cancel the hotel and the flight, and each cancellation is a planned step. You also keep a written ledger of every booking so anyone can see the current state, and a handy summary sheet so you do not read the whole ledger each time.

diagram.title: Order, payment and inventory with an outbox (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: Places the order and sends an idempotency key so a retry after a timeout does not create a second order.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.detail: Owns orders. Saves the order and its outbox event in a single database transaction.

nodes.label: Order DB + outbox table
nodes.detail: The orders table and an outbox table that holds events not yet published. Both are written in one transaction.

nodes.label: Outbox relay
nodes.detail: Reads unpublished outbox rows (by polling or change data capture), publishes them and marks them sent. It may publish twice after a crash.

nodes.label: Event bus (Kafka)
nodes.detail: Carries events such as OrderCreated, PaymentFailed and StockReserved to every interested service.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.detail: Charges the customer. Remembers processed event ids so a duplicate event never charges twice.

nodes.label: Inventory service
nodes.detail: Reserves stock, and releases it when a compensation event arrives. Also idempotent by event id.

nodes.label: Order read model
nodes.detail: A denormalised view built from events, shaped for the order-status screen. This is the query side of CQRS.

steps.text: POST /orders with an Idempotency-Key header. If the client retries after a timeout, the service finds the same key and returns the original order.
In ONE database transaction the service inserts the order (status PENDING) and an OrderCreated row in the outbox table. Either both exist or neither does.
The relay reads outbox rows that are not yet published, in order.
It publishes OrderCreated to the event bus, then marks the row sent. If it crashes in between, it republishes, so consumers must be idempotent.
Payment receives OrderCreated and tries to charge the customer. It records the event id so a duplicate has no effect.
Inventory receives the same event and reserves the items, publishing StockReserved.
The charge is declined, so Payment publishes PaymentFailed. This is the failure branch of the saga.
Inventory receives PaymentFailed and runs its compensation: release the reserved stock.
A projector consumes every event and updates the read model, so the order-status screen shows CANCELLED without joining three services.

blocks.text: How it works

**The dual-write problem.** A service must update its database and publish an event. These are two systems with no shared transaction. If you save and then publish, a crash in between leaves a saved order that nobody hears about. If you publish first and the save fails, other services act on an order that does not exist. Retrying does not fix this: the gap is the problem, not the failure rate.

**Transactional outbox.** Write the business row and an event row into an **outbox table** in the same local database transaction, which is atomic. A separate relay reads the outbox and publishes to the broker, either by polling (`WHERE published = false ORDER BY id`) or by change data capture reading the database log. The relay may publish an event more than once after a crash, so delivery is at-least-once and every consumer must be idempotent. The result: the event is published if and only if the order was saved.

**Saga.** A saga is a business workflow split into local transactions, one per service, with a **compensating action** for each step that can be undone (refund the payment, release the stock). There is no isolation between steps, so other users can briefly see intermediate states such as an order that is PENDING. In **choreography** each service reacts to events from others, with no central coordinator: simple for 2 or 3 steps, but the flow becomes hard to see as services grow. In **orchestration** a coordinator tells each service what to do next and tracks state: more code in one place, but the workflow is explicit, testable and easier to monitor.

**Compensation rules.** Compensations must be idempotent and retried until they succeed, because they cannot be allowed to fail permanently. Some steps cannot be undone, such as an email already sent, so put those last or make them a notification rather than a transaction. Order steps so that the ones most likely to fail and cheapest to undo come first. Give each saga a timeout, so an order stuck waiting for payment is cancelled after, say, 15 minutes.

**Event sourcing and CQRS.** With **event sourcing** the stored truth is the ordered list of events (OrderPlaced, ItemAdded, OrderPaid), and current state is computed by replaying them, often from a periodic snapshot. You get a full audit trail and can rebuild any view, at the cost of event schema versioning and a steeper learning curve. **CQRS** (command query responsibility segregation) separates the model that handles writes from the one that serves reads. Commands change state through the write model; read models are built from events and shaped per screen. The read side is eventually consistent, so a user may briefly not see their own change, which you handle by returning the new state in the command response or reading from the write side right after a write. You can use CQRS without event sourcing, and the outbox is a natural way to feed read models.

**Idempotency keys.** Networks retry. A client sends a unique key with each command; the server stores the key with the result in the same transaction as the work, and a repeated key returns the stored result instead of running again. Consumers do the same with the event id: insert the id into a processed table with a unique constraint inside the same transaction that applies the effect. This turns at-least-once delivery into effectively-once behaviour, and it is what makes outbox, retries and sagas safe together.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: When several services must cooperate, we do the work in small steps, write down what happened, and have a way to undo a step if a later one fails.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: The outbox saves the order and its event together so nothing is lost. A saga runs the steps across services and compensates on failure. CQRS keeps a separate, easy-to-read copy of the data for screens.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Outbox gives at-least-once publishing, so consumers need idempotency keys. Sagas have no isolation, so design for visible intermediate states, idempotent compensations and timeouts. Choose choreography for small flows and orchestration when the flow needs visibility.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Treat events as a public contract: version schemas, keep per-aggregate ordering by key, make the relay and projectors replayable, and monitor outbox age and saga stuck-state counts. Prefer CDC for low latency and no polling load, and use event sourcing only where the audit and replay value justify its cost.
Trade-offs

rows: Transactional outbox
Reliable publishing without distributed transactions; works with an ordinary database.
Extra table and relay to run; at-least-once delivery means duplicates; small publishing delay.
Any service that changes data and must announce it.
Saga with choreography
No central coordinator, services stay loosely coupled, simple for short flows.
The overall flow is implicit and hard to trace; risk of cyclic event chains.
Two or three steps with few participants.
Saga with orchestration
Explicit workflow, central state, easier timeouts, retries and monitoring.
The orchestrator is extra code and can become a bottleneck or a god service.
Longer flows with branching and compensations.
Event sourcing and CQRS
Full audit trail, replayable history, read models shaped per screen and scaled independently.
Eventual consistency on reads, event versioning, higher complexity.
Audit-heavy domains or very different read and write loads; avoid for simple CRUD.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Service crashes after saving the order but before publishing (no outbox)
Order exists but payment and inventory never hear about it.
Use the transactional outbox so saving and publishing intent are one atomic write.
Relay publishes an event twice
Payment could charge the customer twice.
Consumers record processed event ids with a unique constraint in the same transaction as the effect.
A compensation fails
Stock stays reserved for an order that was cancelled.
Make compensations idempotent, retry until success, alert on stuck sagas and add a reconciliation job.
Read model lags behind the write side
User places an order but the status screen does not show it yet.
Return the new state in the command response, or read from the write side briefly, and monitor projection lag.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you update a database and publish an event reliably?
blocks.text: Avoid the dual write. Insert the event into an outbox table in the same transaction as the business change, and have a relay (polling or CDC) publish it. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers deduplicate by event id.

blocks.title: Design order placement across order, payment and inventory services.
blocks.text: Order service saves a PENDING order and an outbox event atomically. Payment and inventory react to OrderCreated idempotently. On PaymentFailed, inventory releases stock and the order becomes CANCELLED. Use a saga timeout, idempotency keys on the API, and a read model for order status. Choose orchestration if the flow grows.

blocks.title: What is CQRS and when should you not use it?
blocks.text: CQRS separates the write model from read models that are built from events and shaped for queries, so each side scales and evolves independently. It adds eventual consistency and operational complexity, so avoid it for simple CRUD where one model and one database are enough.
Takeaways

items: Saving to a database and publishing an event are two writes; the outbox makes them one.
Outbox delivery is at-least-once, so every consumer needs idempotency.
A saga replaces a distributed transaction with local steps plus compensations.
Choreography suits short flows; orchestration suits flows you need to see and control.
Event sourcing stores events as truth; CQRS separates write and read models; they are independent choices.
Idempotency keys on APIs and event ids in consumers make retries safe.

quiz.q: What does the transactional outbox guarantee?
options: The event is published exactly once
The event is recorded if and only if the business change is saved
quiz.why: Both rows are written in one local transaction. Publishing is still at-least-once.

quiz.q: Payment fails in an order saga after stock was reserved. What happens next?
options: The database rolls back everything automatically
A compensating action releases the reserved stock
quiz.why: Sagas have no global rollback. Each completed step needs a compensating step.

quiz.q: Which is a downside of saga choreography?
options: The overall flow is spread across services and hard to follow
quiz.why: Without a coordinator, understanding the end-to-end flow means reading every service reaction.

quiz.q: What is an idempotency key used for?
options: Ensuring a retried request has the effect of running only once
quiz.why: The stored key and result let the server return the original outcome for a repeated request.

modules.title: Docker and Kubernetes
modules.summary: Images, pods, deployments, services, autoscaling and rollouts.

lessons.title: Docker and Kubernetes: from a commit to a running pod

blocks.text: Understand containers vs VMs, images and Dockerfiles, and how Kubernetes runs them with pods, deployments, services, ingress, probes, autoscaling, rolling updates and rollbacks.
In simple words

A container is a sealed box that holds an app and everything it needs to run, so it behaves the same on a laptop and on a server. Kubernetes is the manager that decides which machines run how many boxes, replaces boxes that crash, and sends visitors to a box that is ready.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of shipping containers at a port. Each one is packed the same way no matter what is inside, so cranes can move them anywhere. Kubernetes is the port control: it decides which ship and slot each container goes on, brings in a replacement if one is damaged, and opens or closes the gate to a container depending on whether it is ready.

diagram.title: Request from ingress to a pod (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: A browser or app calling https://shop.example.com/api/orders.

nodes.label: Ingress controller
nodes.detail: A reverse proxy running in the cluster behind a cloud load balancer. It terminates TLS and routes by host and path using Ingress rules.

nodes.label: Service (ClusterIP)
nodes.detail: A stable virtual IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of pods. It selects pods by label and only includes pods that pass readiness.

nodes.label: Pod A (order-api)
nodes.detail: One or more containers sharing a network namespace. Pods are disposable: they get new IPs when replaced.

nodes.label: Pod B (order-api)
nodes.detail: A second replica of the same Deployment, often on another node, so one node failing does not take the service down.

nodes.label: ConfigMap and Secret
nodes.detail: Configuration and credentials injected as environment variables or files at start. Secrets are base64-encoded, so enable encryption at rest and restrict access.

nodes.label: Autoscaler (HPA)
nodes.detail: Watches CPU or custom metrics and changes the Deployment replica count between a minimum and maximum.

steps.text: The request reaches the cloud load balancer and then the ingress controller, which terminates TLS.
The Ingress rule matches host shop.example.com and path /api/orders and forwards to the order-api Service.
The Service picks a pod from its ready endpoints. A pod failing its readiness probe is skipped, so no traffic reaches it.
At startup the pod received its settings from a ConfigMap and its credentials from a Secret. The request is handled with those.
The next request is balanced to pod B. During a rolling update, old and new pods serve side by side.
CPU stays above the target, so the autoscaler raises replicas. New pods start, pass readiness and join the Service.
The response returns along the same path to the client.

blocks.text: How it works

**Containers vs VMs.** A virtual machine runs a full guest operating system on a hypervisor, so it is heavy: gigabytes and minutes to start. A container is an ordinary process isolated by Linux namespaces and limited by cgroups, sharing the host kernel, so it is megabytes and starts in seconds. The trade is weaker isolation than a VM. An **image** is a read-only layered filesystem plus start command, stored in a registry and identified by a tag and an immutable digest. A **Dockerfile** builds it: start FROM a small base image, COPY dependency files first and install them (so the layer is cached), then COPY the code, and set CMD. Use multi-stage builds to leave compilers out of the final image, run as a non-root user, and pin versions. **Docker Compose** describes several containers (app, database, cache) in one file for local development.

**Cluster objects.** A Kubernetes cluster has a control plane (API server, scheduler, controllers, etcd as the state store) and worker **nodes** that run a kubelet and a container runtime. A **Pod** is the smallest unit: one or more containers sharing a network and volumes. You rarely create pods directly. A **Deployment** declares the desired state (image, replica count, update strategy) and a controller keeps reality matching it, replacing pods that die. A **Service** gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name to a set of pods chosen by labels. **Service discovery** works through cluster DNS: other pods call http://order-api.shop.svc.cluster.local and never track pod IPs. An **Ingress** (served by an ingress controller) exposes HTTP routes to the outside world with TLS and host or path routing.

**Configuration, probes and resources.** A **ConfigMap** holds non-secret settings and a **Secret** holds credentials, both injected as environment variables or mounted files so the same image runs in every environment. A **liveness probe** answers "is this process stuck?" and makes the kubelet restart the container when it fails. A **readiness probe** answers "can this pod take traffic now?" and removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. A startup probe protects slow-starting apps from being killed early. **Requests** are what the scheduler reserves for a pod, and **limits** are the ceiling: exceeding the memory limit gets the container killed (OOMKilled), and exceeding the CPU limit throttles it. Set requests close to real usage, or nodes become overcommitted or wasted.

**Scaling and deployment.** The **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler** adds or removes pods to keep a metric such as average CPU near a target, within minimum and maximum replicas. The default **rolling update** replaces pods gradually using maxSurge and maxUnavailable, and uses readiness probes to avoid sending traffic to a new pod before it is ready, so a release causes no downtime. If the new version is bad, `kubectl rollout undo` returns to the previous ReplicaSet in seconds. Graceful shutdown matters: on termination the pod gets a SIGTERM and a grace period, so the app should finish in-flight requests and the Service stops sending it new ones.

**From commit to production.** A developer pushes a commit and the CI pipeline runs tests and static checks. It builds the Docker image, tags it with the commit hash, scans it for vulnerabilities, and pushes it to a registry. A deployment step (a pipeline job, or a GitOps tool such as Argo CD that watches a config repository) changes the image tag in the Deployment manifest. The API server stores the new desired state, the Deployment controller creates a new ReplicaSet and the scheduler places new pods on nodes with enough requested CPU and memory. Each node pulls the image, starts the container and runs probes. Once pods are ready they join the Service, old pods drain and stop, and monitoring watches error rate and latency. If the release is unhealthy, the pipeline or an operator rolls back to the previous tag.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Pack the app in a box that runs the same everywhere. A manager keeps the right number of boxes running, replaces broken ones and sends visitors only to boxes that are ready.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: A Dockerfile builds an image, a Deployment runs several pod replicas from it, a Service gives them one address, and an Ingress exposes it to the internet. Probes tell Kubernetes when to restart or when to send traffic.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Kubernetes is a set of control loops that move actual state toward declared state. The scheduler places pods by requests, probes gate traffic and restarts, HPA adjusts replicas, and rolling updates swap ReplicaSets under readiness checks so releases and rollbacks are safe.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Treat the cluster as shared infrastructure: right-size requests and limits, spread replicas across zones with anti-affinity, set PodDisruptionBudgets for voluntary evictions, drive releases through GitOps with immutable image digests, and watch for CPU throttling, OOM kills, slow image pulls and probe misconfiguration, which cause most production incidents.
Trade-offs

rows: Containers instead of VMs
Fast start, small size, dense packing, identical environments.
Shared kernel gives weaker isolation, and the orchestration layer adds complexity.
Most stateless services, and teams that deploy often.
Kubernetes instead of a simple managed container service
Rich scheduling, autoscaling, self-healing, a large ecosystem, portability across clouds.
Steep learning curve and operational cost, even with a managed control plane.
Many services and a platform team, or a need for fine control. A smaller product may do better with a simpler service.
Rolling update
No downtime, no extra full environment, simple.
Old and new versions run together, so APIs and schemas must be compatible.
The default for stateless services with backward-compatible changes.
Strict CPU limits
Predictable sharing and protection from noisy neighbours.
Throttling raises latency even when the node has idle CPU.
Multi-tenant clusters. Many teams set requests and a memory limit but leave CPU limits loose.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Missing or wrong readiness probe
Traffic reaches a pod that is still starting, so users see errors during every deploy.
Add a readiness probe that checks real dependencies lightly, and a startup probe for slow apps.
Memory limit set too low
The container is OOMKilled and restarts in a loop (CrashLoopBackOff).
Set the limit from measured usage plus headroom, watch restarts, and fix memory leaks.
Aggressive liveness probe
A slow but healthy pod is restarted, causing a restart storm under load.
Use a lenient liveness check that does not depend on downstream services, with sensible timeouts.
A bad release reaches all pods
Errors spike for every user.
Use readiness-gated rolling updates with maxUnavailable, canary or progressive delivery, alerts on error rate, and a fast rollback.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Walk through what happens when I push code until it serves production traffic.
blocks.text: CI tests the commit, builds and scans an image, tags it with the commit hash and pushes it to a registry. A deploy step (or GitOps) updates the image tag in the Deployment. Kubernetes creates a new ReplicaSet, schedules pods, nodes pull the image and run probes, ready pods join the Service and old pods drain. Monitoring watches the release and a rollback is one command.

blocks.title: Liveness vs readiness probe?
blocks.text: Liveness decides whether to restart a stuck container. Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic. A pod can be alive but not ready, for example while it warms up or when a dependency is down. Mixing them up causes restart loops or errors during deploys.

blocks.title: How do requests, limits and the autoscaler relate?
blocks.text: Requests are used by the scheduler to place pods and also as the base for CPU-percentage autoscaling. Limits cap usage: memory over the limit kills the container, CPU over the limit throttles it. HPA changes replica count to keep utilization near the target, so wrong requests give wrong scaling decisions.
Takeaways

items: Containers package an app with its dependencies and share the host kernel, so they are light and start fast.
Deployments keep the desired number of pods, Services give them a stable address, Ingress exposes them outside.
Readiness gates traffic, liveness triggers restarts, and mixing them up causes outages.
Requests drive scheduling and autoscaling, and limits cap usage. Memory over the limit kills the container.
Rolling updates and fast rollbacks make releases safe, but old and new versions must be compatible.
The path to production is commit, test, build image, push, update manifest, schedule, probe, serve.

quiz.q: A pod fails its readiness probe. What does Kubernetes do?
options: Removes the pod from Service endpoints so it gets no traffic
quiz.why: Readiness controls traffic. Liveness is the probe that triggers restarts.

quiz.q: Why copy the dependency file and install dependencies before copying the source code in a Dockerfile?
options: Layer caching: dependencies are rebuilt only when they change
quiz.why: Layers are cached top down. Code changes often, so it goes last to keep the slow install layer cached.

quiz.q: What is the main difference between a container and a VM?
options: A container shares the host kernel, a VM runs its own guest OS
quiz.why: Sharing the kernel makes containers small and fast, at the cost of weaker isolation.

quiz.q: How do pods find each other reliably when pod IPs keep changing?
options: Use a Service name resolved by cluster DNS
Restart pods until the IP matches
quiz.why: A Service provides a stable name and virtual IP in front of changing pods.

modules.title: Distributed Systems
modules.summary: CAP, PACELC, consistency models, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads.

lessons.title: CAP, PACELC, consistency, quorum, consensus and distributed transactions

blocks.text: Why copies of data disagree, what you must give up when the network breaks, and how replication, quorums, Raft-style consensus and 2PC fit together.
In simple words

When the same data is stored on several computers, those copies can briefly disagree. You can make every read wait until all copies agree, which is safe but slower, or answer right away from the nearest copy, which is fast but might be a little out of date. Good designs pick the safe option for money and stock counts and the fast option for things like reviews.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Picture a shop with three branches that each keep a paper ledger. If a customer can only buy when a majority of branches write the sale down, no two branches ever sell the last item twice. If branches just sell and mail each other updates later, the shop is faster, but two branches may briefly both think the last item is theirs.

diagram.title: Replicated write with a quorum (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: Sends a write such as "reserve 1 unit of item 42" and later reads the result.

nodes.label: Inventory service
nodes.detail: Stateless. Sends writes to the shard leader and chooses whether a read goes to the leader (strong) or a follower (possibly stale).

nodes.label: Shard leader
nodes.detail: The one replica that orders writes for this shard. It appends to its log and waits for a majority before calling a write committed.

nodes.label: Follower 1
nodes.detail: Keeps a copy of the log. Acknowledges each entry. If the leader goes quiet it can start an election.

nodes.label: Follower 2
nodes.detail: Second follower in a different zone. Leader plus two followers is N=3, so a majority is 2.

nodes.label: Remote replica
nodes.detail: A far-away region copy fed asynchronously. Reads here are fast for nearby users but can lag by seconds.

steps.text: The client asks to reserve one unit of item 42. Stock must never go below zero, so this is a strong-consistency write.
The service sends the write to the shard leader, the single replica that orders all writes for this shard.
The leader appends the entry to its log and sends it to follower 1.
It sends the same entry to follower 2. With N=3 the write is committed once 2 of 3 replicas (a majority) have it.
Follower 1 acknowledges. The leader now has itself plus one follower, so the write is committed even if follower 2 is slow.
The leader tells the service the write is committed. Any later majority read must see it.
In the background the leader ships the entry to the remote region. This copy is eventually consistent and is not part of the quorum.
A product page asks for review counts. The service reads follower 1 directly: fast, and being a few seconds stale does not matter.
If the leader dies, a follower times out, asks the other for votes and becomes the new leader once it has a majority.
The client gets the confirmed result. During a partition the minority side would refuse writes rather than risk a split brain.

blocks.text: How it works

**CAP.** When the network splits a system into groups that cannot talk, it must choose between **consistency** (reject or delay requests so nobody sees stale or conflicting data) and **availability** (keep answering from whatever copy is reachable). Partitions are not optional in a real network, so the real choice is C versus A only while a partition is happening. A bank balance should choose C: refuse the request. A "likes" counter can choose A: answer and reconcile later.

**PACELC.** CAP says nothing about normal days, so PACELC adds a second rule: if there is a **P**artition choose **A** or **C**; **E**lse (no partition) choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency. Waiting for replicas in other regions costs tens to hundreds of milliseconds on every write even when nothing is broken. That is why many systems are described as PA/EL (available and low latency, eventually consistent) or PC/EC (always consistent, pay the latency).

**Strong versus eventual consistency.** Strong (linearizable) means a read returns the latest committed write, as if there were one copy. Eventual means that if writes stop, all replicas converge, but a read may return older data in between. In-between levels are useful: read-your-writes (you always see your own update), monotonic reads (time never goes backwards for one user) and causal consistency. Scenario: **inventory count** must be strong so two buyers cannot take the last unit; **product reviews** can be eventual because a review appearing 3 seconds late harms no one.

**Replication and quorum.** With N replicas, a write waits for W acknowledgements and a read asks R replicas. If **R + W > N** the read set and write set must overlap in at least one replica, so a read sees the newest write. Example N=3: W=2, R=2 gives overlap and tolerates one failure; W=3, R=1 makes reads fast but any single failure blocks writes; W=1, R=1 is fastest but can read stale data. Synchronous replication waits for followers (safer, slower); asynchronous replication does not (faster, may lose the last few writes if the leader dies).

**Consensus and leader election.** Consensus lets a group agree on one value even when some members crash. Raft, at a high level: one **leader** accepts writes and appends them to a replicated log; followers copy the log; an entry is **committed** when a majority has stored it. Time is split into **terms**. If followers hear no heartbeat they become candidates, increment the term and ask for votes; whoever gets a majority becomes leader, and a node votes only once per term, so two leaders cannot both hold a majority. A 3-node group survives 1 failure and a 5-node group survives 2. Scenario: choosing the single owner of a payment shard or a distributed lock.

**Distributed transactions.** Updating two databases atomically is hard. **Two-phase commit (2PC)** has a coordinator ask every participant to prepare (vote yes and hold locks), then commit if all said yes. It is correct but blocking: if the coordinator crashes after prepare, participants hold locks until it returns, and every call adds latency. Large systems usually avoid it and use a **saga**: a chain of local transactions, each with a compensating action (refund the payment if stock reservation fails), plus idempotent steps and an outbox so events are not lost. Scenario: placing an order touches stock, payment and shipping, so it is a saga, not one 2PC.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Several computers hold copies of the same data. Waiting for most of them to agree keeps data correct but slower. Answering from one copy is faster but may be slightly old. Pick by how much a wrong answer hurts.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: CAP forces a choice between consistency and availability during a network partition. PACELC adds that, even without a partition, you trade latency against consistency. Quorums (R + W > N) let you tune that trade per operation.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: A replicated log with a majority commit rule (Raft) gives linearizable writes and survives minority failures. Followers reads are cheap but stale unless they check with the leader. Cross-shard atomicity needs 2PC or, more often, a saga with compensations and idempotency keys.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Define the consistency level per operation, not per system. Put invariants (stock cannot go negative, balance cannot overdraw) behind one leader or a consensus group, keep everything else eventual, and guard against split brain with terms or fencing tokens. Budget the extra round trip a synchronous cross-region commit costs and decide explicitly which writes deserve it.
Trade-offs

rows: Strong consistency (majority writes, leader reads)
No stale reads, simple reasoning, invariants hold.
Higher latency, blocks on the minority side of a partition, lower throughput per key.
Money, stock, uniqueness checks, permissions.
Eventual consistency (async replicas, read nearest)
Low latency, high availability, scales reads across regions.
Stale reads, conflicting writes need a merge rule, harder to test.
Reviews, feeds, counters, recommendations, analytics.
Two-phase commit
Atomic across several databases.
Blocking, coordinator is a single point of trouble, slow, poor fit for services owned by different teams.
A few tightly coupled databases in one trust domain where correctness beats latency.
Saga with compensations
No cross-service locks, each step is a local transaction, scales well.
Intermediate states are visible, compensations are hard to write, needs idempotency.
Long business flows such as order, payment and shipping.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Network partition splits a 5-node group into 3 and 2
The side with 3 keeps a leader and accepts writes. The side with 2 cannot reach a majority and stops accepting writes.
Use an odd number of nodes, expect minority-side clients to get errors, and retry against the majority side.
Old leader is paused, a new leader is elected, then the old one wakes up
Two nodes believe they are leader and may write conflicting data (split brain).
Terms or epochs on every message and fencing tokens on storage so stale leaders are rejected.
Asynchronous replica lags behind
A user updates their address then sees the old one, or a failover loses the last few writes.
Read-your-writes by routing the writer to the leader for a short time, and monitor replication lag.
2PC coordinator crashes after participants prepared
Participants hold locks and block other work until the coordinator recovers.
Replicate and persist the coordinator log, set timeouts with recovery rules, or replace 2PC with a saga.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Explain CAP and why it is often misunderstood.
blocks.text: During a network partition you can keep consistency or availability, not both. It is not a permanent pick of two out of three because partitions are not optional. Add PACELC: with no partition you still trade latency against consistency. Choose per operation: C for stock and money, A for reviews and feeds.

blocks.title: How does a quorum give consistency, and what are the knobs?
blocks.text: With N replicas, a write waits for W acks and a read contacts R. If R + W > N the sets overlap, so a read sees the latest write. N=3 with W=2, R=2 survives one failure. Raising W slows writes and lowers write availability; raising R slows reads. W=1, R=1 is fast but may be stale.

blocks.title: How would you keep order, payment and stock consistent across three services?
blocks.text: Use a saga: reserve stock, charge payment, confirm shipping, each as a local transaction with a compensating action (release stock, refund). Make each step idempotent with a key, publish events via a transactional outbox, and show the user a pending state. Avoid 2PC because it blocks and couples services.
Takeaways

items: Partitions will happen, so decide per operation whether to be consistent or available.
Even without a partition, consistency costs latency (PACELC).
Quorum rule: R + W > N means reads overlap the latest write.
Consensus (Raft) elects one leader and commits on a majority; use an odd number of nodes.
Prefer sagas with idempotency over 2PC for business flows across services.
Keep invariants strong and everything else eventual.

quiz.q: N=5 replicas. Which choice guarantees a read sees the latest committed write?
options: W=1, R=5 but only when no failures
quiz.why: R + W must be greater than N. 3 + 3 = 6 > 5, so read and write sets always overlap. 2 + 2 = 4 does not.

quiz.q: Which data fits eventual consistency best?
options: Remaining stock of the last unit
quiz.why: A review count that is a few seconds old harms nobody. Stock and balances have invariants that stale data can break.

quiz.q: PACELC adds what to CAP?
options: A rule about trading latency against consistency when there is no partition
A rule that partitions can be avoided
A rule that consensus is not needed
quiz.why: Even on a healthy network, waiting for distant replicas costs latency, so you still choose between latency and consistency.

quiz.q: Why do large systems often avoid 2PC across services?
options: It blocks holding locks if the coordinator fails and adds latency
quiz.why: Participants wait in the prepared state. Sagas with compensating actions avoid cross-service locks.

lessons.title: Resilience patterns: timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, bulkheads and multi-region

blocks.text: How to stop one slow or broken dependency from taking the whole system down, and how to survive losing an entire region.
In simple words

In a big system, one small part will always be slow or broken at some point. Resilience means building so that when it happens, only that part suffers and everything else keeps working. This is done with simple habits: give up waiting after a short time, try again carefully, stop calling something that keeps failing, and have a plan B.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: A ship has sealed compartments. If one compartment floods, the doors shut and the ship stays afloat. A building has fuses so one short circuit does not burn the whole house, and a theatre stops selling tickets when it is full instead of letting the crowd crush the doors.

diagram.title: A call chain where the payment dependency fails (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client
nodes.detail: Sends checkout requests. Retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and gives up after a total deadline.

nodes.label: Gateway
nodes.detail: Applies rate limits per client and sheds low-priority traffic when the system is overloaded, returning a fast 429 or 503.

nodes.label: Checkout service
nodes.detail: Calls dependencies through a bulkhead (its own bounded thread or connection pool per dependency) with a timeout and a retry budget.

nodes.label: Circuit breaker
nodes.detail: Counts failures to the payment service. Closed means calls flow; open means calls fail instantly; half-open lets a few probes through to test recovery.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.detail: The failing dependency in this scenario: slow, then erroring. Without protection its slowness spreads to every caller.

nodes.label: Fallback
nodes.detail: Graceful degradation: a cached or default answer, such as "pay on delivery" or a saved cart, so the page still works.

nodes.label: Retry queue
nodes.detail: Holds orders waiting for payment. A bounded queue gives backpressure: when it is full the producer is told to slow down.

nodes.label: Region B payment
nodes.detail: A standby copy in another region used for failover. Active-passive keeps it idle until needed; active-active serves traffic all the time.

steps.text: A burst of checkout requests arrives. The gateway rate limits each client and sheds optional traffic first so checkout keeps its capacity.
Admitted requests reach the checkout service, which owns a small separate worker pool (bulkhead) just for payment calls.
The service calls payment with a 300 ms timeout, shorter than the client deadline, so a hung call cannot hold a thread for long.
The payment service starts timing out. Each failed call is allowed at most one retry, drawn from a retry budget of about 10 percent of traffic.
Failures pass the threshold, so the breaker opens. Calls now fail in microseconds instead of waiting 300 ms, and payment gets room to recover.
With the breaker open the service degrades gracefully: shows the cart, offers pay on delivery, and skips optional features.
Orders that must complete are put on a bounded queue. When the queue is full the service returns 503 instead of growing memory (backpressure).
After a few minutes of failures the team (or health automation) fails payment traffic over to the standby region.
The client gets a quick answer, success, degraded or a clear retry-later with a Retry-After header, never a long hang.

blocks.text: How it works

**Timeouts and deadlines.** Every network call needs a timeout, otherwise a hung dependency holds a thread forever. Set the timeout near the dependency p99 plus margin, and make it shorter than the caller timeout so layers fail from the inside out. Pass a **deadline** (remaining time) down the chain so a service does not start work its caller has already abandoned. Calls with no timeout are the most common root cause of cascading outages.

**Retries, backoff, jitter and budgets.** Retry only idempotent operations, or use idempotency keys. Wait **exponentially longer** between attempts (100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms) and add **jitter** (random spread) so thousands of clients do not retry in lockstep. Cap attempts and use a **retry budget**: retries may add at most about 10 percent extra load. Without a budget, 3 retries at every layer of a 3-layer chain multiplies a failing call by 27 and turns a slowdown into a retry storm.

**Circuit breaker and bulkhead.** A breaker has three states: closed (normal), open (fail fast after the error rate passes a threshold, for example 50 percent over 20 calls), half-open (let a few probes through; success closes it). It protects both the caller (no wasted threads) and the dependency (no extra load while sick). A **bulkhead** gives each dependency its own bounded pool, so a slow payment service can exhaust only its own 20 workers, not the 200 shared by inventory and search.

**Backpressure, rate limiting, load shedding.** Backpressure pushes slowness upstream: bounded queues, blocking or rejecting producers, and credit-based flow control, instead of unbounded buffers that hide a problem until memory runs out. **Rate limiting** (token bucket per client) protects against one caller using everything. **Load shedding** drops work deliberately when overloaded, lowest priority first, and returns a cheap 503. Serving 80 percent of requests well beats serving 100 percent badly.

**Graceful degradation and fault tolerance.** Decide in advance what the product does without each dependency: show cached recommendations, hide reviews, disable one-click checkout, queue the email. Fault tolerance is the combination of redundancy (no single point of failure), isolation (bulkheads, cells) and fast failure detection (health checks). Test it with fault injection, because an untested fallback usually fails when needed.

**Disaster recovery and multi-region.** Two numbers drive DR: **RPO** (how much data you can lose, for example 5 minutes) and **RTO** (how long you can be down, for example 30 minutes). **Active-passive** keeps a standby region with replicated data that takes over on failure: cheaper and simpler, but failover is slow and the standby is rarely exercised. **Active-active** serves traffic from several regions at once: near-zero RTO and lower latency, but needs conflict handling, regional routing and costs more. Backups are not DR until restore has been tested.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Do not wait forever for a slow friend. Give up after a short time, try again a little later, stop calling someone who keeps failing, and have a backup plan so most of the app keeps working.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Combine timeouts, capped retries with backoff and jitter, circuit breakers and bulkheads so a failing dependency costs a few failed requests instead of a full outage. Shed load and degrade features when overloaded.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Retry amplification is multiplicative across layers, so use a budget and retry at one layer only. Breakers need sensible thresholds and half-open probing. Bulkheads should be sized from Little law: concurrent calls = request rate x latency.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Treat overload as the main failure mode: adaptive concurrency limits, priority-aware shedding, deadline propagation and cell-based isolation limit the blast radius. Define RPO and RTO per service, rehearse regional failover regularly, and prefer active-active only where data can be partitioned by region or merged safely.
Trade-offs

rows: Aggressive retries
Hides short blips from users.
Multiplies load on a struggling dependency and can cause a retry storm.
Idempotent calls with a small budget, backoff and jitter.
Circuit breaker
Fails fast, protects threads and gives the dependency time to recover.
Can open on a false alarm and needs tuned thresholds and a fallback.
Any synchronous call to a remote dependency that can fail or slow down.
Active-passive multi-region
Simpler data model and lower cost.
Slower failover, standby may be stale and untested.
Moderate RTO (minutes to an hour) and a single write region.
Active-active multi-region
Near-zero downtime, users served from the nearest region.
Write conflicts, complex routing, roughly double the cost.
Strict availability goals or a global user base with partitionable data.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Payment service becomes slow, not down
Callers wait on it, threads fill up and unrelated endpoints on the same service start failing.
Timeouts, a bulkhead per dependency and a circuit breaker that opens on slow calls as well as errors.
Every layer retries 3 times
A failing leaf call is attempted 27 times per user request and the dependency never recovers.
Retry at one layer, use retry budgets, backoff with jitter and honour Retry-After.
Traffic spike doubles load for 10 minutes
Queues grow, latency explodes, then the service crashes and restarts into the same spike.
Rate limit, shed low-priority traffic, bound queues and warm up instances gradually.
Entire region is lost
Users in that region get errors until traffic moves and the standby promotes.
Replicated data meeting the RPO, rehearsed failover runbooks, health-based DNS or global routing, regular game days.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: A downstream service is slow and your service is falling over. What do you do?
blocks.text: Confirm with metrics that threads or connections are exhausted. Add timeouts shorter than the caller deadline, a bulkhead and circuit breaker around that dependency, cap retries with a budget, return a fallback or cached answer, shed low-priority load and apply backpressure on queues. Then fix the root cause in the dependency.

blocks.title: What is the difference between rate limiting, load shedding and backpressure?
blocks.text: Rate limiting caps what each caller may send, protecting fairness. Load shedding drops work when the system is overloaded, lowest priority first. Backpressure signals producers to slow down through bounded queues or flow control. All three keep latency bounded.

blocks.title: How do you choose between active-passive and active-active?
blocks.text: Start from RPO and RTO and the cost the business accepts. If minutes of failover are fine and one region writes, use active-passive. If you need near-zero downtime or low latency worldwide and can partition or merge data, use active-active. Whatever you choose, rehearse failover regularly.
Takeaways

items: Every remote call needs a timeout, and inner timeouts must be shorter than outer ones.
Retries need idempotency, exponential backoff, jitter and a budget.
Breakers fail fast; bulkheads confine the damage to one pool.
Backpressure, rate limiting and load shedding keep latency bounded under overload.
Decide the degraded experience in advance and test it with fault injection.
DR is defined by RPO and RTO; untested backups and failovers do not count.

quiz.q: A request passes through 3 layers and each retries a failing call 3 times. How many calls can the failing dependency receive per user request?
quiz.why: Retries multiply across layers: 3 x 3 x 3 = 27. Use a retry budget and retry at one layer.

quiz.q: What does an open circuit breaker do?
options: Fails calls immediately without calling the dependency
Sends all traffic to the database
quiz.why: Open means fail fast. After a cooldown it goes half-open and probes the dependency.

quiz.q: Why add jitter to backoff?
options: So many clients do not retry at the same instant
quiz.why: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together and create waves of load.

quiz.q: Active-active multi-region mainly adds which difficulty compared with active-passive?
options: Handling write conflicts and regional routing
Removing the need for health checks
quiz.why: Several regions accept writes at once, so data must be partitioned or merged safely.

modules.title: Scalability and Performance
modules.summary: Finding the bottleneck, queueing, capacity planning, backpressure.

lessons.title: Capacity planning, queueing, tail latency and scaling reads and writes

blocks.text: Turn users into requests per second and servers, see why latency explodes near full utilisation, and learn what tail latency, hot keys, autoscaling and caching do to load.
In simple words

Scaling starts with arithmetic: how many people use the app, how many requests that makes each second, and how many servers can handle that with room to spare. A busy server is like a busy checkout till: a little spare capacity keeps queues short, but when it is almost full, waiting time suddenly gets very long.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a motorway. At half capacity cars flow freely. At 90 percent full, one slow lorry makes a jam that lasts for miles. Adding lanes (servers) helps, but if everyone wants the same exit (a hot key), that exit jams no matter how many lanes the rest of the road has.

diagram.title: Scaling a read-heavy service (generic reference design; all numbers are assumptions)

nodes.label: Clients
nodes.detail: Assumption: 10M daily active users, 30 requests each per day, with peak traffic about 3x the average.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.detail: Spreads requests across app servers and removes unhealthy ones. Needs its own headroom for peaks.

nodes.label: App servers (autoscaled)
nodes.detail: Stateless. Each handles about 500 rps at full load but is run near 60 percent so queues stay short. Autoscaling adds servers on CPU or request rate.

nodes.label: Cache
nodes.detail: In-memory. With a 90 percent hit ratio it removes 90 percent of reads from the database. A hot key can still overload the single cache node that owns it.

nodes.label: Write queue
nodes.detail: Absorbs write bursts so the database sees a smooth rate. Trades immediate durability for a short delay.

nodes.label: Write workers
nodes.detail: Consume the queue at a steady rate and batch writes to the primary database.

nodes.label: Read replica
nodes.detail: Copy of the primary used for cache misses. Scales reads, but lags slightly behind the primary.

nodes.label: Primary database
nodes.detail: Takes all writes. Hardest tier to scale because writes cannot simply be copied; options are bigger hardware, sharding and batching.

steps.text: Average load: 10M users x 30 requests / 86,400 s = about 3,500 rps. Peak at 3x is about 10,500 rps.
At a safe 60 percent target of 500 rps per server, one server carries 300 rps, so 10,500 / 300 = 35 servers; round up to about 40 for failures and deploys.
Assume 90 percent of requests are reads: 9,450 rps. With a 90 percent cache hit ratio the cache answers 8,505 of them.
Misses reach the replica: 9,450 x 10 percent = 945 rps. Without the cache the replica would take all 9,450 rps, 10x more.
Writes are 10 percent: 1,050 rps at peak. They are put on a queue so a burst does not hit the database directly.
Workers drain the queue at a steady rate, so the database sees a smooth load instead of spikes.
Workers batch rows (for example 50 per insert), cutting the primary load from 1,050 statements to about 21 per second.
The primary replicates changes to the replica asynchronously, so reads there can be seconds behind.
A viral item becomes a hot key: 5,000 rps all hitting one cache node. Fix by replicating that key across nodes or caching it in the app server memory.

blocks.text: How it works

**Capacity planning from users to servers.** Work top down and show every step. Average rps = daily users x requests per user per day / 86,400. Example: 10M x 30 / 86,400 = 3,472, about 3,500 rps. Peak rps = average x peak factor (assume 3) = 10,500. Servers = peak rps / (per-server rps x target utilisation) = 10,500 / (500 x 0.6) = 35, then add N+1 or zone headroom, about 40. All inputs are assumptions to be replaced by measurements from load tests.

**Utilisation and queueing.** When requests arrive at random, waiting time grows sharply as utilisation approaches 100 percent. For a simple single-queue model, response time = service time / (1 - utilisation). With a 20 ms service time: 50 percent gives 40 ms, 80 percent gives 100 ms, 90 percent gives 200 ms, 95 percent gives 400 ms, 99 percent gives 2,000 ms. Latency rises slowly, then explodes, which is why servers are run at 50 to 70 percent, not 95.

**Tail latency.** Averages hide pain. **p50** is the typical request, **p95** and **p99** are the slowest 5 percent and 1 percent. If a page needs 10 backend calls and each has a 1 percent chance of being slow, the page is slow with probability 1 - 0.99^10 = about 9.6 percent. So p99 of each dependency matters far more than its average. Tools: timeouts, hedged requests (send a second copy after the p95 time), smaller fan-out, and removing queues.

**Read versus write scaling.** Reads scale by copying: caches, read replicas and CDNs. Writes are harder because every copy must agree. Options are a bigger primary (vertical), **sharding** by key so each shard takes part of the writes, batching, and queues that smooth bursts. Because read-heavy workloads are common (here 90 percent reads), start with caching and replicas, and shard only when write rate or data size demands it.

**Hot keys.** Sharding spreads load only if keys are spread evenly. One celebrity profile or flash-sale item can send thousands of requests per second to a single shard or cache node, which then becomes the bottleneck while other nodes sit idle. Remedies: replicate the hot key to several nodes, add a short-lived local cache in each app server, split the key (counter:item42:0..9) and sum on read, or rate limit that key.

**Autoscaling and the cache effect.** Autoscaling adds servers when a metric (CPU, rps per server, queue depth) crosses a target and removes them when it drops. It reacts in minutes, so keep headroom for sudden spikes and warm the cache before sending traffic. Caching changes database sizing: at a 90 percent hit ratio the database handles 10 percent of reads; at 99 percent it handles 1 percent. But if the cache is lost, the database suddenly gets 10x to 100x more reads, so size it for a partial cache failure or protect it with load shedding.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Count how many people use the app and how many requests that is each second, then add enough servers that none is ever completely full. Copies of data (a cache) answer most questions so the main database stays calm.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Plan capacity as peak rps divided by per-server rps at 60 percent utilisation. Use caches and read replicas to scale reads, queues and sharding to scale writes, and watch p99 latency, not the average.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Response time follows service time / (1 - utilisation), so headroom is a latency feature, not waste. Fan-out amplifies tail latency: with n calls, P(slow) = 1 - (1 - p)^n. Hot keys break even sharding, so detect them and replicate or split them.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Model with measured service-time distributions and Little law (concurrency = rate x latency) to size pools and queues. Autoscale on leading signals such as queue depth, keep cold-start and cache-warm time in the plan, protect the database with admission control against cache loss, and validate every assumption with load tests that include a hot key and a failure.
Trade-offs

rows: Run servers at low utilisation (about 50 to 60 percent)
Short queues, stable p99, room for spikes and failures.
Pays for idle capacity.
User-facing latency-sensitive services.
Aggressive caching
Cuts database load 10x or more and lowers latency.
Stale data, invalidation bugs, and a dangerous cliff if the cache is lost.
Read-heavy data that tolerates short staleness.
Read replicas
Easy way to scale reads and isolate reporting queries.
Replication lag, so reads may be stale; no help for write load.
Read-heavy workloads where seconds of lag is acceptable.
Sharding for writes
Scales write throughput and data size roughly linearly.
Cross-shard queries and transactions are hard, hot keys, resharding is costly.
A single primary can no longer handle write rate or data volume.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Servers run at 95 percent utilisation at peak
Queues build, p99 latency jumps from 50 ms to seconds, timeouts trigger retries which add more load.
Plan for 60 percent at peak, autoscale on rps or queue depth, shed load beyond capacity.
One viral item becomes a hot key
The single shard or cache node owning it is saturated while other nodes are idle.
Replicate hot keys, add per-server local caches, split counters, and monitor per-key traffic.
Cache cluster restarts
Reads jump from 945 to 9,450 rps on the database, about 10x, and it overloads.
Warm the cache, use request coalescing so one miss triggers one load, and rate limit misses.
Autoscaler reacts too slowly to a flash sale
New servers need minutes to start and warm up, while latency degrades immediately.
Scale on leading metrics, pre-scale before known events, and keep spare headroom.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Estimate the servers needed for 10M daily users.
blocks.text: State assumptions: 30 requests per user per day, so 10M x 30 / 86,400 = about 3,500 rps average. Peak factor 3 gives 10,500 rps. If one server handles 500 rps and I run at 60 percent, each carries 300 rps, so 35 servers, about 40 with failure headroom. Then say I would verify with a load test.

blocks.title: Why does latency explode when a system is nearly full?
blocks.text: Requests arrive randomly, so bursts queue up. In a simple queueing model, response time is service time / (1 - utilisation), so it is 2x at 50 percent, 10x at 90 percent and 100x at 99 percent. Spare capacity absorbs bursts. Retries at high load make it worse.

blocks.title: How do you handle a hot key?
blocks.text: First detect it with per-key metrics. Then replicate it across several cache nodes, add short-lived local caches in app servers, split counters into sub-keys and sum on read, and apply rate limiting. Consistent hashing alone does not help because one key still maps to one node.
Takeaways

items: Capacity planning is a chain of simple divisions; write every assumption and step down.
Run servers at 50 to 70 percent; latency grows as 1 / (1 - utilisation).
Watch p95 and p99, and remember that fan-out multiplies tail risk.
Scale reads by copying (cache, replicas) and writes by batching, queues and sharding.
Hot keys defeat even sharding; replicate or split them.
A high cache hit ratio is a dependency: size the database for cache failure too.

quiz.q: Using 10M DAU x 30 requests per day, what is the average request rate?
With a 20 ms service time, response time at 90 percent utilisation (service time / (1 - utilisation)) is about:
quiz.why: 20 / (1 - 0.9) = 200 ms. At 50 percent it was only 40 ms, which shows how fast latency grows.

quiz.q: A page makes 10 parallel calls, each slower than its threshold 1 percent of the time. How often is the page slow?
quiz.why: 1 - 0.99^10 = about 9.6 percent. Fan-out amplifies tail latency.

quiz.q: Which change cuts database read load the most for a read-heavy service?
options: Raising the cache hit ratio from 90 to 99 percent
quiz.why: At 90 percent the database serves 10 percent of reads, at 99 percent only 1 percent, a 10x reduction.

modules.title: Security and Authentication
modules.summary: Sessions, tokens, OAuth, mTLS, secrets, threat modelling a request path.

lessons.title: Authentication, authorization, tokens, TLS and defence in depth

blocks.text: Who are you, what may you do, and how a system proves and enforces that: sessions, JWT, OAuth2/OIDC, CSRF, TLS and mTLS, secrets, abuse protection and audit.
In simple words

Security answers two questions. First, who is this person (authentication)? Second, what are they allowed to do (authorization)? A secure system checks both on every request, keeps secrets out of code, encrypts traffic and stored data, and writes down who did what so problems can be traced.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: At an office building you show your ID at the front desk (authentication) and receive a badge. The badge opens only the doors you need (authorization, least privilege). Cameras and a visitor log record who went where (audit log), and the master keys stay in a locked safe (secrets management).

diagram.title: Login and a protected API call (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Client app
nodes.detail: Signs the user in, stores tokens safely, and sends the access token with each API call. A browser client also needs CSRF protection if it uses cookies.

nodes.label: Identity provider
nodes.detail: Authenticates the user (password plus a second factor) and issues an ID token and a short-lived access token using OIDC and OAuth2.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Terminates TLS, validates the token signature and expiry, applies rate limits and bot protection, then forwards to services.

nodes.label: Orders service
nodes.detail: Trusts only calls over mutual TLS. Checks the caller scopes and that the order belongs to the user (authorization), not just that a token exists.

nodes.label: Secrets manager
nodes.detail: Holds database passwords and API keys, hands them out at runtime with short leases, and supports rotation. Nothing secret lives in code or images.

nodes.label: Encrypted database
nodes.detail: Data is encrypted at rest with keys held in a key management service. Access is granted to this service only, with minimum privileges.

nodes.label: Audit log
nodes.detail: Append-only record of who did what and when: logins, permission changes, data access. Stored separately so an attacker cannot erase it.

steps.text: The app starts an authorization code flow with PKCE: it redirects the user to the identity provider, where they sign in with password plus a second factor.
The provider returns a one-time code; the app exchanges it for an ID token (who you are), a short-lived access token (about 15 minutes) and a longer-lived refresh token.
The app calls GET /orders over TLS with the access token in the Authorization header. If it used cookies instead, it would also send a CSRF token.
The gateway fetches the provider public signing keys (cached) so it can verify the JWT signature locally without calling the provider on every request.
After checking signature, expiry, audience and the rate limit, the gateway forwards the request to the orders service over mutual TLS, so both sides prove who they are.
The service fetches its database credential from the secrets manager at start-up, with a short lease and automatic rotation.
It runs the query filtered by the user id from the token, enforcing authorization, and reads data that is encrypted at rest.
It writes an audit event (user, action, resource, time, result) to an append-only log, without blocking the response.
When the access token expires, the app sends the refresh token to the provider for a new one. If the refresh token is stolen or reused, the provider revokes the whole chain.

blocks.text: How it works

**Authentication versus authorization.** Authentication (authn) proves identity: password, one-time code, passkey, certificate. Authorization (authz) decides what that identity may do: role-based (admin, support), attribute-based (owner of this order, same tenant) or scope-based (read:orders). A common bug is checking authn but forgetting authz, so user A can fetch user B order by changing an id (broken object-level authorization). Check ownership on every request, server side.

**Sessions versus JWT.** A **server session** stores state on the server; the browser holds only an opaque id in a cookie. It is easy to revoke instantly but needs a shared session store. A **JWT** is a signed token containing claims (user id, scopes, expiry) that any service can verify with a public key, so no lookup is needed. The cost is revocation: a valid JWT works until it expires, so keep access tokens short-lived (5 to 15 minutes), never put secrets in them (they are signed, not encrypted), and keep a deny list only for emergencies.

**OAuth2, OIDC and token refresh.** OAuth2 lets an app act with limited permission without seeing the password; OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds identity on top with an ID token. For apps and browsers use the **authorization code flow with PKCE**: the app proves it started the flow with a one-time secret, so an intercepted code is useless. The client credentials flow is for service-to-service calls. Short access tokens plus a **refresh token** give both safety and good usability; rotate the refresh token on each use and revoke the family if an old one is replayed.

**CSRF.** If the browser sends a cookie automatically, a malicious site can trigger a request using it. Defences: SameSite cookies, and the **double-submit cookie** pattern. The server sets a random CSRF value in a cookie and requires the same value in a request header or form field; a malicious site cannot read the cookie, so it cannot copy the value into the header. Use unguessable values, ideally signed to the session, and require the header on every state-changing request. APIs that use an Authorization header instead of cookies are not exposed to this attack.

**TLS, mTLS and secrets.** **TLS** encrypts traffic and proves the server identity with a certificate, which defeats eavesdropping and tampering. **Mutual TLS (mTLS)** makes the client present a certificate too, so services can verify each other inside the network; service meshes automate issuing and rotating these. **Secrets management**: keep passwords, API keys and signing keys in a dedicated secrets manager, load them at runtime, rotate them regularly, and never commit them to code, logs or container images.

**Abuse protection, least privilege, encryption and audit.** Apply rate limits per user, IP and endpoint (strict on login and password reset), lockouts or backoff after repeated failures, bot detection and a web application firewall. **Least privilege** means every user, service and database role gets only the permissions needed, which limits damage from a leak. **Encryption at rest** protects stolen disks and backups using keys held in a separate key management service. **Audit logs** are append-only records of sensitive actions, kept apart from the system they watch, and are what lets you answer who did what, when and from where.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: First prove who you are, then the system checks what you are allowed to do. Traffic is locked in transit, stored data is locked at rest, and a log records what happened.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Users sign in with an identity provider and receive short-lived tokens. Services verify the token on every call and also check that the user owns the thing they ask for. Secrets live in a vault, traffic uses TLS, and rate limits stop abuse.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Use OIDC with the authorization code flow and PKCE, verify JWT signature, issuer, audience and expiry at the edge, rotate refresh tokens with reuse detection, use mTLS between services and enforce object-level authorization inside each service.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Assume breach: limit blast radius with least-privilege identities per workload, short-lived credentials issued by a secrets manager, tenant-aware authorization, envelope encryption with separate key custody, centralised tamper-evident audit logs and alerts on anomalous token or data access patterns.
Trade-offs

rows: Server-side sessions
Instant revocation, small cookie, easy to reason about.
Needs a shared session store and a lookup on every request.
Browser apps on one domain where central control matters.
JWT access tokens
Stateless verification, works across services and domains.
Cannot be revoked before expiry, easy to leak claims or oversize.
Many services or mobile clients; keep tokens short-lived.
mTLS between services
Strong mutual identity and encryption inside the network.
Certificate issuing, rotation and debugging add operational work.
Zero-trust internal networks and sensitive service-to-service calls.
Strict rate limits and lockouts
Stops brute force, credential stuffing and scraping.
Can block legitimate users or let attackers lock out real accounts.
Login, OTP, password reset and expensive endpoints, with per-IP and per-account rules.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Access token is stolen from a device
The attacker can call the API as the user until the token expires.
Short expiry, secure storage, refresh rotation with reuse detection, revoke on suspicious activity.
API checks the token but not ownership
Changing an order id in the URL returns another customer data.
Authorize every object access against the user or tenant, and add tests for cross-user access.
Secret committed to a repository or log
Anyone with repository access can use the key, even long after deletion.
Secret scanning, rotate immediately, load secrets from a vault at runtime and redact logs.
Credential stuffing against the login endpoint
Attackers try millions of leaked passwords, causing account takeovers and load.
Rate limits, bot detection, multi-factor authentication, breached-password checks and alerts.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Sessions or JWT for a new system?
blocks.text: It depends on revocation and architecture. For a browser app on one domain, server sessions with a secure cookie give simple instant revocation. For mobile apps and many services, short-lived JWT access tokens verified locally plus rotating refresh tokens scale better. Either way use HTTPS, secure storage and server-side authorization checks.

blocks.title: Walk through OAuth2 authorization code flow with PKCE.
