blocks.text: The app creates a random verifier and sends its hash (challenge) while redirecting the user to the identity provider. The user signs in, the provider returns a one-time code, and the app exchanges the code plus the verifier for tokens. An attacker who intercepts the code cannot redeem it without the verifier. Access tokens are short-lived and refreshed with a refresh token.

blocks.title: How do you protect a login endpoint from abuse?
blocks.text: Per-IP and per-account rate limits with backoff, multi-factor authentication, bot detection or a CAPTCHA after failures, breached-password checks, generic error messages that do not reveal which part was wrong, alerts on spikes in failures, and audit logging of attempts.
Takeaways

items: Authentication proves who you are; authorization decides what you may do, on every request.
Short-lived access tokens plus rotated refresh tokens balance safety and usability.
Use authorization code flow with PKCE for apps; never put secrets in a JWT.
CSRF is a cookie problem: SameSite and double-submit tokens defend against it.
TLS protects traffic, mTLS authenticates services, a secrets manager protects keys.
Least privilege, rate limits, encryption at rest and audit logs limit and reveal damage.

quiz.q: A user changes /orders/101 to /orders/102 and sees another customer order. Which control is missing?
quiz.why: The user was authenticated, but the service did not check that order 102 belongs to them.

quiz.q: How does the double-submit cookie pattern stop CSRF?
options: A malicious site cannot read the cookie value, so it cannot also put it in the request header
quiz.why: The server requires the same random value in the cookie and in a header or form field.

quiz.q: What is the main drawback of a long-lived JWT access token?
options: It stays valid until it expires even if the user logs out
It cannot carry a user id
quiz.why: JWTs are verified statelessly, so revocation is hard. Use short expiry plus refresh tokens.

quiz.q: What does mTLS add compared with ordinary TLS?
options: The client also proves its identity with a certificate
quiz.why: In mutual TLS both sides authenticate, so a service can verify exactly which service is calling it.

lessons.title: Mobile client security architecture

blocks.text: How to secure a mobile client and the APIs behind it: token storage in Keychain and Keystore, short-lived access tokens with refresh rotation, biometric gating, certificate pinning and its risks, device attestation, jailbreak and root signals, deep-link and WebView hardening, secrets in binaries and API abuse protection.
In simple words

A phone app runs on a device the company does not own. Anyone can take the app apart, read what is inside it and watch what it sends. So the app can never be trusted to keep a company secret or to enforce a rule by itself. The safe design keeps real decisions on the server, gives the app a short-lived pass that proves who the user is, stores that pass in the locked vault the phone provides, and checks for signs that the request comes from a tampered app or a script.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a hotel guest. The guest gets a key card that opens only their room and stops working after checkout; it is kept in the room safe, not on the table. The front desk, not the guest, decides what the card can open. For the spa or the minibar the guest must show their face at the desk again. Staff notice if a card has been copied because two people try to use the same card. The hotel never gives guests the master key, because anything handed to a guest can be copied.

diagram.title: Token refresh and a protected high-risk request (generic wallet app)

nodes.label: Keychain / Keystore
nodes.detail: OS secure storage. Encrypts items with keys protected by hardware (Secure Enclave or a trusted execution environment) and tied to device unlock state.

nodes.label: Mobile app
nodes.detail: Untrusted from the server point of view. Holds tokens, never long-term secrets. Its binary can be read and modified by an attacker.

nodes.label: Biometric prompt
nodes.detail: System UI for Face ID, Touch ID or fingerprint. Most useful when it unlocks a hardware-held key rather than returning a simple yes or no.

nodes.label: Platform attestation
nodes.detail: App Attest on iOS and Play Integrity on Android. Produce signed evidence that a request comes from a genuine app on a genuine device.

nodes.label: Edge / WAF
nodes.detail: TLS termination, coarse rate limiting, bot rules and DDoS absorption before traffic reaches the origin.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Validates access tokens, enforces per-user and per-device limits, routes high-risk calls through the risk engine.

nodes.label: Auth service
nodes.detail: Issues short-lived access tokens and rotates refresh tokens. Detects refresh token reuse.

nodes.label: Token store
nodes.detail: Refresh token families per device session, stored hashed, with status and last-used time. Enables revocation.

nodes.label: Risk engine
nodes.detail: Verifies attestation evidence and combines it with device, velocity and behaviour signals into allow, step-up or deny.

nodes.label: Payments API
nodes.detail: Performs authorisation checks for every request: does this user own this account and may they do this action.

steps.text: On launch the app reads its tokens from secure storage. The access token has expired; the refresh token is present.
It calls POST /token/refresh over TLS, sending the refresh token and device session id.
The edge applies rate limits per IP and forwards the request.
The gateway routes token requests to the auth service.
The refresh token is valid and unused. The service marks it used, issues a new refresh token in the same family and a new access token valid for minutes.
The app replaces both tokens in secure storage. The old refresh token is now worthless.
The user starts a money transfer. The app asks for biometrics, which unlocks a private key held in hardware for this device.
The app obtains an attestation assertion bound to a server-issued challenge and to the request payload.
It sends POST /transfers with the access token, an idempotency key, the assertion and a signature from the biometric-protected key.
The gateway verifies the access token signature, expiry, audience and scope.
Because the endpoint is high risk, the gateway asks the risk engine for a decision.
The engine verifies the evidence (signature chain or the platform verification service, depending on the platform), checks the challenge is fresh, and scores device and velocity signals.
Decision: allow. The payments API checks that the source account belongs to this user and that limits permit the amount, then executes the transfer.

blocks.text: How it works

**Threat model first.** The server must assume the client is hostile: the binary can be decompiled, patched and re-signed, traffic can be intercepted on a device the attacker controls, and API calls can be replayed by scripts with no app at all. Therefore authentication, authorisation, pricing, limits and validation are enforced on the server for every request. Client-side controls (pinning, tamper checks, obfuscation) raise attacker cost and protect honest users on compromised networks, but they are never the control that prevents fraud. The assets to protect on the device are the user session and personal data.

**Token storage.** Store tokens in the platform secure store: **Keychain** on iOS, and on Android a key in the **Keystore** used to encrypt the stored token. Choose the accessibility class deliberately: items available only while the device is unlocked are safest, items available after first unlock are needed for background work, and device-only classes prevent the token from migrating to another device through backup or restore. Do not put tokens in plain preference files, the app database, logs, crash reports, analytics events or URLs. Hardware-backed keys never leave the secure hardware; the app asks the hardware to sign or decrypt.

**Short-lived access tokens and refresh rotation.** The access token lives for minutes and is sent on every call; if stolen it expires quickly. The refresh token lives longer, is sent only to the token endpoint, and is **rotated**: each use returns a new one and invalidates the old. The server tracks a token family per device session. If an already-used refresh token is presented, a copy exists somewhere, so the server revokes the whole family and forces re-login (**reuse detection**). On the client, refresh must be single-flight: when ten requests receive `401` at once, one refresh runs and the rest wait, otherwise parallel refreshes trip reuse detection and log the user out. Bind sessions to a device id and support server-side revocation (logout everywhere, password change). For sign-in through an identity provider use the system browser with authorisation code flow and PKCE, not an embedded WebView.

**Biometric gating.** A biometric check that only returns true or false to app code can be bypassed on a compromised device by patching the branch. The strong pattern binds a cryptographic key in the secure hardware to biometric authentication: the key can be used only after a successful biometric match, and the server verifies a signature made with it over a server challenge. Then the proof is cryptographic, not a boolean. Decide the policy for biometric enrolment changes (a new fingerprint can invalidate the key, forcing re-authentication) and always keep a fallback such as device passcode or full login. Use biometrics for step-up on sensitive actions and for unlocking a session, not as the only factor at account creation.

**Certificate pinning.** By default the app trusts any certificate that chains to a root in the OS trust store. Pinning narrows this to specific public keys (pin the key, a hash of the subject public key info, of an intermediate or leaf), which defeats interception that relies on a rogue or user-installed root. The operational risk is severe: if the server certificate key changes and no shipped pin matches, every installed app stops connecting and cannot be fixed without a store release, which the broken app may not be able to prompt for. Mitigations: always ship at least one backup pin for a key kept offline, pin to keys you control rather than a leaf that rotates often, have a tested rotation runbook, monitor pin failures, and keep an emergency path (a separately configured endpoint or a remotely fetched, signed pin set). Pinning does not stop an attacker who controls the device and patches the app; it protects users from network attackers.

**Device attestation and integrity signals.** **App Attest** (iOS) creates a key in secure hardware and has the platform certify that the key belongs to a genuine instance of your app; later requests carry assertions signed by that key. **Play Integrity** (Android) returns a signed verdict about app authenticity, device integrity and licensing that your server verifies. In both, the server issues a one-time challenge so evidence cannot be replayed, and the verdict is evaluated on the server, never in the app. Treat results as risk signals with a rollout plan: services have quotas and outages, legitimate users have unusual devices, so decide fail-open or fail-closed per endpoint. Jailbreak and root detection in the client is a weak signal that can be hidden; use it for telemetry and risk scoring, and avoid hard blocks that punish legitimate users while barely slowing attackers.

**Deep links and WebView bridges.** A custom URL scheme can be registered by any app, so another app may intercept links meant for yours; use verified links (Universal Links, Android App Links) that are tied to your domain through a file hosted on it. Treat every incoming link as untrusted input: validate and allow-list routes and parameters, never perform a state-changing action directly from a link without confirmation inside the authenticated app, and never accept tokens or redirect targets from link parameters without validation. For WebViews: load only allow-listed HTTPS origins, expose the smallest possible native bridge, check the origin of the calling frame for every bridge message, never hand the session token to arbitrary web content, disable file access and mixed content, and prefer the system browser component for third-party pages.

**No secrets in the binary.** Anything compiled into the app, placed in its resources or fetched into its memory can be extracted. Obfuscation delays this, it does not prevent it. So an API key in the app identifies the app at best; it does not authenticate it. Calls to third-party services that need a real secret go through your backend, which holds the secret and applies per-user authorisation and quotas. If a client-side key is unavoidable (maps, analytics), restrict it at the provider by app identity and platform, scope it minimally, and be able to rotate it.

**API abuse protection.** Mobile endpoints are public APIs. Layer the defences: rate limits per user, device, IP and token at the edge and gateway; attestation on sensitive endpoints; server-side validation of every business rule (price, quantity limits, ownership checks to prevent access to another user resource by changing an id); velocity and anomaly rules on login, OTP, signup, promo redemption and payments; step-up authentication when risk is high; and idempotency keys so replays do not repeat effects. Log security-relevant events with device and version context, and plan the response: revoke sessions, block versions through the forced-upgrade contract, rotate keys.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The app lives on a device the company cannot control, so the server makes every important decision. The app keeps a short-lived login pass in the secure vault of the phone and gets a new one regularly.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Tokens go in Keychain or a Keystore-encrypted store with a suitable accessibility class. Access tokens last minutes; refresh tokens rotate with reuse detection. Verified links, allow-listed WebView origins and server-side validation close the common holes. Secrets stay on the backend.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Bind high-risk actions to hardware keys unlocked by biometrics and verified by signature. Add attestation as a server-evaluated risk signal with replay-proof challenges. Use pinning only with backup pins and a rotation runbook. Combine edge limits, device signals and business-rule checks into a risk decision with step-up paths.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Design security as a system with failure modes and economics. Each control has an availability cost (pinning outages, attestation quota or downtime, false positives on integrity checks), so define per endpoint whether it fails open or closed, stage enforcement behind flags with shadow mode first, and keep remote levers that reach old binaries: kill switches, minimum version, pin set updates, session revocation. Assume client checks will be bypassed and place detection on the server where attackers cannot observe the logic. Track attacker cost versus fraud loss, treat the long tail of old app versions as part of the attack surface, and make key and certificate rotation routine exercises instead of emergencies.
Trade-offs

rows: Short access token lifetime (minutes)
Stolen tokens expire quickly; revocation takes effect fast.
More refresh traffic; needs careful single-flight refresh and good behaviour on flaky networks.
Default for consumer apps handling money or personal data.
Refresh token rotation with reuse detection
Detects token theft and limits its lifetime.
Lost responses or concurrent refreshes can look like theft and log out real users; needs a short grace window and client discipline.
Any long-lived mobile session.
Certificate pinning
Protects against rogue or user-installed certificate authorities and many interception setups.
Can lock every installed app out if pins and certificates fall out of sync; complicates debugging and certificate operations.
High-value apps with a mature certificate rotation process and backup pins. Skip it if the team cannot operate it.
Hard-block on root or jailbreak detection
Removes some easy tampering paths; satisfies some compliance checklists.
Easily bypassed by determined attackers; false positives block legitimate users.
Rarely as a hard block. Prefer feeding it into risk scoring and limiting only high-risk features.
Attestation enforced on sensitive endpoints
Strong signal that the caller is the genuine app on a real device; raises the cost of scripted abuse.
Platform quotas and outages, latency, devices that cannot attest, operational complexity.
Login, signup, OTP, payments and promo redemption, rolled out in shadow mode first.
Biometric unlock of a hardware-bound key
Cryptographic proof of user presence on a known device; good UX for step-up.
Key invalidation on enrolment change, devices without capable hardware, fallback flows to design.
Approving payments, viewing sensitive data, re-opening a session.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Server certificate rotated without a matching pin in shipped apps
All pinned app versions fail every request. A store release takes days and users may not see the prompt.
Backup pins for offline keys in every release, pin to stable keys, rotation runbook rehearsed in staging, pin-failure monitoring, an emergency unpinned or separately pinned config channel.
Several requests refresh the token in parallel
The second refresh presents an already-used token, reuse detection revokes the family and the user is logged out at random.
Single-flight refresh in the client, a brief server grace window for the immediately previous token, retry queued requests after refresh.
Access token written to logs or a crash report
Anyone with access to logging or the crash vendor can impersonate users.
Redact authorization headers and bodies in logging layers, short token lifetime, scrub breadcrumbs, review third-party SDK data collection.
API trusts an id sent by the client without an ownership check
Changing the id in the request returns another user order or address.
Authorise every object access on the server against the authenticated user; automated tests for cross-user access.
Deep link triggers an action directly
A malicious page or app sends a crafted link that changes settings or starts a payment in the logged-in app.
Verified links, allow-listed routes, parameter validation, explicit in-app confirmation for state changes.
Third-party API secret embedded in the binary
The key is extracted and used at your expense or to access your data at the provider.
Proxy through your backend, restrict any unavoidable client key by app identity, monitor usage, rotate.
Attestation service outage with fail-closed policy everywhere
Legitimate users cannot log in or pay.
Per-endpoint fail policy, cached recent verdicts, fallback to stricter rate limits and step-up authentication, shadow-mode rollout.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Design the session management for a mobile banking style app.
blocks.text: Login through system browser or native flow with strong factors; server creates a device session and issues a minutes-long access token and a rotating refresh token in a family bound to the device. Tokens in Keychain or Keystore with device-only accessibility. Single-flight refresh on 401. Reuse detection revokes the family. App re-entry and sensitive actions require a biometric-unlocked hardware key signing a server challenge. Server supports listing and revoking sessions, global logout on password change, and idle and absolute session timeouts.

blocks.title: Would you implement certificate pinning? How do you avoid breaking the app?
blocks.text: Only if the threat model justifies it and the team can run it. Pin public keys, not leaf certificates; include at least two pins with one backup key stored offline; keep pins valid for longer than the forced-upgrade window; rehearse rotation; monitor pin failures by version; and keep an emergency channel such as a signed remote pin set or a fallback host. Combine with minimum-version enforcement so versions with expiring pins can be retired before rotation.

blocks.title: How do you stop scripts from abusing a signup or OTP endpoint?
blocks.text: Layered controls on the server. Edge rate limits per IP and network; per-phone-number and per-device limits with backoff; attestation required for the genuine app with a server challenge; risk scoring on velocity, device reputation and behaviour; step-up challenges when risk is high; cost controls on SMS per destination; and monitoring with the ability to tighten rules or kill the flow remotely. No single control is trusted alone, and nothing relies on logic inside the app.

blocks.title: How should the app handle deep links securely?
blocks.text: Use verified links bound to the domain so other apps cannot claim them. Parse links through one router with an allow-list of routes and typed parameter validation. Require an authenticated session for protected destinations and resume the link after login. Never execute state-changing actions or accept tokens straight from a link; show a confirmation screen. For links that open web content, allow-list hosts and open others in the system browser.

blocks.title: What is device attestation and what are its limits?
blocks.text: A platform service gives the app cryptographic evidence, verifiable by the server, that the request originates from a genuine build of the app on a device that passes integrity checks. It is bound to a server nonce to stop replay. Limits: quotas and latency, availability dependence on the platform, devices that cannot attest, and determined attackers using real devices at scale. So it is a strong risk signal, not proof of good intent, and enforcement must be staged and combined with other controls.
Takeaways

items: The client is untrusted: authentication, authorisation and business rules are enforced on the server for every request.
Tokens live in Keychain or Keystore-protected storage, never in logs, files, URLs or analytics.
Use minutes-long access tokens with rotating refresh tokens, reuse detection and single-flight refresh.
Bind biometrics to a hardware key and verify a signature; a boolean result is not security.
Pinning helps against network attackers and can brick the fleet; ship backup pins and rehearse rotation.
Attestation and root or jailbreak checks are risk signals evaluated on the server, rolled out gradually.
Anything in the binary is public; keep secrets behind your backend and validate every deep link and bridge message.

quiz.q: Where should a mobile app store its refresh token?
options: In the local database with the other app data
In the Keychain, or encrypted with a Keystore-held key
quiz.why: The platform secure store protects items with hardware-backed keys tied to device state. The other locations are readable from backups or a compromised device far more easily.

quiz.q: A refresh token that was already used is presented again. What should the server do?
options: Issue a new token pair as usual
Treat it as possible theft: revoke the token family and require login
quiz.why: With rotation, each refresh token is valid once. A second use means two parties hold it, so the family is revoked.

quiz.q: What is the main operational risk of certificate pinning?
options: Shipped apps stop working if the certificate key changes and no pin matches
quiz.why: Pins live inside installed binaries. A mismatch cannot be corrected from the server through the pinned channel.

quiz.q: Why is a biometric check that returns only true or false weak?
options: On a compromised device the result can be patched; binding a hardware key to biometrics gives the server a verifiable signature instead
It is not allowed by app stores
quiz.why: A boolean lives in app code the attacker controls. A signature from a key that only unlocks after a biometric match can be verified by the server.

quiz.q: An API key is embedded in the app. What does it prove to the server?
options: That the request comes from an unmodified app
Nothing reliable, since anyone can extract and reuse it
That the device is not rooted
quiz.why: Anything shipped in the binary is public. Real secrets must stay on the backend.

modules.title: Cloud Architecture
modules.summary: Regions, zones, VPCs, managed services, multi-region trade-offs and cost.

lessons.title: Building on the cloud: regions, zones, managed services and autoscaling

blocks.text: How a typical web system is laid out across availability zones, subnets and managed services, and what each choice costs in money and reliability.
In simple words

Instead of buying and housing your own computers, you rent them from a cloud provider by the hour. The provider has buildings full of machines in many cities. You choose where to put your app, how many copies to run, and which jobs (databases, file storage, queues) the provider should run for you.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of renting space in a large shopping mall instead of building your own shop. The mall owns the building, power and security guards. You choose which mall (region), which wing of it (availability zone), and you open a second shop in another wing so that a power cut in one wing does not close your business. Hiring more staff on busy days is autoscaling.

diagram.title: Three-tier web system across two availability zones (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Users
nodes.detail: Browsers and apps on the public internet. They only ever talk to the CDN and the load balancer, never to servers directly.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.detail: Caches static files close to users and forwards dynamic requests. Examples: CloudFront, Cloud CDN, Azure Front Door.

nodes.label: Load balancer
nodes.detail: Sits in a public subnet and spreads traffic over healthy servers in all zones. Example: AWS Application Load Balancer.

nodes.label: App servers (autoscaling group)
nodes.detail: Identical stateless instances in private subnets, spread over at least two zones. The group adds or removes instances based on load.

nodes.label: IAM
nodes.detail: Identity and access management. Each instance gets a role with temporary credentials, so no passwords or keys live in code.

nodes.label: Managed queue
nodes.detail: A queue run by the provider (for example SQS). Slow work is dropped here so the web request can return quickly.

nodes.label: Background workers
nodes.detail: Containers or functions that read the queue and do the slow work such as sending email or resizing images.

nodes.label: Managed DB (primary)
nodes.detail: A relational database run by the provider (for example RDS). It handles backups, patching and failover for you.

nodes.label: DB standby (other AZ)
nodes.detail: A synchronous copy in a second zone. If the primary zone fails, the provider promotes the standby, usually within one to two minutes.

nodes.label: Object storage
nodes.detail: Cheap, very durable storage for files such as images and backups (for example S3). Data is copied across several zones automatically.

steps.text: The browser asks for a page. Static files such as images and scripts are answered by the CDN right away.
The request is personal data, so the CDN forwards it to the load balancer in the region.
The load balancer picks a healthy instance. Instances that fail the health check get no traffic.
The instance uses its attached role to get short-lived credentials for the database secret and storage.
The instance reads and writes the primary database over the private network.
Each write is copied to the standby in another zone before it is acknowledged, so a zone loss does not lose committed data.
Uploaded files are written to object storage, not to the instance disk, because instances can disappear at any time.
The slow part (email, thumbnails) is put on the queue as a message and the instance moves on.
A worker picks up the message and does the job later. If the worker crashes, the message becomes visible again.
The instance returns the response through the load balancer and CDN to the user.

blocks.text: How it works

**Regions and availability zones.** A region is a geographic area such as `ap-south-1`. Inside it are several availability zones (AZs): separate data centres with their own power and network, a few milliseconds apart. Put copies of your system in at least two AZs so a single building failure does not take you down. Use more than one region only when you need to survive a whole-region outage or serve users on another continent, because it multiplies cost and data-consistency problems.

**Network layout.** A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your own private network. You cut it into subnets, each living in one AZ. Public subnets hold the load balancer and have a route to the internet. Private subnets hold app servers and databases and have no inbound internet route. Security groups act as per-resource firewalls: allow the load balancer to reach the app on its port, allow the app to reach the database, and nothing else.

**Compute choices.** Virtual machines give the most control and are billed while running. Containers (ECS, Kubernetes) pack many services on shared machines and start in seconds. Serverless functions run per request, scale to zero and bill per millisecond, but have cold starts and execution time limits. A common rule: steady, predictable load fits containers or VMs; spiky or rare work fits functions.

**Managed services.** Managed databases, queues, caches and object storage move patching, backups and failover to the provider. You pay a premium over running the same software yourself, and you accept the provider limits and some lock-in. For most teams the saved operations time is worth more than the premium. Object storage is the default place for files; keep the database for structured data.

**Identity.** IAM roles give each workload only the permissions it needs (least privilege) through temporary credentials that rotate automatically. Never put long-lived access keys in code or images. Separate roles for the web tier, workers and humans make a leaked credential far less damaging.

**Autoscaling and cost.** An autoscaling group keeps a minimum number of instances, adds more when a metric such as average CPU or requests per instance crosses a target, and removes them when load drops. Scaling out takes minutes, so keep headroom for sudden spikes. Reliability costs money: two AZs roughly double the compute baseline and a multi-AZ database roughly doubles the database cost. Choose per tier: a checkout path deserves multi-AZ, an internal report tool may not.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: You rent computers and services from a provider, keep more than one copy of everything in different buildings, and let the provider add or remove copies when traffic changes.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Place a load balancer in public subnets, stateless app servers in private subnets across two AZs, a managed database with a standby in the second AZ, and use object storage and queues so servers hold no state.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Failure domains are instance, AZ and region. Multi-AZ covers the first two with synchronous replication and health-checked routing. Autoscaling policies, instance warm-up time and connection limits on the database decide whether a spike is absorbed or becomes an outage.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Size for N+1 at the AZ level: if one of three AZs is lost, the remaining two must carry full load, so each runs at no more than about 66 percent. Account for cross-AZ data transfer charges, quota limits, correlated launch failures when an AZ is impaired, and the fact that control-plane calls such as launching instances are less reliable than already-running capacity during provider incidents.
Trade-offs

rows: Single AZ
Cheapest and simplest. No cross-zone traffic cost.
A zone failure is a full outage.
Development environments and internal tools that can be down for hours.
Multi-AZ in one region
Survives a data centre failure with automatic failover. Low latency between zones.
Roughly double the baseline cost; small cross-AZ transfer charges.
The default for production systems that serve customers.
Managed service vs self-run
Backups, patching and failover handled by the provider.
Higher price, provider limits and lock-in.
Unless you have a strong reason and the staff to operate the software yourself.
Serverless vs always-on containers
Scales to zero, pay per use, no servers to patch.
Cold starts, time limits and costly at steady high load.
Spiky or low-volume workloads; use containers for steady heavy traffic.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: An entire availability zone loses power
Instances and the database primary in that zone vanish; half of capacity is gone.
Run in at least two AZs, use a multi-AZ database with automatic failover, and keep enough headroom for the survivors to carry full load.
Autoscaling reacts too slowly to a traffic spike
Existing instances saturate, latency rises and requests fail before new instances are ready.
Keep a higher minimum, scale on a leading metric such as request rate, use scheduled scaling for known events, and shed load with rate limits.
Scaling out opens too many database connections
The database hits its connection limit and every instance starts failing.
Use a connection pool or proxy, cap the autoscaling maximum, and add read replicas for read traffic.
A leaked long-lived access key
An attacker can read storage or launch costly resources.
Use IAM roles with temporary credentials, least-privilege policies, key rotation and billing alerts.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Design a highly available web application on the cloud.
blocks.text: CDN in front, load balancer in public subnets, stateless app servers in an autoscaling group across at least two AZs in private subnets, managed database with a standby in another AZ, object storage for files, queue and workers for slow jobs, IAM roles for access. State what each tier does on an AZ failure and where the single points of failure remain.

blocks.title: When would you choose serverless over containers or VMs?
blocks.text: For spiky, infrequent or event-driven work where scaling to zero saves money and operations effort is the priority. Avoid it for steady high throughput, long-running jobs or latency-critical paths where cold starts and time limits hurt.

blocks.title: How do you balance cost against reliability?
blocks.text: Tier the system. Put multi-AZ and generous headroom on revenue-critical paths, and use single-AZ or smaller capacity for internal tools. Quantify with the cost of an hour of downtime against the monthly cost of the extra redundancy, and revisit as the business grows.
Takeaways

items: An availability zone is the unit of failure you design around; use at least two.
Public subnets hold only the entry points; apps and databases stay private.
Keep servers stateless: files go to object storage, jobs go to queues, data goes to the managed database.
Managed services trade money for less operational work and are the sensible default.
Autoscaling needs headroom, a good metric and limits that protect the database.
Every extra nine of reliability costs money, so spend it where an outage hurts most.

quiz.q: Why place app servers in at least two availability zones?
options: A single data centre failure should not take the whole system down
It is required to use a load balancer
quiz.why: AZs are separate failure domains. Spreading over two or more keeps the system running when one is lost.

quiz.q: Which belongs in a private subnet?
quiz.why: Databases should have no route from the internet. Only the load balancer needs to be public.

quiz.q: Where should user-uploaded images be stored in an autoscaled system?
options: On the local disk of the app instance
quiz.why: Instances are replaced and scaled in and out, so local disk is lost. Object storage is durable and shared.

quiz.q: You run in three AZs and want to survive losing one. Roughly how busy can each AZ be in normal operation?
quiz.why: If one of three is lost, the remaining two must carry the full load, so each normally uses at most two thirds of its capacity.

modules.title: CI/CD and Deployment
modules.summary: Pipelines, canary, blue-green, feature flags, safe schema changes.

lessons.title: From commit to production: CI/CD, safe deployments and rollbacks

blocks.text: How code moves automatically from a commit through build, tests, registry and staging to production, and how rolling, blue-green and canary releases keep users safe.
In simple words

When a developer saves a change, a robot builds the app, runs the tests, packs it into a box and puts it on the live servers. Doing it by machine makes releases boring and safe. If something goes wrong, the robot can quickly put the old version back.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a bakery that tests every new recipe. A baker writes the recipe (commit), a tester bakes a small batch and tastes it (CI), the approved recipe is filed in a binder (registry), a few regular customers try it first (canary), and only then it goes on every shelf. If customers complain, the old recipe is back on the shelves in minutes.

diagram.title: Delivery pipeline with GitOps-style deployment (generic reference design)

nodes.label: Developer
nodes.detail: Pushes a small change to a branch and opens a pull request. Small, frequent changes are easier to test and to roll back.

nodes.label: Git repository
nodes.detail: The single source of truth for code. A merge to the main branch triggers the pipeline.

nodes.label: CI pipeline
nodes.detail: Runs on a build agent (Jenkins-style or hosted). Compiles, runs unit and integration tests, scans dependencies and builds a container image.

nodes.label: Artifact registry
nodes.detail: Stores immutable, versioned images. The same image that passed tests is the one promoted to production.

nodes.label: CD / GitOps controller
nodes.detail: Reads the desired version from a config repository and makes each environment match it. Handles promotion, canary steps and rollback.

nodes.label: Staging + QA
nodes.detail: A production-like environment where integration, end-to-end and manual QA checks run before real users see the change.

nodes.label: Production
nodes.detail: Live servers. A canary slice runs the new version beside the stable one while metrics are compared.

nodes.label: Feature flags
nodes.detail: Runtime switches that turn a feature on or off per user group without a deploy. They separate deploying code from releasing a feature.

nodes.label: Database
nodes.detail: Shared by old and new versions during a rollout, so schema changes must work for both. Migrations run as a separate, controlled step.

steps.text: The developer opens a pull request. A teammate reviews it and it is merged into the main branch.
The merge triggers the pipeline through a webhook.
CI builds, runs unit and integration tests, then builds one container image tagged with the commit id and pushes it to the registry.
The new tag is written to the config repository. The controller notices that the desired version differs from what is running.
The controller deploys the image to staging, where end-to-end tests and QA run against production-like data.
The controller runs the additive (expand) database migration first. Old code keeps working because nothing was removed.
The new version is sent to a small canary slice, for example 5 percent of traffic.
The new feature code is deployed but hidden. The flag releases it to internal users first, then to everyone.
Error rate and latency of the canary are compared with the stable version. If they are worse, the controller rolls back automatically.
If the canary is healthy, the controller increases traffic in steps until the new version serves 100 percent.

blocks.text: How it works

**Continuous integration.** Every merge builds the code and runs fast checks: unit tests, linting, dependency and security scans, then slower integration tests against real components such as a database in a container. The output is one **immutable artifact**, usually a container image tagged with the commit id. The rule is build once, deploy the same artifact everywhere, so what was tested is what runs.

**Pipelines as code.** A Jenkins-style `Jenkinsfile` or a hosted CI config file describes the stages in the repository, so the pipeline is reviewed and versioned like code. Order stages from fastest to slowest so a broken change fails in seconds, and run independent stages in parallel to keep feedback under about ten minutes.

**GitOps.** Instead of the pipeline pushing commands to servers, a controller inside each environment watches a config repository and reconciles the cluster to match it. Deploying means changing a version number in Git; rolling back means reverting the commit. Every change has an author, a review and a history, and drift between Git and reality is corrected automatically.

**Release strategies.** A **rolling** update replaces instances in small batches: cheap, but old and new versions run together for a while. **Blue-green** keeps two full environments and switches traffic at once: instant rollback, but double capacity during the switch. A **canary** sends a small share of traffic to the new version and watches metrics before widening: the safest for risky changes, and it needs good observability to judge the result.

**Feature flags and rollback.** A flag lets you deploy code that is switched off, release it gradually, and turn it off in seconds without redeploying. Rollback of code is fast because the previous image is still in the registry. Keep flags short-lived and delete them after the rollout, or they pile up as hidden complexity.

**Database migrations.** During any rollout old and new code run against the same database, and a rollback must also work. Use **expand and contract**: first expand by adding a nullable column or new table (old code ignores it), then deploy code that writes both and reads the new one, backfill old rows, and only in a later release contract by dropping the old column. Never rename or drop in the same deploy that needs it.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: A robot builds and tests every change, stores the approved build, and releases it to a few users first. If problems appear, it puts the old version back.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Commit triggers CI: build, test, image, registry. A CD step deploys to staging, then production using rolling, blue-green or canary releases, with feature flags to control exposure and a fast rollback path.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Treat the artifact as immutable and the environment as declared state in Git. Canary analysis compares error rate and latency against the baseline, and schema changes follow expand-contract so any version pair that can coexist during a rollout works with the database.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Optimise the lead time and change failure rate together. Gate promotion on service-level indicators rather than time, keep deploy and release decoupled with flags, make migrations backward and forward compatible across at least two versions, and plan for the state that cannot be rolled back, such as data already written in a new format.
Trade-offs

rows: Rolling update
No extra capacity needed and simple to run.
Old and new versions serve traffic together; rollback means rolling again, which is slow.
Low-risk changes on stateless services that are backward compatible.
Blue-green
Instant switch and instant rollback; the new version is fully tested before traffic.
Needs double capacity during the switch; database changes still have to suit both versions.
Releases where a fast, clean rollback matters more than the temporary cost.
Canary
Real traffic reveals problems while only a few users are affected.
Needs strong metrics and more tooling; slower to complete.
High-traffic or risky changes where a bad release is expensive.
Feature flags
Release is decoupled from deploy; instant off switch and gradual exposure.
Flag debt and many untested combinations if flags are not removed.
Any user-visible change that benefits from gradual rollout or a kill switch.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: A bad release passes all tests but raises errors in production
Users see failures until someone notices and acts.
Canary with automatic rollback on error rate and latency, plus a feature flag kill switch.
A migration drops or renames a column in the same deploy
Old instances still running during the rollout crash, and rollback cannot restore the data.
Expand and contract across separate releases, and test the migration on a copy of production data.
The pipeline passes but the artifact differs from what was tested
Production runs code that never went through the tests.
Build once, tag the image with the commit id, deploy by digest, and never rebuild per environment.
Flaky tests are ignored or retried until green
Real failures slip through and engineers stop trusting the pipeline.
Quarantine and fix flaky tests, track their rate, and fail the build on genuine failures.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Describe a CI/CD pipeline from commit to production.
blocks.text: Merge triggers CI: build, unit tests, integration tests, security scan, build one image and push it to a registry. A CD step deploys to staging for end-to-end and QA checks, runs the expand migration, then releases to production by canary with automatic rollback on bad metrics. Mention immutable artifacts and feature flags.

blocks.title: Compare rolling, blue-green and canary deployments.
blocks.text: Rolling replaces instances in batches and needs no extra capacity but mixes versions. Blue-green switches between two full environments for instant rollback at double cost. Canary exposes a small share of traffic first and compares metrics, which is safest but needs good observability.

blocks.title: How do you change a database schema without downtime?
blocks.text: Use expand and contract. Add the new structure in a backward compatible way, deploy code that handles both, backfill data, move reads to the new structure, and remove the old structure in a later release. Each step must work with the previous and next application version.
Takeaways

items: Build one immutable artifact and promote that same artifact through every environment.
Order pipeline stages from fastest to slowest so failures surface early.
GitOps makes deployment a reviewed change in Git and rollback a revert.
Canary releases limit the damage of a bad change; automatic rollback shortens it.
Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature.
Database changes must work for old and new code, so use expand and contract.

quiz.q: What does "build once, deploy many" mean?
options: The same immutable artifact that passed tests is promoted through every environment
Run the build in every environment to be safe
quiz.why: Rebuilding per environment can produce a different artifact from the one that was tested.

quiz.q: Which strategy needs double capacity but gives the fastest rollback?
quiz.why: Blue-green keeps the old environment running, so rollback is just switching traffic back.

quiz.q: You need to rename a database column. What is the safe approach?
options: Rename it in the same deploy as the code change
Add the new column, write to both, backfill, switch reads, and drop the old column in a later release
quiz.why: Expand and contract keeps old and new code working at every step and keeps rollback possible.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of GitOps?
options: Deployments are declared in Git, so they are reviewed, auditable and revertible
It removes the need for tests
quiz.why: The desired state lives in Git and a controller reconciles to it, so rollback is a revert.

lessons.title: Mobile release engineering: shipping what you cannot roll back

blocks.text: Why a mobile release cannot be undone, and the system built around that fact: store review, staged rollout, feature flags and remote config, experiment exposure, server-driven UI, minimum supported version and forced upgrade, crash-free gates, backend compatibility with old versions and hotfix strategy.
In simple words

When a website has a bug, the team puts the old version back within minutes. A phone app cannot do that. Once people have installed a version it stays on their phones until they choose to update, and a fixed version must first pass the store review. So mobile teams release slowly to a few people first, hide new features behind switches they can turn off from the server, and keep the server able to talk to old app versions for a long time.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Publishing an app is like printing a book, while deploying a website is like editing a notice board. A notice can be replaced in a minute. A printed book stays in readers' homes with its mistakes. So a careful publisher prints a small first batch and listens for complaints before printing more, puts the fast-changing material on a website the book points to, and prints "check our website for corrections" in every copy from the first edition onward.

diagram.title: Release train with staged rollout, flags and gates (generic app)

nodes.label: CI / release train
nodes.detail: Builds, signs and tests a release candidate on a fixed schedule. New features are merged dark, behind flags that default to off.

nodes.label: Store review
nodes.detail: App Store and Play review. Takes hours to days and can reject a build. A step you do not control.

nodes.label: Staged rollout
nodes.detail: Store feature that offers the new version to a growing share of users. It can be paused or halted, but installed copies stay installed.

nodes.label: Old app versions
nodes.detail: Many earlier releases still in daily use. Their code can never be changed, only influenced through server responses.

nodes.label: New app version
nodes.detail: The release being rolled out. Contains new code paths that stay inactive until flags enable them.

nodes.label: Release gate
nodes.detail: Automated and human checks that compare health metrics of the new version with the previous one and decide: widen, hold or halt.

nodes.label: Crash and metrics pipeline
nodes.detail: Collects crashes, hangs, startup time, API errors and business metrics, tagged by app version and flag state.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Receives traffic from every version. Reads the app version header for routing, metrics and upgrade enforcement.

nodes.label: Remote config / flags
nodes.detail: Serves feature flags, experiment assignments, kill switches and minimum version, targeted by version, platform and user segment.

nodes.label: Backend services
nodes.detail: Deployed many times a day and reversible in minutes. Must remain compatible with every supported app version.

steps.text: The weekly release candidate is submitted. It contains the new checkout flow, compiled in but switched off by a flag.
Review passes. The release manager starts a staged rollout at a small percentage.
A small share of users receive the update. Everyone else stays on earlier versions.
On launch the new version fetches remote config: new checkout off, minimum supported version unchanged.
It calls the APIs with its version in a header. Behaviour is the same as the previous release because the flag is off.
The backend already supports both old and new checkout contracts; it was deployed before the app was submitted.
Older versions keep calling the same APIs and keep working, because no contract they depend on was removed.
Crash, hang, startup and error telemetry flows in, tagged with the new version.
After enough sessions, the gate compares crash-free rate and key funnels with the previous version at the same stage.
Metrics are within thresholds. The rollout is widened step by step toward 100 percent.
Separately, the new checkout flag is turned on for 5 percent of users on the new version, and exposure is logged.
Payment errors rise sharply for the flagged cohort only.
The kill switch turns the flag off for everyone. Within one config refresh the old flow is back, with no new binary and no store review.
Months later, a very old version falls below the minimum supported version in config and shows the forced-upgrade screen.

blocks.text: How it works

**Why there is no rollback.** A backend deploy is reversible: redeploy the previous image and every user is on it within minutes. A mobile binary is distributed to devices you do not control. You can stop offering a version, but you cannot uninstall it. The fix path is roll-forward: build, test, submit, pass review, then wait for users to update, which takes days for most users and never happens for some. The whole discipline of mobile release engineering follows from that asymmetry: reduce how much risk each binary carries, limit how many users get it at first, and keep as many controls as possible on the server side where change is fast.

**Store review and the release train.** Review adds a delay you cannot fully predict, and a rejection restarts the clock. Teams therefore use a **release train**: a fixed cadence (weekly or fortnightly) with a branch cut, a stabilisation period and a submission date. Features that are not ready do not delay the train; they ship dark behind a flag or wait for the next one. A predictable train keeps each release small, which makes regressions easier to find and makes missing a train cheap. Both stores provide pre-release channels (internal and beta testing tracks) to exercise a build on real devices before production.

**Staged and phased rollout.** Both major stores can release a new version to a fraction of users and grow that fraction over days. This is the mobile equivalent of a canary. Its limits must be understood: halting stops new users from receiving the version but does not remove it from those who already have it; users can often update manually regardless of the stage; and exact percentages and controls differ by store and change over time. A staged rollout limits blast radius for binary-level problems (crashes at startup, a broken migration). It is too slow and coarse for controlling individual features, which is what flags are for.

**Feature flags and remote config.** Decouple **deploy** (code reaches devices) from **release** (users see behaviour). New code is wrapped in a flag evaluated from remote config, targeted by app version, platform, user segment and percentage. This gives progressive exposure independent of the store, instant disable (the kill switch), and the ability to ship unfinished work safely. Design rules: flags have safe compiled-in defaults (normally off); the app caches the last fetched config and works when the config service is unreachable; decide when a new value takes effect (next launch is safest, mid-session changes can break a flow); the server enforces the same flag for anything security or money related; and every flag has an owner and a removal date, because stale flags multiply untested combinations.

**Experiment exposure.** An A/B test is a flag with random assignment and measurement. Assignment must be sticky per user or device (hash of a stable id and experiment id) so a user does not flip between variants. Log an **exposure event** at the moment the user actually encounters the variant, not at assignment; otherwise users who never reached the feature dilute the result. Compare variants within the same app version, since version adoption itself is biased toward engaged users. Guardrail metrics (crash rate, latency, checkout conversion) are watched alongside the target metric and can stop an experiment automatically.

**Server-driven UI as a release valve.** If the server describes screen composition from a set of components the app already contains, then ordering, content, copy, promotions and many layout changes need no binary release at all. The same idea applies in smaller forms: server-provided strings, thresholds, validation rules and polling intervals. The boundary is clear: the server can rearrange and configure what is shipped, but new native capability still needs a release, and store policies restrict using downloaded code to change what an app fundamentally does, so check current guidelines before relying on any over-the-air code mechanism.

**Minimum supported version and forced upgrade.** The server holds a minimum supported version per platform. An app below it is blocked with an upgrade screen; an app below a recommended version gets a dismissible prompt. This is the only tool that retires a version with a security hole, a data-corrupting bug or a contract the backend can no longer afford to support. It must exist from the first release, since it cannot be retrofitted into installed binaries. Use it carefully: confirm the new version is fully available in the store before enforcing, account for devices whose OS cannot run the new version, and raise the minimum on a published schedule so support and product teams are not surprised.

**Crash-free gates and health metrics.** A rollout advances only when the new version is at least as healthy as the old one. Typical gates: crash-free users and crash-free sessions, hang or not-responding rate, cold start time, API error rate from that version, and a few business funnels such as login success and checkout completion. Compare against the previous version at the same rollout stage and with a minimum sample size, because early adopters differ from the general population and small samples are noisy. Thresholds are choices your team makes; write them down before the rollout so the decision to halt is mechanical, not a debate.

**Backend compatibility and hotfix strategy.** The backend serves N app versions at once, so API changes follow expand and contract: deploy the backend that supports both old and new behaviour first, ship the app that uses the new behaviour, and remove the old path only when usage by version has fallen below the support threshold. Never deploy a backend change that requires a new app to already be installed. When something breaks in production, work down a ladder from fastest to slowest: (1) kill switch or config change, effective in minutes; (2) server-side fix or compensating response for the affected versions; (3) halt the staged rollout; (4) hotfix build from the release branch with only the fix, submitted with a request for expedited review where the store offers one; (5) forced upgrade past the bad version once the fix is live. Design each feature so that step 1 or 2 is possible.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: An app release cannot be taken back once people have installed it. So teams release to a few users first, watch for crashes, keep new features behind remote switches, and make sure the server still works with old app versions.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Ship on a regular release train with features dark behind flags. Use staged rollout to limit binary risk and remote config to control feature exposure and kill switches. Gate each rollout step on crash-free rate and key funnels compared with the previous version. Keep APIs backward compatible and maintain a minimum supported version.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Separate deploy from release completely: binaries carry inactive code, config activates it for targeted cohorts with logged exposure, and guardrail metrics trigger automatic rollback of the flag. Backend changes follow expand and contract ordered around app adoption curves. Incident response follows a ladder from config change to forced upgrade, and every feature is designed to be recoverable at the top of that ladder.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: At Staff level this is a control-plane design problem. Remote config becomes production-critical infrastructure that can break every app version at once, so it needs staged rollout of its own, validation and schema checks, audit, instant revert and safe client defaults. Define the organisation-wide compatibility policy (supported version window, deprecation timelines, contract tests against real old binaries), the ownership and lifecycle of flags to keep the combination space testable, and the release health SLOs that gate automation. Model the cost of the long tail explicitly, and treat "what can we change without a release" as an architectural quality you invest in before the incident that needs it.
Trade-offs

rows: Fast release cadence (weekly train)
Small changes per release, quick fixes on the next train, less pressure to cram features in.
More review cycles and release overhead; users see frequent updates; needs strong automation.
Teams with good CI, automated tests and flagging in place.
Slow staged rollout over many days
Small blast radius; time to observe rare crashes and slow-burn issues.
Fixes and features reach users late; long periods with several versions in rollout at once.
Risky releases such as database migrations or large refactors. Go faster for small low-risk releases.
Feature flag for every change
Instant disable, progressive exposure, experiments, unfinished work can merge.
Both code paths must be tested; stale flags create debt and unexpected combinations; config becomes a risk surface.
User-facing features and risky changes. Remove the flag soon after full release.
Server-driven UI and server-side logic
Change behaviour without store review; fix all versions at once.
More backend complexity, weaker offline behaviour, limited to shipped components, extra latency on first load.
Frequently changing surfaces and rules. Keep core interaction and offline paths native.
Aggressive forced upgrade
Short version tail, simpler backend, fast retirement of bad versions.
Users blocked at the moment they want to use the app; some devices cannot upgrade; churn and bad reviews.
Security issues, data-corrupting bugs or legal requirements. Otherwise prefer soft prompts and a long notice period.
Supporting many old versions on the backend
No user is locked out; less churn.
Compatibility code accumulates, testing matrix grows, old vulnerabilities stay reachable.
While old-version usage is material. Retire by data on a published schedule.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Crash at startup in a fully released version
Users cannot open the app, so in-app kill switches and upgrade prompts never run. Recovery waits for store review and user updates.

Staged rollout with startup-crash gates, minimal work before first frame, fetch config resiliently, and consider a crash-loop detector that resets risky state or disables optional modules on next launch.
Backend deploy removes a field old versions still read
Older apps break immediately for a large share of users while the team tests only the latest version.
Expand and contract, contract tests using fixtures from old versions, dashboards of API usage by app version before removal.
Bad remote config pushed to all users at once
Every version of the app changes behaviour or crashes simultaneously, faster than any binary bug could spread.
Schema validation, staged rollout of config changes, review and audit, one-click revert, clients that validate values and fall back to defaults.
Feature shipped without a flag or kill switch
A bug in it can only be fixed by a new binary; exposure lasts days.
Policy that risky features ship behind a flag with a server-side enforcement point, verified in release review.
Forced upgrade enforced before the new build is available to everyone
Users are told to update but the store shows no update, or their OS cannot install it. They are locked out.
Enforce only after 100 percent availability is confirmed per store and region; exempt OS versions that cannot run the new build or give them a clear message.
Rollout widened on a small or biased sample
A crash affecting a specific device family or locale appears only at high rollout percentages.
Minimum sample sizes per gate, segment health by device, OS and region, hold periods that cover a full day cycle.
Flags never removed
Hundreds of flags interact in untested ways; an old flag flipped by mistake revives dead code.
Owner and expiry per flag, alerts on stale flags, cleanup as part of the definition of done.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: A crash is affecting 3 percent of sessions in a version at 20 percent rollout. What do you do?
blocks.text: Halt the staged rollout to stop the spread. Check whether the crash is tied to a flagged feature; if so, turn the flag off and confirm the crash rate drops. If it is in unflagged code, look for a server-side mitigation such as changing the response that triggers it. In parallel prepare a hotfix from the release branch containing only the fix, run the release checks, submit with an expedited review request if available, and roll it out staged but faster. Afterwards review why the gate at the earlier stage did not catch it and add the missing flag or test.

blocks.title: How do you design feature flags for a mobile app?
blocks.text: A config service with targeting by version, platform, segment and percentage, with sticky bucketing. The client has compiled defaults, caches the last good config, fetches at launch and periodically, and applies changes at safe points. Each flag has an owner, type (release, experiment, ops kill switch) and expiry. Sensitive behaviour is also enforced on the server. Config changes are validated, staged and auditable with instant revert. Flag state is attached to telemetry so metrics can be split by it.

blocks.title: How many old app versions should the backend support, and how do you decide?
blocks.text: By data and policy rather than a fixed number. Track active users and revenue by version, publish a support window (for example the versions released in the last N months, where N is a business choice), and raise the minimum supported version on a schedule with soft prompts first. Exceptions force earlier retirement: security flaws and data-corrupting bugs. Weigh the engineering and risk cost of each extra version against the users who would be blocked, including those whose OS cannot run newer builds.

blocks.title: What are release gates and which metrics would you use?
blocks.text: Predefined conditions that must hold before widening a rollout. Stability: crash-free users and sessions, hang rate, startup crash rate. Performance: cold start, key screen load times. Network: API error rate and latency from the new version. Business: login success, add-to-basket and checkout conversion. Each is compared with the previous version at the same stage with a minimum sample, segmented by device and OS. Breaching a gate pauses the rollout automatically and pages the owner.

blocks.title: What can you change in a shipped app without a new store release?
blocks.text: Anything the binary was built to take from the server: feature flags and kill switches, experiment variants, remote config values such as thresholds and intervals, copy and localisation, server-driven screen composition from shipped components, API behaviour and responses for specific versions, minimum version enforcement and web content in allow-listed WebViews. You cannot add new native capability or fix native crashes that way, and store policies limit downloading code that changes the app purpose, so the investment has to be made in advance.
Takeaways

items: Mobile releases are roll-forward only; design every release so recovery does not depend on a new binary.
Separate deploy from release: ship code dark and expose it through remote flags with logged exposure.
Staged rollout limits binary risk; flags and kill switches control feature risk in minutes.
Gate each rollout step on crash-free rate, performance and business funnels compared with the previous version.
Deploy backward-compatible backend changes before the app, and remove old paths only by usage data.
Minimum supported version and forced upgrade must exist from the first release and be used sparingly.
Know the hotfix ladder: config change, server fix, halt rollout, hotfix build, forced upgrade.

quiz.q: Why can a mobile release not be rolled back like a backend deploy?
options: Installed binaries stay on user devices; you can only ship a newer version and wait for users to update
quiz.why: You control distribution of new versions, not the copies already installed. Recovery is always roll-forward or a server-side control.

quiz.q: What does halting a staged rollout do?
options: Removes the new version from devices that installed it
Stops offering the new version to more users, while existing installs keep it
quiz.why: Halting limits further spread. Users already on the version need a flag change or a fixed build.

quiz.q: What is the fastest way to stop a broken feature that is already on user devices?
options: Turn off its remote flag (kill switch)
Unpublish the app from the store
Wait for the next release train
quiz.why: A config change takes effect in minutes and needs no review or user action, provided the feature was built behind a flag.

quiz.q: In which order should a breaking API change be shipped?
options: Backend that supports old and new first, then the app, then remove the old path once old-version usage is low
Backend removes old path first to force upgrades
quiz.why: The backend must never require an app version users do not have yet. Expand, migrate, then contract.

quiz.q: When should an experiment exposure event be logged?
options: When the user is assigned to a variant at config fetch
When the user actually encounters the experimental experience
quiz.why: Counting users who never saw the feature dilutes the measured effect. Exposure marks the population that could be affected.

modules.title: Observability and Reliability
modules.summary: Metrics, logs, traces, SLOs, error budgets, incident response.

lessons.title: Observability and reliability: metrics, logs, traces, SLOs and incidents

blocks.text: How to see inside a running system with metrics, logs and traces, define how reliable it must be with SLOs, alert on what users feel, and learn from incidents.
In simple words

A running system is like a car driving at night. You need dashboard gauges to see speed and fuel, a diary of what happened, and a way to follow one trip from start to end. You also need to decide how reliable is good enough, and be woken up only when users are really suffering.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a hospital. Monitors on the patient show numbers over time (metrics). The nurse notes record events (logs). A wristband follows one patient through every department (a trace). The hospital promises that most patients are seen within a set time (SLO), and an alarm sounds only when that promise is at risk, not whenever a single reading wobbles.

diagram.title: Telemetry pipeline and alerting path (generic reference design)

nodes.label: User
nodes.detail: Sends a request. The edge or first service attaches a correlation id (trace id) that travels with the request through every hop.

nodes.label: Checkout service
nodes.detail: Instrumented code. It counts requests and errors, times each call, writes structured logs and starts a trace span.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.detail: A downstream dependency. It receives the trace id in a request header and adds its own span to the same trace.

nodes.label: Telemetry collector
nodes.detail: An agent or collector that receives metrics, logs and spans, batches them, drops noise and forwards each to the right store without slowing the request.

nodes.label: Metrics store
nodes.detail: A time-series database of numbers such as request rate, error rate and latency percentiles. Cheap to keep and fast to query.

nodes.label: Log store
nodes.detail: Searchable structured log lines. Rich detail about single events, but costly in volume, so retention is limited.

nodes.label: Trace store
nodes.detail: Holds spans grouped by trace id so you can see the full path of one request and which hop was slow. Usually sampled.

nodes.label: Alert manager
nodes.detail: Evaluates rules on metrics, for example error budget burn rate, and routes a page to the right team with a runbook link.

nodes.label: Dashboards
nodes.detail: Graphs of the key signals for each service, built so an engineer can go from a symptom to the failing component in a few clicks.

nodes.label: On-call engineer
nodes.detail: The person paged. Uses the dashboard, then logs and traces, to find the cause and mitigate first, then fix properly.

steps.text: A request arrives with a correlation id. If none exists, the service creates one and puts it in every log line.
The service calls the payment service and passes the trace id in a header, so both appear in one trace.
The payment service answers slowly. The service records the call duration and counts the result as success or error.
Metrics, structured logs and spans are sent to a collector asynchronously so telemetry never blocks the user.
Counters and latency histograms are stored as time series: request rate, error rate and duration.
Spans are stored by trace id. Only a sample is kept for normal traffic, but slow and failed requests are kept.
A rule sees the error budget burning 10 times faster than allowed for the last 10 minutes.
The alert pages the on-call engineer with the symptom (checkout success rate down) and a link to the runbook.
The engineer opens the service dashboard and sees the payment dependency latency has jumped.
The engineer opens slow traces and finds one payment call retrying three times. Mitigation: switch it off with a flag or fail over.

blocks.text: How it works

**Three signals.** **Metrics** are numbers over time: cheap, aggregated, good for alerting and trends. **Logs** are timestamped records of single events: detailed, good for finding what happened, expensive at scale. **Traces** follow one request across services as a tree of spans: good for finding which hop is slow. Use metrics to detect, traces to locate and logs to explain. Write logs as structured JSON with fields such as `trace_id` and `user_id` hash, never as free text with secrets in it.

**RED and USE.** For request-driven services use the **RED** method: Rate (requests per second), Errors (failed requests per second or percentage) and Duration (latency percentiles such as p50, p95 and p99, not averages). For resources such as CPU, disks, queues and connection pools use **USE**: Utilisation, Saturation (queue length, waiting) and Errors. Start every dashboard with these, because they cover most failures.

**SLI, SLO, SLA and error budgets.** A service level indicator (SLI) is a measurement, for example the share of checkout requests that succeed within 500 ms. A service level objective (SLO) is the target, for example 99.9 percent over 30 days. A service level agreement (SLA) is a contract with penalties, and is usually looser than the SLO. The **error budget** is 100 percent minus the SLO: 99.9 percent allows about 43 minutes of failure in 30 days (30 x 24 x 60 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes). Spend it on releases and experiments; when it is gone, slow down and fix reliability.

**Alert on symptoms.** Page a human when users are affected or about to be, such as a high error budget burn rate or a failing user journey, not on causes such as high CPU that may be harmless. A multi-window burn-rate alert catches fast and slow burns with few false alarms. Every page must be actionable and link to a runbook. Causes belong on dashboards and low-priority tickets.

**Tracing and correlation.** Generate a trace or correlation id at the edge, pass it in a header such as `traceparent` through every service and queue message, and add it to every log line. Then one id links the user complaint, the logs and the full request path. Keep full traces for errors and slow requests, and sample the rest to control cost.

**Health checks, incidents and postmortems.** A liveness check says the process is running and should be restarted if it fails; a readiness check says it can take traffic and removes it from the load balancer. Keep readiness cheap and do not make it depend on every downstream, or one outage empties the whole fleet. During an incident, mitigate first (roll back, flag off, fail over), then find the cause. Afterwards write a blameless postmortem with a timeline, root causes, what went well, and action items with owners.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Numbers, notes and request trails let you see what the system is doing. You decide how reliable it should be and get an alarm only when that promise is in danger.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Collect metrics, logs and traces with a shared correlation id. Track rate, errors and duration for services, and utilisation and saturation for resources. Define SLOs and alert when the error budget burns too fast.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Use latency histograms and percentiles, multi-window burn-rate alerts, trace sampling that keeps errors and slow requests, and readiness checks that do not cascade. Instrument at service boundaries and propagate context through queues too.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Control cardinality in metrics, since each label combination is a new series. Tie release policy to the error budget, run game days to test alerts and runbooks, and measure the observability system itself, because telemetry that fails during an incident leaves you blind exactly when you need it.
Trade-offs

rows: Metrics
Cheap, fast to query and ideal for alerts and long trends.
Aggregated, so they show that something is wrong but not which request.
Always: they are the first signal for detection and SLOs.
Logs
Rich detail about individual events and errors.
High volume and cost, hard to search without structure.
For explaining a failure once metrics or traces point to a component.
Distributed tracing
Shows the full path and time of one request across services.
Needs instrumentation everywhere and sampling to control cost.
Systems with several services where latency problems cross boundaries.
Tight SLO such as 99.99 percent
Very high user trust.
Allows only about 4 minutes of failure a month and costs a lot in redundancy and effort.
Only for truly critical paths; most services are fine at 99.9 percent.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Alerts fire on every CPU spike
Engineers get alert fatigue and start ignoring pages, so a real outage is missed.
Alert on user-facing symptoms and burn rate, send cause-based signals to dashboards, and delete alerts nobody acts on.
A readiness check calls every downstream service
One dependency outage marks all instances not ready and the whole service goes down.
Keep readiness local and cheap, handle dependency failure with timeouts, fallbacks and circuit breakers.
A metric label holds user id or request id
Millions of time series overload the metrics store and queries slow down or fail.
Use low-cardinality labels only; put high-cardinality detail in logs and traces.
The monitoring system runs in the same failure domain as the app
An outage also takes out the dashboards and alerts, so nobody is notified.
Run monitoring in a separate zone or account, add an external synthetic check, and alert on missing data.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you monitor a microservices system?
blocks.text: Instrument each service with RED metrics, resource USE metrics, structured logs and distributed traces linked by a trace id.
