Define SLOs for key user journeys, alert on error budget burn rate, keep dashboards that go from symptom to component, and add health checks and synthetic probes. Mention sampling and cardinality control.

blocks.title: What is an error budget and how is it used?
blocks.text: It is 100 percent minus the SLO, the amount of unreliability you may spend, for example 43 minutes a month at 99.9 percent. While budget remains the team ships features and takes risks; when it is exhausted, releases slow and work shifts to reliability until it recovers.

blocks.title: Walk through how you would handle a production incident.
blocks.text: Acknowledge the page, assess user impact and declare severity, assign roles, mitigate first by rolling back, turning off a flag or failing over, communicate status, then find the root cause using dashboards, traces and logs. Afterwards write a blameless postmortem with timeline, causes and owned action items.
Takeaways

items: Metrics detect, traces locate and logs explain; you need all three.
RED covers services, USE covers resources, and percentiles beat averages.
An SLO sets the reliability target and the error budget makes it a decision tool.
Page on user-visible symptoms and burn rate, not on every cause.
A correlation id passed through every hop makes one request traceable end to end.
In an incident, mitigate first; afterwards write a blameless postmortem with owned actions.

quiz.q: A 99.9 percent monthly SLO allows roughly how much downtime?
quiz.why: 0.1 percent of 30 days (43,200 minutes) is 43.2 minutes.

quiz.q: Which is the best thing to page a human about?
options: CPU is at 85 percent on one server
Checkout success rate is burning the error budget quickly
A log line contains the word warning
quiz.why: Alerts should reflect user-visible symptoms. CPU and warnings are causes or noise that can go on dashboards.

quiz.q: What do the letters in the RED method stand for?
quiz.why: RED covers request rate, error rate and latency of a service.

quiz.q: Why pass a correlation id through every service?
options: To link logs and spans from different services to one user request
quiz.why: The same id lets you follow one request across services and find where it failed or slowed.

modules.title: Real-World Case Studies
modules.summary: Netflix, Uber, food delivery, Amazon, YouTube, WhatsApp, Instagram and five classic designs.

lessons.title: Case study: Netflix-style video streaming

blocks.text: A subscription streaming service splits into a control plane (cloud microservices that decide what you may watch and where to fetch it) and a data plane (a purpose-built CDN that actually moves the video bytes). This lesson walks through encoding, playback start, adaptive bitrate, caching and resilience as a reference design.
In simple words

Pressing play does two separate things. First a set of cloud services checks your account, picks the right version of the video for your device and hands back a list of nearby servers. Then your device downloads the video in small pieces from one of those nearby servers, switching quality up or down as your network changes. The clever part is that the videos were prepared and copied close to you long before you pressed play.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a library chain. The head office keeps the catalogue, checks your membership card and tells you which branch has your book. The branches in each neighbourhood hold the actual books, restocked by truck overnight. Head office never carries books to readers, and a branch never decides who is a member.

diagram.title: Video streaming platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Device player
nodes.detail: TV, phone or browser player. Runs the adaptive bitrate logic, buffers segments and reports playback quality.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Single cloud entry point for all device calls. Terminates TLS, authenticates, routes to backend services and sheds load.

nodes.label: Playback service
nodes.detail: Orchestrates a play request: entitlement check, stream selection for the device, licence and steering. Returns the manifest.

nodes.label: DRM licence service
nodes.detail: Issues short-lived content keys bound to a device and a title so encrypted segments can be decoded.

nodes.label: Steering service
nodes.detail: Ranks the CDN appliances that hold the requested files and are healthy and close to this client network.

nodes.label: Distributed cache
nodes.detail: In-memory key-value tier in front of the databases for membership, viewing position and title metadata.

nodes.label: Wide-column store
nodes.detail: Multi-region, always-writable store for viewing history, bookmarks and metadata. Tuned for availability over strict consistency.

nodes.label: Event pipeline
nodes.detail: Durable log that carries playback telemetry and business events to analytics, recommendations and alerting.

nodes.label: Encoding pipeline
nodes.detail: Splits each source into chunks, encodes them in parallel into a bitrate ladder, validates quality and packages segments.

nodes.label: Origin object store
nodes.detail: Durable home for every encoded file. Appliances fill from here; it is never on the hot playback path.

nodes.label: CDN appliance in ISP
nodes.detail: Storage-dense cache server placed inside or next to the ISP network. Serves video segments over HTTPS.

steps.text: Days before launch, the encoding pipeline turns the studio master into a ladder of bitrates and resolutions per codec and publishes the files to the origin.
During the off-peak window, appliances pull the files predicted to be popular in their region so the bytes sit inside the ISP before anyone asks.
Each appliance regularly reports its health, load and the list of files it holds, so the control plane knows where every title lives.
The viewer presses play. The device sends a play request with its capabilities (codecs, screen, DRM level) to the cloud gateway.
The gateway authenticates the session and routes to the playback service in the nearest healthy cloud region.
Playback reads membership status, plan limits and the resume position from the in-memory cache in around a millisecond.
On a cache miss the value is read from the wide-column store and written back to the cache for the next request.
Playback obtains a DRM licence scoped to this device and title, with a short validity period.
Steering returns several ranked appliance URLs per stream, so the client has fallbacks without another round trip.
The manifest (available bitrates, segment URLs, licence) travels back through the gateway to the device.
The player fetches segments from the top-ranked appliance, measures throughput and buffer level, and moves up or down the ladder segment by segment.
Start-up time, rebuffers and bitrate switches are posted as events and flow asynchronously to analytics and steering feedback.

blocks.text: How it works

**Control plane versus data plane.** The two halves have opposite profiles. The control plane handles many small, personalised, stateful requests (sign-in, browse, play, licence) and runs as stateless microservices in several cloud regions. The data plane handles few request types but an enormous byte volume, almost all of it immutable files. Splitting them lets each scale on its own axis: add cloud instances for request rate, add appliances and network ports for bitrate. It also separates failure: if the control plane is degraded, sessions that already hold a manifest keep playing.

**Encoding pipeline.** A source file is inspected, split into chunks (ideally on shot boundaries so each chunk is visually uniform), and each chunk is encoded independently on a large worker fleet, then stitched and quality-checked. Because chunks are independent the job is embarrassingly parallel and retryable per chunk. **Per-title encoding** chooses the bitrate ladder from the complexity of the content rather than one fixed ladder: a flat cartoon reaches high quality at a far lower bitrate than a grainy action film. Per-shot encoding pushes the same idea down to individual shots. Output is segmented (a few seconds per segment) and aligned across renditions so the player can switch at any segment boundary.

**Content placement.** Video files are immutable and demand is highly predictable, so the CDN is filled proactively rather than on demand. A placement job ranks files by predicted regional popularity and each appliance pulls its share during the quiet hours. Popular titles are replicated on many appliances; the long tail lives on larger storage nodes at interconnection points. The origin object store is the source of truth but is not consulted during playback.

**Playback start.** The play call is a small orchestration: authenticate, check entitlement and concurrent-stream limits, select the streams this device can decode, get a DRM licence, and ask steering for ranked URLs. Independent calls run in parallel and each has a timeout and a fallback. The response is a manifest. Time to first frame is dominated by this call plus the first segment fetches, so clients often start at a conservative bitrate and ramp up, and may prefetch manifests for titles the viewer is likely to play.

**Adaptive bitrate.** The server is plain HTTP file serving; the intelligence is in the client. The player keeps a buffer of several segments and picks the next rendition from measured throughput and buffer occupancy. Throughput-only algorithms react fast but oscillate; buffer-based algorithms are steadier but slower to climb. Practical players blend both, and optimise for a quality-of-experience mix: fast start, few rebuffers, high average quality and few visible switches. If an appliance becomes slow or fails, the client moves to the next URL in the manifest.

**State, caching and eventing.** Hot read paths go through a replicated in-memory cache so that a play request does not depend on database latency. The system of record for viewing history and bookmarks is a multi-region wide-column store chosen for write availability and linear scale, accepting eventual consistency (a resume position that is a few seconds stale is harmless). Everything observable is published to a durable event log: playback telemetry feeds dashboards and steering, while business events feed recommendations and billing downstream without coupling them to the request path.

**Resilience.** Every remote call has a timeout, a bounded retry, a circuit breaker and a **fallback** (for example an unpersonalised but cached row of popular titles when recommendations are down). Failure is rehearsed continuously: randomly terminating instances proves that services are stateless, and injecting latency or errors proves that fallbacks work. The largest drill is **regional evacuation**: shift all traffic out of one cloud region by scaling up the others and moving DNS and gateway routing, which requires data to be replicated across regions already.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: A streaming service has a brain and a delivery fleet. The brain (cloud services) decides whether you can watch and which server is closest. The delivery fleet (CDN servers inside internet providers) sends the video in small pieces. Quality goes up and down automatically so the video keeps playing.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Videos are pre-encoded into a ladder of bitrates, cut into aligned segments and pushed to edge caches ahead of demand. A play request returns a manifest listing renditions and ranked edge URLs plus a DRM licence. The client runs adaptive bitrate logic, while the control plane leans on an in-memory cache in front of an eventually consistent store.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Design choices follow from immutability and predictability: proactive fill beats pull-through caching, steering can be computed from appliance inventory and client network, and control-plane failure can be isolated from active sessions. Encoding is a chunked DAG with per-chunk retries and content-aware ladders. Multi-region active-active demands idempotent writes and conflict-tolerant data models.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: The hard problems are economic and operational: placing petabytes on heterogeneous appliances under popularity uncertainty, steering with stale health signals without causing herd shifts, tuning ABR against a multi-objective quality metric via experiments, and keeping regional evacuation fast enough to be a routine mitigation. Capacity is planned to peak bitrate per ISP, not global average, and every dependency needs an explicit degradation contract.
Functional requirements

items: Browse a personalised catalogue and search titles.
Start playback on many device types and resume where the viewer left off.
Adapt video quality continuously to network conditions.
Enforce plan rules such as concurrent stream limits and maximum resolution.
Ingest studio masters and make them playable in every supported codec and resolution.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Play start succeeds with very high availability; active streams survive control-plane incidents.
Time to first frame in low single-digit seconds on a typical connection.
Rebuffering kept to a small fraction of viewing time.
Survive loss of an availability zone or a whole cloud region.
Delivery cost per hour streamed falls as volume grows.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 200M subscribers, 20M concurrent streams at peak, average 5 Mbps. 20M x 5 Mbps = 100 Tbps of peak egress, which is why delivery sits inside ISP networks.
Assumption: 4-second segments. 20M streams / 4 s = 5M video segment requests per second at peak, served entirely by edge appliances.
Assumption: 100M daily active users x 300 control-plane calls per day / 86,400 s = ~350k rps average; plan for roughly 3x at evening peak, ~1M rps.
Assumption: 50,000 hours of content x 20 GB per hour across all renditions and codecs = 1 PB for one full copy of the catalogue.
Assumption: a 2-hour title = 7,200 s / 4 s shots = 1,800 chunks x 10 renditions = 18,000 encode tasks. At 2 minutes each on 1,000 workers: 36,000 worker-minutes / 1,000 = ~36 minutes wall clock.

blocks.text: APIs

rows: POST
`/v1/playback/start`
Body: titleId, device capabilities. Returns manifest: renditions, ranked segment base URLs, licence, resume position.
POST
`/v1/license`
Exchange a DRM challenge from the device for a short-lived licence.
PUT
`/v1/profiles/{profileId}/bookmarks/{titleId}`
Idempotent upsert of the playback position; last write by timestamp wins.
POST
`/v1/telemetry/playback`
Batched playback events (start, rebuffer, bitrate switch, stop). Accepted asynchronously.
GET
`/v1/profiles/{profileId}/home`
Personalised rows for the home screen; falls back to cached popular rows.
GET
`/{fileId}/range/{start}-{end}`
Edge appliance: fetch a segment of an immutable file using a signed, expiring URL.

blocks.text: Data model

rows: viewing_history

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Playback start fans out to entitlement, stream selection, licence and steering in parallel with a per-call deadline derived from the overall budget.
Steering input: client network prefix, appliance inventory, appliance health and load; output: 2-3 ranked URLs per stream.
Cache keys are namespaced and versioned (for example `profile:{id}:bookmark:{title}`); writes go to the store first, then the cache, replicated to other regions.
Encoding workflow is a durable DAG: inspect, split, encode chunk x rendition, assemble, validate, package, publish; each task is idempotent on (job, chunk, rendition).
Client ABR: start low, estimate throughput with a smoothed average, never pick a rendition that would drain the buffer below a safety threshold.

blocks.text: Security

items: Content is encrypted at rest and in transit; keys are released only through DRM licences bound to device and title.
Segment URLs are signed and expire, so a leaked URL is short-lived.
Device and account authentication at the gateway; plan limits enforced server-side, never trusted to the client.
Least-privilege service identities and mutual TLS between control-plane services.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Own CDN appliances inside ISPs
Shortest network path, lowest transit cost at scale, full control of hardware and steering.
Capital cost, hardware logistics, ISP relationships, and a dedicated operations team.
Very large and predictable video volume concentrated in known networks.
Commercial multi-CDN
No hardware, global reach on day one, vendor redundancy.
Per-GB cost grows with success, less control over placement and cache behaviour.
Early and mid-scale services, or regions with little traffic.
Proactive fill versus pull-through cache
Proactive fill gives a warm cache at launch and uses off-peak bandwidth; pull-through needs no prediction.
Proactive fill wastes space on wrong predictions; pull-through gives cold misses and origin spikes on a big launch.
Proactive for a known catalogue with predictable demand; pull-through for unpredictable or user-generated content.
Per-title ladder versus fixed ladder
Per-title saves bits on simple content and adds quality on complex content.
Extra analysis encodes and compute cost per title, more complex pipeline.
A curated catalogue where each title is watched many times; fixed ladders suit huge volumes of rarely watched uploads.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: An appliance or its ISP link fails mid-stream
Segment requests time out and the buffer starts to drain.
The manifest already lists ranked alternatives; the client fails over to the next URL and steering stops recommending the unhealthy appliance.
A non-critical service such as recommendations is slow
Without isolation, threads pile up and the gateway latency rises for every request.
Timeouts, circuit breakers and bulkheads per dependency, with a cached generic fallback response.
A whole cloud region is impaired
New play requests and sign-ins fail for users routed there; existing streams continue from the CDN.
Evacuate: pre-scale the healthy regions, shift traffic at DNS and gateway level, rely on cross-region data replication.
Cache tier loses a large share of nodes
Reads fall through to the database, which may not be sized for the full read rate.
Replicate cache data across zones, warm replacements from peers, and rate-limit the fall-through path.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Walk through what happens between pressing play and the first frame.
blocks.text: Device calls the gateway with its capabilities. The playback service checks auth and entitlement, selects decodable streams, fetches a DRM licence and asks steering for ranked edge URLs, running independent calls in parallel. It returns a manifest. The player requests the first segments at a conservative bitrate from the top edge, decrypts and renders, then ramps quality. I would call out the latency budget and the fallback for each dependency.

blocks.title: How would you design the encoding pipeline for a two-hour title?
blocks.text: Ingest and validate the source, split into chunks on shot boundaries, fan out encode tasks per chunk and per rendition onto a queue-driven worker fleet, retry failed chunks individually, assemble, run automated quality checks, package into aligned segments and publish to origin. A complexity analysis pass picks the ladder. The workflow is a durable DAG so a crash resumes rather than restarts.

blocks.title: How do you keep the service up when a cloud region fails?
blocks.text: Run active-active in several regions with data replicated asynchronously, keep services stateless, and keep enough headroom or fast autoscaling to absorb another region. Evacuation is a practised procedure: scale targets, shift traffic, verify. Data models must tolerate concurrent writes in two regions, and active streams are unaffected because the CDN is separate.

blocks.title: What would you measure to know the system is healthy?
blocks.text: A business-level signal such as successful play starts per second, compared with the expected curve, plus time to first frame, rebuffer ratio, average delivered bitrate and error rates per device family, ISP and region. Play starts per second catches most serious outages faster than per-service metrics.
Takeaways

items: Separate the control plane (decisions, small requests) from the data plane (bytes); they scale and fail differently.
Immutable content plus predictable demand means you can encode once, place proactively and serve from caches near the viewer.
Chunked, parallel, content-aware encoding trades compute at ingest for bandwidth and quality on every later view.
Adaptive bitrate lives in the client; the manifest gives it renditions and several ranked servers to fail over to.
Resilience is designed and rehearsed: timeouts, fallbacks, failure injection and regional evacuation.

quiz.q: Why can viewers who are already watching often continue during a control-plane outage?
options: The player holds a manifest and licence and fetches segments directly from CDN appliances
The cloud region buffers the whole film on the device at start
The database serves video segments as a backup
quiz.why: Segment delivery is on the data plane. Once the client has URLs and keys, it does not need the control plane until a renewal or a new play.

quiz.q: What does per-title encoding change?
options: It encrypts each title with a different algorithm
It picks the bitrate ladder from the visual complexity of each title instead of using one ladder for all
It stores each title in a separate database
quiz.why: Simple content needs fewer bits for the same quality, so a content-aware ladder saves bandwidth or raises quality.

quiz.q: Where does the adaptive bitrate decision run?
quiz.why: The client sees its own throughput and buffer level, so it chooses the next rendition; servers just serve files.

quiz.q: Why is proactive fill a good fit for a subscription video catalogue?
options: Files are immutable and regional demand is predictable, so caches can be warm before requests arrive
It removes the need for an origin store
It guarantees strong consistency of viewing history
quiz.why: Predictable demand plus immutable content lets you ship bytes during quiet hours and avoid cold misses at peak.

lessons.title: Case study: Uber-style ride matching

blocks.text: A ride-hailing platform must track millions of moving drivers, find the best one for each rider within seconds, and guarantee that a driver is never given two trips at once. This lesson covers location ingestion, geospatial indexing, dispatch, ETA, the trip state machine, surge pricing and failure handling as a reference design.
In simple words

Every driver phone reports where it is every few seconds. The map is divided into small tiles, and the system remembers which drivers are in which tile. When you ask for a ride, it looks at the tiles around you, works out which nearby driver can reach you soonest, and offers the trip to that one driver. A trip then moves through clear stages: requested, accepted, arriving, on trip, completed.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Picture a taxi dispatcher with a wall map covered in a honeycomb grid and a pin for each cab. Cabs radio in their position and the dispatcher moves the pins. When a customer calls, the dispatcher looks at the cells around the caller, picks the cab that can get there fastest, and radios only that cab, marking its pin as spoken for until the driver answers.

diagram.title: Ride matching platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Rider app
nodes.detail: Requests quotes and rides, then receives live trip updates over a persistent connection.

nodes.label: Driver app
nodes.detail: Streams GPS position every few seconds and receives trip offers over a persistent connection.

nodes.label: API + realtime gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates requests, holds long-lived connections for push, and routes traffic to the right city shard.

nodes.label: Location ingestion
nodes.detail: Validates and smooths GPS pings, snaps them to a grid cell and updates the live index. Built for very high write rates.

nodes.label: Geo index (hex cells)
nodes.detail: In-memory map from cell id to the available drivers in it, with a short expiry on each entry. Partitioned by city.

nodes.label: Pricing + surge
nodes.detail: Computes the fare quote from route estimate and a per-area multiplier derived from supply and demand.

nodes.label: Dispatch / matching
nodes.detail: Finds candidate drivers near the pickup, scores them by ETA and other factors, and chooses an assignment.

nodes.label: ETA + routing
nodes.detail: Computes travel time over the road graph with live traffic. Much more accurate than straight-line distance.

nodes.label: Trip service
nodes.detail: Owns the trip state machine and the driver reservation. The single authority for who is on which trip.

nodes.label: Trip store
nodes.detail: Durable, replicated store for trips and their state transitions. Sharded by city and trip id.

nodes.label: Payments worker
nodes.detail: Consumes trip-completed events and charges the rider asynchronously with retries and idempotency keys.

steps.text: An available driver app sends a position ping (latitude, longitude, heading, timestamp) every few seconds over its open connection.
The gateway forwards pings to location ingestion for that city. Pings are small, frequent and loss-tolerant: the next one replaces the last.
The ping is converted to a hexagonal cell id. If the driver changed cell, it is removed from the old cell set and added to the new one, with a short expiry.
A rider enters a destination and asks for a price.
Pricing combines the route estimate with the current multiplier for the pickup area, computed from open requests versus available drivers, and returns an upfront quote.
The rider confirms. The request, carrying an idempotency key, reaches dispatch on the shard that owns the pickup city.
Dispatch asks for available drivers in the pickup cell and the rings of cells around it, widening the ring if too few are found.
Road-network ETAs are computed for the candidates. The closest driver in a straight line may be across a river or facing the wrong way.
Dispatch asks the trip service to reserve the chosen driver. The reservation is a conditional write with a lease, so only one request can win a given driver.
The trip is persisted as OFFERED with the driver id and lease expiry before anything is sent to a phone.
The offer is pushed to the driver. On accept, state moves to ACCEPTED and the rider is pushed driver details and live position; on timeout the lease lapses and dispatch tries the next candidate.
When the trip reaches COMPLETED, an event triggers fare finalisation and payment in the background, so a slow card network never blocks the ride ending.

blocks.text: How it works

**Location ingestion.** Driver positions are the highest-volume write in the system and also the most disposable: each ping is superseded seconds later. So the live position lives in memory with a time-to-live rather than in a transactional database, and a driver whose pings stop simply expires from the index. Ingestion filters GPS noise, may snap points to roads, and can batch or adapt ping frequency (faster when on a trip or near demand, slower when idle) to save battery and bandwidth. A sampled copy goes to a log for trip-path reconstruction and analytics.

**Geospatial indexing.** "Find drivers near this point" must not scan every driver. The map is divided into cells and each driver is filed under a cell id, so a proximity query becomes a few key lookups. **Geohash** interleaves latitude and longitude bits into a string prefix; it is simple and works with any key-value store, but cells are rectangles whose size varies with latitude and neighbours across a boundary can have unrelated prefixes. A **quadtree** subdivides adaptively where density is high, at the cost of a mutable tree. **S2** projects the sphere onto a cube and uses a space-filling curve for good range scans. **H3** uses hexagons: every cell has six neighbours all at the same centre distance, which makes "ring of radius k" queries and smoothing across neighbours natural. Hexagons do not nest exactly into parents, which is the price paid.

**Matching and dispatch.** The naive rule is nearest available driver. Better is lowest road ETA, and better again is to hold requests for a short window and solve the batch: assign several riders and drivers together to minimise total wait, because the greedy best match for one rider can be a poor outcome for the next. Scoring can include driver heading, the chance the driver accepts, and drivers who are about to finish a trip nearby. The dispatch service is stateless in the sense that all truth about reservations sits in the trip service.

**One driver, one trip.** This is the correctness core. Two dispatch workers can pick the same driver at the same moment. The reservation must therefore be an atomic conditional write: set driver X to RESERVED for trip T only if X is currently AVAILABLE, using compare-and-set or a row version. The reservation carries a **lease** with an expiry, so if the driver never answers or a server dies, the driver becomes available again without manual cleanup. A fencing token (the version) stops a stale accept from a lapsed lease being honoured. Partitioning drivers by city, with one owner for each partition, keeps this a single-shard operation.

**Trip state machine.** A trip moves through REQUESTED, OFFERED, ACCEPTED, ARRIVING, IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED, with CANCELLED and NO_DRIVERS as exits. Each transition is validated against the current state, written durably and then published. Client actions carry idempotency keys so a retried "accept" or "end trip" on a flaky mobile network applies once. Long-running orchestration (offer timeouts, re-dispatch, post-trip steps) suits a durable workflow engine that persists timers and progress instead of in-memory timers.

**ETA, pricing and surge.** ETA runs shortest-path queries on a road graph weighted by live and historical speeds, with precomputation (such as contraction hierarchies) to answer in milliseconds, often corrected by a learned model. Surge is a control loop: per cell and time window, compare open requests to available drivers and raise a multiplier when demand outruns supply, smoothing across neighbouring cells and over time so prices do not flicker at cell borders. The quoted price is locked for the rider for a short period.

**Sharding, push and the async tail.** Rides are local: a rider in one city is never matched with a driver in another. That makes **city** (or region) a natural shard key for the index, dispatch and trip state, and it limits the blast radius of an incident to one city. Riders and drivers hold persistent connections to a realtime gateway; a routing table maps user to gateway node, with mobile push notifications as the fallback. Payment, receipts, ratings and fraud checks hang off the trip-completed event and run asynchronously with retries, because none of them should delay the next ride.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Drivers send their location every few seconds. The system keeps a live map of who is where, finds drivers close to a rider, picks the one who can arrive soonest and offers the trip to that single driver. The trip is then tracked step by step until it ends, and payment happens afterwards.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Live positions sit in an in-memory index keyed by grid cell with a TTL. A ride request queries the surrounding cells, ranks candidates by road ETA and reserves one driver with an atomic conditional write and a lease. Trip state is a persisted state machine with idempotent transitions, and updates are pushed over persistent connections.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Choices to defend: hexagonal cells for uniform neighbours versus geohash simplicity; batched assignment versus greedy; lease duration versus offer timeout; city sharding with a cross-shard path for trips that cross borders. Surge is a damped feedback loop over cell-level supply and demand. Workflows with durable timers replace ad hoc retries.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: At scale the difficult parts are global optimisation under latency limits (matching as a streaming assignment problem with forecasts), marketplace stability (surge and incentives interacting with driver behaviour), consistency during shard movement or failover (who owns a driver while membership is changing), and graceful degradation: stale ETAs, straight-line fallback and a simple nearest-driver mode when the optimiser is unavailable.
Functional requirements

items: Drivers go online and report position continuously.
Riders get an upfront price and ETA, then request a ride.
The system matches a rider to one driver and handles accept, decline and timeout.
Both parties see live trip status and position until completion.
Fare is finalised and charged after the trip; either side can cancel under defined rules.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Match decision within a few seconds of the request.
A driver is never committed to two trips at once.
Location freshness within a few seconds.
A failure in one city does not affect other cities.
Core request-to-trip loop stays available when payments or analytics are degraded.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 5M drivers online at global peak, one ping every 4 s. 5M / 4 = 1.25M location writes per second.
Assumption: 200 bytes of index state per driver. 5M x 200 B = 1 GB, so the live index fits in memory with room for replicas.
Assumption: 30M trips per day / 86,400 s = ~350 requests per second average; at a 5x peak factor, ~1,750 per second.
Assumption: 20 candidate drivers per request. 1,750 x 20 = 35,000 ETA computations per second at peak, which is why routing is precomputed and cached.
Assumption: 5 KB per trip record. 30M x 5 KB = 150 GB of trip data per day before replication.

blocks.text: APIs

rows: POST
`/v1/drivers/{driverId}/location`
Body: lat, lng, heading, speed, ts. Usually sent as a stream message; no response body needed.
POST
`/v1/quotes`
Body: pickup, dropoff, product. Returns upfront fare, pickup ETA and a quote id with an expiry.
POST
`/v1/rides`
Body: quoteId. Header: Idempotency-Key. Creates a trip in REQUESTED and starts matching.
POST
`/v1/trips/{tripId}/accept`
Driver accepts an offer. Body: offer version. Fails if the lease expired.
POST
`/v1/trips/{tripId}/transitions`
Body: event (arrived, start, end, cancel). Validated against the state machine; idempotent.
GET
`/v1/trips/{tripId}`
Current state, driver position and ETA. Live updates arrive over the persistent connection.

blocks.text: Data model

rows: driver_live
driver_id, cell_id, lat, lng, heading, status, updated_at (TTL)
In-memory geo index, per city
driver_state
driver_id (key), status, current_trip_id, lease_expires_at, version
Strongly consistent KV, per city shard
trip
trip_id (key), city_id, rider_id, driver_id, state, pickup, dropoff, quote_id, fare, created_at, updated_at
Replicated document or relational store, sharded by city
trip_event
trip_id, seq, from_state, to_state, actor, ts
Append-only log
surge_cell
cell_id, window_start, open_requests, available_drivers, multiplier
In-memory with periodic snapshot

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Geo index: `cell_id -> set(driver_id)` plus `driver_id -> cell_id`; a ping that changes cell does remove-then-add; entries expire if not refreshed.
Candidate search: ring k = 1 around the pickup cell covers 7 cells, k = 2 covers 19; grow k until enough candidates or a maximum radius is reached.
Reservation: `UPDATE driver_state SET status = RESERVED, current_trip_id = T, version = v + 1 WHERE driver_id = D AND status = AVAILABLE AND version = v`.
Trip transitions are a table of allowed (state, event) pairs; anything else is rejected, and each accepted transition appends to `trip_event`.
Offer timeout and re-dispatch run as a durable workflow with persisted timers so a process restart does not lose an in-flight match.

blocks.text: Security

items: Authenticate every app call; a driver can only post location and accept offers for their own id.
Share only what is needed: the rider sees the assigned driver position, not all drivers; phone numbers are masked through a relay.
Detect spoofed GPS with plausibility checks on speed and jumps, and rate-limit ride requests per account.
Location history is sensitive personal data: restrict access, encrypt at rest and apply retention limits.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Hexagonal cells (H3 style)
Uniform neighbour distance, simple ring queries, good for smoothing surge across cells.
Children do not nest exactly in parents; needs a library rather than plain string prefixes.
Proximity and aggregation over moving objects, analytics by area.
Geohash
Trivial to compute, prefix search works in any ordered key-value store.
Rectangular cells that distort with latitude; edge cases at cell boundaries need neighbour lookups.
Simple nearby search, small teams, storage engines with prefix scans.
Greedy nearest-ETA match
Instant response, simple to reason about and debug.
Locally best choices can raise total wait across riders.
Low density markets or as a degraded mode.
Batched assignment over a short window
Lower average wait and fewer wasted kilometres across the whole batch.
Adds a few seconds of delay and an optimiser to operate.
Dense cities with many concurrent requests.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Two requests pick the same driver simultaneously
Without protection the driver receives two trips and one rider is stranded.
Atomic compare-and-set reservation with a lease; the loser immediately tries its next candidate.
Driver app loses connectivity after an offer is sent
The rider waits on a driver who never saw the offer.
Offer timeout tied to the lease; on expiry the driver is released (or marked unreachable) and dispatch re-offers to the next candidate.
A geo index node crashes
Drivers in that partition disappear from search for a moment.
Replicate partitions; because every driver re-reports within seconds, a replacement node rebuilds its state from the live stream quickly.
Payment provider is down at trip end
If payment were synchronous, trips could not be completed and drivers would be stuck.
Complete the trip first, queue the charge with an idempotency key, retry with backoff and reconcile later.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you find nearby drivers efficiently?
blocks.text: Map each driver position to a grid cell id and keep cell to driver-set in memory, partitioned by city. For a request, compute the pickup cell, fetch that cell plus k rings of neighbours, filter by status and vehicle type, then rank by road ETA. Expand k if results are thin. I would compare geohash, quadtree, S2 and H3 and justify the choice by neighbour uniformity and tooling.

blocks.title: How do you guarantee a driver gets only one trip?
blocks.text: Make the trip service the single owner of driver availability. Reservation is a compare-and-set from AVAILABLE to RESERVED with a version and a lease expiry, done on the shard that owns the driver. Accept must present the current version. If the lease lapses, the driver is released automatically. Idempotency keys make client retries safe.

blocks.title: How would you shard this system?
blocks.text: By city or region, since matching never crosses cities. Each shard holds its geo index, dispatch workers and trip state. Large cities can be split into sub-regions with overlap handling at the borders. A consistent-hash ring or a directory maps city to nodes, and a global layer handles users, payments and trips that cross regions.

blocks.title: What happens when the ETA service is slow?
blocks.text: Dispatch has a deadline. If ETA misses it, fall back to cached recent travel times or straight-line distance with a speed factor, accept a slightly worse match, and record the degradation. A request should not fail because one ranking input is unavailable.
Takeaways

items: Treat live location as high-rate, ephemeral data: in memory, keyed by cell, expiring on its own.
A spatial grid turns nearby search into a handful of key lookups; hexagons give uniform neighbours, geohash gives simplicity.
Rank candidates by road ETA, and consider batching requests to optimise the whole city rather than one rider.
One driver, one trip is enforced by an atomic conditional reservation with a lease and a version, owned by one service.
Shard by city, model the trip as a persisted state machine with idempotent transitions, and push payments to an async tail.

quiz.q: Why keep live driver positions in memory with a TTL rather than in a relational table?
options: Positions are written very often, are superseded within seconds, and stale entries should disappear automatically
Relational databases cannot store latitude and longitude
Memory is more durable than disk
quiz.why: The data is high-rate and ephemeral. Losing it is cheap because drivers re-report, while durable writes for each ping would be wasteful.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of hexagonal cells over square cells for proximity search?
options: All six neighbours are at the same centre distance, so ring expansions approximate circles evenly
Hexagons nest perfectly inside larger hexagons
quiz.why: Squares have edge and corner neighbours at different distances. Hexagons do not nest exactly, which is their downside.

quiz.q: What prevents one driver being assigned to two trips?
options: The driver app rejecting the second offer
An atomic conditional reservation with a lease in the service that owns driver state
quiz.why: Only a single-writer conditional update makes the guarantee; client behaviour and speed cannot.

quiz.q: Why is payment processed after the trip completes rather than inside the end-trip request?
options: External payment calls are slow and can fail; they should not block the driver from taking the next ride
Cards cannot be charged while a car is moving
quiz.why: Decoupling through an event with retries and idempotency keeps the core loop fast and available.

lessons.title: Food delivery (Swiggy / Zomato style): discovery, ordering, dispatch and live tracking

blocks.text: Design a food delivery platform: find restaurants near you, place an order, assign a delivery partner, track the ride live and show a believable ETA.
In simple words

You open the app, see restaurants that can reach you, pick dishes and pay. The restaurant cooks while the system finds a nearby delivery person to collect the food. You watch the rider move on a map until the food arrives. Three things must work together: finding things fast, never losing an order, and matching orders to riders quickly.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Picture a busy pizza shop with a dispatcher. Customers call in, the dispatcher writes a ticket, the kitchen cooks, and the dispatcher looks at a wall map of where every driver is to pick the one closest to the shop who is not already carrying too much. While the driver is out, the dispatcher can tell the customer roughly when to expect the pizza, and updates that guess as traffic changes.

diagram.title: Food delivery platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Customer app
nodes.detail: Browses restaurants, places the order and shows live status. Sends an idempotency key with each order so a retry never creates a second order.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates the user, rate limits and routes requests to the discovery, order and tracking services.

nodes.label: Discovery service
nodes.detail: Answers "what can deliver to me now". Reads a geo-aware search index of restaurants, menus and open/closed state.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.detail: Owns the order state machine. Validates the cart, takes payment and publishes an OrderConfirmed event.

nodes.label: Orders DB
nodes.detail: Relational store, source of truth for orders and their status history. Needs transactions because money is involved.

nodes.label: Event bus
nodes.detail: Durable log of order events. Dispatch, notifications and analytics read it independently so the order path stays short.

nodes.label: Dispatch service
nodes.detail: Picks a delivery partner for each confirmed order using distance, current load and acceptance history, then offers the job.

nodes.label: Partner geo index
nodes.detail: In-memory index of partner positions bucketed by map cell. Answers "who is within 3 km of this restaurant" in milliseconds.

nodes.label: Partner app
nodes.detail: Sends GPS pings every few seconds, receives job offers and reports pickup and drop-off.

steps.text: The user opens the app. The app sends its coordinates and asks for restaurants that deliver there.
Discovery queries a geo-aware index, filters out closed or out-of-range restaurants and ranks the rest. Results are cached for a short time per map cell.
The user fills a cart and taps pay. The request carries an idempotency key.
The gateway authenticates and forwards the checkout to the Order service.
The order is written in a transaction with status CREATED. A repeated idempotency key returns the existing order instead of making a new one.
After payment succeeds the status becomes CONFIRMED and an OrderConfirmed event is published. The restaurant is notified from the same event.
Dispatch consumes the event. It does not need to start when the food is ready; it starts early so a partner arrives as cooking finishes.
Dispatch asks the geo index for partners near the restaurant and scores them by distance, current load and recent acceptance rate.
The best partner gets a time-limited offer. If it is declined or times out, the next candidate is tried.
While riding, the partner app sends a location ping every few seconds. Only the latest position per partner is kept in the index.
The customer app polls or streams the order status and rider position, and shows an ETA that is recomputed as the ride progresses.

blocks.text: How it works

**Discovery is a read-heavy search problem.** Menus and restaurant availability change slowly, but they are read by far more users than place orders. A search index keyed by geography answers "who can deliver to this address", and results are cached per map cell for tens of seconds. Open or closed state and item stock must be fresh, so they are pushed into the index as updates rather than waiting for a nightly rebuild.

**Ordering is a transaction, not a search.** The Order service writes the order and its payment intent in one transaction, then publishes an event. The client sends an **idempotency key** so a retry after a network timeout returns the same order. Status moves through a small state machine (created, confirmed, accepted by restaurant, preparing, picked up, delivered, cancelled) and only valid transitions are allowed.

**Events decouple the slow parts.** Dispatch, restaurant notifications, push messages and analytics all react to the order event. The checkout call stays short, and a slow dispatcher cannot make a customer wait on the pay button. Events are delivered at least once, so every consumer must treat a repeated event as a no-op.

**Dispatch is a matching problem.** For each order the system finds candidate partners near the restaurant, scores them (distance, how many orders they already carry, whether they are heading that way, past acceptance) and offers the job with a short timeout. Batching a few orders per partner raises efficiency but lengthens delivery time, so the scoring is a tuned trade-off, not a fixed formula.

**Live location is a high-write, low-value-per-write stream.** Thousands of partners ping every few seconds, but only the latest position matters for dispatch and tracking. An in-memory geo index that overwrites by partner id handles this; a sampled copy can go to a log for later analysis. The customer sees the position through polling or a pushed stream.

**ETA has three parts.** Estimated food preparation time, partner travel to the restaurant and travel from the restaurant to the customer. Preparation time is the hardest to predict, so it is learned per restaurant from history and corrected by the restaurant marking the order ready. The ETA is recomputed at every state change so it does not drift.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: You pick food, pay, and the app finds a nearby rider. The app keeps showing where the rider is and when the food should arrive.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: A search index serves restaurant lists, an order service stores orders safely, an event feeds a dispatch service that looks up nearby riders in a fast location index, and riders send location pings that customers see.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Orders are transactional with idempotency keys and a state machine. Everything downstream is event-driven with at-least-once delivery and idempotent consumers. Dispatch scores candidates from an in-memory geo index and offers jobs with timeouts and reassignment.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: The hard parts are the peak-hour spike at lunch and dinner, hot map cells during rain, prepare-time prediction error and the cost of reassigning an order after a partner cancels. Cell-level sharding of the geo index, backpressure on dispatch, surge controls and graceful degradation (show fewer restaurants rather than none) keep the system usable.
Functional requirements

items: Search and filter restaurants that can deliver to the user location, with menus and open/closed state.
Build a cart, apply offers and pay; create exactly one order per checkout.
Notify the restaurant, track the order through its states and allow cancellation within rules.
Assign a delivery partner automatically and let the partner accept, pick up and deliver.
Show live partner location and a continuously updated ETA to the customer.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Availability of ordering above 99.9 percent; discovery may degrade to cached results.
No lost or duplicated orders and no double charges (strong consistency on the order record).
Search p95 under 300 ms; checkout p95 under 1 s; dispatch decision within a few seconds of confirmation.
Handle a 5x peak at lunch and dinner without manual intervention.
Location updates visible to the customer within about 5 seconds.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 5M orders/day. Average = 5,000,000 / 86,400 s = ~58 orders/s. Peak assumed 5x = ~290 orders/s.
Assumption: 30 browse requests per order. 5M x 30 = 150M/day / 86,400 = ~1,740 rps average, ~8,700 rps at 5x peak.
Assumption: 300,000 active partners at peak, one ping per 4 s. 300,000 / 4 = 75,000 location writes/s.
Ping size ~100 bytes. 75,000 x 100 B = 7.5 MB/s of ingest; the live index holds 300,000 x ~100 B = ~30 MB.
Assumption: 2 KB per order record. 5M x 2 KB = 10 GB/day = ~3.6 TB/year.

items: Order state machine: CREATED -> CONFIRMED -> ACCEPTED -> PREPARING -> READY -> PICKED_UP -> DELIVERED, with CANCELLED reachable from early states. A transition table rejects invalid moves.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you design partner assignment?
blocks.text: Index partner positions by map cell in memory. On a confirmed order, query the cells around the restaurant, filter by availability and load, score candidates, and send a time-limited offer. On decline or timeout move to the next. Keep the scoring pluggable and measure delivery time and idle time.

blocks.title: How do you avoid losing or duplicating orders?
blocks.text: Write the order in a transaction with an idempotency key, publish the event after commit (outbox pattern), make consumers idempotent, and run reconciliation between payments and orders.

blocks.title: How do you scale the live location stream?
blocks.text: Shard the geo index by map cell, keep only the latest position per partner, batch writes, and let customers read position by cheap polling or a push channel. Sample positions into a log for analytics.
Takeaways

items: Discovery is a cached, geo-aware read problem; ordering is a transactional write problem.
Idempotency keys and a strict order state machine prevent duplicate and invalid orders.
Events decouple dispatch and notifications from checkout; consumers must be idempotent.
Dispatch is matching over a fast in-memory geo index with timeouts and reassignment.
Location is a high-write stream where only the latest value matters.
ETA is prepare time plus two travel legs, recomputed as the order moves.

quiz.q: Why does the client send an idempotency key when placing an order?
options: So a retried request returns the same order instead of creating a duplicate
quiz.why: Networks time out. Without the key a retry can charge and create the order twice.

quiz.q: Why keep only the latest partner location in the geo index?
options: Dispatch and tracking need current position, and overwriting is cheap at thousands of writes per second
Old locations are illegal to store
quiz.why: The live path needs the latest value. History, if needed, goes to a separate log.

quiz.q: Which is the main reason to publish an OrderConfirmed event instead of calling dispatch directly?
options: Checkout stays fast and survives a slow or down dispatcher
quiz.why: Decoupling keeps the pay button independent of downstream work. Delivery is usually at least once, so consumers must be idempotent.

lessons.title: Amazon-style e-commerce: catalog, cart, checkout, inventory and the order pipeline

blocks.text: Design an online store: a fast catalog, a cart that never loses items, a checkout that never oversells, and an order pipeline that fulfils each purchase.
In simple words

You search for a product, add it to a basket, pay, and a few days later it arrives. Behind the scenes the store must show product pages instantly, remember your basket, make sure the last item is not sold to two people, and then pass the order to the warehouse. Each of those jobs is handled by a separate part of the system.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a big bookshop. Browsing the shelves is free and anyone can do it at the same time. The basket you carry is yours alone. At the till, the cashier puts a sold tag on the exact copy you picked so nobody else can take it while you pay. After payment a ticket goes to the stockroom, which packs and ships it.

diagram.title: E-commerce platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Shopper app / web
nodes.detail: Browses products, manages the cart and checks out. Sends an idempotency key with checkout so a double tap does not create two orders.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates the shopper, rate limits and routes by path to catalog, cart or order services.

nodes.label: Catalog + search
nodes.detail: Serves product pages and search. Heavily cached and backed by a search index; stale by seconds is acceptable.

nodes.label: Cart service
nodes.detail: Stores each shopper cart in a highly available key-value store. Must accept writes even during partial failures.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.detail: Coordinates checkout: reads the cart, reserves stock, authorises payment and records the order. Owns the order state machine.

nodes.label: Payment provider
nodes.detail: External processor. Checkout authorises the amount first and captures it when the order ships.

nodes.label: Inventory service
nodes.detail: Tracks available and reserved quantity per item and warehouse. Reservations expire if checkout is abandoned.

nodes.label: Inventory DB
nodes.detail: Source of truth for stock counts. Updates use conditional writes so the count can never go below zero.

nodes.label: Order events
nodes.detail: Durable event log. OrderPlaced is consumed by fulfilment, email, fraud checks and analytics independently.

nodes.label: Fulfilment pipeline
nodes.detail: Picks a warehouse, creates pick and pack tasks, books shipping and updates order status as events arrive.

steps.text: The shopper searches and opens a product page. The request is read-only and cache friendly.
Catalog serves the page from cache or its search index. Price and rough availability are shown; the exact stock is not guaranteed yet.
The shopper adds an item to the cart.
The cart service writes to a key-value store. Writes favour availability, and conflicting edits to the same cart are merged rather than rejected.
The shopper taps place order. The request carries an idempotency key.
The Order service starts checkout and creates an order in PENDING state.
It reads the cart and re-prices every line from the catalog so a stale cart price is never trusted.
It asks Inventory to reserve each line. A reservation holds the stock for a short time.
Inventory runs a conditional update (decrement only if available is at least the requested quantity). Two buyers racing for the last unit cannot both succeed.
With stock held, the order authorises payment. On failure the reservation is released.
The order moves to CONFIRMED and an OrderPlaced event is published after the database commit.
Fulfilment consumes the event, chooses a warehouse and starts pick, pack and ship. Status updates flow back as events.

blocks.text: How it works

**Split browse from buy.** Browsing is read-heavy, tolerant of stale data and benefits from CDN and cache layers. Buying is write-heavy, needs correctness and cannot be cached. Putting them in separate services lets each scale and fail independently, so a catalog slowdown does not block checkout.

**The cart favours availability.** A shopper should always be able to add an item. The Dynamo paper describes exactly this goal for the Amazon shopping cart: accept the write even during failures and reconcile conflicting versions later, merging cart contents instead of losing items. Merging can occasionally resurrect a deleted item, which is an acceptable product trade-off.

**Checkout favours correctness.** Checkout is a saga: create the order, reserve inventory, authorise payment, confirm. If any step fails, the earlier steps are compensated (release the reservation, void the authorisation). Each step is idempotent, and the whole flow is keyed by the client idempotency key so retries are safe.

**Inventory reservation prevents overselling.** Stock is tracked as available and reserved. A reserve call does a conditional update so the count cannot go negative, and a reservation has an expiry so abandoned checkouts return stock. For a very popular item all buyers hit the same row, so hot items need techniques such as splitting the counter into several buckets or queueing requests per item.

**The order pipeline is event driven.** After payment is authorised, an OrderPlaced event is published using an outbox so it is never lost or sent for a rolled-back order. Fulfilment, email, fraud scoring and analytics each consume it independently. Consumers are idempotent because delivery is at least once.

**Peak events change the design.** During a big sale, traffic is a multiple of normal. Catalog caches absorb reads, checkout is rate limited with a waiting room, and non-critical work (recommendations, emails) is deferred. The system sheds optional features before it sheds orders.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The store shows products, remembers your basket, holds the item for you while you pay, and then tells the warehouse to send it.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Separate services handle catalog, cart, inventory and orders. Checkout reserves stock, charges payment and publishes an event that the warehouse system consumes.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Checkout is an idempotent saga with compensation. Inventory uses conditional writes and reservation expiry. The order event is published through an outbox and consumed idempotently by fulfilment and other consumers.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Key design choices are per-path consistency (available cart, correct inventory), hot-SKU contention handling (bucketed counters or per-item serialisation), warehouse selection under stock and cost constraints, and load shedding with a waiting room during sale peaks.
Functional requirements

items: Browse and search products with prices, images and reviews.
Add, remove and update items in a persistent cart.
Check out with address and payment; produce exactly one order per attempt.
Reserve stock so an item is never sold beyond availability.
Track the order through packing, shipping and delivery; support cancellation and returns.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Catalog read p95 under 200 ms with high availability; stale by seconds is acceptable.
Cart always writable (high availability).
Checkout correctness: no oversell, no double charge, no lost order.
Survive a sale peak of 10x to 20x normal traffic.
Full audit trail of order state changes.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 100M product page views/day. 100,000,000 / 86,400 s = ~1,160 rps average; assume 10x sale peak = ~11,600 rps.
Assumption: 95 percent of page views served by CDN and cache. Origin load = 5 percent x 11,600 = ~580 rps at peak.
Assumption: 2M orders/day. 2,000,000 / 86,400 = ~23 orders/s average; assume 20x peak = ~460 orders/s.
Hot item assumption: 50,000 buyers in a 10 s window = 5,000 reservation attempts/s against one inventory key.
Assumption: 3 KB per order record. 2M x 3 KB = 6 GB/day = ~2.2 TB/year before replication.

blocks.title: How do you prevent overselling during a flash sale?
blocks.text: Reserve with an atomic conditional decrement in the inventory store, expire reservations, reject early when stock is zero, split hot counters into buckets or serialise per item, and put a waiting room in front of checkout.

blocks.title: How would you design checkout so retries are safe?
blocks.text: Use a client idempotency key, make each saga step idempotent, store order state, and compensate on failure. Reconcile uncertain payment results asynchronously.

blocks.title: Where would you use caching in this system?
blocks.text: CDN and cache for product pages and images, search results caching, price and promo caches with short TTLs. Never trust a cached price or stock number at checkout; re-read from the source.

items: Separate browse (cache heavy, tolerant) from buy (correct, uncached).
Carts favour availability; inventory and payment favour correctness.
Checkout is an idempotent saga with compensating actions.

Publish order events through an outbox and consume them idempotently.

quiz.q: Why does a cart usually favour availability over strict consistency?
options: Rejecting an add-to-cart loses a sale, while a rare merge anomaly is cheap to fix
quiz.why: The business cost of refusing a write is higher than the cost of occasionally merging two cart versions.

quiz.q: What stops two buyers from purchasing the last unit?
options: A conditional update that decrements only if enough stock remains
quiz.why: The check and the decrement must be one atomic operation in the source of truth.

quiz.q: Why publish OrderPlaced through an outbox?
options: So the event is sent only if the order transaction committed, and never lost
quiz.why: Writing the event row in the same transaction guarantees the order and event agree.

lessons.title: YouTube-style video platform: upload, transcoding, storage, CDN and recommendations

blocks.text: Design a video platform: accept large uploads, convert each video to many formats, store petabytes, stream through a CDN and suggest what to watch next.
In simple words

Someone uploads a video from their phone. The platform cannot show that file directly, because viewers have different screens and internet speeds. So it makes several smaller copies, stores them, and sends the right copy to each viewer from a server near them. It also remembers details about the video and suggests other videos you might like.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Imagine a printing house. An author hands over one master manuscript. The printing house makes a hardcover, a paperback and a pocket edition, stores the copies in a warehouse, and ships stock to local bookshops so readers pick up a copy nearby instead of ordering from the warehouse. A catalogue lists every book and suggests others you may enjoy.

diagram.title: Video platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Uploader / viewer
nodes.detail: Uploads a video in chunks and later plays videos. The player picks a quality level based on measured bandwidth.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates users, rate limits and routes upload, metadata and watch requests.

nodes.label: Upload service
nodes.detail: Receives resumable chunked uploads so a dropped connection continues instead of restarting a multi-gigabyte file.

nodes.label: Metadata service
nodes.detail: Holds title, description, owner, visibility and processing status of each video. Small records, read very often.

nodes.label: Raw object storage
nodes.detail: Durable blob storage for the original uploaded files. Kept so videos can be re-encoded with newer codecs later.

nodes.label: Job queue
nodes.detail: Holds transcoding jobs. Decouples fast uploads from slow, compute-heavy processing and smooths bursts.

nodes.label: Recommendation service
nodes.detail: Suggests videos using watch history and video features. Runs as precomputed candidates plus a light ranking step at request time.

nodes.label: Transcoding workers
nodes.detail: Split the video into segments, encode each into several resolutions and bitrates in parallel, and write playlists.

nodes.label: Rendition storage
nodes.detail: Object storage holding the encoded segments and manifests for every quality level. Origin for the CDN.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.detail: Caches popular segments close to viewers. Most playback traffic is served here and never reaches the origin.

steps.text: The creator starts an upload. The service creates a video record in PROCESSING state and returns an upload session.
The gateway authenticates and routes the chunked upload to the Upload service.
Chunks are written to object storage and assembled. A failed connection resumes from the last stored chunk.
When the file is complete, a VideoUploaded job is queued. The creator gets a quick response while processing continues in the background.
A worker takes the job. Large videos are split into segments so many workers can encode them in parallel.
The worker reads the original file from object storage.
It writes short segments for each resolution and bitrate plus a manifest listing them.
The video status changes to READY, so it becomes visible according to its privacy setting.
A viewer opens the video page. Metadata is read from a cache or store and returns title, owner and the manifest location.
The page also asks for up-next suggestions from precomputed candidates, lightly re-ranked for this viewer.
The player fetches the manifest and the first segments from the nearest CDN node and adapts quality to the available bandwidth.
On a cache miss the CDN pulls the segment from rendition storage once and caches it for the next viewers.

blocks.text: How it works

**Upload must survive bad networks.** Videos are large, and mobile connections drop. The client splits the file into chunks, uploads each with an offset, and can ask the server which chunks it already has. This is a resumable upload, and it avoids restarting a multi-gigabyte transfer from zero.

**Transcoding is an offline pipeline.** One original file is converted into a ladder of renditions (for example several resolutions, each at a few bitrates) cut into short segments of a few seconds. Work is queued, and the video is split so segments are encoded in parallel on many workers. The queue absorbs bursts, retries failed jobs and lets the platform add cheaper capacity for non-urgent work.

**Adaptive streaming makes one video fit every connection.** The player downloads a manifest that lists segments per quality level and switches quality segment by segment depending on measured throughput. Formats such as HLS and MPEG-DASH work this way over plain HTTP, which is why a normal CDN can serve them.

**Storage is huge and mostly cold.** Originals and renditions live in object storage with replication or erasure coding. A small share of videos get most views, so popular segments sit in CDN caches while the long tail is read rarely and can move to cheaper storage tiers. Metadata lives separately in a database because it is small, structured and queried often.

**The CDN carries almost all the bandwidth.** Playback is far larger than upload traffic. Edge caches serve most requests, a regional tier shields the origin, and the origin only sees first requests for unpopular content. Cache hit ratio is the main cost and latency lever.

**Recommendations are a separate, mostly offline system.** At a high level, offline jobs build candidate lists per user from watch history and video similarity, and an online step ranks a few hundred candidates with fresh context such as the current video. Recommendation failures must never block playback; the page simply shows fewer or generic suggestions.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: A video is uploaded once, converted into several sizes, stored, and sent to viewers from a nearby server so it starts quickly.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Upload is chunked and resumable, a queue feeds transcoding workers that produce multiple resolutions in short segments, and a CDN serves those segments to players that choose a quality level.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Segments are encoded in parallel, manifests describe each rendition, metadata is a separate store, and recommendations use precomputed candidates plus an online ranker. CDN hit ratio and origin shielding dominate cost.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Trade-offs include encoding cost versus bandwidth saved (more expensive codecs for popular videos), per-title encoding ladders, tiering cold storage, handling live ingest differently from on-demand, and keeping the recommendation path off the critical path of playback.
Functional requirements

items: Upload videos of many gigabytes with resume support.
Process each video into multiple resolutions and make it playable when ready.
Stream with adaptive quality on phones, TVs and browsers.
Store and show metadata: title, description, owner, visibility, view counts.
Suggest relevant videos on the home and watch pages.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Playback start under about 2 seconds at p95 for popular videos.
Durability of originals and renditions (no lost uploads).
Upload-to-ready within minutes for typical videos; durable queue so no job is lost.
Scale to petabytes of storage and hundreds of Gbps of egress.
Graceful degradation: recommendations and counters may be stale or missing.

items: Assumption: 200,000 uploads/day. 200,000 / 86,400 s = ~2.3 uploads/s average.
Assumption: 300 MB average original. 200,000 x 300 MB = 60,000 GB = ~60 TB/day of raw uploads.
Assumption: renditions total ~0.8x the original size. 60 TB x 0.8 = ~48 TB/day; total new storage ~108 TB/day x 365 = ~39 PB/year before replication.
Assumption: 100M views/day, 5 minutes each at 2.5 Mbps. One view = 300 s x 2.5 Mb/s = 750 Mb = ~94 MB.
Egress: 100M x 94 MB = ~9.4 PB/day; 9.4e15 B x 8 / 86,400 s = ~870 Gbps average, served mostly by the CDN.
