lessons.title: WhatsApp-style messaging: persistent connections, delivery receipts, offline queues and encryption

blocks.text: Design a chat system: keep millions of phones connected, route 1:1 and group messages, show sent, delivered and read ticks, and hold messages for offline users.
In simple words

A chat app keeps an open line between your phone and the company servers. When you send a message, it travels along that line to the server, and the server pushes it down the receiver line. If the receiver is offline, the server keeps the message safe until their phone reconnects. Ticks on the message tell you which step it reached.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a post office with a direct phone line to every customer. A letter handed in at the counter gets a stamp (sent). The clerk rings the recipient and hands it over if they answer (delivered). If nobody answers, the letter waits in a pigeonhole until the recipient comes by. The letters are sealed in envelopes only the recipient can open, so the clerk never reads them.

diagram.title: Messaging platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Sender phone
nodes.detail: Encrypts the message on the device and sends it over its persistent connection. Shows one tick when the server acknowledges.

nodes.label: Connection gateway
nodes.detail: Holds long-lived connections from phones. Stateless about content: it forwards frames and knows only which connection belongs to which user.

nodes.label: Message router
nodes.detail: Finds where the recipient is connected, forwards the message or stores it, and relays delivery and read receipts.

nodes.label: Session map
nodes.detail: Fast in-memory map from user to the gateway that holds their connection. Entries expire if a gateway disappears.

nodes.label: Group service
nodes.detail: Stores group membership and expands one group message into one delivery per member.

nodes.label: Offline queue
nodes.detail: Durable store holding encrypted messages for users who are not connected. Deleted after delivery is acknowledged.

nodes.label: Push provider
nodes.detail: Platform push service used to wake a sleeping phone so it reconnects and fetches queued messages.

nodes.label: Recipient gateway
nodes.detail: The gateway instance that holds the recipient connection. It pushes the message frame down that connection.

nodes.label: Recipient phone
nodes.detail: Decrypts the message locally and sends back a delivery receipt, and later a read receipt.

steps.text: The sender encrypts the message on the phone and sends it over the open connection with a client-generated message id.
The gateway forwards the frame to the router, which immediately acknowledges so the sender sees one tick (server received).
The router looks up which gateway holds the recipient connection. A missing entry means the recipient is offline.
For a group chat the router asks the Group service for the member list and treats each member as one recipient.
For each online member the message is sent to the gateway that holds that member connection.
The gateway pushes the still-encrypted message down the connection and the phone decrypts it.
The phone sends a delivery receipt, which is relayed back to the sender as the second tick.
If a recipient is offline, the ciphertext is written to the offline queue with the message id.
A small push notification wakes the phone. The push carries no message content.
The phone reconnects and announces it is online; the session map is updated.
The router drains queued messages for that user in order. Each message is deleted from the queue once the phone acknowledges it.
Receipts travel back over the sender connection: delivered, then read when the recipient opens the chat.

blocks.text: How it works

**Persistent connections.** Instead of polling, each phone keeps one long-lived connection to a gateway. A server can hold a very large number of idle connections if the runtime is built for many lightweight concurrent tasks. WhatsApp has publicly described using Erlang for exactly this reason. Gateways are stateless about message content, so a failed gateway only means its users reconnect to another one.

**Routing needs a session map.** The router must know which gateway holds a given user connection. A fast in-memory map from user id to gateway id answers this, with short expiry so stale entries heal. If the lookup finds nothing, the recipient is treated as offline and the message goes to the offline queue.

**Delivery guarantees come from ids and acks.** Every message has a client-generated id. The server acknowledges receipt, the recipient acknowledges delivery, and each hop retries until it gets an ack. Retries make delivery at least once, so receivers de-duplicate by message id. Ordering is guaranteed per conversation, not globally, by assigning sequence numbers within a conversation.

**Offline queues hold ciphertext temporarily.** When the recipient is unreachable, the encrypted message waits in a durable queue and a content-free push wakes the phone. On reconnect the queue is drained in order and entries are removed after acknowledgement. The server should keep messages only as long as needed for delivery.

**Groups multiply work.** One group message becomes one delivery per member. The Group service expands membership and the router fans out. Large groups cost more, so groups have size limits, and fan-out is done asynchronously with per-member acks. Read receipts in groups are aggregated rather than shown per member in the transport path.

**End-to-end encryption at a high level.** Messages are encrypted on the sender device with keys only the endpoints hold, so servers route ciphertext they cannot read. The Signal protocol is a widely used design for this, using per-device identity keys, one-time prekeys uploaded to a key server for first contact, and a ratchet that changes keys every message. Groups use a shared sender key distributed to members. The server still sees metadata such as who talks to whom and when.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Your phone stays connected to the chat server. Messages go in one end and come out the other, and if the other phone is off, the server holds the message until it turns on.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Phones hold persistent connections to gateways, a router finds the recipient via a session map, messages are acknowledged at each hop, and offline users get queued messages after a push wakes their phone.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Delivery is at least once with client message ids for de-duplication and per-conversation sequence numbers for ordering. Groups fan out through a membership service. Gateways are stateless about content, so connection failover is a reconnect.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Scaling limits are connection count per host, reconnect storms after an outage, large group fan-out and key distribution. End-to-end encryption moves trust to devices, which complicates multi-device sync, server-side search and abuse detection, and leaves only metadata for the server to protect.
Functional requirements

items: Send and receive 1:1 text and media messages in real time.
Create groups and deliver a message to all members.
Show sent, delivered and read status.
Deliver messages sent while the recipient was offline once they reconnect.
Keep message content private with end-to-end encryption.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Online delivery latency under about 500 ms at p95 within a region.
No message loss: acknowledged messages are delivered at least once.
Per-conversation ordering.
Support hundreds of millions of concurrent connections with horizontal scaling.
Recover from gateway failure by reconnect, without user action.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 500M daily users x 40 messages sent/day = 20B messages/day. 20,000,000,000 / 86,400 s = ~231,000 messages/s average; assume 3x peak = ~700,000 msgs/s.
Assumption: 200M concurrent connections and 250,000 connections per gateway host. 200,000,000 / 250,000 = 800 gateway hosts, plus headroom.
Assumption: 1 KB per encrypted message. 231,000 x 1 KB = ~231 MB/s average through routers.
Assumption: 10 percent of messages wait in the offline queue. 20B x 10% x 1 KB = ~2 TB/day of transient queued data.
Group example: a message to a 200-member group creates 200 deliveries, so 1,000 such messages/s produce 200,000 deliveries/s.

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Connection state machine in the gateway: CONNECTING -> AUTHENTICATED -> ACTIVE -> CLOSING, with heartbeat timeout moving ACTIVE to CLOSING and clearing the session map entry.
MessageRouter.route(msg): look up session; if present forward to that gateway, otherwise append to the offline queue; always ack the sender after durable acceptance.
Per-conversation sequence numbers are assigned by the router so clients can detect gaps and request resends.
GroupService.expand(groupId) returns the member device list for fan-out; membership changes bump a version used in the encryption key.
OfflineDrainer streams queued messages in order and deletes each after the client ack.

blocks.text: Security

items: End-to-end encryption: servers store and route ciphertext only; private keys never leave devices.
Authenticate connections with device-bound credentials and rate limit connection attempts.
Protect metadata: minimise logs, expire queue entries and session data, restrict internal access.
Verify identity keys on first contact (safety numbers) to detect man-in-the-middle attacks.

Server cannot read content; strong privacy.

Private messaging products.

Simple delivery per member.
Cost grows with group size.
Moderate group sizes; cap membership.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: A gateway crashes
All its connected phones drop.
Clients reconnect with jittered backoff to another gateway; session map entries expire; queued messages are delivered on reconnect.
Reconnect storm after an outage
Millions of phones connect at once and overload gateways.
Exponential backoff with random jitter, connection rate limiting and gradual admission.
Duplicate delivery due to retry
User sees the same message twice.
De-duplicate by client message id on the receiver and server.
Offline queue grows without bound
Storage cost and slow drain.
Expire old queued messages, cap per-user queue, drain in batches.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you route a message to a user connected to some gateway?
blocks.text: Keep a session map from user to gateway in a fast store with expiry. The router looks it up, forwards to that gateway, or writes to the offline queue if there is no entry.

blocks.title: How do you show sent, delivered and read ticks?
blocks.text: Server ack on receipt gives sent, recipient device ack gives delivered, and an app-level read event when the chat is opened gives read. Each receipt is itself a small message routed back to the sender with its own retries.

blocks.title: How would you handle a large group chat?
blocks.text: Store membership in a group service, fan out asynchronously per member with per-member acks, cap group size, and use a shared sender key so the message is encrypted once for the group.
Takeaways

items: Persistent connections give instant delivery but require careful connection scaling and reconnect handling.
A session map tells the router where a user is connected; no entry means offline.
Ids and acknowledgements give at-least-once delivery; receivers de-duplicate.
Offline queues store ciphertext only until delivery; push is a content-free wake-up.
End-to-end encryption hides content from servers, but metadata remains visible to them.

quiz.q: Why does each message carry a client-generated id?
options: So retries can be de-duplicated and acknowledgements matched
quiz.why: Retries make delivery at least once, so ids let the receiver ignore duplicates.

quiz.q: What does the push notification for an offline user contain?
options: No message content, only a wake-up so the phone reconnects and fetches
quiz.why: Content stays end-to-end encrypted and flows through the normal channel; push is only a wake-up signal.

quiz.q: What can the server still learn under end-to-end encryption?
options: Metadata such as who messaged whom and when
quiz.why: Encryption hides content, not routing metadata, which the server needs to deliver messages.

lessons.title: Instagram-style feed: photo upload, follower graph, fan-out and caching

blocks.text: Design a photo-sharing feed: store images, track who follows whom, build each home feed fast, and decide between fan-out on write and fan-out on read.
In simple words

People post photos, and each person sees a home feed made of photos from the people they follow. The hard part is making that feed appear instantly even when millions of people post and follow each other. The system prepares feeds in advance for most users and builds them on demand for a few special ones.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a newspaper delivery service. For ordinary writers, when a story is published a copy is dropped in every subscriber mailbox straight away, so reading is instant. For a famous columnist with fifty million subscribers, dropping that many copies would take forever, so subscribers fetch the columnist latest story from the newsstand when they open their paper.

diagram.title: Photo feed platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Mobile app
nodes.detail: Uploads photos, creates posts and opens the feed. Requests the next page of the feed with a cursor.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates users, rate limits and routes to the media, post and feed services.

nodes.label: Media service
nodes.detail: Accepts the photo, creates resized versions and returns a media id. Images are served through a CDN.

nodes.label: Post service
nodes.detail: Stores the post record (author, caption, media id, time) and publishes a PostCreated event.

nodes.label: Feed service
nodes.detail: Builds a feed page: reads the precomputed list, merges in posts from celebrity accounts, filters and ranks.

nodes.label: Photo storage + CDN
nodes.detail: Object storage for originals and resized images, fronted by a CDN so most image bytes never hit storage.

nodes.label: Post events
nodes.detail: Durable event log. Fan-out workers consume PostCreated at their own pace so posting stays fast.

nodes.label: Fan-out workers
nodes.detail: For each new post, look up followers and push the post id into their feed lists. Skip accounts above a follower threshold.

nodes.label: Follower graph
nodes.detail: Stores who follows whom in both directions: followers of a user and followees of a user. Sharded by user id.

nodes.label: Feed cache
nodes.detail: Per-user list of recent post ids in memory, capped to a few hundred entries. Reads are a single list fetch.

steps.text: The user picks a photo. The app uploads it first and the caption is sent separately.
The Media service validates the file and returns quickly with a media id while resizing continues.
The original and several resized versions are stored in object storage and served later through a CDN.
The user taps share; the app sends the media id and caption to create the post.
The Post service saves the post record and returns success, so the user is not waiting for any fan-out.
A PostCreated event is published after the database commit.
A fan-out worker picks up the event.
The worker loads the author followers from the follower graph in pages.
It pushes the post id onto each follower feed list. Accounts above the follower threshold are skipped (pull model).
A follower opens the app and requests the feed.
The gateway routes the request to the Feed service.
The Feed service reads the precomputed id list, adds recent posts from followed celebrity accounts, ranks them and loads post details for the page.

blocks.text: How it works

**Two data shapes drive everything.** Posts and photos are write-once and read-many, so they cache well. The follower graph is a many-to-many relation that needs two lookups: who follows me (used to fan out) and whom I follow (used to build a feed on read). Both directions are stored, sharded by user id.

**Fan-out on write (push).** When a user posts, workers copy the post id into the feed list of every follower. Reading the feed is then one fast cache read. The cost moves to write time: a user with 200 followers causes 200 list inserts, which is cheap, but an account with 50 million followers causes 50 million.

**Fan-out on read (pull).** Nothing is precomputed. When a user opens the feed, the service fetches the recent posts of everyone they follow and merges them. Writes are cheap and always fresh, but reads touch many accounts, so latency grows with the number of people followed.

**Hybrid is the practical answer.** Push for ordinary accounts, pull for accounts above a follower threshold. At read time the feed service merges the precomputed list with fresh posts from the few high-follower accounts the user follows. This bounds write amplification while keeping reads fast, at the price of a slightly more complex read path.

**Photos are served by CDN.** Upload creates several resized variants so each device downloads an appropriately sized image. The CDN caches them near users, and image bytes dominate traffic. The feed itself carries only ids and small metadata, which is why the feed cache can hold hundreds of entries per user cheaply.

**Stories and caching.** Stories are short-lived posts, so they use the same graph but with a time-to-live: a per-user list of story ids that expires after 24 hours, which suits a cache with TTL. Feeds, post records and hot follower lists are cached; cache entries are rebuilt from the database when missing, so a cache loss slows the system but does not lose data.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: When someone posts, the app puts that post into the feeds of their followers ahead of time, so opening the app is instant. For very famous people it fetches their posts when you look instead.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Posts are stored once, an event triggers fan-out workers that push post ids into each follower feed list in a cache, and the read path loads that list. Accounts with huge followings use fan-out on read.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Write amplification equals follower count, so a threshold splits push and pull. The graph stores both edge directions, the feed cache holds capped lists of ids, and ranking happens after retrieval. Events make fan-out asynchronous and retryable.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Design questions include the threshold choice, backfilling a feed when a user follows someone new, removing posts from feeds after a delete or block, hot-key handling for celebrity graphs, cache warming after failures, and keeping ranking models separate from retrieval so each can change independently.
Functional requirements

items: Upload photos with a caption and share them as posts.
Follow and unfollow users.
Show a home feed of recent posts from followed accounts, paginated.
Show stories that disappear after 24 hours.
Like and comment on posts (counts shown on the feed).

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Feed load p95 under 500 ms.
Posting returns in about a second; the post appears in followers feeds within seconds.
High availability for reads; eventual consistency for feeds is acceptable.
Durable storage of photos and posts.
Handle accounts with tens of millions of followers without delaying other users.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 200M daily users and 20M new posts/day. 20,000,000 / 86,400 s = ~231 posts/s average.
Assumption: 200 followers on average. 20M x 200 = 4B feed inserts/day; 4,000,000,000 / 86,400 = ~46,000 inserts/s.
Assumption: 10 feed opens per user per day. 200M x 10 = 2B/day; 2,000,000,000 / 86,400 = ~23,000 feed reads/s average, ~70,000 at 3x peak.
Feed cache sizing: 800 post ids x 8 bytes = 6.4 KB per user; 200M x 6.4 KB = ~1.3 TB.

Celebrity case: 1 post to 50M followers at 46,000 inserts/s = 50,000,000 / 46,000 = ~1,090 s (about 18 minutes), which is why such accounts use pull. Photo storage: 20M x 1 MB total across sizes = ~20 TB/day.

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: PostService.create(): write post row, write outbox row in the same transaction, relay publishes PostCreated.
FanoutWorker.handle(event): if author follower_count is above the threshold, stop; otherwise page through followers and LPUSH post id to each feed list with a cap, idempotent by post id.

Feed rebuild path: if a list is missing, rebuild from followees recent posts, then cache it.

blocks.text: Security

items: Authenticate every call; enforce account privacy so private accounts only expose posts to approved followers.
Respect blocks at read time so blocked users never see each other content, even from stale feed lists.
Validate and re-encode uploaded images; strip location metadata unless the user opts in.
Rate limit follow, like and post actions to resist spam and scraping.

Avoids writing to dormant feeds.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Fan-out on write or on read?
blocks.text: Use a hybrid. Push post ids to follower feed lists for ordinary accounts so reads are one cache fetch, and pull posts from high-follower accounts at read time. The threshold limits write amplification while keeping reads fast.

blocks.title: How do you store the follower graph?
blocks.text: Store edges in both directions (followers-of and followees-of), sharded by user id, with paginated reads. Cache hot lists and handle celebrity keys with replication or dedicated storage.

blocks.title: How would stories differ from posts?
blocks.text: Same graph, but entries expire after a fixed time, so a TTL list per user fits. Viewing state (who has seen the story) is tracked separately and also expires.
Takeaways

items: Feeds are lists of post ids; photos and details are loaded separately and served via CDN.
Fan-out on write makes reads fast but costs one write per follower.
Fan-out on read keeps writes cheap but makes reads slow for people who follow many accounts.
A follower-count threshold gives a hybrid that bounds both costs.
Make fan-out asynchronous with events and idempotent workers.
Caches speed reads, but the database and graph remain the source of truth.

quiz.q: Why not use fan-out on write for every account?
options: An account with tens of millions of followers causes tens of millions of writes per post
quiz.why: Write amplification equals follower count, which is unbounded for very popular accounts.

quiz.q: What does the feed cache store?
options: A capped list of post ids per user
quiz.why: Ids are tiny, so hundreds per user fit in memory; post details and images are loaded separately.

quiz.q: Why publish PostCreated as an event instead of fanning out inside the post request?
options: So the poster is not kept waiting and fan-out can be retried and scaled separately
quiz.why: Asynchronous fan-out keeps posting fast and lets workers retry independently.

lessons.title: Design a payment gateway: authorize, capture, never charge twice

blocks.text: A payment gateway moves money safely between a merchant and a card network. The hard parts are idempotency, a trustworthy ledger, webhooks and keeping card data out of your systems.
In simple words

A payment gateway is the middleman that lets a shop take a card payment. The shop sends the amount, the gateway asks the card network if the money is available, and then reports back. The main promise is simple: a customer is never charged twice, and no payment is ever lost, even when networks fail halfway through.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a hotel that puts a hold on your card at check-in and takes the real payment at check-out. The hold is the authorization and the final charge is the capture. A careful cashier writes every movement of money in a book with two columns, so the book always balances. If the phone line drops mid-payment, the cashier looks up the receipt number instead of charging again.

diagram.title: Payment gateway (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Merchant
nodes.detail: The shop checkout page and backend. The page sends card details straight to the vault; the backend creates the payment using only a token.

nodes.label: Payment API
nodes.detail: Authenticates the merchant, validates the request and enforces idempotency keys before any money logic runs.

nodes.label: Idempotency store
nodes.detail: Maps (merchant, idempotency key) to the first request hash and its saved response. A retry returns the saved response instead of running again.

nodes.label: Token vault
nodes.detail: The only place that holds real card numbers, encrypted, in a small isolated network zone. Everyone else handles random tokens.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.detail: Owns the payment state machine: CREATED, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED, VOIDED, REFUNDED, FAILED. Every transition is a conditional update.

nodes.label: Card network / acquirer
nodes.detail: The external bank-side system that approves the hold and moves the money. Slow and sometimes unreachable, so calls need timeouts.

nodes.label: Ledger (double-entry)
nodes.detail: Append-only rows of debits and credits that always sum to zero. Balances are derived from it, never edited directly.

nodes.label: Event queue
nodes.detail: Durable queue carrying payment events. Written in the same transaction as the state change through an outbox table.

nodes.label: Webhook worker
nodes.detail: Signs and delivers events to the merchant, retrying with backoff until acknowledged.

nodes.label: Reconciliation job
nodes.detail: Daily job that compares the ledger with the settlement file from the acquirer and flags every mismatch for review.

steps.text: The customer types the card into a field served by the gateway. The number goes straight to the vault, which returns a token such as tok_abc. The merchant servers never see the card number.
The merchant backend sends POST /payments with the token, amount, currency and an Idempotency-Key header it generated for this checkout attempt.
The API looks up the key. If it is new, it is stored as in progress. If it exists with the same request hash, the saved response is returned. If the hash differs, the request is rejected.
The validated request reaches the payment service, which creates the payment row in state CREATED.
The service asks the vault to use the token. The vault attaches the real card data inside its own zone when it calls the acquirer, so the service still never holds it.
Authorization request with a timeout. On approval the state moves CREATED to AUTHORIZED. A timeout leaves the state as unknown and a status check is scheduled.
In one database transaction the service writes the state change and the journal entry: debit customer funds in flight, credit merchant pending balance.
When the merchant ships, a capture call turns the hold into a charge. The state becomes CAPTURED and the ledger gets a second entry.
An outbox row written in the same transaction is published as a payment.captured event.
The webhook worker picks up the event and builds the signed payload.
The merchant endpoint returns 2xx to acknowledge. Anything else is retried with growing delays for several days.
Next day the reconciliation job downloads the settlement file and compares each line with the ledger, flagging missing, extra or different amounts.

blocks.text: How it works

**Authorize then capture.** Authorization reserves funds without moving them. Capture takes them. Splitting the two lets a merchant authorize at order time and capture at shipping, and void the hold if the order is cancelled. A payment is a state machine, and each transition is a conditional update such as `UPDATE ... SET state = CAPTURED WHERE id = ? AND state = AUTHORIZED`. This makes two racing capture calls safe: only one row update succeeds.

**Idempotency keys.** Networks drop responses, so clients retry, and a retry must not charge twice. The client generates a unique key per logical attempt and sends it in a header. The server stores the key with a hash of the request and the final response, using a unique constraint on (merchant, key). A repeat with the same key returns the stored response; the same key with a different body is an error. Keys are kept for roughly a day or more. The same idea applies on the outbound call to the acquirer, using a reference the acquirer treats as unique.

**Double-entry ledger.** Every money movement is a journal entry with at least two lines, and debits equal credits. Rows are append-only: a mistake is fixed by a reversing entry, never by an update. Balances are sums over entries, often cached in a balance table updated in the same transaction. Because the books always balance, any bug that creates or destroys money shows up as a non-zero total, which is easy to alert on.

**Unknown outcomes.** The hardest case is a timeout after the request was sent. The money may or may not have moved. The service must not retry blindly or mark the payment failed. It records the state as pending, queries the acquirer for the status using the same reference, and resolves it. Reconciliation is the final safety net for anything this process misses.

**Webhooks.** The gateway delivers events at least once, so merchants must handle duplicates using the event id. Payloads are signed with a shared secret so the merchant can verify the sender, and delivery is retried with exponential backoff. The merchant should also be able to fetch the payment by id, because webhooks can arrive late or out of order.

**PCI scope reduction.** Card numbers are the most sensitive data in the system. Tokenization keeps them in one small vault zone, and everything else works with tokens. Hosted fields or a redirect mean the merchant page never touches the number either. The smaller the zone that stores, processes or transmits card data, the less infrastructure falls under the strictest compliance rules and the smaller the blast radius of a breach.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The shop asks the gateway to charge a card. The gateway checks with the bank, records the result in a careful book, and tells the shop. If the shop asks twice because of a bad connection, the gateway recognises the repeat and does not charge twice.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: A payment moves through states: created, authorized, captured. An idempotency key makes retries safe. A double-entry ledger records every movement. Webhooks tell the merchant the outcome, and a nightly reconciliation compares the ledger with the bank report.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: State changes are conditional updates, the ledger entry and outbox event commit in the same transaction, and timeouts create an explicit unknown state resolved by status queries. Idempotency uses a unique constraint on merchant and key plus a request hash to catch key reuse with different data.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Correctness comes from invariants rather than happy paths: debits equal credits, every external call has a durable intent recorded before it is made, and every unknown outcome has an owner that resolves it. Shard by merchant to keep ledger transactions local, keep the vault in a separate network and key-management boundary, and treat reconciliation as a first-class pipeline with its own SLOs.
Functional requirements

items: Create a payment from a token with amount, currency and merchant reference.
Authorize, capture (full or partial), void and refund a payment.
Accept a client-supplied idempotency key on every write call.
Deliver signed webhooks for every state change and let the merchant fetch payments by id.
Record every money movement in a ledger and produce settlement reports per merchant.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Correctness over availability: never double charge, never lose a payment.
Authorization latency p99 under about 2 seconds, mostly bound by the acquirer.
High availability of the create-payment path, with graceful degradation to pending states.
Durable and auditable: every state change and ledger entry is persisted and immutable.
Card data confined to the vault zone with encryption, access logging and key rotation.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 20M payments per day. 20,000,000 / 86,400 s = ~230 payments per second on average.
Assumption: peak is 10x average during a sale. 230 x 10 = ~2,300 payments per second at peak.
Assumption: each payment writes about 1 payment row, 4 ledger lines and 3 events. About 8 rows x 2,300 = ~18,000 row writes per second at peak.
Assumption: ~1 KB per payment row plus ledger. 20M x 1 KB x 365 = ~7.3 TB per year before indexes and replicas.
Assumption: idempotency keys kept 24 hours at 200 bytes each. 20M x 200 B = ~4 GB, which fits in memory or a small table.

POST

Capture an authorized payment, full or partial amount.
POST

POST

blocks.text: Data model

rows: payments
id, merchant_id, amount, currency, state, token_id, acquirer_ref, created_at, version
Relational database sharded by merchant_id
idempotency_keys
merchant_id, key, request_hash, response_body, status, created_at
Relational table with unique (merchant_id, key); optional cache in front

entry_id, txn_id, account_id, direction, amount, currency, created_at
Append-only relational table; per-transaction sum of debits equals credits
outbox_events
id, payment_id, type, payload, published_at
Same database as payments, drained to the queue

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: PaymentStateMachine: a table of allowed transitions (CREATED to AUTHORIZED, AUTHORIZED to CAPTURED or VOIDED, CAPTURED to REFUNDED). Every transition is a conditional update that checks the current state and bumps a version.

IdempotencyGuard: begin(merchant, key, hash) inserts a row; on a unique violation it loads the existing row and either returns the saved response, reports in-progress, or raises key-reuse error if the hash differs.
AcquirerClient: wraps the external call with timeout, a stable reference per attempt, and a status-query method. Returns APPROVED, DECLINED or UNKNOWN; UNKNOWN schedules a resolver job.
LedgerPoster: takes a list of balanced lines, verifies sum of debits equals credits, and inserts them with the payment state change in one transaction.
WebhookDispatcher: reads outbox events, signs the payload with HMAC, posts to the merchant URL and reschedules with exponential backoff until a 2xx arrives.

blocks.text: Security

items: Keep card numbers only in the vault zone, encrypted with keys held in a key management service and rotated; never log card data.
Authenticate merchants with API keys or signed requests, scope keys to test or live mode, and rate limit per merchant.
Sign webhooks with HMAC and a timestamp so merchants can verify the sender and reject replays.
Restrict ledger and vault access by role, audit every read of sensitive data and alert on unusual volumes.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Synchronous authorize and capture in one call
Simple for the merchant and one fewer state.
No way to adjust or cancel before the charge; refunds are needed for every cancellation.
Digital goods that are delivered instantly.
Separate authorize, then capture later
Holds can be voided free of charge; suits shipping and hotels.
Holds expire, so capture must happen inside the authorization window; more states to manage.
Physical goods, travel, anything fulfilled after ordering.
Idempotency in a fast cache only
Very quick lookups.
Losing the cache can allow duplicate charges.
Never as the only guard. Use a database unique constraint, optionally with a cache in front.
Own the vault vs use a third-party tokenization service
Own vault gives control and lower per-call cost at scale.
Full compliance burden and security operations.
Build only at large scale; otherwise buy.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Timeout after the authorization request was sent
The customer may be on hold without the system knowing, or a retry may create a second hold.
Mark the payment pending, retry only with the same unique reference, query the acquirer for status, and rely on reconciliation as backup.
Client retries the same payment during a slow response
Without protection the customer is charged twice.
Idempotency key with a unique constraint; return the stored response for repeats and reject key reuse with a different body.
Merchant webhook endpoint is down for hours
The merchant never learns the order was paid and may not ship.
Retry with backoff for days, expose a fetch-payment API and a dashboard for failed deliveries, and alert on rising backlog.
Ledger and acquirer disagree after settlement
Money is missing or extra in merchant balances.
Daily reconciliation, a mismatch queue with human review, and reversing entries instead of editing history.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you guarantee a customer is never charged twice?
blocks.text: Idempotency keys enforced by a unique constraint on merchant and key, a request hash to catch misuse, conditional state transitions so concurrent captures cannot both win, a stable reference on the acquirer call, and reconciliation to catch anything that slips through.

blocks.title: Why double-entry bookkeeping instead of a balance column?
blocks.text: Each movement is recorded as balanced debit and credit lines, so money cannot appear or vanish unnoticed. Balances are derived or cached from entries, history is append-only, and errors are corrected by reversing entries. A single balance column loses the audit trail.

blocks.title: How do you reduce PCI scope?
blocks.text: Collect card data with hosted fields or a redirect so merchant systems never see it, store it only in an isolated encrypted vault, and pass tokens everywhere else. Restrict network access and keys around the vault and keep logs free of card data.
Takeaways

items: A payment is a state machine; every transition is a conditional update.
Idempotency keys with a database unique constraint make retries safe.
A timeout is an unknown outcome, so check the status instead of guessing.
Double-entry, append-only ledgers make money bugs visible.
Webhooks are at-least-once, signed, and backed by a fetch API.
Tokenization keeps card data in one small, isolated zone.

quiz.q: A client times out and retries POST /payments with the same Idempotency-Key. What should the server do?
options: Create a second payment because the first response was never seen
Return the stored result of the first attempt without charging again
Reject all retries with an error
quiz.why: The key identifies one logical attempt, so a repeat must return the original outcome.

quiz.q: Why is the ledger append-only?
options: It keeps a complete audit trail and corrections are visible as reversing entries
Databases cannot update rows with foreign keys
quiz.why: History that can be edited cannot be trusted for audit or reconciliation.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of tokenization for PCI scope?
options: Tokens are faster to process than card numbers
Only the small vault zone handles real card data, so the rest of the system is out of the strictest scope
It removes the need for TLS
quiz.why: Fewer systems touching card data means less to secure and audit.

quiz.q: An acquirer call times out. What is the safest next move?
options: Mark the payment failed and let the customer try again
Retry immediately with a new reference
Mark it pending and query the status using the same reference
quiz.why: The outcome is unknown, so it must be resolved by checking, not by guessing.

lessons.title: Design a ticket booking system: holds, double booking and flash demand

blocks.text: Selling a seat exactly once under a rush of buyers needs temporary holds with a time limit, atomic claims, a payment timeout and a queue to protect the system.
In simple words

When a popular show goes on sale, thousands of people try to buy the same few seats at once. The system must make sure each seat is sold to only one person. While you pay, the seat is kept aside for you for a few minutes, and if you do not finish, it goes back on sale.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a cinema box office with one till. When you pick a seat, the clerk puts a reserved card on it and starts a timer. If you pay before the timer ends, the seat is yours. If not, the clerk takes the card off. Outside, a doorman lets people in a few at a time so the counter is never crushed.

diagram.title: Ticket booking (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Buyer app
nodes.detail: Shows the seat map and a countdown for the hold. Polls or listens for queue position during high demand.

nodes.label: Waiting room
nodes.detail: Virtual queue that admits buyers at a rate the booking path can handle and hands out short-lived admission tokens.

nodes.label: Booking API
nodes.detail: Verifies the admission token, authenticates the user and applies per-user limits before touching inventory.

nodes.label: Inventory service
nodes.detail: Owns seat state and the rules for holding, confirming and releasing seats.

nodes.label: Hold store (Redis)
nodes.detail: Short-lived keys such as hold:event:seat with a TTL. Created with set-if-not-exists, so only one buyer can win a seat.

nodes.label: Seat database
nodes.detail: Source of truth for seat status AVAILABLE, HELD, SOLD and for bookings. Confirmation is a conditional update.

nodes.label: Payment service
nodes.detail: Creates a payment for the hold and reports success, failure or timeout back to inventory.

nodes.label: Payment provider
nodes.detail: External card or wallet processor. Can be slow, so the hold TTL must be longer than the normal payment time.

nodes.label: Expiry sweeper
nodes.detail: Background job that finds holds past their expiry and returns the seats to AVAILABLE, as a backup to TTL expiry.

steps.text: On sale day 500,000 people open the page at once. Each is put in the waiting room and given a place in line.
The room admits a few thousand buyers per minute. Each admitted buyer receives a signed token valid for a short time.
The buyer picks seats 14 and 15. The API checks the token and forwards the request to inventory.
Inventory tries to create a hold key for each seat with set-if-not-exists and a 10 minute TTL. If any seat fails, the whole request is rolled back and the buyer is told those seats are gone.
With the seats held, inventory asks the payment service to start a payment for the total and sends the buyer to the pay page with a countdown.
The payment provider charges the card. The idempotency key is the hold id, so a retry never charges twice.
Payment success is reported to inventory. A failure or timeout is reported too, so the hold can be released early.
On success inventory runs a conditional update: set seat SOLD where status is HELD by this hold id. If zero rows change, the hold expired and the payment is refunded.
For holds that expired without payment, the sweeper sets seats back to AVAILABLE so they can be sold again.

blocks.text: How it works

**The core problem is a race.** Two buyers click the same seat within the same millisecond. Whatever the design, claiming a seat must be one atomic operation: set-if-not-exists in Redis, or a conditional update in the database such as `UPDATE seats SET status = HELD WHERE id = ? AND status = AVAILABLE`. Reading the seat and then writing it in two steps always leaves a window where both buyers win.

**Temporary holds with a TTL.** Payment takes minutes, so a seat cannot be sold at click time nor left free. A hold marks the seat as taken for a fixed time, commonly a few minutes. A key with an expiry in Redis releases itself automatically, which removes the need for a cleanup job on the hot path. The database stores the hold id and expiry as well, so the final confirmation can verify the hold is still valid, and a sweeper corrects any drift.

**Confirm with a conditional update.** After payment succeeds, the seat moves to SOLD only if it is still held by this hold id. This is the line that prevents double booking, because even if the cache was lost or a hold expired during a slow payment, the database refuses the second claim. If the update fails, the money is refunded automatically and the buyer is told.

**Payment timeouts.** The hold TTL must be longer than the normal payment time plus a margin, but short enough that abandoned seats return quickly. If the provider is slow and the hold expires while a charge is in flight, the result is ambiguous. The safe approach is to accept a late success only if the seat is still free or still held by the same buyer, otherwise refund.

**Flash demand.** Popular events create a spike far above normal traffic. A waiting room admits buyers at a controlled rate, which protects inventory and the database, and makes the experience fair and predictable. Seat map reads are served from a cache or CDN with short staleness, since showing a seat as free that has just been taken is acceptable but selling it twice is not. Hot events can be placed on their own shard so they do not affect others.

**Best-available and group seating.** Holding several seats must be all-or-nothing. Seats are claimed in a fixed order, for example sorted by seat id, to avoid two buyers each holding part of what the other needs. If any claim fails, previously claimed seats in that request are released immediately.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: When you choose a seat, the system keeps it for you for a few minutes while you pay. If you pay in time it is yours. If not, it becomes free again. Only one person can hold a seat at any moment.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: A hold is created with an atomic set-if-not-exists and a TTL. Payment runs while the hold is active. Confirmation is a conditional database update, and a waiting room limits how many buyers reach the booking path at once.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Redis provides fast hold claims, but the database is the final arbiter through a conditional update keyed by hold id. Multi-seat holds are all-or-nothing with a fixed claim order, payment uses the hold id as an idempotency key, and late payments after expiry follow a refund rule.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Treat the hold store as an optimisation and the database as the authority, so cache loss degrades throughput but never correctness. Partition inventory by event, size the waiting room admission rate from measured database write capacity, and design for the ambiguous case of a charge succeeding after hold expiry with an explicit reconciliation path.
Functional requirements

items: Show events, venues and a live seat map with availability.
Hold selected seats for a limited time and show a countdown.
Pay for a hold and confirm the booking, issuing tickets after success.
Release seats automatically when a hold expires or payment fails.
Admit buyers through a waiting room during high-demand sales.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Strong correctness: a seat is never sold twice.
Seat claim latency p99 under about 200 ms once admitted.
Survive spikes of 100x normal traffic for minutes without failing.
Fairness: first-in-line is served first within the waiting room.
Availability of browsing even when booking is throttled.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: one big on-sale with 500,000 buyers arriving within 5 minutes. 500,000 / 300 s = ~1,700 arrivals per second.
Assumption: venue has 50,000 seats and each purchase takes 2 seats. At most 25,000 successful purchases for the event.
Assumption: waiting room admits 3,000 buyers per minute. 3,000 / 60 = 50 admissions per second, so 500,000 buyers drain in about 500,000 / 3,000 = ~170 minutes.
Assumption: about 5 hold attempts per admitted buyer. 50 x 5 = ~250 claim operations per second, well within one Redis node.
Assumption: 10 minute hold and 50,000 seats. Worst case 50,000 hold keys at 100 bytes = ~5 MB of memory.

POST
`/queue/join`
Join the waiting room for an event; returns position and a polling token.
POST
`/holds`
Hold one or more seats; requires an admission token; returns hold id and expiry.
POST
`/holds/{id}/pay`
Start payment for a hold with an idempotency key equal to the hold id.

rows: seats
event_id, seat_id, status, hold_id, hold_expires_at, booking_id

holds
hold_id, user_id, event_id, seat_ids, expires_at, state

bookings
booking_id, user_id, event_id, seat_ids, payment_id, status, created_at
Relational database

event_id, user_id, position, admitted_at, token_expires_at

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: SeatState: AVAILABLE to HELD (with hold id and expiry) to SOLD, and HELD back to AVAILABLE on expiry or release. SOLD never goes back except by an explicit cancellation flow.
HoldService.hold(seatIds, user): sorts seat ids, claims each with set-if-not-exists, and on the first failure releases the ones already claimed and returns the conflicting seats.
BookingSaga: states HOLD_CREATED, PAYMENT_PENDING, PAID, CONFIRMED, REFUNDED. A late payment after expiry moves to REFUNDED unless the seat is still free or held by the same buyer.
ExpirySweeper: scans seats where status is HELD and hold_expires_at is in the past, and sets them AVAILABLE with a conditional update on the same hold id.
AdmissionController: releases N buyers per interval from the queue and signs tokens containing user id, event id and expiry.

blocks.text: Security

items: Sign admission tokens and bind them to user and event so they cannot be shared or reused for another event.
Rate limit per user, device and IP, and add bot checks at the waiting room entrance.
Never trust seat availability sent by the client; the server decides on every hold and confirmation.
Use idempotency keys on payment and keep payment data with the payment provider, not in the booking database.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Pessimistic hold (reserve then pay)
Buyer is sure of the seat while paying; no failed purchases after card entry.
Abandoned holds block inventory until they expire.
Scarce, high-demand seats where a failed purchase after paying is unacceptable.
Optimistic booking (pay then claim)
No inventory is locked by people who do not pay.
Buyers can pay and then lose the seat; refunds and anger.
Plentiful inventory such as general admission.
Redis holds with database confirmation
Very fast claims, correctness guarded by the database.
Two stores to keep consistent and a sweeper to repair drift.
Large events with heavy claim traffic.
Database-only locking
One store, simple reasoning.
Row contention and lock waits under a rush on few seats.
Smaller events or moderate demand.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Redis loses all hold keys
Seats appear free while buyers are mid-payment, so two people could try to pay for one seat.
Database conditional update at confirmation rejects the second claim; rebuild holds from the database; refund the loser automatically.
Payment provider is slow and the hold expires mid-charge
Money is taken for a seat that may now belong to someone else.
Accept late success only if the seat is still free or held by the same buyer, otherwise refund; extend the hold once while a payment is in progress.
Bots grab seats and never pay
Inventory is locked and real fans are shut out.
Waiting room tokens, per-user and per-device limits, CAPTCHA at admission, and shorter holds after repeated abandoned carts.
Traffic spike overwhelms the booking path
Timeouts, retries and a cascade of failures.
Admit buyers at a fixed rate from the waiting room, serve seat maps from cache, and shed load early with clear messages.

blocks.text: Evidence for claims

rows: Atomic set-if-not-exists with a TTL is a standard way to implement temporary holds.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you prevent double booking?
blocks.text: Make every seat claim atomic: set-if-not-exists in the hold store and a conditional update in the database where status must be HELD by this hold id. The database decision is final, so even a cache failure cannot sell a seat twice. Multi-seat requests are all-or-nothing in a fixed order.

blocks.title: How long should a seat hold last and what happens when it expires?
blocks.text: Long enough for normal payment plus a margin, typically a few minutes, but short so abandoned seats return fast. On expiry the key disappears and a sweeper resets the database row. A late payment is accepted only if the seat is still available or held by the same buyer, else refunded.

blocks.title: How do you handle a million users arriving at once?
blocks.text: Put a waiting room in front that admits users at a rate matching measured write capacity, issue short-lived admission tokens, serve seat maps from cache, limit per user and device to stop bots, and isolate hot events on their own capacity.
Takeaways

items: Seat claiming must be one atomic operation, never read then write.
Holds with a TTL make seats temporarily unavailable and release themselves.
The database conditional update is the final guard against double booking.
Payment timeouts need a clear rule for late success: accept or refund.
A waiting room turns a flash spike into a controlled flow.

quiz.q: Two buyers choose the same seat at the same instant. What makes only one succeed?
options: Reading the seat and then writing it
An atomic claim such as set-if-not-exists or a conditional update
quiz.why: Check-then-write has a gap; an atomic claim has none.

quiz.q: Why does the database still do a conditional update at confirmation when Redis already held the seat?
options: The cache can lose data or the hold can expire, and the database is the authority
It makes the page load faster
quiz.why: Correctness must not depend on the cache surviving.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a waiting room?
options: To make buyers wait for no reason
To admit users at a rate the booking path can handle and keep it fair
quiz.why: It converts a huge spike into a steady controlled flow.

lessons.title: Design live streaming: ingest, transcode, segment, CDN and chat

blocks.text: A live stream is cut into small video files while it is being made, converted to several qualities and delivered through a CDN. Latency, cost and scale pull against each other, and live chat is a separate fan-out problem.
In simple words

In a live stream, one person films and thousands of people watch at almost the same moment. The video is chopped into tiny pieces a few seconds long, copied in several qualities so slow phones and fast TVs can both watch, and spread to servers near the viewers. A separate system carries the chat messages.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a live radio show passed through a relay of local stations. The studio sends the show to a central plant, which makes loud, medium and quiet copies and cuts them into short tapes. Each local station keeps the latest tapes and hands them to listeners in its area, so the studio never serves each listener directly.

diagram.title: Live streaming (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Broadcaster
nodes.detail: Encoder software or app that captures camera and microphone and sends one high-quality stream upward.

nodes.label: Ingest edge
nodes.detail: Accepts the incoming stream over RTMP or WebRTC at a point close to the broadcaster and authenticates the stream key.

nodes.label: Transcoder
nodes.detail: Decodes the stream and re-encodes it into a ladder of resolutions and bitrates. CPU or GPU heavy, one job per live stream.

nodes.label: Packager
nodes.detail: Cuts each rendition into short segments and writes playlists (HLS) or manifests (DASH) listing the newest segments.

nodes.label: Origin storage
nodes.detail: Holds the latest segments and playlists. The single source the CDN pulls from.

nodes.label: CDN
nodes.detail: Caches segments close to viewers. Many viewers of the same segment cost the origin one fetch.

nodes.label: Viewer player
nodes.detail: Downloads the playlist, picks a quality that fits its bandwidth and keeps requesting the next segment.

nodes.label: Chat service
nodes.detail: Receives chat messages, applies moderation and rate limits, and publishes them to the channel topic.

nodes.label: Pub/sub bus
nodes.detail: Fan-out layer. One message published to a channel is delivered to every gateway holding viewers of that channel.

nodes.label: WebSocket gateways
nodes.detail: Hold long-lived connections to viewers and push each message down the socket.

steps.text: The broadcaster presses Go Live. The encoder connects to the nearest ingest server using a secret stream key and sends a 1080p stream at about 6 Mbps.
The ingest edge forwards the stream to a transcoder assigned to this channel.
The transcoder produces a ladder of renditions, for example 1080p, 720p, 480p and 360p, with keyframes aligned across all of them.
Each rendition is cut into segments of about 2 to 6 seconds. Segments are uploaded and the playlist is updated to list the newest ones.
A viewer opens the stream. The player requests the master playlist, then a rendition playlist, then segments, starting at the newest ones.
On the first request for a new segment the CDN edge pulls it from the origin and caches it. The next 10,000 viewers on that edge are served from cache.
The player measures download speed each segment and switches renditions up or down to avoid buffering.
A viewer types a message. It goes over the open connection to the chat service, which checks rate limits and moderation rules.
The message is published to the topic for this channel.
Every gateway that holds viewers of this channel receives one copy from the bus.
Each gateway writes the message to its connected viewers. Very busy channels sample or batch messages so screens remain readable.

blocks.text: How it works

**Ingest protocols.** RTMP is the long-standing way encoders push to a server and is simple and widely supported, with a delay of a few seconds. WebRTC ingest cuts that to well under a second and works from a browser, but is harder to scale because it is connection-oriented and uses UDP. Ingest nodes sit at the edge close to broadcasters, authenticate the stream key, and hand the stream to the processing pipeline.

**Transcoding ladder.** Viewers have very different bandwidth and devices, so each stream is re-encoded into several renditions, for example 1080p at 6 Mbps down to 360p at 0.8 Mbps. Keyframes are aligned so the player can switch quality at any segment boundary. Transcoding is the biggest compute cost, so popular channels get the full ladder while small ones may get fewer rungs or are transcoded only when someone watches.

**Segments and playlists.** HLS and DASH split the stream into short files plus a text playlist that lists them. Plain HTTP means ordinary caches and CDNs work with no special support. The player downloads a few segments ahead before it starts, so end-to-end delay is roughly the segment length times the number of segments buffered, plus encode and upload time. Segments of 6 s with 3 buffered gives about 18 s; 2 s segments give about 6 s.

**Latency tradeoffs.** Shorter segments lower latency but multiply the number of requests and reduce compression efficiency. Low-latency HLS and chunked transfer deliver partial segments before they are complete to reach about 2 to 5 seconds. WebRTC reaches sub-second but needs many more servers per viewer and loses CDN caching. The right choice depends on the use: a sports stream accepts 20 seconds, an auction or live Q&A does not.

**CDN and origin protection.** All viewers fetch from the CDN, so the origin sees roughly one request per segment per edge region. Segment URLs are cache friendly, playlists have very short TTLs because they change every segment, and request collapsing makes sure many simultaneous cache misses become one origin fetch. Multi-CDN setups add resilience at the cost of complexity.

**Live chat fan-out.** Chat is the reverse problem: many writers, many readers, small messages, and strict order matters little. Viewers hold WebSocket connections to gateways. A message is published once to a pub/sub topic, and every gateway with viewers of that channel pushes it down its sockets. Cost grows with messages times viewers, so very large channels rate limit senders, sample messages and batch writes.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The streamer sends video to a server. The server makes copies in different qualities, cuts them into short pieces and sends them to nearby servers. Your phone downloads the pieces one after another. Chat runs on a separate system.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: RTMP or WebRTC ingest feeds a transcoder that creates an HLS or DASH ladder. The packager writes segments and playlists to an origin, a CDN caches them, and players adapt quality to bandwidth. Chat uses WebSockets and pub/sub fan-out.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Latency equals encode time plus segment duration times player buffer plus CDN and network delay. Low-latency HLS delivers partial segments to cut it. Playlist TTLs are very short while segments are cached long, and request collapsing protects the origin.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Budget the pipeline: ingest 0.5 s, transcode and package under 2 s, segment duration and player buffer chosen per product tier. Place transcoders by ingest region, make ladders adaptive to channel popularity, run multi-CDN with real-time steering, and shard chat by channel with per-room sampling so a hot channel cannot starve others.
Functional requirements

items: A broadcaster can start and stop a live stream using a stream key.
Viewers can watch with automatic quality switching on phones, web and TVs.
Viewers can see the stream with a delay of a few to a few tens of seconds depending on tier.
Viewers can send and read live chat for the channel.
The live stream can be recorded for replay after it ends.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Playback starts in under about 3 seconds and rebuffering stays rare.
Handle a viral channel with hundreds of thousands of concurrent viewers.
End-to-end latency target chosen per product tier, from 3 s to 30 s.
Ingest availability matters most: a dropped broadcaster connection is visible to everyone.
Cost-aware: transcoding and egress bandwidth dominate the bill.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 100,000 concurrent viewers on one stream at an average 3 Mbps. 100,000 x 3 Mbps = 300 Gbps of egress, served by the CDN, not the origin.
Assumption: ladder of 4 renditions totalling about 10 Mbps. The origin stores 10 Mbps / 8 = 1.25 MB per second, or 1.25 MB x 3,600 = 4.5 GB per hour per stream.
Assumption: 4 second segments. Each rendition produces 1 / 4 = 0.25 new segments per second, so 4 renditions give 1 new origin object per second per stream.
Assumption: 5,000 concurrent live streams, each with a 4 rung ladder. 5,000 x 4 = 20,000 concurrent encodes, which sets the transcoder fleet size.
Assumption: a chat of 100,000 viewers receives 50 messages per second. 50 x 100,000 = 5 million socket writes per second across gateways, so sampling is needed at this size.

blocks.text: APIs

rows: POST
`/streams`
Create a stream and return an ingest URL and a secret stream key.
POST
`/streams/{id}/end`
End the stream and finalize the recording.
GET
`/streams/{id}/playlist.m3u8`
Master playlist listing available renditions (served via CDN).
GET
`/streams/{id}/{rendition}/{segment}.ts`
A media segment; immutable and cacheable.
GET
`/chat/{channel}/connect`
WebSocket upgrade to receive and send chat messages.
POST
`/chat/{channel}/messages`
Send a chat message when sockets are not available.

blocks.text: Data model

rows: streams
stream_id, channel_id, stream_key_hash, status, started_at, ended_at, ingest_region
Relational database
segments
stream_id, rendition, sequence, duration_ms, object_key, created_at
Object storage plus an index in a key-value store
channel_presence
channel_id, gateway_id, viewer_count, updated_at
In-memory store with short TTL
chat_messages
channel_id, message_id, user_id, text, created_at
Wide-column or log store, retained for a short time

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: StreamSession state machine: CREATED, LIVE, RECONNECTING, ENDED. A dropped ingest connection moves to RECONNECTING with a grace timer before ENDED.
TranscodeJob: one job per stream with a list of rendition profiles; a supervisor restarts failed jobs and reports lag as the gap between ingest time and newest segment time.
Packager: keeps a sliding window of the last N segments per rendition, writes playlists with media sequence numbers, and inserts discontinuity tags after gaps.
ChatGateway: tracks sockets per channel, subscribes to a channel topic only while at least one viewer is connected, and drops messages for clients whose send buffer is full.

blocks.text: Security

items: Treat the stream key as a secret: store only its hash, allow rotation, and reject ingest from unknown keys.
Protect paid or private streams with signed, short-lived playlist and segment URLs or tokens checked at the CDN.
Moderate chat with rate limits, banned words and user blocks, and authenticate sockets before accepting messages.
Limit ingest by account and region to prevent abuse of expensive transcoding capacity.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: HLS/DASH with 4-6 s segments
Cheap, scales through any CDN, resilient to bad networks.
Delay of about 15 to 30 seconds.
Large audience broadcasts where delay does not matter.
Low-latency HLS or chunked segments
About 2 to 5 seconds of delay while still using CDNs.
More complex, more requests, fewer compatible players.
Sports, interactive shows, live commerce.
WebRTC delivery
Under one second delay.
Heavy servers per viewer, hard to cache, cost grows with audience.
Small interactive sessions such as auctions or video calls.
Full transcoding ladder for every stream
Best viewer experience everywhere.
Very high compute cost for channels with few viewers.
Premium or popular channels; use fewer rungs or on-demand ladders elsewhere.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Transcoder crashes mid-stream
Viewers see a frozen picture or an error until segments resume.
Run a hot standby per channel or restart quickly with aligned timestamps, keep the broadcaster connection on the ingest edge, and alert on a stalled playlist.
Broadcaster connection drops and returns
Gaps in segments and timestamp jumps confuse players.
Accept reconnect with the same stream key, insert discontinuity markers in the playlist and keep the channel session alive for a grace period.
Viral stream causes a CDN cache miss storm
The origin is flooded with requests for each new segment.
Request collapsing, an origin shield tier between edge and origin, and pre-warming popular channels.
Chat flood on a huge channel
Gateways and phones are overwhelmed by thousands of messages per second.
Per-user rate limits, sampling or batching on the server, slow mode, and dropping the oldest messages for slow clients.

blocks.text: Evidence for claims

rows: Ingest over RTMP or WebRTC, transcoding to a bitrate ladder and delivery as HLS or DASH segments through a CDN is the standard live pipeline.

Delay is roughly segment duration times player buffer plus processing time.

WebSocket gateways with a pub/sub bus are a common pattern for live chat fan-out.
