blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How would you reduce live stream latency from 20 seconds to 5?
blocks.text: Shorten segments to 1-2 seconds, use low-latency HLS or chunked CMAF so partial segments are delivered early, reduce player buffer to a couple of segments, keep transcoding close to ingest, and use shorter playlist TTLs. Accept more requests and slightly lower efficiency in exchange.

blocks.title: Why is transcoding the expensive part and how do you control the cost?
blocks.text: Re-encoding video in real time is CPU or GPU heavy and runs once per rendition per stream. Control it with a ladder sized to channel popularity, hardware encoders, skipping rungs nobody watches, and transcoding on demand for small channels.

blocks.title: How would you design live chat for a channel with one million viewers?
blocks.text: WebSocket gateways hold viewer connections, a pub/sub topic per channel fans out messages to gateways, and each gateway pushes to its sockets. Rate limit senders, sample or batch messages, shard channels across the bus, and drop messages for slow clients rather than slowing everyone.
Takeaways

items: Live video is a pipeline: ingest, transcode, package, origin, CDN, player.
Segments are plain files, so the CDN scales delivery by caching them.
Latency is segment length times buffer plus processing time; shortening it costs requests and efficiency.
The transcoding ladder is the main compute cost and can be sized to popularity.
Chat is a separate fan-out system using sockets and pub/sub with rate limiting.

quiz.q: A stream uses 6 second segments and the player buffers 3 segments before playing. Roughly what is the delay behind live?
quiz.why: Segment length times buffered segments gives 18 s, plus encode and network time.

quiz.q: Why is the same stream encoded at several resolutions and bitrates?
options: So each viewer can switch to a quality that fits their bandwidth
quiz.why: Adaptive bitrate keeps playback smooth on slow and fast connections.

quiz.q: Why do CDNs reduce load on the origin for live video?
options: Many viewers share one cached copy of each segment
quiz.why: Segments are ordinary cacheable files, so thousands of viewers cost one origin fetch per edge.

quiz.q: Which approach delivers under one second of delay?
quiz.why: WebRTC trades CDN cacheability and low cost for very low latency.

lessons.title: Design a URL shortener: keys, redirects, caching and click analytics

blocks.text: A URL shortener turns a long link into a short code and redirects millions of times per day. The design choices are how to generate unique keys, how to make reads fast and how to count clicks without slowing redirects.
In simple words

A URL shortener gives you a short link such as short.example/aZ3kQ that opens a long web address. When someone visits the short link, the service looks up the long address and sends the visitor there. It also counts the visits. The service is read-heavy: a link is created once but clicked many times.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a coat check. You hand over a big coat and get a small numbered ticket. Later, anyone with the ticket gets the coat back in seconds. The attendant never searches through all coats: the number tells exactly where to look. And a clipboard by the door ticks off every time a ticket is used.

diagram.title: URL shortener (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Browser / client
nodes.detail: Creates links through the API and follows short links by sending a GET to the short code.

nodes.label: CDN / load balancer
nodes.detail: Terminates TLS, spreads traffic and can cache redirects for very hot links for a short time.

nodes.label: Shortener service
nodes.detail: Stateless service that handles both create and redirect requests. Scales horizontally behind the load balancer.

nodes.label: Key generator
nodes.detail: Hands out unique numeric ids in ranges, so each service instance can create codes without asking the database every time.

nodes.label: Cache (Redis)
nodes.detail: Holds code to long URL mappings. Most redirects are served here in about a millisecond.

nodes.label: URL store
nodes.detail: Durable key-value or wide-column store keyed by short code. The source of truth.

nodes.label: Click event queue
nodes.detail: Receives one small event per redirect so counting never blocks the redirect itself.

nodes.label: Aggregator
nodes.detail: Consumes events in batches, groups by link and time bucket and writes counts.

nodes.label: Analytics store
nodes.detail: Column store or time-series store holding clicks per link per hour, plus country and device breakdowns.

steps.text: A user sends POST /links with a long URL. The request arrives over HTTPS at the edge.
The load balancer forwards the request to any healthy shortener instance.
The service takes the next number from its reserved id range, for example 125,000,001.
The number is converted to base62, giving a code like aZ3kQ. The service stores code to long URL with owner and expiry.
Later, a visitor opens short.example/aZ3kQ. The browser sends GET /aZ3kQ.
The service looks up the code in the cache. For a popular link this is almost always a hit.
On a miss it reads the URL store and then fills the cache with a TTL.
The service answers with an HTTP 302 redirect and the Location header set to the long URL. The browser goes to the destination.
Before returning, the service drops a tiny click event (code, time, country, device) onto the queue. This is fire and forget.
The aggregator reads events in batches of thousands and counts them per link per hour.
Counts are written to the analytics store, which powers the dashboard showing clicks over time.

blocks.text: How it works

**Key space.** A code of 7 characters from base62 (a-z, A-Z, 0-9) gives 62^7, about 3.5 trillion, combinations. Even at 100 million new links per month that lasts for thousands of years, so 6 or 7 characters is enough. Shorter codes look nicer but run out sooner: 62^6 is about 56 billion.

**Counter with base62.** Take a unique increasing number and write it in base 62. There are no collisions by construction and codes are short and compact. To avoid a single hot counter, each service instance reserves a range of, say, 1,000 numbers from a central allocator and uses them locally. If an instance dies, the unused part of its range is simply skipped. The weakness is predictability: sequential codes can be guessed and enumerated, so if privacy matters the number is passed through a reversible shuffle or the code is made random.

**Hashing.** The alternative is to hash the long URL and take the first 7 characters. The same URL gives the same code, which helps deduplicate, but two different URLs can collide, so the insert must check for existing codes and retry with a salt. Random codes have the same collision issue and need a unique constraint on the code column. Counters avoid collisions entirely; hashing and random avoid a central allocator.

**Redirect path.** Redirects are the hot path. The service reads the cache first and falls back to the store. Because the mapping almost never changes, cache hit rates are very high, and a few viral links dominate traffic, so a small cache holds most of the load. A 301 is permanent and lets browsers and CDNs cache the redirect, which cuts load but hides later clicks from analytics. A 302 is temporary, so every click reaches the service and can be counted.

**Analytics pipeline.** Counting inside the redirect request would slow it and could lose clicks on failure. Instead each redirect emits a small event to a queue and returns. Consumers aggregate in batches by link and time bucket, which turns millions of events into far fewer writes. The analytics store is separate from the URL store, so a slow dashboard query never affects redirects.

**Scaling reads.** The service is stateless and scales behind a load balancer. The URL store is partitioned by short code, so every lookup goes to one partition. Read replicas and the cache absorb read traffic. Hot keys are handled by CDN caching of redirects and, if needed, replicating the hottest entries across cache nodes.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The service stores a short code and the long address it stands for. Opening the short link looks up the code and sends you to the long address. A counter records how many times each link was used.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Each new link gets a unique number turned into a base62 code. Redirects read from a cache before the database. Clicks are sent to a queue and counted in the background so redirects stay fast.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Id ranges are leased to service instances to avoid a hot counter, the URL store is partitioned by code, and the cache absorbs most reads. A 302 keeps clicks visible to analytics while a 301 trades analytics for lower load.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Read:write is commonly 100:1 or more, so optimise the redirect path first: cache with request coalescing, replicate hot keys, keep the service stateless and put analytics strictly off the critical path with at-least-once events and idempotent aggregation. Make codes non-guessable when links are private, and protect against abuse by scanning destinations and rate limiting creation.
Functional requirements

items: Create a short link for a long URL, optionally with a custom alias and expiry.
Redirect a short link to its destination quickly.
Show click counts over time with country and device breakdown.
Let owners edit, disable or delete their links.
Reject or flag links to known malicious destinations.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Redirect latency p99 under about 50 ms at the service.
Very high availability for redirects; creation can degrade briefly.
Short codes are unique and, for private links, not easy to guess.
Handle viral links with a sudden 100x traffic jump on one code.
Analytics may lag by minutes but must not lose a significant share of clicks.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 100M new links per month. 100,000,000 / (30 x 86,400 s) = ~39 writes per second on average.
Assumption: read to write ratio of 100:1. 39 x 100 = ~3,900 redirects per second on average; with a 10x peak about 39,000 per second.
Assumption: each record is about 500 bytes (code, long URL, owner, timestamps). 100M x 500 B = 50 GB per month, or 600 GB per year.
Assumption: 20% of links get 80% of traffic. Caching 20% of one month of links = 20M x 500 B = ~10 GB, which fits in a small cache cluster.
Assumption: one click event is about 100 bytes. 3,900 per second x 100 B = ~390 KB per second, or ~34 GB per day of raw events before aggregation.

blocks.text: APIs

rows: POST
`/api/links`
Create a short link from a long URL with optional alias and expiry; returns the short URL.
GET
`/{code}`
Redirect to the long URL with a 302 and record a click event.
GET
`/api/links/{code}`
Fetch link details for the owner.
PATCH
`/api/links/{code}`
Change the destination or expiry, or disable the link.
DELETE
`/api/links/{code}`
Delete a link; the cache entry is invalidated.
GET
`/api/links/{code}/stats`
Click counts by time bucket, country and device.

blocks.text: Data model

rows: links
code (primary key), long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at, status
Key-value or wide-column store partitioned by code
id_ranges
allocator_id, range_start, range_end, leased_to, leased_at
Small relational table or consensus store
click_events
code, ts, country, device, referrer
Log or queue topic partitioned by code
click_stats
code, hour_bucket, clicks, by_country, by_device
Column or time-series store

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: CodeGenerator: nextCode() takes the next number from a local range, asks the allocator for a new range when empty, and returns base62(number) after an optional reversible shuffle.
Base62 codec: encode(n) repeatedly divides by 62 and maps remainders to the alphabet; decode is the inverse. Both are pure functions that are easy to test.
RedirectHandler: cache lookup, then store lookup, then cache fill; checks expiry and status; emits a click event without waiting for it; returns 302 with Location.
ClickAggregator: consumes batches, groups by (code, hour), adds counts in memory and flushes upserts; replays are safe because events carry ids and writes are idempotent.

blocks.text: Security

items: Validate and normalise destination URLs, allow only http and https, and check them against a malware and phishing blocklist.
Rate limit link creation per account and IP, and require authentication for custom aliases and edits.
Make codes for private links unguessable and block enumeration with rate limits on 404 responses.
Never log full long URLs when they may contain tokens in query strings; store and show them only to the owner.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Counter plus base62
No collisions, shortest codes, simple.
Needs an allocator; codes are predictable unless shuffled.
Most public shorteners where scale and simplicity matter.
Hash of the long URL
Same URL gives same code; no central counter.
Collisions must be detected and retried; longer codes for safety.
You want deduplication and stateless creation.
301 permanent redirect
Browsers and CDNs cache it, so far less server load.
Later clicks are invisible to analytics and the target cannot be changed easily.
Links that never change and analytics is not needed.
302 temporary redirect
Every click reaches you for counting and the destination can change.
More load on the service.
Analytics matter or links can be edited.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Cache is flushed or a node fails
All redirects fall through to the database at once.
Replicated cache, request coalescing so one miss triggers one read, read replicas and rate limits on the database path.
Key allocator is down
New links cannot be created once local ranges run out.
Lease large ranges, run the allocator with replicas and keep enough headroom that a short outage never exhausts a range.
Analytics queue backs up
Dashboards lag; if redirects wait for it, redirects slow down.
Make event publishing non-blocking with a bounded local buffer, drop or sample under pressure, and scale consumers.
Abuse: links to malware or spam
The domain is flagged by browsers and email providers.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you generate short, unique codes at scale?
blocks.text: Use a unique counter written in base62, with each service instance leasing a range of ids from a central allocator so there is no per-request coordination. Add a reversible shuffle if codes must not be guessable. Alternatives are random or hashed codes with a unique constraint and collision retry.

blocks.title: How would you scale the redirect path to 100,000 requests per second?
blocks.text: Stateless service instances behind a load balancer, a replicated cache holding most mappings, a partitioned store keyed by code for misses, CDN caching for very hot links, and analytics events sent asynchronously so they never add latency.

blocks.title: How do you track clicks without slowing redirects?
blocks.text: Emit a small event per redirect to a queue, aggregate in batches by link and time bucket, and write to a separate analytics store. Use at-least-once delivery with idempotent aggregation, and allow sampling or dropping under overload.
Takeaways

items: The workload is read-heavy, so optimise the redirect path first.
Base62 of a unique counter gives short collision-free codes; leased id ranges avoid a hot counter.
Hashing and random codes need collision checks with a unique constraint.
301 saves load but hides clicks; 302 keeps analytics accurate.
Count clicks through a queue and a separate store, never in the redirect request.

quiz.q: How many unique codes can 7 base62 characters represent?
quiz.why: 62^7 is roughly 3.5 trillion.

quiz.q: Why does a 301 redirect hide clicks from analytics?
options: Browsers cache it and do not contact the service again
quiz.why: A permanent redirect is remembered, so later visits never reach your servers.

quiz.q: Why send click events to a queue instead of updating a counter during the redirect?
options: To keep the redirect fast and not lose or block on counting
quiz.why: Counting off the critical path keeps latency low and isolates failures.

lessons.title: Design a notification system: push, SMS and email at scale

blocks.text: A notification system takes events from many services and delivers the right message on the right channel, once, in time. The hard parts are priorities, preferences, provider failures, rate limits and duplicates.
In simple words

Apps send many messages: an order update, a password code, an offer. A notification system is the single place that decides who should get each message, which channel to use (phone alert, text message or email), and then sends it. It also makes sure nobody gets the same message twice or gets bothered when they said no.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a post office with a sorting room. Letters arrive from many senders. Urgent ones go to the front of the line, each is written on the right paper, and the clerk checks the address book to see how the person wants to be reached. If one delivery van breaks down, the clerk uses another. A logbook records every delivery.

diagram.title: Notification system (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Producer services
nodes.detail: Order, account and marketing services that call the notification API with an event, a recipient and data for the template.

nodes.label: Notification API
nodes.detail: Validates the request, assigns a priority, checks deduplication and rate limits, then enqueues. Returns quickly with a notification id.

nodes.label: Preferences and templates
nodes.detail: Stores per-user channel settings, quiet hours and opt-outs, plus the message templates per channel and language.

nodes.label: Dedup and rate limit
nodes.detail: Redis keys that record recently seen idempotency keys and per-user and per-provider counters with short TTLs.

nodes.label: Priority queues
nodes.detail: Separate queues for critical, normal and bulk traffic so a marketing blast can never delay a login code.

nodes.label: Channel workers
nodes.detail: Render the template, choose the channel and provider, call the provider, and retry or fail over on errors.

nodes.label: Push provider
nodes.detail: Mobile push gateway that delivers alerts to iOS and Android devices using device tokens.

nodes.label: SMS providers A/B
nodes.detail: Two SMS providers so traffic can fail over when one is slow or down. SMS is the most expensive channel.

nodes.label: Email provider
nodes.detail: Email delivery service handling sending reputation, bounces and unsubscribe links.

nodes.label: Delivery log
nodes.detail: Records each attempt and status: queued, sent, delivered, failed, opened. Updated from provider callbacks.

steps.text: The order service sends POST /notifications: user id, event type order_shipped, template data and an idempotency key.
The API checks that this idempotency key has not been seen in the last 24 hours and that the user is under their rate limit. A repeat is acknowledged but dropped.
It loads the user settings: push is allowed, SMS is off, email is on, and quiet hours apply from 22:00 to 07:00.
A message is placed on the normal-priority queue for the chosen channels. A login code would go to the critical queue instead.
A worker pulls the message. Critical queues have dedicated workers so bulk traffic cannot starve them.
The worker renders the push template in the user language and calls the push provider with the device token.
For a critical SMS the worker uses provider A. After repeated errors or timeouts a circuit breaker switches new sends to provider B.
The provider later calls back with a delivery receipt, which is written to the delivery log.
The worker records each attempt and result so support can answer where a message went, and failures are retried with backoff up to a limit.
The email is sent with an unsubscribe link. Bounces and complaints come back later and update the suppression list.

blocks.text: How it works

**One API, many channels.** Producers describe what happened and who it is for, not how to send it. The notification service decides the channels from the event type, user preferences and policy. This keeps provider details out of every other team and gives one place to enforce limits and opt-outs. The API is asynchronous: it validates, enqueues and returns an id, so a slow SMS provider never slows an order.

**Templates and preferences.** Messages are rendered from versioned templates per channel and language, filled with data from the event. Preferences include channel opt-in, topic subscriptions and quiet hours. Transactional messages such as a password reset bypass marketing opt-outs but never bypass legal opt-outs. The preference check happens at enqueue time and again at send time for messages that waited a long time in the queue.

**Priority queues.** Traffic has very different urgency: one-time passwords must arrive in seconds, order updates in a minute, promotions within hours. Using separate queues per priority with separately scaled workers prevents a large marketing campaign from delaying critical messages. Bulk sends are also throttled to the rate the providers and users can tolerate.

**Provider failover and retries.** Providers fail and slow down. Each call has a timeout, retries use exponential backoff with jitter, and a circuit breaker stops calling a provider that keeps failing and routes to a backup. Retries are only safe if the provider call carries a unique message id, otherwise the user may receive the message twice. After the retry budget the message goes to a dead-letter queue for inspection.

**Rate limiting and deduplication.** There are three kinds of limit: per user (do not send 30 pushes an hour), per provider (stay under their throughput limits and cost caps) and per producer (stop a buggy service from flooding). Deduplication uses the idempotency key and, for some event types, a content-based key such as user plus event plus order id within a time window. Both use fast counters with TTLs in a cache.

**Delivery tracking.** Sent does not mean delivered. Providers send asynchronous receipts: delivered, bounced, opened or failed. These update a delivery log keyed by notification id, which supports support queries, retry decisions (for example, fall back to SMS when a push token is invalid) and analytics. The log is append-oriented and partitioned by time, with old data archived.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Services tell the notification system what happened. It checks how the user likes to be contacted, picks the channel, sends the message and writes down what happened, making sure the same message is not sent twice.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: An API enqueues events into priority queues. Workers render templates, check preferences, and call push, SMS or email providers with retries and failover. A delivery log is updated from provider callbacks.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Idempotency keys and content keys deduplicate at enqueue time, per-user and per-provider limits protect people and budgets, and circuit breakers fail over between providers. Preferences are rechecked at send time, and unknown outcomes are resolved from delivery receipts.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Isolate priorities all the way down: separate queues, worker pools and provider quotas so a campaign cannot affect critical traffic. Make every send idempotent with a stable message id, treat provider receipts as an event stream that drives channel fallback, and design bulk campaigns as rate-planned jobs that respect time zones, quiet hours and suppression lists.
Functional requirements

items: Accept notification requests from internal services with an event type, recipient and data.
Send over push, SMS and email using per-channel templates and languages.
Respect user preferences, opt-outs and quiet hours.
Support priorities, scheduled sends and bulk campaigns.
Track delivery status per notification and expose it to support and analytics.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Critical messages delivered within a few seconds; normal within a minute; bulk within hours.
At-least-once delivery with strong duplicate suppression.
Horizontal scale for campaign peaks without affecting critical traffic.
Provider outages do not stop delivery for critical channels.
Auditable: every attempt and outcome is logged.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Assumption: 10M users and 5 notifications per user per day. 10,000,000 x 5 = 50M notifications per day, or 50,000,000 / 86,400 = ~580 per second on average.
Assumption: peak is 20x average during campaigns. 580 x 20 = ~11,600 per second at peak, mostly on the bulk queue.
Assumption: channel split is 70% push, 20% email, 10% SMS. SMS = 5M per day. At 0.5 cents per SMS (illustrative price) that is 5,000,000 x $0.005 = $25,000 per day, so SMS use must be controlled.
Assumption: each delivery log row is about 300 bytes with 3 status updates. 50M x 300 B = 15 GB per day, or ~5.5 TB per year before compression and archiving.
Assumption: dedupe keys of 100 bytes held 24 hours. 50M x 100 B = ~5 GB of cache memory.

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: NotificationRouter: given an event and preferences, returns a list of (channel, template) targets; applies quiet hours and policy such as always-send for security codes.
ChannelSender interface with PushSender, SmsSender and EmailSender; each wraps provider clients, handles timeouts and maps provider errors to RETRYABLE or PERMANENT.
ProviderSelector with a circuit breaker per provider: CLOSED, OPEN and HALF_OPEN states, choosing the primary unless OPEN, then the backup.
DedupeGuard: tryAcquire(key, ttl) uses an atomic set-if-not-exists; returns false for a duplicate so the caller acknowledges without enqueueing.
RetryPolicy: exponential backoff with jitter, a maximum attempt count per priority, and routing to a dead-letter queue when exhausted.

blocks.text: Security

items: Authenticate producers with service credentials, scope what event types each may send, and apply per-producer quotas.
Keep provider credentials in a secrets manager, never in templates or logs, and rotate them regularly.
Mask phone numbers and email addresses in logs; honour unsubscribe and legal opt-out lists across all channels.
Verify provider callbacks with signatures and sign unsubscribe links so they cannot be forged.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Single queue for all traffic
Simple to build and operate.
Bulk campaigns delay time-critical messages.
Very small systems only.
Separate priority queues and worker pools
Critical messages are protected; each tier scales independently.
More infrastructure and capacity planning.
Any system that sends both transactional and marketing messages.
At-least-once sending with idempotent providers
No message is lost; duplicates are suppressed by message id.
Relies on providers honouring the id; otherwise duplicates can reach users.
Default for most notifications.
Multiple providers per channel
Survives provider outages and lets you control cost.
Different APIs and delivery behaviour to maintain; routing logic.
SMS and email where outages directly hurt the business.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: SMS provider has an outage
Login codes and alerts stop arriving.
Circuit breaker, automatic failover to a second provider, and alerts on rising failure or latency.
A producer bug sends the same event thousands of times
Users are spammed and sending costs spike.
Idempotency and content-based dedupe, per-user limits, per-producer quotas and a kill switch.
Marketing campaign floods the queues
Critical messages are delayed behind millions of promotions.
Separate priority queues and worker pools, rate-planned bulk sends, and a lower provider quota for bulk traffic.
Worker crashes after calling the provider but before recording the result
The message is retried and the user may get it twice.
Send with a stable message id the provider can dedupe on, and record intent before the call so retries can check status.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you make sure a user does not get the same notification twice?
blocks.text: Require an idempotency key from producers and store it with a TTL for fast dedupe at enqueue, add a content key such as user, event type and entity id for a time window, send to providers with a stable message id, and keep workers idempotent so retries after a crash are safe.

blocks.title: How do you handle a provider outage?
blocks.text: Timeouts and retries with backoff and jitter, a circuit breaker that opens after repeated failures, automatic routing to a secondary provider, a dead-letter queue for exhausted retries, and alerts. Keep both providers warm with a small share of traffic so failover is proven.

blocks.title: How would you design a campaign to 20 million users?
blocks.text: Treat it as a throttled batch job on the bulk queue: split recipients into chunks, filter by preferences and suppression lists, spread sending over time zones and hours at a rate within provider limits, track progress, and allow pause and cancel. Keep critical queues and providers separate.
Takeaways

items: Producers send events; the notification service decides channel, template and timing.
Priority queues with separate workers protect critical messages from bulk traffic.
Idempotency keys and stable message ids make retries safe.
Circuit breakers and multiple providers handle provider failures.
Rate limits protect users, providers and budgets.
Delivery receipts, not send calls, tell you what really happened.

quiz.q: Why use separate queues for critical and bulk notifications?
options: So a large campaign cannot delay time-critical messages
quiz.why: Isolation by priority keeps latency of urgent traffic predictable.

quiz.q: A worker retries a send after a timeout. How do you avoid a duplicate?
options: Send with a stable message id that the provider or system can deduplicate on
quiz.why: A stable id turns an at-least-once retry into an effectively once delivery.

quiz.q: What does a circuit breaker do for a failing SMS provider?
options: Stops sending to it for a while and routes to a backup
quiz.why: It prevents wasting time on a dead dependency and enables failover.

quiz.q: Why record provider delivery receipts?
options: Sent does not mean delivered; receipts show the real outcome and drive fallbacks
quiz.why: Receipts close the loop for tracking, support and channel fallback.

lessons.title: Case study: Quick commerce and 10-minute delivery

blocks.text: Quick commerce promises groceries in about ten minutes by serving each neighbourhood from a small warehouse called a dark store. This lesson covers store selection by location, per-store inventory that must not oversell, picking and packing, slotless dispatch and rider assignment, and how the promise time is computed and defended, as a reference design in the style of Blinkit, Zepto and Instamart.
In simple words

Instead of one big warehouse far away, the company runs many small stock rooms, each serving the few kilometres around it. When you open the app it works out which stock room serves your address and shows only what is on its shelves right now. When you order, a staff member picks the items in a couple of minutes while a delivery rider who is already waiting at the store is chosen, so the ride to you is short.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a pizza shop that only delivers within its own neighbourhood. The menu on the counter lists only what is in the kitchen today, the cook starts the moment you call, and a delivery person is already standing at the door. Ten minutes is possible because the shop is close, the menu is small and nobody waits for a delivery slot.

diagram.title: Quick commerce order-to-doorstep platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Customer app
nodes.detail: Sends the delivery location, browses a catalog scoped to one store, places the order and follows live status.

nodes.label: Picker handheld
nodes.detail: Device used by store staff. Receives pick lists sorted by shelf path and confirms each item by barcode scan.

nodes.label: Rider app
nodes.detail: Reports rider state and location, receives one assignment at a time and confirms pickup and delivery.

nodes.label: API + realtime gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates calls, routes them by city and store, and holds persistent connections for pushing tasks and status.

nodes.label: Serviceability + catalog
nodes.detail: Maps a latitude and longitude to the dark store whose delivery polygon contains it, then serves that store assortment with prices and a promise time.

nodes.label: Hyperlocal inventory
nodes.detail: Owns available and reserved quantity for every store and item pair. The only component allowed to change stock.

nodes.label: Inventory store
nodes.detail: Strongly consistent store keyed by store id and item id, partitioned by store so a reservation touches one partition.

nodes.label: Order service
nodes.detail: Validates the cart, reserves stock, records payment intent and owns the order state machine.

nodes.label: Order event stream
nodes.detail: Durable log of order events, partitioned by store id so events for one store stay in order.

nodes.label: Store fulfilment
nodes.detail: Turns confirmed orders into pick tasks, balances them across pickers, handles missing items and marks orders packed.

nodes.label: Rider assignment
nodes.detail: Keeps the queue of riders waiting at each store and matches a rider to an order so the rider is ready when packing ends.

steps.text: The app opens and sends the selected delivery address as latitude and longitude.
Serviceability finds the store whose delivery polygon contains the point. If the store is closed, overloaded or the area is not covered, the app is told so before anything is shown.
The catalog for that one store is joined with current availability, so out-of-stock items are hidden or greyed. The read may be a few seconds stale; that is acceptable for browsing.
The customer taps checkout. The request carries the cart, the store id it was built against and an idempotency key.
The order service re-validates prices and the store, then creates the order in a CREATED state.
It asks inventory to reserve every line. This is the first strongly consistent stock check; browsing was only a hint.
Each line is a conditional decrement: reduce available and raise reserved only if available is at least the requested quantity. Lines that fail are reported back so the cart can be adjusted.
After payment is authorised (or cash on delivery is chosen) the order moves to CONFIRMED and an event is appended to the stream for that store.
Fulfilment creates a pick task, orders the lines by shelf location and assigns the task to the least loaded picker.
The pick list is pushed to a picker handheld within a second or two of confirmation. The clock for the promise is already running.
The picker scans each item. A scan mismatch or an empty shelf is reported immediately so stock is corrected and the customer is offered a refund or substitute for that line.
In parallel with picking, dispatch takes the same confirmed event and selects a rider from the queue at that store, timed so the rider reaches the handover counter as the bag is sealed.
The assignment is pushed to the rider app with the order, the handover counter and the drop location.
The rider confirms pickup, streams location during the short trip and confirms delivery, which releases the rider back to the store queue and closes the order.

blocks.text: How it works

**The promise is built from fixed budgets.** Ten minutes is a sum: time to accept the order, time to pick and pack, time to hand over, and ride time. Ride time is bounded by geography, so each dark store serves a small **delivery polygon** drawn from road travel time, not a circle. Pick time is bounded by a small assortment and a store layout designed for walking speed. Everything else in the design exists to stop software from eating into those budgets: no slot selection, no batch planning window, no waiting for a rider to be found after the bag is ready.

**Serviceability comes first.** Every screen in the app is scoped to exactly one store, so the first call resolves the delivery point to a store. Polygons are stored as geometry and indexed by grid cell, so the lookup is a cell lookup followed by a point-in-polygon test on a handful of candidates. Polygons are operational data that change during the day: an operations tool can shrink a polygon in heavy rain, pause a store that is overloaded, or hand part of an area to a neighbouring store. The mapping is cached at the edge with a short time-to-live and the cart remembers the store id it was built against, so a change in mapping forces a re-validation instead of silently mixing two stores.

**Hyperlocal inventory is the correctness core.** Stock is tracked per store and per item as `available`, `reserved` and `on_hand`. A reservation is a conditional write on the row for that store and item, so two customers cannot both buy the last unit. Because the key includes the store id, the data partitions naturally by store and a hot item in one neighbourhood does not contend with the rest of the city. Browsing reads come from a cache or read replica that lags by seconds; the checkout path always goes to the authoritative store. Reservations carry an expiry so an abandoned payment returns stock without manual cleanup.

**Physical truth drifts from the database.** Items get damaged, misplaced or expire, so the count in the system is only an estimate of the shelf. The design closes the loop in three places: every pick is a barcode scan that confirms the unit existed; a picker reporting an empty shelf triggers an immediate stock correction to zero and removes the item from the catalog for that store; and cycle counts by staff reconcile the rest. Inbound stock from the mother warehouse is scanned in as a putaway event. Inventory is therefore modelled as a ledger of movements (inbound, reserve, pick, release, adjust) from which the current quantities are derived.

**Slotless dispatch.** Scheduled grocery delivery batches orders into time slots and plans routes hours ahead. Quick commerce does the opposite: every order is dispatched the moment it is confirmed. That removes the planning problem but requires spare capacity to be standing by, so riders are attached to a home store and wait there. Assignment is then mostly a queue: take the rider who has been waiting longest at that store, with adjustments for riders who are about to return. The interesting timing question is when to commit the rider: too early and the rider idles at the counter, too late and the packed bag waits. Dispatch predicts pack-ready time from the number of lines and current picker load and commits the rider to meet it.

**Batching is the pressure valve.** When orders outnumber riders, strict one-order-per-rider makes every wait longer. A limited batch, two orders whose drops are close together and whose pack times nearly coincide, raises throughput at a small cost to the second customer. The rule is conservative: batch only if both orders still meet their promised time. When even batching is not enough, the system lengthens the promise shown to new customers, adds a surge fee, or temporarily marks the store as not accepting orders. Admitting fewer orders honestly is preferred to accepting them and breaking the promise.

**Order state and events.** The order is a persisted state machine: CREATED, CONFIRMED, PICKING, PACKED, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, with CANCELLED and PARTIALLY_FULFILLED as side exits. Each transition is written durably and then published to a stream partitioned by store id, which keeps events for a store in order and lets fulfilment, dispatch, notifications and analytics consume independently. Payment capture, refunds for missing items and rider payouts hang off these events with idempotency keys. A short pick is a normal path, not an error: the line is removed, the amount is refunded automatically and the order continues.

**The mobile clients.** The customer app must cope with a location that changes between browse and checkout, so the cart is validated against the store again when the address changes. The picker handheld works inside a building with poor connectivity: it holds the pick list locally, queues scans with client-generated ids and replays them when the connection returns, and the server treats repeats as no-ops. The rider app is restricted by the operating system when in the background, so it reports location at a low rate while idle at the store and at a higher rate only during a trip, and it falls back to push notifications to wake up for an assignment when the persistent connection has been closed.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Each neighbourhood has a small stock room. The app shows only what that stock room has, staff pick the order in a couple of minutes, and a rider who is already at the store carries it a short distance. It is fast because everything is close and nothing waits for a schedule.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: A serviceability lookup maps the delivery point to one dark store polygon. Stock is kept per store and item and reserved at checkout with a conditional write. A confirmed order emits an event that starts picking and rider assignment in parallel, and the order moves through a persisted state machine until delivery.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: The decisions to defend are consistency levels (stale reads for browse, strong writes for reserve), reservation expiry versus payment timeout, when to commit a rider relative to predicted pack time, the batching rule, and admission control when a store saturates. Inventory is a movement ledger with reconciliation against physical scans, because system stock and shelf stock diverge.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: At scale the hard problems are economic and operational as much as technical: placing stores and drawing polygons from demand density, forecasting per-store demand by hour to set stock and rider headcount, pricing the promise honestly under load, and keeping the system usable when a store loses connectivity. Degraded modes matter: a store should be able to pick from a local cache of confirmed orders, and the platform should shed load one store at a time instead of city-wide.
Functional requirements

items: Resolve a delivery address to a serving store and show a promise time.
Browse and search a catalog limited to items in stock at that store.
Place an order with stock reservation and payment, with idempotent retries.
Create pick tasks, confirm items by scan and handle missing items with automatic refunds.
Assign a rider, track the delivery and confirm handover.
Let operations edit polygons, pause stores and adjust stock.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: No overselling: a unit is never promised to two orders.
Pick task reaches a handheld within about two seconds of order confirmation.
A failure or overload in one store does not affect other stores.
Checkout stays available when notifications, analytics or recommendations are degraded.
Clients in the store tolerate short network loss without losing scans.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Illustrative assumption: 1,000 dark stores x 1,500 orders per store per day = 1.5M orders per day; 1.5M / 86,400 s = ~17 orders per second average.
Illustrative assumption: evening peak is 6x the average. 17 x 6 = ~100 orders per second across all stores, about 0.1 per second per store.
Illustrative assumption: 8 lines per order. 100 x 8 = 800 conditional stock writes per second at peak, spread over 1,000 store partitions.
Illustrative assumption: 6,000 items per store. 1,000 x 6,000 = 6M inventory rows; at 200 bytes each that is 1.2 GB, small enough to cache fully.
Illustrative assumption: 30 browse requests per order. 100 x 30 = 3,000 catalog reads per second at peak, served from cache.
Illustrative assumption: 40 riders per store reporting every 5 s. 1,000 x 40 / 5 = 8,000 location updates per second.

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Reservation: `UPDATE store_inventory SET available = available - :q, reserved = reserved + :q WHERE store_id = :s AND item_id = :i AND available >= :q`; zero rows updated means the line is unavailable.
All lines of an order are reserved in one transaction on the store partition; a partial failure returns the failed lines and releases the rest.
Reservation expiry: a sweeper releases reservations older than the payment timeout whose order is not CONFIRMED, writing a release movement.
Rider queue per store is a sorted set scored by `queued_at`; assignment pops the head with a compare-and-set on `rider_state.version`.
Pack-ready estimate: `picker_queue_wait + lines x seconds_per_line + packing_constant`; the rider is committed when the estimate minus the walk to the counter reaches zero.
Scan events carry a client-generated id; the server stores processed ids per task so a replay after reconnect changes nothing.

blocks.text: Security

items: Authenticate every app; a picker token is bound to one store and a rider can act only on the order assigned to that rider.
Never trust client prices or store ids: the server re-resolves the store from the address and re-prices the cart.
Stock adjustments and polygon edits are privileged operations with an audit trail and dual approval above a threshold.
Customer address and phone number are shown to the rider only for the active order, with calls routed through a masking relay.
Rate-limit order creation per account and device to limit stock-hoarding abuse through abandoned reservations.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Slotless immediate dispatch
Shortest possible delivery time and a simple customer experience with no slot picker.
Needs idle riders and pickers standing by, so cost per order is higher when demand is low.
Small baskets, dense areas and a promise measured in minutes.
Slotted delivery with route planning
High vehicle utilisation, large baskets and predictable labour planning.
Delivery is hours away and a planning engine must be operated.
Weekly grocery shopping from a large warehouse.
Strong reservation at checkout only
Browsing stays fast and cacheable; the single contended write happens once per order.
A customer can add an item that is gone by checkout and must be told then.
High browse-to-order ratio, which is the normal case.
Reserve stock on add-to-cart
Checkout never fails for stock reasons.
Abandoned carts hold scarce stock; needs short expiries and creates heavy write load.
Flash sales of very limited items, not general grocery.
Store-attached riders
Assignment is a local queue with no travel to the store; the rider is ready when the bag is.
Riders cannot easily cover a neighbouring store that is busier.
Dense demand around each store with predictable peaks.
Batching two nearby orders
Raises rider throughput in peaks and lowers cost per order.
Adds minutes to the second drop and complicates handover.
Rider supply is short and both orders still meet their promise.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Two customers check out the last unit at the same instant
Without protection both orders are confirmed and one cannot be filled.
Conditional decrement on the store and item row; the loser is told the item is unavailable before payment.
System shows stock but the shelf is empty
The picker cannot fill a line after the customer has paid.
Picker marks the line short, stock is set to zero immediately, the line is refunded automatically or a substitute is offered, and the event feeds a shrinkage report.
Payment gateway times out during checkout
Stock is reserved but the order is neither confirmed nor failed.
Reservation has an expiry slightly longer than the payment timeout; a status check resolves the payment, then the order is confirmed or the reservation is released.
No rider available when the bag is packed
The packed order waits and the promise is broken.
Predict the shortfall from queue length before accepting orders: extend the displayed promise, allow limited batching, borrow riders from a neighbouring store, or pause the store.
Dark store loses connectivity
Pickers stop receiving new orders and scans cannot be sent.
Handhelds keep assigned tasks locally and replay scans with idempotent ids; serviceability stops routing new orders to the store after missed heartbeats.
Order event consumer falls behind
Pick tasks appear late, which directly consumes the delivery budget.
Alert on consumer lag per store partition, scale consumers, and keep the pick-task path free of slow downstream calls.
Delivery polygon is edited while carts are open
A cart built for one store is submitted for an address now served by another.
The order request carries the store id; the server re-resolves the address and rejects a mismatch so the app rebuilds the cart.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you prevent overselling when stock is per store?
blocks.text: Key inventory by store id and item id and make reservation a conditional update: decrement available only where available is at least the requested quantity. Partition by store so the write is single-partition. Give reservations an expiry tied to the payment timeout, and convert them to a permanent deduction when the item is scanned at pick. Browse reads can be cached; checkout always hits the authoritative row.

blocks.title: How does the app decide which store serves a customer?
blocks.text: Each store has a delivery polygon derived from road travel time. Index polygons by grid cell, look up the cell of the delivery point, then run point-in-polygon on the few candidates. Cache the result briefly. Polygons are editable operational data, so the order request includes the store id and the server re-checks it.

blocks.title: When should the rider be assigned: at order time or at pack time?
blocks.text: Neither extreme. Assign so the rider arrives at the counter when the bag is ready. Predict pack-ready time from line count and picker load, and commit a rider from the store queue shortly before it. Under shortage, start the search at confirmation because finding a rider becomes the bottleneck.

blocks.title: How do you compute the promise time shown to the customer?
blocks.text: Sum the current estimates of each stage for that store: queue wait for a picker, pick time for a typical basket, expected wait for a rider, and ride time from the store to the address over the road network. Add a safety margin, recompute every few seconds from live load, and show the larger number when the store is busy.

blocks.title: What changes if a store must run for ten minutes with no network?
blocks.text: Orders already pushed to handhelds are picked from local storage and scans are queued with client ids. No new orders reach the store, and after a few missed heartbeats serviceability removes it from routing. On reconnect the queued scans replay idempotently and stock is reconciled.
Takeaways

items: The ten-minute promise is a budget of pick time plus ride time, protected by small delivery polygons and small assortments.
Resolve the address to one store first; catalog, price and availability are all scoped to that store.
Inventory is keyed by store and item, read loosely for browsing and reserved with a conditional write at checkout.
Treat system stock as an estimate and correct it continuously from barcode scans and shortage reports.
Dispatch is slotless: riders wait at the store, and assignment is timed to predicted pack-ready time.
When a store saturates, lengthen the promise or stop admitting orders for that store instead of failing silently.

quiz.q: Why is every catalog request scoped to a single dark store?
options: Because prices must be the same everywhere
Because only items physically in the store that serves the address can arrive within the promise
Because the database cannot join two stores
Because the app can only cache one store
quiz.why: The promise depends on picking from one nearby location, so availability is a property of that store, not of the company.

quiz.q: Which read can safely be a few seconds stale?
options: The stock check inside the reserve call
The payment status before confirming the order
The availability shown while browsing the catalog
quiz.why: Browsing is a hint. The authoritative check is the conditional reservation at checkout.

quiz.q: What makes dispatch "slotless"?
options: Orders are grouped into hourly windows
Each order is dispatched as soon as it is confirmed, using riders already waiting at the store
Delivery is done only at night
quiz.why: There is no planning window; capacity stands by so the order can leave immediately.

quiz.q: A store is saturated and riders are all out. What is the preferred system response?
options: Accept all orders and deliver late
Raise the displayed promise or stop accepting orders for that store until capacity returns
Route the orders to a warehouse in another city
quiz.why: Admission control per store keeps the promise honest and limits the damage to one store.

quiz.q: Why does a picker scan every item?
options: To confirm the physical unit matches the order and keep system stock aligned with the shelf
Because the rider needs the barcode
quiz.why: Scans are the feedback loop that corrects drift between the database and reality.

lessons.title: Case study: UPI payments app (PhonePe / Google Pay style)

blocks.text: A UPI app moves money between two bank accounts in a few seconds without holding the money itself. This lesson follows a payment through the app, the PSP bank, the NPCI switch and the remitter and beneficiary banks, and explains pay versus collect, idempotency, the pending state, reversals and reconciliation as a reference design.
In simple words

A UPI app is a messenger, not a wallet. When you pay, the app sends a signed instruction through its partner bank to a central switch run by NPCI. The switch asks your bank to take the money out and asks the other bank to put it in, then tells everyone the result. If any party is slow to answer, the payment is marked pending until the banks agree on what really happened.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Imagine paying a shopkeeper by handing a signed note to a trusted courier. The courier carries it to a central clearing desk, which phones your bank to deduct the amount and phones the shopkeeper bank to add it. You and the shopkeeper both get a call back with the outcome. If one phone line is busy, the desk keeps the note marked "waiting" and follows up until both banks confirm.

diagram.title: UPI payment flow across app, PSP, switch and banks (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Payer UPI app
nodes.detail: Collects payee address and amount, captures the UPI PIN inside the NPCI-supplied secure component and shows the transaction status.

nodes.label: Payee app / merchant
nodes.detail: Shows a QR code or raises a collect request, and receives the credit confirmation.

nodes.label: App backend (TPAP)
nodes.detail: Backend of the third-party app. Owns user profiles, device binding records, transaction history and risk checks. Never sees the PIN in clear.

nodes.label: Transaction store
nodes.detail: Durable record of every payment attempt keyed by transaction id, with its state and the last known response.

nodes.label: Payer PSP bank
nodes.detail: The sponsor bank through which the app connects to UPI. Validates and forwards messages to the switch and relays responses.

nodes.label: Status + reconciliation worker
nodes.detail: Polls for the final status of pending payments and compares daily settlement files with the transaction store.

nodes.label: NPCI UPI switch
nodes.detail: Central switch that resolves payment addresses, routes debit and credit legs between banks and records the outcome for settlement.

nodes.label: Remitter bank
nodes.detail: Bank holding the payer account. Verifies the PIN, checks balance and limits, and debits the account in its core banking system.

nodes.label: Beneficiary bank
nodes.detail: Bank holding the payee account. Credits the account and confirms to the switch.

nodes.label: Payee PSP bank
nodes.detail: Bank that issued the payee payment address. Resolves the address to an account and notifies the payee app.

steps.text: The payer scans a QR code or types a payment address such as `name@bank`. The app asks the backend to verify the address before any money moves.
The backend sends an address validation request through its PSP bank.
The PSP bank forwards it to the switch, which works out from the handle after the `@` which PSP owns the address.
The payee PSP resolves the address to a bank account and returns the registered name, which the payer sees and confirms.

The payer enters the amount and the UPI PIN. The PIN is captured by a secure component supplied by NPCI and encrypted on the device, so the app and its backend only carry an opaque credential block. The request includes a unique transaction id.

Before sending anything outward, the backend runs risk checks and writes the payment as PENDING under that transaction id. A retry with the same id finds this row instead of creating a second payment.
The pay request, signed by the app backend, goes to the PSP bank.
The PSP bank signs and forwards the payment request to the switch.
The switch sends the debit leg to the payer bank. That bank decrypts and verifies the PIN, checks balance and limits, debits the account and answers.
Only after a successful debit, the switch sends the credit leg to the payee bank, which credits the account and answers.
The switch returns the final result with a reference number. If the credit answer never arrived, the result is not success but a pending or deemed state to be resolved later.
The backend updates the stored transaction and pushes the outcome to the payer app, which was showing a waiting screen.
The payee side is notified of the credit, which is what makes a merchant sound box or app announce the payment.

For any payment still PENDING after the response window, a worker issues status checks with the original transaction id until a final answer arrives, then updates the store. The next day, settlement files are compared against the store to catch anything missed.

blocks.text: How it works

**Who does what.** UPI is a four-party model plus a switch. The **payer app** is often a third-party application provider (TPAP) that is not a bank; it connects through a sponsor **PSP bank**. The **NPCI switch** routes messages. The **remitter bank** holds the payer account and the **beneficiary bank** holds the payee account. The app never holds customer funds in this flow: it originates an instruction, and the money moves between banks. This shapes the whole design, because the app owns the user experience and the record of attempts but does not own the source of truth for money.

**Addresses and onboarding.** A user is identified by a virtual payment address of the form `user@handle`, which hides the account number. Onboarding binds the app to a device and a mobile number: the app sends an SMS from the SIM so the number can be verified against the bank record, lists the accounts linked to that number, and lets the user set a UPI PIN with the issuing bank. Two factors therefore protect a payment: possession of the bound device and knowledge of the PIN. The app backend stores the binding (user, device fingerprint, address, linked account reference) and refuses payment requests from an unbound device.

**The PIN never touches the app.** The PIN entry screen is rendered by a common library provided by NPCI and embedded in every UPI app. It encrypts the PIN on the device with a key the app cannot read, producing a credential block that only the issuing bank path can open. The app, the app backend and the PSP forward this block without being able to inspect it. In design terms this is a trust boundary drawn inside the client: the least trusted party carries the secret as opaque bytes.

**Pay versus collect.** In a **pay** (push) transaction the payer starts the flow and authorises it immediately. In a **collect** (pull) transaction the payee asks for money: the request travels to the payer PSP, appears in the payer app as a pending request with an expiry, and only becomes a debit when the payer approves it with the PIN. Push is simpler and safer because the person losing money is the one who began the action. Collect supports invoices and subscriptions but is a favourite tool for fraud, where a victim is tricked into approving a request believing it is a receipt. Systems therefore restrict collect by amount, category and counterparty, and show clear warnings.

**Idempotency end to end.** A mobile network can drop the response after the bank has debited. If the app then simply retried, the user would pay twice. The defence is one transaction id generated at the start, stored before the first outbound call and carried through every hop. The backend treats a repeated request with the same id as a query for the existing payment. Downstream parties treat a repeated id as a duplicate and return the original outcome. A retry is therefore never a new payment; it is a status check under the same identity.

**Pending is a real state.** Each hop has a timeout. If the remitter debits but the beneficiary bank does not answer in time, nobody at the app layer knows whether the credit happened. Reporting failure would be a lie if the credit went through; reporting success would be a lie if it did not. So the payment is stored as PENDING and shown as such. The state machine is INITIATED, PENDING, SUCCESS, FAILED, with REVERSED for a debit that was returned. Only a final response or a reconciliation result moves a payment out of PENDING, and the app must never invent a terminal state from a timeout.

**Reversal and reconciliation.** When the debit succeeded but the credit failed or timed out, the switch drives a reversal of the debit leg so the payer is made whole. If the beneficiary bank is merely slow, the credit may be treated as deemed successful and confirmed later. The app side runs two safety nets: a status-check worker that asks for the outcome of pending payments with backoff, and a daily reconciliation that compares settlement and report files from the PSP bank with its own store. Interbank settlement itself is a separate, later step in which net positions are settled between banks; the user-visible payment is a real-time message exchange, not the movement of settlement funds.

**Scale and availability.** The app backend sees extreme peaks around salary days, festivals and evening hours, and it depends on banks whose availability it cannot control. It keeps a health score per bank from recent success rates and warns the user before they pay from an account whose bank is struggling. Calls to the PSP are protected by timeouts, circuit breakers and bulkheads per bank, so one slow bank cannot exhaust shared threads. Transaction history, rewards and notifications are driven from events after the payment state changes, so they never sit on the payment path.

**The mobile client angle.** A phone can lose signal, switch from Wi-Fi to cellular, or have the app killed in the middle of a payment. The client persists the transaction id before sending, and on next launch asks the backend for the status of any payment it believes is in flight. The result screen is driven by server state, not by whether the HTTP call returned. Push notifications deliver the final outcome if the app is in the background. Device binding is re-checked when the SIM or device changes, which forces re-registration instead of trusting a restored backup.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: A UPI app sends a payment instruction through its partner bank to a central switch. The switch tells your bank to debit you and the other bank to credit the receiver. The app shows success only when the switch confirms both, and shows pending if someone has not answered yet.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: The flow is address validation, then a pay request carrying an encrypted PIN block and a unique transaction id. The backend persists PENDING before calling the PSP, the switch runs debit then credit, and the final response updates the stored state. Timeouts lead to status checks, and a failed credit after a successful debit leads to a reversal.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: The design choices are where to anchor idempotency (one id across all hops), how to model uncertainty (an explicit pending state with bounded resolution time), how to isolate failing banks (per-bank circuit breakers and health-based warnings), and how to restrict collect requests to contain fraud. Reconciliation against bank files is the final authority over the app database.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: The app is a coordinator with no authority over money, so correctness is about never asserting more than it knows. Hard problems include success-rate engineering across many banks with different failure patterns, real-time fraud scoring under a latency budget of a few hundred milliseconds, handling duplicate and out-of-order callbacks, and running reconciliation at very high volumes so that every unresolved payment has an owner and a deadline.
Functional requirements

items: Register a user by binding device and mobile number, link bank accounts and set a UPI PIN.
Validate a payment address and show the registered payee name.
Send money by address, QR code or contact, with PIN authorisation.
Receive and approve or decline collect requests with an expiry.
Show real-time status and a complete transaction history.
Raise and track a dispute for a payment.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: No duplicate debits under retries, crashes or duplicate callbacks.
Never report a terminal state that is not confirmed by the payment network.
Normal payment completes in a few seconds end to end.
A degraded bank affects only payments involving that bank.
Every pending payment is resolved within a bounded time and is auditable.
The PIN is never visible to the app, its backend or its logs.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Illustrative assumption: 300M payments per day on one app. 300M / 86,400 s = ~3,500 payments per second average.
Illustrative assumption: peak is 3x average. 3,500 x 3 = ~10,500 payments per second at peak.
Illustrative assumption: each payment causes 1 validation, 1 pay call and 2 status reads. 10,500 x 4 = ~42,000 backend requests per second at peak.
Illustrative assumption: 1 KB per transaction record. 300M x 1 KB = 300 GB per day, ~110 TB per year before replication, so history is partitioned by time and user.
Illustrative assumption: 1% of payments go pending. 300M x 0.01 = 3M status-check workflows per day, about 35 per second on average.
Illustrative assumption: 5 s end-to-end budget split as 0.3 s app backend, 0.5 s PSP, 0.5 s switch, 1.5 s each bank leg, leaving ~0.7 s for network.

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Create payment: `INSERT payment (txn_id, ..., state = PENDING)` with a unique constraint on `txn_id`; on conflict return the existing row.
Transition: `UPDATE payment SET state = :new, version = version + 1 WHERE txn_id = :id AND state IN (:allowed) AND version = :v`; zero rows means a stale or duplicate event.
Allowed transitions: INITIATED to PENDING; PENDING to SUCCESS or FAILED; SUCCESS to REVERSED only when the network reports a reversal.
Status worker: schedule checks at increasing intervals after the response window; stop on a terminal state; escalate to reconciliation after a maximum age.
Callbacks: verify signature, look up `txn_id`, apply the conditional transition, acknowledge even when it is a duplicate.
Outbox: the state change and an outbox row are written in one transaction; a relay publishes the event for notifications, history and rewards.
Per-bank isolation: separate connection pool, timeout and circuit breaker keyed by bank code.

blocks.text: Security

items: Device binding plus UPI PIN gives two factors; requests from an unbound device are rejected.
The PIN is captured and encrypted by the NPCI-supplied component; it is never logged, stored or visible to the app backend.
All messages between app backend, PSP and switch are mutually authenticated and signed; callbacks are verified before processing.
Risk engine scores each payment on device, counterparty age, amount and velocity within a strict latency budget.
Collect requests have limits, expiries and explicit warnings; reported addresses are blocked.
Account references are tokenised; full account numbers are not stored in the app database.
Rate-limit address verification to prevent enumeration of who holds which address.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Pay (push) flow
Payer starts and authorises in one step; low fraud surface; simplest state machine.
Payee cannot initiate, so it does not fit invoices raised by a merchant system on its own.
Person-to-person transfers and QR payments at a shop.
Collect (pull) flow
Payee can request a precise amount with a reference; fits online checkout and bills.
Easy to abuse through social engineering; needs expiries, limits and warnings.
Merchant-initiated requests where the payer is not at a QR code.
Show pending until confirmed
Never misreports money movement; trust is preserved.
The user waits and may be anxious; support load rises.
Any time a hop timed out and the outcome is unknown.
Optimistic success on timeout
Feels faster to the user.
Sometimes wrong, which means telling a user that money moved when it did not.
Never for payments; acceptable only for cosmetic, reversible actions.
Synchronous wait for final status
Simple client logic and an immediate result in the normal case.
Long-held connections under peak load; breaks when the app is backgrounded.
The first few seconds of a payment, with a fall back to push and polling.
Multiple PSP bank partners
If one sponsor bank degrades, traffic can move to another; better overall success rate.
More integrations, more handles, more reconciliation streams.
Large apps where a single bank outage would affect many users.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Response lost after the bank debited
The app sees a timeout and the user may try again, risking a double payment.
One transaction id persisted before sending; retries become status checks; the backend rejects a second payment with the same id.
Debit succeeded, beneficiary bank timed out
Money has left the payer but the credit is unconfirmed.
Keep the payment PENDING; the switch either confirms the credit later or drives a reversal of the debit; status checks and reconciliation close it.
Remitter bank is degraded
A large share of payments from that bank fail or hang, hurting all users if threads are shared.
Per-bank bulkheads and circuit breakers; show a warning on that account and suggest another linked account.
Duplicate or out-of-order callbacks
A late FAILED could overwrite a SUCCESS, or a reward could be issued twice.
State transitions are conditional on the current state and terminal states are immutable; downstream consumers deduplicate on transaction id.
App killed during payment
The user reopens the app with no result screen and does not know if they paid.
Client stores the transaction id before sending and queries status on launch; push notification delivers the final state.
Fraudulent collect request
A user approves a request thinking money will be received.
Clear wording that approving sends money, limits and cooling periods for new counterparties, risk scoring, and blocking of reported addresses.
SIM swap or device change
An attacker with the number could try to register the victim account on a new device.
Re-binding requires SMS from the SIM in the device plus bank-side checks; the PIN is still required; risk rules add a hold after re-binding.
