Illustrative reference design

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you guarantee a user is not charged twice?
blocks.text: Generate one transaction id on the client when the user confirms, persist it on the client and in the backend before any outbound call, and carry it on every hop. The backend enforces uniqueness on the id, so a repeated request returns the existing payment. On timeout the client and a server worker do status checks with the same id. Downstream duplicates are rejected on that id, so no path creates a second debit.

blocks.title: Walk through what happens when the beneficiary bank is down.
blocks.text: Address validation may still work because it goes to the payee PSP. The pay request reaches the switch, the remitter debits, and the credit leg times out or is declined. The switch then returns a failure with a reversal of the debit, or a pending state if the credit outcome is unknown. The app shows pending, the status worker polls, and the payment ends as REVERSED or SUCCESS. Reconciliation the next day confirms it.

blocks.title: How would you design the transaction state machine?
blocks.text: States: INITIATED, PENDING, SUCCESS, FAILED, REVERSED. Transitions are conditional updates checked against the current state and version. SUCCESS and FAILED are terminal except that a debit-side SUCCESS with a failed credit moves to REVERSED. Every transition appends to an event log, and all side effects such as notifications and rewards consume that log idempotently.

blocks.title: How do you keep success rates high when some banks are unreliable?
blocks.text: Measure success, failure and timeout rates per bank and per transaction type over short windows. Isolate each bank with its own connection pool and circuit breaker. Surface the health to the user before they pay, suggest another linked account, and spread traffic across more than one sponsor PSP. Tune timeouts so a slow bank fails fast to pending instead of holding resources.

blocks.title: What does the mobile app do if it is killed mid-payment?
blocks.text: It has already stored the transaction id locally. On next start it calls the status endpoint for any payment marked in flight and renders the server state. Meanwhile the backend keeps resolving the payment and sends a push notification with the final result. The client never treats the absence of a response as failure.
Takeaways

items: A UPI app is a coordinator of messages between banks; it does not hold the money or decide the outcome.
The path is app, PSP bank, NPCI switch, remitter bank for debit, beneficiary bank for credit, then the response returns the same way.
One transaction id, stored before sending and carried on every hop, turns retries into status checks.
Pending is a first-class state: a timeout means unknown, not failed.
A debit without a confirmed credit is resolved by reversal or late confirmation, and reconciliation is the final authority.
Pay is safer than collect because the person losing money starts the action.
Isolate each bank with its own limits so one failing bank cannot take the app down.

quiz.q: Where is the money while a UPI payment is in progress?
options: In a wallet held by the UPI app
In the bank accounts; the app and switch only pass messages
In the PSP bank pooled account of the app
quiz.why: The app originates an instruction and banks move the money. That is why the app must wait for confirmation instead of deciding the outcome.

quiz.q: Why does the backend write PENDING before calling the PSP bank?
options: To make the screen load faster
So that a crash or retry can find the existing attempt by its transaction id instead of creating a new one
Because banks require a database row
To reserve the balance in the app
quiz.why: Persist-then-send makes the attempt recoverable and is the anchor for idempotency.

quiz.q: The debit succeeded and the credit response timed out. What should the app show?
options: Pending, until the switch reports a final outcome or a reversal
quiz.why: The outcome is unknown. Only a final response or reconciliation may move the payment to a terminal state.

quiz.q: Why is the collect flow riskier for users than the pay flow?
options: The request is started by the party receiving money, so a victim can be tricked into approving it
quiz.why: Collect still needs the PIN, but the initiator is the beneficiary, which enables social engineering.

quiz.q: Who can read the UPI PIN in this design?
options: The PSP bank and the app
Only the issuing bank side that verifies it; the app carries an encrypted block
Anyone on the same Wi-Fi network
quiz.why: The PIN is encrypted on the device by the NPCI-supplied component, so intermediaries forward opaque bytes.

lessons.title: Case study: Google Maps-style navigation

blocks.text: A navigation product draws a map of the whole world, finds a fast route across a road network with hundreds of millions of segments in well under a second, predicts arrival time from live traffic reported by phones, and keeps working with no signal. This lesson covers map tiles, the routing graph, probe-based traffic, ETA and offline maps as a reference design.
In simple words

The map you see is cut into many small square pictures, and the app downloads only the squares for the area and zoom level on screen. Roads are also stored as a network of junctions and connecting stretches, each with a travel time. To give directions the system finds the quickest chain of stretches, using speeds learned from phones that are currently driving on those roads.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a giant paper atlas cut into numbered squares so you only pull out the pages you need. Separately, a control room keeps a string-and-pin model of every road, where each string has a tag saying how long it takes to drive right now. Drivers phone in their speed, the tags are updated, and when you ask for directions the control room traces the shortest path through the strings.

diagram.title: Maps and navigation platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Maps app
nodes.detail: Renders tiles, runs turn-by-turn guidance, reports location probes while navigating and stores offline regions.

nodes.label: Tile CDN
nodes.detail: Caches immutable, versioned map tiles close to users. Serves the vast majority of map reads.

nodes.label: Tile store
nodes.detail: Pre-generated vector tiles keyed by zoom, x, y and version, produced by an offline build pipeline from map data.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates and rate-limits requests and routes them to search, routing and probe ingestion.

nodes.label: Search + geocoding
nodes.detail: Turns text into places and coordinates, and coordinates into addresses, using a text index combined with a spatial index.

nodes.label: Routing service
nodes.detail: Computes candidate routes over a preprocessed road graph and returns geometry, steps and travel time.

nodes.label: Road graph store
nodes.detail: Road segments and junctions with attributes such as length, class, turn restrictions and one-way flags, partitioned by region and held in memory by routing nodes.

nodes.label: ETA prediction
nodes.detail: Predicts travel time along a route for the time the driver will reach each part, combining live and historical speeds with a learned model.

nodes.label: Probe stream
nodes.detail: Durable stream of anonymised location samples from devices that are moving, partitioned by region.

nodes.label: Map matching + speeds
nodes.detail: Snaps noisy GPS traces to road segments and aggregates them into a speed per segment per short time window.

nodes.label: Live traffic store
nodes.detail: Current speed and confidence for each road segment with a short expiry, falling back to the historical profile when there is no fresh data.

steps.text: The app computes which tiles cover the visible area at the current zoom and requests those not already in its local cache.
On a cache miss the CDN fetches the tile from the tile store. Tiles are versioned and immutable, so they can be cached for a long time.
The user types a destination. The app sends the text with the current map position to bias results toward nearby places.
Search returns ranked places with coordinates. The chosen place becomes the route destination.
The app requests directions from the current position to the destination with a travel mode and departure time.
The request is routed to routing nodes that hold the graph partitions for the regions involved.

The origin and destination are snapped to the nearest road segments. A hierarchical shortest-path search runs over the preprocessed graph, exploring local roads only near the ends and long-distance shortcuts in between.
Edge costs use current segment speeds where fresh data exists, so a jammed highway becomes more expensive than a clear side road.
For each candidate route the ETA service predicts the total time, accounting for how traffic is expected to change by the time the driver reaches later segments.
The best route and a few alternatives are returned as compact encoded geometry with turn instructions and arrival time.
During navigation the app reports its position periodically. Guidance itself runs on the device against the downloaded route, so a brief loss of signal does not stop instructions.
Location samples are stripped of account identity and appended to the probe stream for the region.
Workers snap each trace to the most likely sequence of road segments, discarding points that fit no road, and compute a speed for each traversed segment.

Speeds from many devices on the same segment are combined into one estimate with a confidence value. Routing and ETA read the new value within a minute or so, and active trips are re-evaluated for a faster route.

blocks.text: How it works

**Tiles.** The world is projected onto a square and divided into a pyramid: zoom level 0 is one tile, and each level splits every tile into four, so level `z` has `4^z` tiles addressed by `z/x/y`. A client only needs the dozen or so tiles under the viewport. **Raster tiles** are pre-drawn images: simple but heavy and fixed in style. **Vector tiles** carry geometry and labels that the device draws itself, so they are smaller, rotate and tilt smoothly, restyle for night mode without a download and stay sharp at any zoom. Tiles are built offline from map data, given a version, and served as immutable objects, which makes a CDN extremely effective.

**The road graph.** Routing does not use tiles. It uses a directed graph in which nodes are junctions and edges are road segments carrying length, road class, speed, one-way and turn-restriction data. A continent has hundreds of millions of edges. Plain Dijkstra explores outward in all directions and would touch millions of nodes for a long trip; A* with a distance heuristic helps but not enough. Production systems preprocess the graph. **Contraction hierarchies** rank nodes by importance and add shortcut edges so a query climbs from local streets to major roads and back down, visiting only a few thousand nodes. The cost is that shortcuts bake in edge weights.

**Routing with changing weights.** Live traffic changes weights every minute, which conflicts with heavy preprocessing. The standard answer is to separate structure from weights. The graph is cut into cells along natural boundaries such as rivers and sparse areas; the expensive partitioning is done once, and only the small per-cell tables of crossing costs are recomputed when traffic changes, which takes seconds and can be done per cell in parallel. Queries then search inside the origin and destination cells and jump across the cells in between. This is the idea behind customisable route planning, and it is why a traffic update does not require rebuilding the world.

**Traffic from probes.** The main source of live speed is the phones themselves. A device that is navigating or has location sharing enabled sends periodic position samples. These are noisy, so a **map matching** step picks the most likely sequence of road segments for each trace, typically with a hidden Markov model that weighs how close each point is to a road against how plausible the movement between consecutive points is. Matched traces yield a traversal time per segment, and samples from many devices are aggregated per segment over a short window. Segments with too few samples fall back to a historical profile for that hour and day of week.

**ETA.** Arrival time is not the sum of current segment times, because by the time a driver reaches a segment forty minutes ahead, conditions there will have changed. ETA prediction estimates the speed each segment will have at the moment the vehicle arrives, using live conditions near the start and learned patterns further along. Models that treat neighbouring road segments as a graph capture how a jam spreads backward along a road. The route is re-scored during the trip, and if another route becomes meaningfully faster the driver is offered it.

**Search and geocoding.** Turning text into a place needs a text index for names and addresses joined with a spatial index, so that results near the viewport rank higher. Reverse geocoding, turning a coordinate into an address, is a nearest-feature query on the spatial index. The world is indexed by hierarchical cells so that "what is near this point" becomes a small set of cell lookups, the same technique used for drivers in a ride-hailing system.

**Serving topology.** Tile reads dominate by request count and are almost entirely absorbed by the CDN. Routing is CPU and memory heavy: each routing node keeps graph partitions for some regions in memory, and requests are routed by region. Long routes that cross regions are stitched through boundary nodes. The probe pipeline is a high-volume, loss-tolerant stream: losing a few samples changes nothing, so it favours throughput over per-message durability. Map data updates flow through a build pipeline that validates changes, produces a new graph and tile version, and rolls it out gradually.

**Offline maps and the mobile client.** A user can download a region. The package contains vector tiles for a range of zooms, the road graph for that region, and a search index of places, all compressed and versioned. With no signal the device runs routing itself on the regional graph, using historical speeds instead of live traffic, and resumes server routing when connectivity returns. The package has an expiry and is refreshed in the background on Wi-Fi with a delta where possible. During normal navigation the client prefetches tiles along the route corridor, keeps guidance fully on the device, batches probe uploads to save battery and radio time, and lowers location sampling when the phone is stationary.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: The map is a stack of small square pictures at many zoom levels, and the app fetches only the squares it needs. Directions come from a separate model of roads as connected stretches with travel times, updated from the speeds of phones on the road.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Vector tiles addressed by `z/x/y` are served from a CDN. Routing runs a preprocessed shortest-path search on a directed road graph whose edge costs come from live traffic. Traffic is built by snapping device location samples to road segments and aggregating speeds per segment per time window.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: The central tension is fast queries versus fresh weights: heavy preprocessing gives millisecond queries but resists traffic updates, so structure and weights are separated by partitioning the graph into cells. ETA must predict future segment speeds, not sum current ones. Sparse probe data needs confidence values and historical fallback.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: Hard problems at scale include feedback effects when many drivers are sent down the same alternative road, privacy of probe data at trip ends, detecting map errors from probe traces that disagree with the graph, consistent rollout of tile and graph versions so the picture and the route agree, and running an on-device router within phone memory limits for offline use.
Functional requirements

items: Display a pannable, zoomable map of any location.
Search for places and addresses and convert between coordinates and addresses.
Return driving, walking or transit routes with alternatives and arrival time.
Provide turn-by-turn guidance with rerouting when the driver deviates or traffic changes.
Show live traffic conditions on roads.
Download a region for offline map display, search and routing.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Map tiles appear within a few hundred milliseconds on a good connection.
Route response within about one second for typical trips.
Traffic reflected in routing within a minute or two of conditions changing.
Guidance continues through short connectivity gaps.
Probe data is anonymised and not linkable to an account in the traffic pipeline.
A regional failure degrades that region only.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Illustrative assumption: zoom 0 to 16 covers the globe with (4^17 - 1) / 3 = ~5.7 billion tile positions; most are ocean and are stored as one shared empty tile.
Illustrative assumption: 1 billion map sessions per day x 60 tile requests = 60 billion tile requests per day; 60B / 86,400 s = ~700,000 per second, nearly all served by CDN and device cache.
Illustrative assumption: at a 98% CDN hit rate, origin sees 700,000 x 0.02 = ~14,000 tile requests per second.
Illustrative assumption: 500M route requests per day / 86,400 s = ~5,800 per second average; at 3x peak, ~17,000 per second.
Illustrative assumption: 50M devices navigating at peak, one sample every 5 s. 50M / 5 = 10M probe samples per second.
Illustrative assumption: 300M road segments x 20 bytes of live state = 6 GB for the live traffic store, which fits in memory per replica.
Illustrative assumption: an offline city package of 200 MB = 120 MB tiles + 50 MB graph + 30 MB place index.

blocks.text: APIs

rows: GET
`/tiles/{version}/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`
One vector tile. Immutable for a given version and cacheable for a long time.
GET
`/v1/places/search?q={text}&near={lat},{lng}`
Ranked places matching the text, biased to the given location.
GET
`/v1/geocode/reverse?lat={lat}&lng={lng}`
Nearest address or place for a coordinate.
POST
`/v1/routes`
Body: origin, destination, waypoints, mode, departure time, options. Returns routes with encoded geometry, steps and ETA.
POST
`/v1/routes/{routeId}/refresh`
Body: current position. Returns updated ETA and a faster alternative if one exists.
POST
`/v1/probes`
Batch of timestamped positions with speed and heading under a rotating anonymous id. No response body.
GET
`/v1/offline/regions/{regionId}/manifest`
Versions, sizes and download locations of the tile, graph and index packages for a region.

blocks.text: Data model

rows: tile
version, z, x, y (key), payload (compressed vector data)
Object store behind a CDN
road_segment
segment_id (key), from_node, to_node, length_m, road_class, speed_limit, one_way, geometry, cell_id
Region-partitioned graph files loaded in memory
turn_restriction
from_segment, via_node, to_segment, type
Part of the graph build
cell_cost_table
cell_id, profile, entry_node, exit_node, cost, built_at
In-memory per routing node, rebuilt on traffic updates
segment_speed_live
segment_id (key), speed_kph, sample_count, updated_at (TTL)
In-memory cache, partitioned by region
segment_speed_history
segment_id, day_of_week, time_slot, median_speed_kph
Columnar store, loaded into routing nodes
place
place_id (key), name, category, location, cell_id, address
Search index with a spatial field

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Tile addressing: for zoom `z`, `n = 2^z`; `x = floor((lng + 180) / 360 x n)` and `y` from the Mercator latitude formula; the viewport maps to a small rectangle of `x, y` values.
Snapping: find candidate segments in the grid cells around the point, project the point onto each, and choose by distance and heading agreement.
Query: bidirectional search from origin and destination inside their cells, then over the boundary-node overlay using `cell_cost_table` for cells in between.
Traffic update: for each cell whose segment speeds changed beyond a threshold, recompute its cost table and swap it atomically.
Map matching: for each GPS point keep a few candidate segments; score transitions by the difference between road distance and straight-line distance; pick the best path through the candidates.
Speed aggregation: per segment and one-minute window, take a trimmed mean of traversal speeds and store it with the sample count.
Reroute rule: offer an alternative only if it saves more than a set number of minutes and a set fraction of the remaining time.

blocks.text: Security

items: Probe samples use a rotating identifier not tied to the account, and trace ends near origins and destinations are trimmed before aggregation.
Publish traffic only for segments with enough distinct devices so a single vehicle cannot be identified.
Location history is opt-in, encrypted at rest, access-controlled and has retention limits.
Rate-limit and key-protect routing and geocoding APIs to prevent scraping of map data.
Offline packages are signed so a tampered package is rejected by the app.
Detect fabricated traffic from devices sending implausible or coordinated samples and exclude them from aggregation.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Vector tiles
Small, restylable, smooth rotation and zoom, labels stay upright.
Rendering work moves to the device and needs a capable graphics pipeline.
Modern mobile and web clients.
Raster tiles
Trivial client, identical look everywhere.
Larger downloads, fixed style, blurry between zoom levels.
Very simple clients or imagery such as satellite photos.
Contraction hierarchies
Extremely fast queries after preprocessing.
Weight changes invalidate shortcuts, so live traffic is expensive to apply.
Static or slowly changing weights, such as distance-based routing.
Cell-partitioned routing with customisable weights
Traffic updates are applied in seconds per cell; supports several cost profiles.
Queries are somewhat slower than pure hierarchies; more complex to build.
Live traffic and per-user options such as avoiding tolls.
Server-side routing
Uses the freshest traffic and the full graph; easy to improve centrally.
Needs connectivity for each new route.
The default whenever the device is online.
On-device routing from an offline package
Works with no signal and has no network latency.
No live traffic, limited to the downloaded region, uses device storage and memory.
Travel through areas with poor coverage or when roaming.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Probe volume drops for a region
Segments lose fresh speeds and the map would show roads as clear when they may not be.
Each speed carries a sample count and age; below a threshold the system uses the historical profile and widens the ETA uncertainty.
GPS traces are noisy in dense city streets
Samples snap to the wrong parallel road and corrupt segment speeds.
Map matching uses the whole trace and movement plausibility, drops low-confidence matches, and aggregation uses robust statistics that ignore outliers.
Routing nodes for a region are unavailable
Directions for that region fail.
Replicate each graph partition across nodes and zones, route requests by region with failover, and let the client fall back to on-device routing if an offline package exists.
Tile origin is down
New areas cannot be fetched.
Long CDN cache lifetimes on immutable tiles, serving stale content on origin errors, and the device tile cache keep most map views working.
Many drivers are rerouted onto the same small road
The alternative becomes congested and the advice makes things worse.
Dampen rerouting with a minimum time saving, account for capacity of road classes, and spread drivers across alternatives.
A road closure is not yet in the map data
Routes send drivers into a closed road.
Detect closures from the absence of probes on a normally busy segment and from user reports, then apply a temporary penalty or block on the edge without waiting for a full map build.
Device loses signal during navigation
Without care, guidance would stop.
The full route and corridor tiles are already on the device, guidance runs locally, and rerouting uses the offline graph if present or waits for signal.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you compute a route across a country in under a second?
blocks.text: Preprocess. Partition the road graph into cells and precompute the cost between the boundary nodes of each cell, or add shortcut edges with contraction hierarchies. A query then searches locally near the origin and destination and uses the precomputed layer in between, visiting thousands of nodes instead of millions. Keep the partitions in memory on routing nodes and route requests by region.

blocks.title: How do you incorporate live traffic without redoing the preprocessing?
blocks.text: Separate topology from weights. The partition into cells depends only on the road structure and is built rarely. When segment speeds change, recompute only the crossing-cost tables for affected cells, which is fast and parallel. Queries always read the current tables, so traffic takes effect within a minute or so.

blocks.title: How is live traffic derived, and how do you handle sparse data?
blocks.text: Devices send location samples; a map-matching stage assigns each trace to road segments and computes traversal times; an aggregator combines samples per segment per window with outlier-resistant statistics. Each estimate has a sample count and age. When data is thin, blend with or fall back to the historical speed profile for that segment and time slot.

blocks.title: Design the tile serving path for a global user base.
blocks.text: Pre-generate vector tiles per zoom from map data in a batch pipeline, store them keyed by version and `z/x/y`, and serve through a CDN with long cache lifetimes. Clients request only viewport tiles, keep a local disk cache, and prefetch along the route. A new map build publishes a new version so old and new tiles never mix.

blocks.title: What should the app do when connectivity is lost mid-trip?
blocks.text: Continue guidance from the route already on the device, draw from cached corridor tiles, and queue probe samples. If the driver leaves the route and an offline region is installed, reroute on the device with historical speeds; otherwise show the last known route and reconnect in the background. When signal returns, refresh the route and ETA from the server.
Takeaways

items: Drawing and routing use different data: tiles for pictures, a directed graph for paths.
Tiles are an immutable, versioned pyramid addressed by zoom, x and y, which makes them ideal for a CDN and for device caching.
Continental routing is made fast by preprocessing; partitioning into cells keeps it compatible with weights that change every minute.
Live traffic comes from device location samples that are map-matched to segments and aggregated, with historical fallback where data is thin.
ETA predicts the speed of each segment at the time the vehicle will reach it.
Offline packages bundle tiles, graph and place index so the device can draw, search and route alone.

quiz.q: Why are map tiles so well suited to a CDN?
options: They are personalised for each user
They are immutable for a given version and many users request the same ones
They must be encrypted individually for each device
quiz.why: Shared, versioned, unchanging objects have very high cache hit rates and long lifetimes.

quiz.q: Why is plain Dijkstra not used directly for long routes?
options: It gives wrong answers on road networks
It explores far too many nodes on a continental graph to answer within the latency budget
It only works on undirected graphs
quiz.why: It is correct but too slow at this scale; preprocessing with shortcuts or cells cuts the search space by orders of magnitude.

quiz.q: What does map matching do?
options: Snaps a noisy sequence of GPS points to the most likely sequence of road segments
quiz.why: Raw points fall beside roads; speeds per segment can only be computed after the trace is matched to the graph.

quiz.q: Why can ETA not be computed by adding up current segment travel times?
options: Segments do not have travel times
Conditions on later segments will have changed by the time the vehicle reaches them
quiz.why: ETA needs the predicted speed at the time of arrival at each segment, which requires historical patterns and a model.

quiz.q: What must an offline map package contain for directions to work without signal?
options: Only raster images of the area
Tiles, the road graph for the region and a place index
Only the list of saved places
A copy of the live traffic store
quiz.why: Drawing needs tiles, routing needs the graph and search needs an index; live traffic is not available offline.

lessons.title: Case study: Spotify-style music streaming

blocks.text: A music service must start any of a hundred million tracks almost instantly, keep playing on a train with no signal, keep playlists consistent across devices, recommend what to play next and count every play accurately because plays decide royalties. This lesson covers the catalog, audio delivery through a CDN, offline downloads with DRM, playlists, recommendations and the play-count pipeline as a reference design.
In simple words

Every song is stored as a few files at different sound qualities and copied to servers near listeners. When you press play, the app asks for permission to play that song, gets a short-lived link, and downloads the audio in pieces a little ahead of what you are hearing. Songs you save for offline use are kept on the phone in a locked form that only the app can open, and the app reports what you played the next time it is online.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a library with branches in every town. The catalogue desk tells you which shelf a recording is on, and your library card proves you may borrow it. For a trip you can take sealed boxes home that open only with your card and stop opening if the card is not renewed. Every time you listen, a slip goes into a box at the desk so the library can pay the artists.

diagram.title: Music streaming platform (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Player app
nodes.detail: Plays audio from a local buffer, stores offline tracks encrypted, edits playlists and reports play events in batches.

nodes.label: Audio CDN
nodes.detail: Edge caches that serve encrypted audio files by byte range from locations close to listeners.

nodes.label: Encoded audio store
nodes.detail: Origin object store holding every track in several codecs and bitrates, encrypted, keyed by file id.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates the session, applies rate limits and routes calls to backend services. Also holds a connection for cross-device control.

nodes.label: Catalog + search
nodes.detail: Read-heavy metadata for tracks, albums and artists, including which territories each track may be played in, plus a search index.

nodes.label: Playlist service
nodes.detail: Stores each playlist as an ordered list with a revision and applies edits as operations so several devices can change it.

nodes.label: Playlist store
nodes.detail: Wide-column or key-value store holding playlist heads and their operation logs, partitioned by playlist id.

nodes.label: Playback + license
nodes.detail: Checks subscription, territory and device limits, chooses a file for the requested quality, and issues signed URLs and decryption keys.

nodes.label: Recommendations
nodes.detail: Serves personalised home, radio and next-track suggestions from precomputed candidates and a lightweight online ranker.

nodes.label: Play event stream
nodes.detail: Durable, replayable log of client events such as play started, seconds played and skip.

nodes.label: Play-count + royalty pipeline
nodes.detail: Deduplicates events, applies the rule for what counts as a stream, filters fraud and produces counts and royalty reports.

steps.text: The listener searches for a song. The request carries the session token and the account country.
The catalog returns matching tracks that are licensed for that country, with ids, titles, artwork references and durations. This data is cached heavily.
The listener presses play. The app asks to resolve the track id for its preferred audio quality.
Playback checks the subscription tier, territory and concurrent-stream rule, picks the matching encoded file and returns a short-lived signed CDN URL and the key to decrypt it.

The app requests the first byte range of the file from the CDN, starts playing as soon as a small buffer is filled, and keeps fetching ahead. It also fetches the start of the next track so the transition is gapless.
Popular tracks are already at the edge. A rarely played track is fetched from the origin store once and then cached.
The listener marks a playlist for offline use. The app first syncs the playlist to make sure it has the latest revision.
The playlist service returns the changes since the revision the app already holds, or accepts a queued edit from the device.
An edit is appended as an operation against a base revision. If another device changed the playlist in between, the operation is transformed and applied on top, and a new revision is produced.

For each track to download, playback issues an offline license bound to the account and device with an expiry. The app downloads the encrypted files over Wi-Fi and stores the keys in protected device storage.
While playing, online or offline, the app records play events locally. When connected it uploads them in batches, each with a unique event id.
Events are acknowledged once they are durably appended to the stream. The app deletes them locally only after the acknowledgement.
The pipeline removes duplicates by event id, applies the minimum listening time for a play to count, discards suspicious traffic and updates public play counts and royalty totals.
The same events become listening features. Recommendations use them to refresh what the listener sees on the home screen and what plays after an album ends.

blocks.text: How it works

**Catalog.** The catalog is a large, read-dominated dataset: tracks, albums, artists, credits, artwork and, critically, **availability**. A track may be licensed in some countries and not others, may appear on several albums, and may be replaced by a new master. Deliveries from labels arrive through an ingestion pipeline that validates metadata, transcodes the audio and publishes a new catalog version. Because reads vastly outnumber writes and can tolerate minutes of staleness, the catalog is denormalised into read-optimised views, cached aggressively and paired with a search index that supports typo tolerance and popularity ranking.

**Audio delivery.** A track is a few megabytes, far smaller than video, which changes the design. Each track is encoded once per quality level into a small number of files and stored encrypted. The client requests the file from a CDN by HTTP byte range, so it can begin playback after a few hundred kilobytes and can seek by requesting a different range. Popularity is extremely skewed: a small share of tracks accounts for most plays, so the CDN hit rate is high, while the long tail is fetched from origin on demand. Adaptive quality is simpler than for video: the client picks a bitrate from network type and user settings and may switch at track boundaries.

**Fast start.** The goal is that pressing play feels instant. Three techniques matter. The client **prefetches** the head of the next track in the queue and of likely choices such as the first item of a playlist being viewed. The resolve call that returns URL and key is small and can be batched for a whole queue. And the device keeps a bounded disk cache of recently played encrypted audio, so replays need no network at all. Together these mean the network is usually not on the critical path at the moment the user taps.

**Offline downloads and DRM.** Offline listening means the encrypted audio file is on the device together with a **license**: the content key wrapped so that only this app on this device can use it, with rules such as an expiry. The key is kept in hardware-backed storage where available. The app must contact the service periodically to renew licenses; if it does not, offline tracks stop playing until it does. This lets the service honour subscription cancellations, device limits and catalog takedowns even for content already on the phone. Downloads are scheduled as background transfers that respect the Wi-Fi-only setting, storage limits and operating system background rules, and they resume from the last byte after an interruption.

**Playlists.** A playlist is an ordered list that several devices, and sometimes several people, edit, sometimes while offline. Storing it as a single blob and overwriting on save loses edits. A better model stores a **head revision** plus a log of operations (add at position, remove, move). A client sends an operation with the revision it was based on. If the head has moved, the server rebases the operation over the intervening ones, and the client receives the merged result. Large playlists are synced as diffs from the revision the client holds, not as full copies. The store is partitioned by playlist id, and a separate index lists the playlists a user follows.

**Recommendations.** Suggestions are produced in two stages. Offline and near-real-time jobs build representations of tracks and listeners from listening history (people who played this also played that), from audio analysis and from playlist co-occurrence, and generate candidate sets per user. At request time a ranker orders candidates using fresh context such as time of day, device and what was just skipped. Approximate nearest-neighbour search over track vectors powers "radio" and "more like this". Weekly personalised playlists are a batch product computed ahead of time and stored as ordinary playlists.

**Play-count pipeline.** Play events are money: they drive royalty payments and public charts. The client emits events with a unique id, the track, how long it actually played, and the context. They are appended to a durable stream and processed by a pipeline that must be effectively exactly-once: duplicates from retries are removed by event id, late events from offline devices are assigned to the period in which the play happened, and a play counts only if it passes the minimum listening rule. A fraud stage removes artificial streaming. Public counters are updated in near real time for display, while royalty reports come from a batch recomputation over the complete, deduplicated log, which is the authoritative figure.

**Cross-device and client architecture.** A listener may control playback on a speaker from a phone. Each active device keeps a connection to a state service; the "now playing" state lives on the server and devices subscribe to it, so a command from one device is delivered to the one producing sound. On mobile, the player runs as a foreground media service so the operating system keeps it alive, handles audio focus when a call arrives, and survives a switch from Wi-Fi to cellular because the buffer already holds the next seconds and range requests simply continue on the new network.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Songs are stored in a few quality levels and copied close to listeners. Pressing play gets a permission and a link, and the app downloads the song in pieces slightly ahead of playback. Saved songs stay locked on the phone and the app reports plays when it is online again.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Catalog reads are cached and filtered by territory. A playback service authorises each play and returns a signed CDN URL plus a decryption key; the client streams by byte range and prefetches the next track. Playlists are revisioned operation logs. Play events flow through a durable stream into a deduplicating counter.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Key decisions: where to enforce entitlements (at license issue, not at the CDN), license lifetime versus offline tolerance, operation-based playlist merge versus last-write-wins, and separating a fast approximate play counter from an authoritative batch computation for royalties. Late offline events require event-time processing with long allowed lateness.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: At scale the difficult parts are rights management across territories and time, fraud-resistant counting when plays have direct monetary value, keeping recommendation quality while avoiding feedback loops that only promote what is already popular, cost control for the long tail at the CDN, and consistent behaviour across many device types with different DRM capabilities.
Functional requirements

items: Search and browse a catalog filtered by the listener territory.
Play any available track with fast start, seek and gapless transitions.
Download tracks and playlists for offline listening under subscription rules.
Create, edit, follow and share playlists across devices.
Receive personalised recommendations and automatic next-track selection.
Count plays for public display and for royalty reporting.
Control playback on one device from another.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Time from tap to audio is a few hundred milliseconds in the common case.
Playback survives short network loss and network type changes.
Each qualifying play is counted exactly once, including plays made offline.
Entitlement and territory rules are enforced for streamed and downloaded content.
Catalog reads stay available when write pipelines or recommendations are degraded.
Playlist edits are never silently lost.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Illustrative assumption: 100M tracks x 4 quality files x 5 MB average = 2,000 TB = 2 PB of audio before replication.
Illustrative assumption: 250M daily listeners x 25 tracks per day = 6.25 billion plays per day; 6.25B / 86,400 s = ~72,000 plays started per second average.
Illustrative assumption: 3.5 minutes at 160 kbps = 210 s x 20 KB/s = ~4.2 MB per play; 72,000 x 4.2 MB = ~300 GB per second, about 2.4 Tbps average egress from CDN before local caching.
Illustrative assumption: each play emits 3 events (start, progress, end). 72,000 x 3 = ~216,000 events per second average into the stream.
Illustrative assumption: 300 bytes per event. 6.25B x 3 x 300 B = ~5.6 TB of raw event data per day.
Illustrative assumption: 4 billion playlists x 2 KB average = 8 TB of playlist data before replication.

rows: track

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Resolve: check `available_territories` contains the account country, check tier allows the quality, pick `file_id`, sign a URL with a short expiry, return the content key wrapped for the device.
Client buffer: start playback when a small target buffer is filled; keep fetching ranges until a high-water mark; fetch the head of the next track when the current one is near its end.
Playlist append: `INSERT playlist_op (playlist_id, revision = head + 1, ...) IF head = :expected`; on conflict read the missed operations, transform the incoming operation and retry.
Snapshot compaction: every N operations write a new snapshot and allow old operations to be trimmed.
Event upload: the client keeps events in a local queue and removes them only after the batch is acknowledged; the server deduplicates by `event_id`.
Qualifying play: count an event when `ms_played` meets the minimum listening threshold; group late events by `played_at`, not `received_at`.
License renewal: on each app start with connectivity, renew licenses close to expiry in one batched call.

blocks.text: Security

items: Audio is encrypted at rest and in the CDN; content keys are released only by the playback service after entitlement checks.
Signed URLs expire quickly and are scoped to a file, limiting the value of a leaked link.
Offline keys are wrapped for hardware-backed storage and bound to account and device.
Limit registered offline devices and concurrent streams per account to deter account sharing abuse.
Treat play events as untrusted input: validate plausibility and run fraud detection before they affect payments.
Listening history is personal data: restrict access, support export and deletion, and keep private sessions out of recommendations.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Whole-file progressive download by byte range
Simple, cache friendly, instant seek with range requests, few objects per track.
Quality cannot change in the middle of a track.
Audio, where files are small and bitrate switching per track is enough.
Segmented adaptive streaming
Bitrate can adapt every few seconds to the network.
Many more objects, manifests and requests for little benefit at audio sizes.
Video, podcasts with video, or very long audio on unstable networks.
Long offline license lifetime
Listeners can be offline for weeks without interruption.
Cancellations and takedowns take longer to reach devices.
Travel-heavy audiences; balanced against rights-holder requirements.
Operation log for playlists
Concurrent and offline edits merge without losing changes; efficient diff sync.
More complex server logic and periodic compaction of the log.
Collaborative or multi-device editing.
Last-write-wins playlist blob
Trivial to implement and reason about.
An offline device can overwrite newer edits from another device.
Single-device products or small, rarely edited lists.
Streaming counter plus batch recomputation
Fresh numbers for display and an auditable authoritative total for payments.
Two pipelines to operate and reconcile.
Any metric that is both shown live and used for money.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: CDN edge fails or is slow
Playback stalls for listeners mapped to that edge.
The resolve response lists more than one CDN host; the client switches host on error or slow throughput and keeps playing from its buffer meanwhile.
Playback service is unavailable
New tracks cannot be authorised even though the audio is cached at the edge.
Batch-resolve the queue ahead of time, cache URLs and keys for their short lifetime, and allow offline and locally cached tracks to play without the call.
Phone is offline past the license renewal deadline
Downloaded tracks refuse to play.
Renew licenses opportunistically whenever online, warn the user before expiry, and keep the files so a single renewal call restores them.
Play events are sent twice after a timeout
Counts and royalties would be inflated.
Each event has a client-generated id; the pipeline deduplicates on it and the gateway acknowledges only after a durable append.
Two devices edit the same playlist while one is offline
With overwrite semantics one set of edits disappears.
Edits are operations against a base revision and are rebased on the server; both sets of changes survive.
Bots loop a track to earn royalties
Payments are diverted and charts are distorted.
Fraud detection on device, account and listening patterns before counts feed royalty reports; suspicious streams are excluded and accounts reviewed.
A track is withdrawn by its rights holder
It must stop being playable everywhere, including offline copies.
Catalog availability is updated, new licenses are refused, and existing offline licenses are not renewed so copies become unplayable at the next check-in.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you make playback start in a fraction of a second?
blocks.text: Keep the network off the critical path. Resolve URLs and keys for the queue in advance, prefetch the first few hundred kilobytes of the next track and of likely selections, keep a disk cache of recent audio, and serve from a nearby CDN edge by byte range so playback begins once a small buffer is filled. Measure time from tap to first audio and treat it as a top-level metric.

blocks.title: Design offline downloads so that rights can still be enforced.
blocks.text: Download the same encrypted files the CDN serves. Issue a license per track or per batch, bound to account and device, with the content key wrapped for hardware-backed storage and an expiry. The app renews licenses whenever it is online. Renewal is refused if the subscription lapsed, the device limit is exceeded or the track was withdrawn, so the files become unusable without being deleted.

blocks.title: How do you count plays accurately for royalties?
blocks.text: Clients log events locally with unique ids and actual seconds played, and upload in batches until acknowledged. The gateway appends to a durable stream. A pipeline deduplicates by id, applies the qualifying-play rule, handles late events by event time and removes fraudulent traffic. A streaming job feeds display counters; a batch job recomputes from the full log for payment, and the two are reconciled.

blocks.title: How would you sync a 5,000-track playlist across devices?
blocks.text: Give the playlist a monotonically increasing revision. Clients keep the revision they hold and ask for changes since then, receiving a list of operations instead of 5,000 entries. Edits are sent as operations with a base revision and rebased if needed. Periodically compact the log into a snapshot so a new device can load snapshot plus recent operations.

blocks.title: What does the mobile player do when the network changes from Wi-Fi to cellular mid-track?
blocks.text: Nothing visible. Audio continues from the buffer, the in-flight range request fails or is cancelled, and the next range is requested over the new network, possibly from another CDN host. The client may choose a lower bitrate for the next track according to the data-saver setting, and it pauses offline downloads if they are restricted to Wi-Fi.
Takeaways

items: Audio is small: one encrypted file per quality served by byte range from a CDN is enough, with a skewed popularity curve that caches well.
Access control lives in the service that issues signed URLs and keys, not in the CDN.
Instant start comes from prefetching, batched resolution and a local cache.
Offline playback is encrypted files plus expiring, device-bound licenses that must be renewed.
Playlists are revisioned operation logs so multi-device and offline edits merge.
Play events are financial data: unique ids, durable ingestion, deduplication, fraud filtering and an authoritative batch total.

quiz.q: Why does audio streaming usually not need per-segment adaptive bitrate like video?
options: Audio files are small, so a whole track at one bitrate downloads quickly even on modest networks
Phones cannot decode more than one bitrate
quiz.why: A few megabytes per track means range requests on a single file are enough; switching at track boundaries is sufficient.

quiz.q: Where should the entitlement check for a play happen?
options: Only in the app user interface
At the CDN for every byte range
In the playback service that issues the signed URL and decryption key
quiz.why: The CDN serves encrypted bytes to anyone with a valid signed URL; control lies in who is given the URL and the key.

quiz.q: What allows the service to revoke downloaded tracks after a subscription ends?
options: Deleting files remotely from the phone
Offline licenses that expire unless renewed by contacting the service
quiz.why: The files stay on the device but the key to open them is time-limited and renewal is refused.

quiz.q: Why are play events given a unique id on the client?
options: So retries and replays can be deduplicated and each play is counted once
quiz.why: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing by id gives an effectively exactly-once count.

quiz.q: Why store a playlist as revisions and operations instead of one overwritten document?
options: Concurrent and offline edits can be merged instead of one overwriting the other
It removes the need for a database
quiz.why: Operations against a base revision can be rebased, so no edit is lost and clients sync small diffs.

lessons.title: Case study: Twitter-style home timeline

blocks.text: A home timeline shows each user the recent posts of everyone they follow, and it is read far more often than anything is posted. This lesson covers fan-out on write versus fan-out on read, the celebrity problem and the hybrid that solves it, the timeline cache, ranking, and real-time search and trends as a reference design.
In simple words

There are two ways to build your home feed. The system can collect posts from everyone you follow at the moment you open the app, which is slow if you follow many people. Or, each time someone posts, it can drop a copy of that post into the waiting feed of every follower, so opening the app is instant. Most people get the second approach, but for accounts with millions of followers the copies are skipped and their posts are added when you open the app.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Picture a block of mailboxes. One way to deliver news is for you to walk to every friend and ask what is new each morning. The other is for each friend to put a copy of their note into the mailbox of everyone who wants it, so your box is already full when you look. That works until a celebrity with a million fans writes a note: instead of filling a million boxes, their notes are pinned on a public board that you check as you collect your mail.

diagram.title: Home timeline, search and trends (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Client app
nodes.detail: Posts, reads the home timeline page by page, searches and views trends. Keeps a local cache of the last timeline.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates, rate-limits and routes write, timeline and search traffic to separate backends.

nodes.label: Post service
nodes.detail: Validates a new post, assigns a time-sortable id, stores it and publishes an event.

nodes.label: Post store
nodes.detail: Durable store of post content keyed by post id, fronted by a cache because recent posts are read constantly.

nodes.label: Post event stream
nodes.detail: Durable log of new posts and deletions consumed independently by fan-out, search indexing and trend counting.

nodes.label: Fan-out workers
nodes.detail: For each new post, look up the author followers and insert the post id into each follower timeline cache.

nodes.label: Social graph service
nodes.detail: Answers who follows whom in both directions, with follower lists paged for accounts with huge audiences.

nodes.label: Timeline cache
nodes.detail: In-memory list of recent post ids for each active user, capped in length and replicated.

nodes.label: Timeline service
nodes.detail: Reads the cached id list, merges in posts from high-follower accounts, ranks, hydrates ids into full posts and returns a page.

nodes.label: Search + trends service
nodes.detail: Fans a query out to index shards and merges results; serves the current list of trending terms by region.

nodes.label: Real-time index
nodes.detail: Inverted index over recent posts that becomes searchable within seconds, plus sliding-window term counts for trends.

steps.text: A user submits a post. The request carries a client-generated idempotency key so a retry on a weak network does not publish twice.
The post service validates length and media references and assigns an id that embeds a timestamp, so ids sort by creation time.
The post is written durably. From this point the author sees it on their own profile; delivery to followers happens asynchronously.
A "post created" event is appended to the stream. The write request returns to the user now, without waiting for fan-out.
A fan-out worker picks up the event and checks the author follower count against a threshold.
For an ordinary author it pages through the follower list. For an author above the threshold it stops here: no per-follower writes are made.
The post id is pushed onto the cached timeline list of each follower who has been active recently, and each list is trimmed to a maximum length.
In parallel, the indexing consumer tokenises the post and adds it to the newest index segment, and increments windowed counters for its hashtags and phrases.
A follower opens the app and asks for the home timeline, passing a cursor if they are scrolling.
The timeline service handles the read. Its work is bounded: it never scans all followed accounts.
It reads the precomputed list of post ids for this user. If the list is missing because the user was inactive, it is rebuilt from the followed accounts and cached again.
It fetches the short list of high-follower accounts this user follows, whose posts were not fanned out.
It pulls recent posts for those accounts, merges them with the cached ids, ranks the candidates, then hydrates the chosen ids into full posts with author and counts in one batched read.

Separately, when the user searches or opens trends, the search service queries every index shard in parallel, merges the top results, and returns terms whose recent counts are far above their usual level.

blocks.text: How it works

**The shape of the workload.** A timeline product is read-dominated by a wide margin: people open and scroll the home timeline many times for each post they write. A design should therefore spend effort at write time to make reads cheap. The second defining property is skew: most accounts have a few hundred followers, while a few have tens of millions. Any design must handle both ends.

**Fan-out on read (pull).** The simplest design stores each post once under its author. To build a home timeline the service fetches the list of followed accounts, queries recent posts for each, and merges them by time. Writes are trivial and there is no duplicated data. But a user who follows 2,000 accounts triggers thousands of lookups for every refresh, and this cost is paid on the most frequent operation in the system. Latency grows with the number of accounts followed and tail latency is poor.

**Fan-out on write (push).** The alternative precomputes each user timeline. When a post is created, workers look up the author followers and insert the post id into a per-user list held in memory. Reading the home timeline is then a single list read followed by a batched fetch of post bodies. Reads are fast and predictable. The cost moves to writes: a post by an account with a million followers causes a million list inserts, and many inserts go to users who will not open the app before the entry is trimmed away.

**The celebrity problem and the hybrid.** Pure push breaks for accounts with enormous audiences. A single post creates a burst of tens of millions of cache writes, delays fan-out for everyone else in the queue, and delivers unevenly, so some followers can see replies before the original. The standard solution is a **hybrid**: authors below a follower threshold are pushed; authors above it are not fanned out at all. At read time the timeline service takes the precomputed list and merges in recent posts from the handful of very large accounts the reader follows. That merge is cheap because the number of such accounts per reader is small and their recent posts are heavily cached.

**The timeline cache.** Each cached timeline is a bounded list of entries, each holding little more than a post id and an author id, kept in an in-memory store and replicated. Storing ids instead of full posts keeps entries tiny and means an edit or deletion needs no fan-out: hydration simply fails to find the post or returns the new version. Lists are capped at several hundred entries. Timelines are kept only for users active in recent weeks; a returning user triggers a rebuild using the pull path once. Because the cache is derived data, losing a node is recoverable: the timeline is recomputed.

**Ranking and hydration.** A purely chronological list is the base. A ranked timeline treats the cached list and other sources (posts liked by people you follow, suggested accounts) as candidates, scores them with a model that predicts engagement, and applies rules for diversity and freshness. Hydration turns ids into renderable objects by batched reads of post content, author profiles and counters, each behind its own cache. Counters such as likes are updated asynchronously and are allowed to be slightly stale.

**Ids, ordering and pagination.** Post ids are generated without coordination by combining a timestamp, a worker number and a sequence number in a 64-bit value. They are unique, roughly time-ordered and usable as a sort key, which makes merging lists by id equivalent to merging by time. Pagination uses the id as a cursor ("older than this id"), not an offset, so new posts arriving at the top do not shift pages and cause duplicates or gaps while a user scrolls.

**Search and trends.** Search over posts must be fresh: a post should be findable within seconds. The index is an inverted index split into time-ordered segments; new posts go into a small, mutable in-memory segment that is optimised for concurrent writes and reads, and older segments are immutable and compact. A query is scattered to all shards and the top results are gathered and merged, usually searching newest segments first. Trends are computed from the same stream: count terms in sliding windows, compare each count with the expected baseline for that term, and surface terms with unusual acceleration, per region. Comparing with a baseline prevents words that are always common from appearing as trends.

**The mobile client.** The app shows the cached last timeline immediately on launch and then asks the server for entries newer than the newest id it holds, so a cold start does not wait on the network. It prefetches the next page before the user reaches the end and prefetches media for posts about to scroll into view when on an unmetered connection. New-post delivery while the app is open uses a streaming connection or periodic polling for a small "new posts" indicator instead of rearranging the list under the user.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: When someone posts, a copy of the post reference is placed in the ready-made feed of each follower, so opening the app is quick. For accounts with millions of followers this copying is skipped and their posts are added when you load your feed.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Posts are stored once and an event triggers fan-out workers that push the post id into per-user lists in an in-memory cache. Reads fetch that list, merge posts from high-follower accounts pulled at read time, hydrate ids into full posts and paginate by id cursor. Search and trends consume the same event stream.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: The trade is write amplification against read latency, with the push/pull threshold as the tuning knob. Cache only active users, store ids not bodies, and bound list length. Fan-out is asynchronous, so the system is eventually consistent and must handle deletes, blocks and out-of-order delivery during hydration. Search needs a write-optimised recent segment and scatter-gather with partial-result tolerance.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: At scale the difficult parts are fan-out queue fairness so one viral author cannot starve others, cache memory economics per active user, ranking with a latency budget of tens of milliseconds over thousands of candidates, graph changes (follow, unfollow, block) that should retroactively alter timelines, multi-region replication of derived caches, and trend integrity against coordinated manipulation.
Functional requirements

items: Publish a short post with optional media.
Follow and unfollow accounts.
Read a home timeline of posts from followed accounts, with infinite scroll.
Read a profile timeline of one account.
Search recent posts by keyword and hashtag.
View trending topics for a region.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Home timeline responds within a couple of hundred milliseconds at the tail.
A post reaches most followers within seconds; eventual consistency is acceptable.
Posting stays available when fan-out or search is degraded.
A viral post or very large account does not delay delivery for others.
New posts are searchable within seconds.
Deleted posts and blocked accounts never appear after the change is accepted.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Illustrative assumption: 300M daily users x 20 timeline loads per day = 6 billion reads per day; 6B / 86,400 s = ~70,000 timeline reads per second average.
Illustrative assumption: 500M posts per day / 86,400 s = ~5,800 posts per second average.
Illustrative assumption: average fan-out of 200 active followers per post. 5,800 x 200 = ~1.16M timeline cache inserts per second.
Illustrative assumption: read to write ratio = 70,000 / 5,800 = ~12 timeline reads per post written, before counting scroll pagination.
Illustrative assumption: 300M cached timelines x 800 entries x 16 bytes = ~3.8 TB of memory per replica; x3 replicas = ~11.5 TB.
Illustrative assumption: one account with 50M followers posting under pure push = 50M inserts; at 1.16M inserts per second that single post equals ~43 s of the whole system fan-out capacity.
Illustrative assumption: 500M posts x 300 bytes of text and metadata = 150 GB of new post data per day, excluding media.

Body: text, media ids, reply-to id. Header: Idempotency-Key. Returns the created post with its id.

GET

Recent posts matching the query, newest first or ranked.
GET

Current trending terms for the region.

rows: post
post_id (key, time-sortable), author_id, text, media_refs, reply_to, created_at, deleted
Distributed key-value or sharded relational store, cached

Wide-column store, partitioned by author_id

In-memory cache, replicated

Small replicated lookup table

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Id layout: 64 bits = timestamp in milliseconds, then worker id, then per-millisecond sequence; sort by id equals sort by time.
Fan-out: `if follower_count(author) > THRESHOLD: skip; else for each page of followers: for active followers: LPUSH timeline:{user} post_id; LTRIM timeline:{user} 0 MAX`.
Read: `ids = cache.get(timeline:{user})`; `big = followed_big_accounts(user)`; `extra = recent_posts(big)`; merge by id, filter blocked and deleted, rank, take page, hydrate with one multi-get.
Cache miss: rebuild by pulling recent ids from `author_posts` for each followed account, merge, store, and limit concurrent rebuilds per node.
Pagination: `WHERE post_id < :cursor ORDER BY post_id DESC LIMIT :n`; the last id returned becomes the next cursor.
Indexing: append to the active segment; readers see a consistent prefix; seal and replace the segment when it reaches a size limit.
Trend score: `(current_rate - expected_rate) / sqrt(expected_rate)` per term and region, with a minimum distinct-account count.

blocks.text: Security

items: Enforce visibility at hydration: protected accounts, blocks and mutes are checked against the current graph before a post is returned.
Rate-limit posting, following and search per account and per device to slow spam and scraping.
Idempotency keys on post creation prevent duplicates from retries.
Validate and scan media and links asynchronously and withhold flagged content from timelines and trends.
Protect trends against manipulation by weighting account reputation and counting distinct accounts.
Audit privileged tools that can view or alter timelines and account state.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Fan-out on write (push)
Home timeline read is a single list fetch; fast and predictable.
Write amplification proportional to follower count; wasted work for inactive followers.
Authors with modest audiences, which is nearly everyone.
Fan-out on read (pull)
Cheap writes, no duplicated data, always fresh.
Read cost grows with accounts followed; poor tail latency on the most common request.
Very high-follower authors, inactive readers and timeline rebuilds.
Hybrid with a follower threshold
Bounded write bursts and fast reads; the read-time merge covers only a few accounts.
Two code paths and a threshold to tune; merge and ranking logic is more complex.
Any large network with skewed follower counts.
Cache post ids only
Small entries; edits and deletes need no fan-out.
Every read needs a hydration step with batched lookups.
Default choice for timeline caches.
Chronological timeline
Simple, predictable, easy to cache and paginate.
Important posts are missed when a user follows many active accounts.
A "latest" tab, or small networks.
Ranked timeline
Surfaces the most relevant posts first and can blend in other sources.
Needs feature pipelines, models and a strict latency budget; harder to reason about.
Default home view on large networks.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: An account with tens of millions of followers posts
With pure push, a huge burst of cache writes delays delivery for all other posts.
Hybrid: do not fan out above the threshold; merge those posts at read time from a hot cache.
Fan-out queue backs up
Followers see posts minutes late.
Partition the queue, scale workers on lag, prioritise small fan-outs, and let the read path pull recent posts from followed accounts when the cached list looks stale.
Timeline cache node is lost
Timelines for users on that node disappear.
Replicate lists across nodes; on a miss rebuild from the social graph and post store, with rate limiting to avoid a rebuild stampede.
A post is deleted after fan-out
Its id remains in millions of cached lists.
Do not chase the copies; hydration drops ids whose post no longer exists, and the entries age out.
User unfollows or blocks an account
Posts from that account are still in the cached timeline.
Filter at read time against the current graph and block list during hydration; optionally clean the list asynchronously.
One search index shard is slow
Scatter-gather waits on the slowest shard and the whole query is slow.
Per-shard deadlines and replicas; return partial results marked as such instead of failing.
Coordinated accounts push a term into trends
Trends show manipulated content.
Count distinct, reputable accounts instead of raw posts, discount bursts from new or linked accounts, and apply review for sensitive terms.
