blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Design the home timeline for a network with 300 million daily users.
blocks.text: Store posts once, keyed by a time-sortable id. On post, publish an event; fan-out workers push the id into per-user in-memory lists for followers of authors below a threshold. On read, fetch the list, merge recent posts from the few very large accounts the reader follows, rank, hydrate by batched lookups and return a page with an id cursor. Keep timelines only for active users and rebuild on demand.

blocks.title: How do you choose the push versus pull threshold?
blocks.text: It balances write cost against read cost. Estimate fan-out writes saved by excluding authors above N followers against the extra read-time merges for their followers. In practice the threshold sits where a single post would noticeably delay the queue. It can also be dynamic: consider follower count, posting rate and how many followers are active.

blocks.title: A user follows someone new. What happens to their timeline?
blocks.text: The graph is updated immediately. For the timeline, either backfill by merging the new account recent posts into the cached list asynchronously, or mark the timeline for rebuild on next read. Unfollow and block are enforced by a read-time filter so they take effect at once, with cleanup later.

blocks.title: How do you make a post searchable within seconds?
blocks.text: Consume the post stream into an indexer that writes to a small in-memory segment designed for concurrent appends and reads. Periodically seal it into an immutable, compressed segment. Shard the index and answer queries by scatter-gather, searching newest segments first, with per-shard deadlines and replicas.

blocks.title: How would you compute trends?
blocks.text: From the same stream, extract hashtags and phrases and count them in sliding windows per region. Score each term by how far its current rate exceeds its own historical baseline, so everyday words are ignored. Use approximate counting structures to bound memory, count distinct accounts to resist spam, and publish the top terms every short interval.
Takeaways

items: Timelines are read far more than written, so precompute at write time.
Fan-out on write gives fast reads; fan-out on read gives cheap writes; neither alone survives a skewed follower distribution.
The hybrid pushes for ordinary authors and pulls for very large ones, merging at read time.
The timeline cache holds bounded lists of post ids for active users and is rebuildable derived data.
Deletes, blocks and unfollows are enforced at hydration time instead of by chasing copies.
Search and trends are separate consumers of the same post event stream.

quiz.q: Why do large timeline systems favour fan-out on write for most users?
options: Writes are more frequent than reads
Reads are far more frequent than writes, so doing work at write time makes the common operation cheap
It uses less memory than pull
It removes the need for a database
quiz.why: Precomputing timelines moves cost from the very frequent read to the infrequent write.

quiz.q: What is the celebrity problem?
options: A single post by an account with millions of followers causes millions of timeline writes
Verified accounts need a different database
quiz.why: Write amplification scales with follower count, which is extremely skewed.

quiz.q: How does the hybrid approach handle very large accounts?
options: It skips fan-out for them and merges their recent posts into each reader timeline at read time
It limits how many followers they may have
quiz.why: Each reader follows only a few such accounts, so the read-time merge is small and cacheable.

quiz.q: Why store only post ids in the timeline cache?
options: Entries stay small and edits or deletions do not have to be propagated to every copy
Ids load faster on mobile screens
quiz.why: The body is fetched once at hydration, so there is a single source of truth for content.

quiz.q: Why paginate with an id cursor instead of an offset?
options: Offsets are not supported by caches
New posts arriving at the top would shift offsets and cause duplicates or gaps
quiz.why: A cursor is stable against inserts at the head of the list.

lessons.title: Case study: Dropbox-style file sync

blocks.text: A file sync service keeps the same folder identical on many devices, uploads only what changed, never stores the same data twice and never loses an edit when two devices change a file at once. This lesson covers chunking, content hashing, deduplication, the split between metadata and block storage, delta sync, conflict handling and mobile background upload as a reference design.
In simple words

Each file is cut into pieces, and each piece gets a fingerprint computed from its contents. The service keeps two things: a store of pieces looked up by fingerprint, and a list saying which pieces, in which order, make up each file. When you change a file, your device sends only the pieces the service does not already have, then updates the list. Other devices are told the list changed and fetch only the pieces they are missing.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a book kept as numbered pages in a shared warehouse, with a table of contents listing which pages form the book. To publish a new edition you send only the pages you rewrote and a new table of contents. If the warehouse already has an identical page from any book, you do not send it again. If two editors submit different new editions based on the same old one, the librarian keeps both and labels the second as a conflicting copy.

diagram.title: File sync with separate metadata and block planes (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Sync client
nodes.detail: Watches the local folder, splits changed files into blocks, hashes them, uploads missing blocks and commits new file versions.

nodes.label: Other device
nodes.detail: Another device on the same account. Holds a cursor into the change journal and waits to be told when something changes.

nodes.label: API gateway
nodes.detail: Authenticates devices and routes block traffic, metadata traffic and long-lived notification connections to separate backends.

nodes.label: Block service
nodes.detail: Accepts and serves blocks addressed by content hash, verifying that the bytes match the hash before storing.

nodes.label: Block store
nodes.detail: Immutable, replicated or erasure-coded storage for block contents. Holds almost all of the bytes in the system.

nodes.label: Block index
nodes.detail: Maps a block hash to its storage location and reference information, so the service can tell whether a block already exists.

nodes.label: Metadata service
nodes.detail: Owns the file tree: paths, versions and the ordered list of block hashes for each file. Decides whether a commit is accepted.

nodes.label: Metadata store
nodes.detail: Transactional store of file entries and an ordered change journal for each namespace. Small in bytes, critical in consistency.

nodes.label: Change stream
nodes.detail: Events for committed changes, consumed by notification and by background processing.

nodes.label: Notification service
nodes.detail: Holds long-poll connections from idle devices and wakes those whose namespace has changed.

nodes.label: Preview + index workers
nodes.detail: Generate thumbnails and previews and update search indexes after a commit, without delaying sync.

steps.text: A file is saved locally. The client splits it into blocks, hashes each one, and sends a commit proposal: path, parent version and the ordered list of block hashes.
The metadata service receives the proposal. It will not accept a file that refers to blocks the system does not hold.
It asks which of the listed hashes are already stored. For an edit to a large file, most are. The commit is answered with the short list of hashes that are missing.
The client uploads only the missing blocks, several in parallel, each addressed by its hash. Unchanged blocks and blocks that already exist anywhere are never sent.
The block service recomputes the hash of each received block and rejects any whose bytes do not match the claimed hash.
It records the hash in the block index. If a concurrent upload already stored the same hash, this one is simply acknowledged.
The bytes are written durably to the block store and never modified again.
With all blocks in place the client repeats the commit with the same content and the same parent version.

In one transaction the service checks that the file is still at the parent version the client saw, writes the new file entry with its block list, and appends an entry to the namespace change journal. If the parent version no longer matches, the commit is rejected as a conflict.
After the transaction commits, a change event is published.
The notification service learns that this namespace has a new journal position.
It completes the pending long-poll request of every other device linked to that namespace, telling them only that something changed.

The other device asks the metadata service for journal entries after its cursor, compares the new block list with the blocks it has locally, downloads only the missing blocks and reassembles the file.
Independently, workers create previews and update the search index for the new version.

blocks.text: How it works

**Two planes.** The system is split into a **metadata plane** and a **block plane** because they have opposite needs. Metadata (the file tree, versions, block lists, sharing) is small, changes often, and must be strictly consistent: two devices must agree on which version is current. Block data is enormous, immutable once written, and only needs to be durable and retrievable by key. Keeping them apart lets metadata live in a transactional database while blocks live in cheap, massively scalable object storage, and lets each scale on its own.

**Chunking and content addressing.** A file is split into blocks of a few megabytes and each block is identified by a cryptographic hash of its contents. A file version is then just an ordered list of hashes. Content addressing has three consequences. Integrity is built in, since anyone can verify a block by rehashing it. Blocks are immutable, since changing the bytes changes the name. And identical content is stored once regardless of which file or user it belongs to. **Fixed-size** chunking is simple but fragile: inserting one byte at the start of a file shifts every boundary and changes every block. **Content-defined** chunking places boundaries where a rolling hash of the data hits a pattern, so an insertion only disturbs nearby blocks.

**Deduplication and delta sync.** Before uploading, the client tells the server the hashes it intends to store and the server replies with the ones it lacks, so the client sends only those. Editing one part of a large file uploads one or two blocks. Copying a folder uploads nothing. For changes smaller than a block, a further step compares the new block with the old one using rolling checksums and sends only the differing byte ranges plus instructions to rebuild. Deduplication across users saves the most space but can leak information (a client could learn that some file already exists by observing that no upload was needed), so cross-user dedup must be handled carefully or limited to within an account.

**The commit protocol.** Sync is a two-phase interaction that keeps the invariant "metadata never points at a missing block". The client proposes a commit; the server lists missing blocks; the client uploads them; the client commits again and this time it succeeds. The commit is conditional on the **parent version**: it applies only if the file is still at the version the client based its edit on. Every accepted change gets a position in a per-namespace **journal**, a strictly ordered log. A device keeps a cursor into the journal and syncs by asking for entries after its cursor, which makes catching up after days offline the same operation as catching up after a second.

**Conflicts.** If two devices edit the same file from the same parent version, the first commit wins and the second is rejected because its parent is no longer current. Automatically merging arbitrary binary files is not possible, so the safe policy is to keep both: the losing client saves its version under a new name marked as a conflicted copy and syncs it as a new file. No data is lost and the user decides. Deletes and renames need the same care: a delete racing with an edit should not silently discard the edit, and a move is modelled as a change of path on a stable file id so that edits follow the file.

**Notification.** Devices should learn of changes quickly without polling constantly. Each idle device holds a long-poll or streaming connection to a notification service that knows only "namespace N has advanced". When a commit lands, the waiting requests for that namespace are completed, and each device then pulls the journal delta from the metadata service. Separating the cheap wake-up signal from the authoritative data fetch means the notification path can be lossy and stateless: a missed signal is corrected by a periodic fallback poll.

**Block storage durability.** Blocks are written once and read rarely, so the store optimises for durability and cost. Data is replicated across zones or erasure-coded, which gives high durability with less overhead than full copies. Background verification rereads blocks and compares them with their hashes to detect silent corruption, repairing from redundancy. Deleting is not immediate: a block may be referenced by many files and by old versions kept for recovery, so space is reclaimed by reference counting or by a periodic mark-and-sweep over the metadata, after retention windows have passed.

**The desktop client.** The client is a small distributed system of its own. It keeps a local database of three trees: the last synced state, the current local state and the current remote state. A file watcher feeds local changes, and a planner computes the operations needed to make the three trees agree. It must tolerate editors that save by writing a temporary file and renaming it, files that are open and locked, case-insensitive file systems, and crashes mid-download, which it handles by writing to a temporary location and renaming atomically once all blocks are verified.

**Mobile background upload.** A phone does not sync a whole folder; it shows the tree from metadata and downloads files on demand, keeping a bounded cache and explicit offline pins. Camera upload is the heavy path. The operating system limits background execution, so uploads are handed to system-managed background transfer facilities that can continue when the app is suspended, with constraints such as Wi-Fi only and charging. Each upload is a resumable session: blocks are sent with their offsets, the session id is persisted, and after an interruption or a switch between Wi-Fi and cellular the client asks the server which blocks it already has and continues from there. The final commit carries an idempotency key so a retry cannot create a duplicate photo.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Files are cut into pieces with fingerprints. The service stores each unique piece once and keeps a list of which pieces make each file. Changing a file sends only the new pieces and an updated list, and other devices fetch only what they lack.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Blocks are addressed by content hash and kept in an immutable block store; a transactional metadata store holds file entries and a per-namespace journal. A commit lists block hashes and a parent version, the server reports missing blocks, the client uploads them and commits. Other devices are woken by long-poll and pull the journal delta.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: The points to defend are fixed versus content-defined chunking, the invariant that metadata never references a missing block, optimistic concurrency on parent version with conflicted copies as the resolution, journal cursors for sync, and garbage collection of blocks that are shared and versioned. Cross-user deduplication trades storage for a side channel.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: At scale the hard parts are the correctness of the client planner across file-system quirks, sharding metadata while shared folders span users, verifying exabyte-scale storage continuously against bit rot, safe garbage collection racing with new commits that reference an old block, and migrating storage back ends with no downtime. Much of the reliability comes from testing the sync engine against randomised and adversarial event orders.
Functional requirements

items: Upload, download, rename, move and delete files and folders.
Keep a folder in sync across several devices of one account.
Share folders between users with shared edits.
Keep version history and allow restoring a previous version or deleted file.
Upload photos automatically from a phone in the background.
Show previews and search by file name.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: No acknowledged data is ever lost; durability is the first requirement.
Concurrent edits never overwrite each other silently.
Bandwidth is proportional to what changed, not to file size.
Other devices learn of a change within seconds when online.
Uploads and downloads resume after interruption.
Metadata stays strictly consistent within a namespace.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Illustrative assumption: 500M users x 20 GB stored on average = 10,000 PB = 10 EB of logical data.
Illustrative assumption: deduplication and compression remove 30%. 10 EB x 0.7 = 7 EB unique; with erasure coding overhead of 1.5x, 7 x 1.5 = 10.5 EB raw.
Illustrative assumption: 4 MB blocks. 7 EB / 4 MB = ~1.75 trillion blocks to index.
Illustrative assumption: 60 bytes of index per block. 1.75 trillion x 60 B = ~105 TB of block index, which must itself be sharded.
Illustrative assumption: 1 billion file commits per day / 86,400 s = ~11,600 metadata commits per second average.
Illustrative assumption: 100M devices connected and long-polling at once; at 10 KB of state per connection that is 1 TB of memory across the notification tier.
Illustrative assumption: a 2 GB file is 500 blocks; an edit touching 2 blocks uploads 8 MB, 0.4% of the file.

rows: POST
`/v1/files/commit`
Body: namespace id, path or file id, parent version, size, ordered block hashes. Returns the new version, or the list of missing hashes, or a conflict.
PUT

Uploads one block. The server verifies the hash. Idempotent.
GET
`/v1/blocks/{hash}`

POST

blocks.text: Data model

rows: namespace
ns_id (key), owner_id, type (root or shared), journal_head
Transactional store, sharded by ns_id
file_entry
ns_id, file_id (key), path, is_dir, version, size, block_list, modified_at, deleted
Transactional store, sharded by ns_id
journal
ns_id, seq (key), file_id, op, version, block_list, ts
Transactional store, same shard as the namespace
block_index
hash (key), location, size, created_at
Sharded key-value store
block_data
location (key), bytes
Immutable erasure-coded object storage

Transactional store, sharded by user_id
upload_session

Key-value store with TTL

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Client chunking: read the file, cut blocks at fixed size or at rolling-hash boundaries, compute a SHA-256 for each; cache hashes by path, size and modification time to avoid rehashing unchanged files.

Commit: `BEGIN; SELECT version FROM file_entry WHERE ns_id = :n AND file_id = :f FOR UPDATE; if version != :parent then CONFLICT; verify all hashes exist; UPDATE file_entry; INSERT journal (seq = journal_head + 1); COMMIT`.
Missing-block reply: the commit handler checks `block_index` for every hash and returns the absent ones without changing any state.
Download plan: diff the new block list against local blocks, fetch missing blocks in parallel, assemble into a temporary file, verify, rename atomically.
Conflict: on CONFLICT the client renames its local file to a conflicted-copy name and commits it as a new file with no parent.
Long-poll: the server keeps `ns_id -> waiting connections`; a change event completes them; clients reconnect immediately with updated cursors.
Garbage collection: periodically mark every hash referenced by live entries and retained versions, then delete unmarked blocks older than the grace period.

blocks.text: Security

items: Encrypt in transit and at rest; block encryption keys are managed separately from block data.
A block can be fetched only through a file the caller is authorised to read, never by guessing a hash alone.
Verify block hashes on the server so a client cannot poison a shared hash with wrong bytes.
Limit or scope cross-user deduplication so upload behaviour does not reveal whether someone else holds a file.
Shared folder permissions are checked on every commit and listing against the current mount table.
Version history and deferred deletion provide recovery from ransomware and accidental mass deletion.
Device links can be revoked, which invalidates tokens and can trigger a remote wipe of the local cache.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Fixed-size blocks
Simple to compute, parallel, easy random access by offset.
An insertion near the start shifts all later boundaries and defeats deduplication.
Files that are appended to or overwritten in place, and when simplicity matters.
Content-defined chunking
Boundaries survive insertions and deletions, so more blocks are reused.
More CPU on the client; variable block sizes complicate storage and offsets.
Documents and archives edited in the middle; backup-style workloads.
Global cross-user deduplication
Largest storage saving; popular files are stored once.
Upload behaviour can reveal that content already exists; complicates deletion and encryption per user.
When storage cost dominates and the side channel is mitigated.
Per-account deduplication
No information leak between users; simpler key management.
Less saving overall.
Privacy-sensitive or enterprise deployments.
Conflicted copy on concurrent edit
Never loses data; works for any file type.
The user must merge by hand and may accumulate copies.
General file sync of opaque files.
Automatic merge
No user action when it works.
Only possible for formats the system understands; a wrong merge corrupts data silently.
Structured collaborative documents with a known data model.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Upload interrupted halfway through a large file
Without care the whole file would be re-sent.
Blocks are independent and idempotent by hash; on resume the client asks which hashes exist and sends only the rest.
Two devices edit the same file offline
Both try to commit a child of the same parent version.
Conditional commit on parent version; the second is rejected and saved as a conflicted copy, so both edits survive.
Metadata commits but a block is missing
A file exists that cannot be downloaded.
The commit transaction verifies that every hash exists before accepting, and garbage collection never removes a block younger than a safety window.
Silent corruption of a stored block
A file would download with wrong bytes.
Hash is verified on write and on read; background scrubbing detects mismatches and repairs from replicas or erasure-coded fragments.
Notification service outage
Devices are not told about changes.
Clients fall back to periodic polling of the journal with their cursor; correctness never depends on the wake-up signal.
Client crashes while writing a downloaded file
A half-written file could replace a good one.
Download into a temporary file, verify all block hashes, then rename atomically over the destination.
Mobile app is suspended during camera upload
Uploads stall until the user reopens the app.
Use system background transfer sessions with persisted upload session ids, resume by offset, and commit with an idempotency key.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: How do you sync a 2 GB file after a small edit?
blocks.text: The client rechunks and hashes the file, which gives a new block list that differs from the old one in a few entries. It proposes the commit, the server replies with the few hashes it lacks, the client uploads those blocks, then commits with the parent version. Other devices receive the new block list, see they already hold all but the changed blocks, download those and rebuild the file locally.

blocks.title: How do you guarantee the file tree never references data that does not exist?
blocks.text: Order the operations: blocks first, metadata second. The metadata transaction checks that every listed hash is present before it commits. Block uploads are idempotent, so retries are safe. Garbage collection only removes blocks unreferenced for longer than a grace period, so a block that is about to be referenced is not collected.

blocks.title: How does a device that was offline for a week catch up?
blocks.text: It stores a cursor, the last journal position it applied for each namespace. On reconnect it asks for entries after the cursor, receives them in order in pages, and applies them, downloading missing blocks. If the cursor is too old or the namespace was reset, the server tells it to do a full listing and reconcile against local state.

blocks.title: Design the metadata schema and its sharding.
blocks.text: Use a namespace as the unit: a personal root or a shared folder. Entries are keyed by namespace id and path or file id, with a version and block list, and each namespace has a monotonically increasing journal. Shard by namespace id so a commit is a single-shard transaction. Shared folders are their own namespaces mounted into several users, which avoids cross-user transactions.

blocks.title: How would you implement reliable photo upload on a phone?
blocks.text: Create an upload session on the server and persist its id locally. Hand block uploads to the operating system background transfer mechanism with Wi-Fi and battery constraints. After any interruption or network switch, ask the server for the received offset and continue. When all blocks are in, commit with an idempotency key derived from the asset id and content hash so retries never duplicate the photo.
Takeaways

items: Split the system into a consistent metadata plane and a durable, immutable block plane.
A file version is an ordered list of content hashes; identical blocks are stored once.
Upload blocks first, then commit metadata conditionally on the parent version.
Concurrent edits are detected by version mismatch and preserved as conflicted copies.
Devices sync by reading a per-namespace journal from a cursor; notifications are only a wake-up.
Block deletion is deferred garbage collection, never an immediate delete.
Mobile uploads are resumable sessions run through system background transfers.

quiz.q: Why separate metadata storage from block storage?
options: Because blocks are confidential and metadata is not
Metadata is small and needs strict consistency, while blocks are huge, immutable and only need durable key lookup
Because databases cannot store binary data
quiz.why: The two have opposite requirements, so each gets a storage system suited to it and scales independently.

quiz.q: What does addressing a block by the hash of its contents give you?
options: Built-in integrity checking, immutability and automatic deduplication of identical content
quiz.why: The name is derived from the bytes, so equal bytes share a name and any change produces a different name.

quiz.q: A user inserts one paragraph at the start of a large document. Which chunking limits the upload best?
quiz.why: Content-defined boundaries move with the data, so only the blocks near the insertion change.

quiz.q: Two devices commit different edits based on the same version. What is the safe outcome?
options: The later timestamp silently overwrites the earlier
Both commits are rejected and both edits discarded
The first commit is accepted and the second is kept as a conflicted copy
quiz.why: Optimistic concurrency on the parent version detects the race, and keeping both versions loses nothing.

quiz.q: Why does the notification only say "something changed" instead of carrying the change?
options: So the wake-up path can be simple and lossy while the authoritative delta is fetched from the journal by cursor
quiz.why: Correctness comes from the journal; a missed signal is repaired by a later poll.

lessons.title: Case study: Zoom-style video calls

blocks.text: A video meeting must deliver audio and video between many people with a delay small enough for natural conversation, over networks that drop packets, block ports and change mid-call. This lesson covers signalling, the WebRTC media stack, mesh versus SFU versus MCU, simulcast, TURN relays, recording and mobile network switches as a reference design.
In simple words

A call has two separate conversations. First, the apps talk to a coordination server to agree who is in the meeting and how to reach each other. Then the audio and video flow as a fast stream of small packets. In a group call each person sends their video once to a relay server, which passes it on to everyone else and gives each viewer a picture quality their connection can handle.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Think of a conference with interpreters. A receptionist checks you in and tells you which room to go to; that is the coordination step. In the room, each speaker talks into one microphone, and a sound desk routes every voice to every listener. The desk does not re-record anything; it only decides who gets which feed, sending a lighter feed to people at the back with poor reception.

diagram.title: Group video call with signalling, SFU and relay (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Participant A
nodes.detail: Captures camera and microphone, encodes several video qualities, sends them to the media server and renders the streams it receives.

nodes.label: Participant B (restricted network)
nodes.detail: A participant behind a firewall that blocks direct UDP, so media must go through a relay.

nodes.label: Signalling gateway
nodes.detail: Long-lived WebSocket connections carrying join, leave, session descriptions, network candidates and in-meeting controls such as mute.

nodes.label: Meeting service
nodes.detail: Authorises joins, owns the participant roster and picks which media server region hosts the meeting.

nodes.label: Room state store
nodes.detail: Fast replicated store of live meeting state: participants, roles, assigned media servers and recording status.

nodes.label: STUN / TURN relay
nodes.detail: STUN tells a client its public address. TURN relays media for clients that cannot send UDP directly, including over TCP or TLS on port 443.

nodes.label: SFU media server
nodes.detail: Selective forwarding unit. Receives each participant streams once and forwards chosen streams and quality layers to each receiver without decoding video.

nodes.label: SFU in another region
nodes.detail: A media server near distant participants. The two servers exchange streams over a backbone link so each user connects to a nearby server.

nodes.label: Recording worker
nodes.detail: Joins the meeting as a silent receiver, writes the incoming streams to disk and later composes them into a single playable file.

nodes.label: Recording store
nodes.detail: Object storage for raw captures and final recordings, encrypted, with access rules and retention.

steps.text: Participant A opens a WebSocket to the signalling gateway and sends a join request with a meeting id and an access token.
The meeting service validates the token, applies rules such as waiting room and capacity, and adds A to the roster.
It reads or creates the room record. If the meeting has no media server yet, it chooses a region close to the first participants and records the assignment.
It asks the chosen media server to create a session for A and gets back the server address and security fingerprint.
A and the media server exchange session descriptions through signalling: which codecs each supports, the encryption fingerprint, and the list of candidate network addresses to try.
A runs connectivity checks against the candidates, picks the best working path, completes an encrypted handshake and starts sending audio plus three video qualities of the same camera picture.
Participant B joins the same way and receives the same media server assignment.
B is on a network that blocks outgoing UDP. Direct checks fail, so B allocates an address on the TURN relay over TLS on port 443 and sends media to it.
The relay forwards B packets to the media server and returns the packets going the other way. It cannot read the media, which stays encrypted.
The server forwards B audio and video to A. For each receiver it chooses which quality layer to send based on that receiver estimated bandwidth and how large the video is drawn on screen.
Participants on another continent connect to a server near them. The two servers exchange only the streams actually needed on the other side.
When the host starts recording, a recording worker joins as a hidden receiver and is sent the audio and the high-quality video layers.
After the meeting the worker composes the streams into one file with a layout, uploads it, and the host is notified when it is ready.
A walks out of Wi-Fi range. The signalling connection reconnects over cellular and triggers a restart of connectivity checks, so media resumes on the new network without leaving the meeting.

blocks.text: How it works

**Two planes with different rules.** The **signalling plane** carries small, reliable, ordered messages: join, leave, session descriptions, mute, raise hand, chat. It runs over a WebSocket on TCP and looks like any stateful web service. The **media plane** carries audio and video as RTP packets over UDP, because for conversation a late packet is useless and waiting for a retransmission, as TCP does, adds delay for everything behind it. The target is end-to-end delay under a few hundred milliseconds. Every design choice on the media plane prefers timeliness over completeness.

**Establishing a connection.** Most devices sit behind network address translation and do not know their public address. **STUN** lets a client ask a server what address its packets appear to come from. **ICE** gathers all possible addresses (local, STUN-discovered, relay) as candidates, exchanges them through signalling, and tests pairs until one works, preferring direct paths. When no direct path works because a firewall blocks UDP or uses strict translation, **TURN** relays the media through a server, if necessary inside TCP or TLS on port 443 so it looks like ordinary web traffic. The session description (SDP) carries codecs and security parameters. Media is encrypted with SRTP using keys agreed in a DTLS handshake.

**Mesh, MCU and SFU.** With **mesh**, every participant sends to every other directly: no media server, but each client uploads `n - 1` copies, so it stops working beyond three or four people. An **MCU** receives all streams, decodes them, composes one mixed picture and encodes a single stream per receiver: clients are simple and bandwidth is low, but the server does heavy decode and encode work and the extra processing adds delay and removes layout freedom. An **SFU** receives each stream once and forwards packets to the other participants without decoding video. Server cost is mostly network, delay is minimal, and each client can lay out streams as it likes. SFU is the standard choice for large interactive meetings.

**Simulcast and layer selection.** An SFU cannot re-encode, so how does it serve a viewer on fibre and a viewer on weak mobile data from the same sender? With **simulcast**, the sender encodes the camera at several resolutions and bitrates at once and sends them all. With **scalable video coding**, one stream is built in layers that can be dropped. The SFU chooses a layer for each receiver from that receiver bandwidth estimate and from what the client says it is displaying: a thumbnail needs only the lowest layer, the active speaker gets the highest that fits. Receivers also tell the server which streams are visible, so off-screen video is not forwarded at all.

**Surviving bad networks.** Each receiver continuously estimates available bandwidth from packet delay and loss and reports it; senders and the SFU adapt bitrate within a second or two. Loss is repaired selectively: a NACK asks for one missing packet when there is time, forward error correction adds redundancy for audio, and a jitter buffer smooths uneven arrival at the cost of a little delay. When bandwidth collapses, the system degrades in a fixed order: lower video resolution, lower frame rate, stop video, and protect audio last, because a meeting with audio only is still a meeting.

**Placing and scaling media servers.** A meeting is stateful: all participants of a small meeting should be on one server. The meeting service assigns a server by region and load when the meeting starts and stores the mapping. For global meetings, each participant connects to a nearby server and servers are **cascaded**: they forward streams to each other over well-provisioned links, which is better than one participant crossing the public internet to a distant region. Very large meetings and webinars spread receivers over many servers in a tree, and viewers who never speak can be served by a low-delay streaming path instead of a full interactive session.

**Recording.** Recording should not affect the live call. A recording worker joins as a receive-only participant, stores the raw encrypted-in-transit streams with timestamps, and a later job decodes, aligns audio and video, applies a layout and encodes a standard file. Doing the composition after the meeting keeps real-time capacity for the call itself. If meetings use true end-to-end encryption, where the servers never hold the keys, a server-side recorder cannot decode the media, so recording must happen on a client or be disabled; this is a product trade-off, not a bug.

**Failure handling.** If a media server dies, its meetings lose media but signalling survives. Clients detect the loss within a second or two by missing packets, ask signalling for a new assignment, and reconnect to a replacement server; the roster and mute state are in the room store, so the meeting continues after a short freeze. Signalling gateways are stateless apart from the connection and reconnect to any node. TURN relays are pooled per region and chosen by the client from a list.

**The mobile client.** A phone changes networks often. When the active network changes, the client does an **ICE restart**: it gathers fresh candidates on the new interface and renegotiates while keeping the same meeting session, so the gap is about a second. Phones have limited upload and get hot, so they send fewer simulcast layers, use hardware encoders, and reduce resolution when the device signals thermal pressure. When the app goes to the background, video capture stops but audio continues through the platform call and audio session facilities. Battery and data use are reduced by not receiving video that is not on screen.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: A coordination server checks you into the meeting and helps your app find a route. Then your audio and video go as small fast packets to a relay server that passes them to everyone else, choosing a lighter or heavier picture for each person depending on their connection.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Signalling over WebSocket exchanges session descriptions and ICE candidates; media flows as SRTP over UDP to an SFU, or through a TURN relay when UDP is blocked. Senders use simulcast and the SFU forwards one layer per receiver based on bandwidth estimates. Recording is a hidden participant plus an offline composition job.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: The design turns on SFU versus MCU cost and delay, simulcast versus scalable coding, where congestion control runs, and how meetings are placed and cascaded across regions. Loss recovery mixes NACK, forward error correction and jitter buffering under a fixed delay budget. End-to-end encryption removes the server ability to record or transcode.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: At scale the hard problems are capacity allocation for meetings whose size is unknown at start, fair bandwidth distribution among dozens of forwarded streams per receiver, large-meeting topologies with active-speaker selection, interoperability across browsers and native clients with different codec support, relay cost for the share of users who need TURN, and measuring quality from client telemetry instead of server metrics.
Functional requirements

items: Create, schedule and join meetings with a link or id.
Send and receive audio and video among many participants, with screen sharing.
Mute, raise hand, chat and host controls such as waiting room and remove participant.
Adapt quality to each participant network and device.
Record a meeting and make the recording available afterwards.
Join from restrictive networks and keep the call across network changes.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: End-to-end audio delay low enough for natural turn-taking, a few hundred milliseconds at most.
Join completes within a few seconds.
Audio continues under conditions where video cannot.
Loss of one media server interrupts its meetings for only a few seconds.
Media is encrypted in transit on every hop.
Capacity scales with predictable daily peaks at the start of each hour.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Illustrative assumption: 10M participants in meetings at peak, average meeting size 5, so 10M / 5 = 2M concurrent meetings.
Illustrative assumption: each participant uploads 1.5 Mbps total (audio plus three simulcast layers). 10M x 1.5 Mbps = 15 Tbps into media servers.
Illustrative assumption: each participant downloads 2 Mbps of forwarded streams. 10M x 2 Mbps = 20 Tbps out of media servers.
Illustrative assumption: one media server forwards 2 Gbps. 20 Tbps / 2 Gbps = 10,000 servers at peak, before headroom and regional spread.
Illustrative assumption: 10% of participants need TURN at 3.5 Mbps combined up and down. 1M x 3.5 Mbps = 3.5 Tbps of relay traffic.
Illustrative assumption: mesh with 6 people needs each client to upload 5 streams of 1 Mbps = 5 Mbps; an SFU needs 1.5 Mbps upload regardless of group size.
Illustrative assumption: 5% of 2M meetings are recorded for 40 minutes at 1 Mbps. 100,000 x 2,400 s x 0.125 MB/s = 30 TB of recordings for that set of concurrent meetings.

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Join: validate token; add participant to `room_state` with compare-and-set on `version`; if `media_servers` is empty, pick by region and load and write it in the same update.
Negotiation: client sends an offer listing audio, simulcast video layers and data channel; server answers with accepted codecs and its DTLS fingerprint; candidates are trickled as they are found.
Candidate order: host and server-reflexive UDP first, then relay UDP, relay TCP, relay TLS on 443.

Layer selection per receiver and stream: choose the highest layer whose bitrate fits the share of estimated bandwidth allotted to that stream and whose resolution does not exceed the tile size the client reported.
Subscription: clients send the set of visible participant ids; the SFU forwards video only for those and audio only for the loudest few speakers.
Layer switch: on change, request a keyframe from the new layer and switch on its arrival so the decoder never sees a broken picture.
ICE restart: client sends new credentials and candidates over signalling; the server keeps the session and stream state and swaps the transport when the new path is validated.
Recording: worker subscribes to all audio and top video layers, writes packets with capture timestamps, and a post-processing job composes and encodes the result.

blocks.text: Security

items: Join tokens are short-lived, bound to meeting and user, and checked by the meeting service; hosts can lock a meeting and use a waiting room.
Media is encrypted with SRTP using keys from a DTLS handshake whose fingerprint is exchanged over authenticated signalling.
TURN credentials are time-limited and per session so relays cannot be used as open proxies.
An SFU can read media unless end-to-end encryption is layered on top, in which case only participants hold the content keys and server recording is unavailable.
Recordings are encrypted at rest, access-controlled and subject to retention; participants are notified when recording starts.
Rate-limit join attempts and meeting id guesses to prevent uninvited entry.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Mesh (peer to peer)
No media servers; lowest delay for two people; end-to-end encryption is natural.
Upload and CPU grow with each participant; unusable beyond a handful.
One-to-one calls and very small groups.
SFU
Low server CPU, minimal added delay, per-receiver quality through layers, flexible client layouts.
Each client decodes many streams and download grows with visible participants.
Interactive group meetings from a few to hundreds of people.
MCU
One stream per receiver; works for weak devices and legacy room systems.
Expensive decode and encode per meeting, added delay, fixed layout, no end-to-end encryption.
Dial-in gateways and devices that can handle only a single stream.
Simulcast
Works with widely supported codecs; the SFU just picks a stream.
Sender spends extra upload and CPU encoding several versions.
Default for group calls on capable devices.
TURN relay over TCP/TLS 443
Connects users behind restrictive firewalls.
Extra hop and relay bandwidth cost; TCP adds delay under loss.
Fallback only, after direct UDP fails.
Server-side recording
Reliable, independent of any participant device, composed offline.
Requires the service to access the media, so it conflicts with end-to-end encryption.
Standard meetings where the organisation accepts provider-held keys.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Firewall blocks UDP
Direct connectivity checks fail and there is no media.
ICE falls back to TURN over UDP, then TCP, then TLS on port 443; the client is told when it is on a relayed path.
SFU node crashes mid-meeting
All participants on it lose audio and video.
Clients detect missing media quickly, signalling reassigns the meeting to another server from room state, and clients reconnect with an ICE restart.
A receiver bandwidth drops sharply
Video freezes and audio breaks up if the bitrate is not reduced.
Bandwidth estimation triggers a switch to a lower simulcast layer within about a second; audio is prioritised and video is paused if needed.
Packet loss burst
Missing frames cause visual artefacts or a frozen picture.
NACK retransmission for recent packets, forward error correction for audio, and a keyframe request when the decoder cannot recover.
Signalling connection drops
Controls stop working although media may continue for a while.
Client reconnects to any gateway with a resume token; room state is in the shared store; media is left running during the reconnect window.
Phone moves from Wi-Fi to cellular
The old network path disappears and packets go nowhere.
Network change event triggers an ICE restart on the new interface while the meeting session stays alive.
Region runs out of media capacity
New meetings cannot be placed nearby.
Spill over to the next closest region, cascade as needed, and keep headroom by scaling on predicted calendar load.

blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Design a group video call for 50 participants.
blocks.text: Signalling over WebSocket to a stateless gateway backed by a meeting service and a room state store. Media through an SFU chosen by region and load. Senders publish audio and simulcast video; receivers subscribe only to visible streams and the SFU picks a layer for each from bandwidth estimates and tile size. STUN and TURN for connectivity, SRTP for encryption, active-speaker detection to limit high-quality video to a few streams.

blocks.title: Compare mesh, SFU and MCU.
blocks.text: Mesh has no server but each client sends n - 1 streams, so it suits two to four people. An MCU decodes and mixes to one stream per receiver: light clients, heavy servers, more delay. An SFU forwards without decoding: cheap servers, low delay, flexible layouts, but clients receive many streams. For interactive meetings SFU with simulcast is the usual answer; MCU remains for gateways to simple endpoints.

blocks.title: A user reports frozen video but clear audio. What is happening and what should the system do?
blocks.text: Their downlink cannot carry the video bitrate, or loss is breaking frames. The bandwidth estimator should drive the SFU to a lower layer or lower frame rate, request a keyframe after a switch, and pause video for off-screen tiles. Audio is prioritised with redundancy. Client telemetry of loss, jitter, bitrate and freezes confirms it and feeds quality dashboards.

blocks.title: How do you support participants on different continents in one meeting?
blocks.text: Connect each participant to a media server in a nearby region and cascade the servers over a backbone, forwarding only the streams needed on each side. This keeps the lossy last mile short. The meeting service tracks which servers host the meeting, and active-speaker selection limits how many streams cross between regions.

blocks.title: What happens on the client when a phone switches from Wi-Fi to cellular during a call?
blocks.text: The operating system reports the network change. The signalling socket reconnects and resumes the session. The client gathers new ICE candidates on the cellular interface and performs an ICE restart toward the same media server, keeping encryption context where possible. Media resumes in about a second, bitrate starts low and ramps up as the new path is measured.
Takeaways

items: Signalling is reliable and stateful over TCP; media is real-time over UDP and prefers losing data to delaying it.
ICE tries direct paths first and falls back to a TURN relay, including over TLS on port 443.
SFU is the default group topology: forward, do not transcode.
Simulcast or scalable coding lets the server match quality to each receiver without re-encoding.
Degrade in order: resolution, frame rate, video off, and protect audio to the end.
Recording is a hidden receiver plus offline composition, and it is incompatible with end-to-end encryption on the server side.
Mobile clients handle network switches with an ICE restart while the meeting session stays alive.

quiz.q: Why is media sent over UDP instead of TCP?
options: A late packet is useless in conversation, and TCP retransmission would delay everything behind it
quiz.why: Real-time media prefers losing a packet to waiting for it; TCP head-of-line blocking adds delay.

quiz.q: What does an SFU do with incoming video?
options: Decodes all streams and mixes them into one picture
Stores it and plays it back later
Forwards the packets to other participants, choosing which streams and layers each receives, without decoding
quiz.why: Forwarding without transcoding is what keeps server cost and added delay low.

quiz.q: What problem does simulcast solve?
options: Finding the public address of a client
Serving receivers with different bandwidths from one sender when the server cannot re-encode
quiz.why: The sender provides several qualities and the SFU picks one for each receiver.

quiz.q: When is a TURN relay used?
options: When no direct path between the client and its peer or media server can be established
quiz.why: TURN is the fallback of last resort because it adds a hop and costs relay bandwidth.

quiz.q: Why does true end-to-end encryption conflict with server-side recording?
options: Recordings are too large to encrypt
The servers never hold the media keys, so a server-side recorder cannot decode the streams
quiz.why: If only participants hold the keys, any server-side processing of media content is impossible.

lessons.title: Case study: Short-video feed (TikTok / Reels style)

blocks.text: A short-video app shows an endless, personalised stream of clips where the next video must already be playing the instant you swipe. This lesson covers upload and transcoding, two-stage recommendation with candidate generation and ranking, feed prefetch on mobile and the engagement event pipeline that feeds the models, as a reference design.
In simple words

Creators upload a clip, and the service converts it into several sizes so it plays on any phone and connection. For each viewer, the system first gathers a few thousand clips that might interest them, then scores those carefully and picks the best handful. The app downloads the start of the next few clips before you swipe, and it reports how long you watched each one so the next choices get better.

blocks.title: Analogy
blocks.text: Imagine a television channel programmed just for you. A scout walks through a huge warehouse of tapes and grabs a trolley of likely ones. An editor then looks closely at the trolley and decides the running order. A stagehand has the next two tapes already loaded in the player, so there is no gap when one ends. Someone notes which shows you watched to the end and which you switched off, and gives the notes to the scout and the editor.

diagram.title: Short-video upload, recommendation and playback (illustrative reference design)

nodes.label: Creator app
nodes.detail: Records and edits a clip, compresses it on the device and uploads it in resumable chunks.

nodes.label: Viewer app
nodes.detail: Plays the feed full screen, prefetches upcoming clips and batches engagement events.

nodes.label: Upload service
nodes.detail: Manages resumable upload sessions, stores the original file and creates the video record in a processing state.

nodes.label: Transcode + moderation
nodes.detail: Produces several resolutions and bitrates, a cover image and a fast-start first segment, and runs automated safety checks before a video can be distributed.

nodes.label: Rendition store
nodes.detail: Object storage for the encoded versions of each video, the origin for the CDN.

nodes.label: Video CDN
nodes.detail: Edge caches serving video segments close to viewers. Popular clips are served almost entirely from the edge.

nodes.label: Feed service
nodes.detail: Orchestrates one feed request: gets candidates, has them ranked, applies policy and diversity rules and returns a short ordered batch.

nodes.label: Candidate generation
nodes.detail: Quickly narrows hundreds of millions of videos to a few thousand using several cheap sources such as embedding similarity, followed creators and trending.

nodes.label: Ranking
nodes.detail: Scores each candidate with a heavier model that predicts watch time, completion, likes and shares, and combines them into one value.

nodes.label: Engagement event stream
nodes.detail: Durable log of impressions, watch durations, likes, shares, skips and follows from all clients.

nodes.label: Realtime feature store
nodes.detail: Low-latency store of user and video features and embeddings, updated by stream jobs within seconds to minutes of an event.

steps.text: The creator app compresses the clip and uploads it in chunks under an upload session id. If the connection drops, it resumes from the last confirmed chunk.
When the last chunk arrives, the original is stored and an event starts processing. The creator sees the post as "processing".

Workers encode a ladder of resolutions and bitrates in parallel, cut each into short segments, extract a cover frame and write everything to the rendition store. Automated moderation runs on frames, audio and text.

Once the video passes checks, its content embedding and metadata are added to the candidate indexes. A new video has no engagement history, so it is first shown to a small audience to learn how it performs.
A viewer opens the app or nears the end of the batch it holds. The app requests the next batch with a session cursor and the ids it has already seen.
Candidate generation runs several sources in parallel and returns a few thousand video ids in tens of milliseconds.

The main source looks up the viewer embedding and runs an approximate nearest-neighbour search over video embeddings. Other sources add recent posts from followed creators and regionally popular clips.
Candidates are filtered for already seen, blocked and ineligible videos, and the remainder is sent for scoring.
The ranker fetches fresh features for the viewer and for each video, including what the viewer did seconds ago in this session, and predicts several outcomes for every candidate.
The feed service re-orders the top results for variety, such as not repeating a creator or a sound back to back, and returns a batch of around eight to ten items with playback URLs.
While the current clip plays, the app downloads the first segment of the next two or three clips at a moderate bitrate, so a swipe starts playback from local data.
A clip not yet at the edge is fetched from the origin once and cached. Clips predicted to become popular can be pushed to edges in advance.
The app records each impression, how many milliseconds were watched, loops, likes, shares and swipes away, and uploads them in small batches with unique ids.
Stream jobs update counters and embeddings in the feature store within seconds to minutes, so the next batch already reflects what the viewer just did. The same log is stored for model training.

blocks.text: How it works

**Upload and transcoding.** Uploads come from phones on unreliable networks, so they use a **resumable** protocol: the client opens a session, sends fixed-size chunks with offsets, and can query the last received offset after a failure. The client usually compresses before upload to save data. On completion the original is stored and a job is queued. Transcoding produces an **encoding ladder**, several resolutions and bitrates, each cut into segments of a few seconds, plus a cover image. Short clips let the whole file be encoded in parallel quickly, so a post can be live within seconds to a minute. Popular videos may later be re-encoded with slower, more efficient settings, because the saved bandwidth multiplied by millions of views repays the compute.

**Fast-start playback.** In a swipe feed the measure that matters is time from swipe to first frame. Each rendition is packaged so that the first segment is small and begins with a keyframe, and the manifest information the player needs is delivered inside the feed response instead of by a separate request. The player starts at a conservative bitrate that it has already prefetched and moves up after the first segment. Because most clips are watched for only a few seconds, the system optimises the first seconds of every clip above all else.

**Two-stage recommendation.** There are far too many videos to score each one with a good model for every request. The funnel has two main stages. **Candidate generation** (recall) uses cheap methods to cut hundreds of millions of items to a few thousand. **Ranking** then applies an expensive model to those few thousand. Splitting the problem lets recall optimise for coverage and speed and ranking optimise for precision. A final **re-ranking** step applies rules that a per-item score cannot express: variety of creators and topics, limits on repetition, freshness, safety and business policy.

**Candidate generation.** The main source is embedding retrieval. A two-tower model learns a vector for each user and each video such that users are close to videos they engage with; video vectors are stored in an **approximate nearest-neighbour index** and the request retrieves the nearest videos to the user vector in milliseconds. Other sources run in parallel: videos similar to what the user just watched, new posts from followed creators, trending items in the region, and an **exploration** source that deliberately includes new or uncertain videos. Mixing sources keeps the feed from collapsing into one topic and gives new videos a chance to gather signal.

**Ranking.** The ranker is a multi-task model: for each viewer and candidate it predicts several outcomes, such as expected watch time, probability of finishing, liking, sharing, following, and negative signals such as a quick swipe away or "not interested". The predictions are combined into one score by a weighted formula, which is where product priorities are expressed. Inputs include long-term user features, video features, creator features and, critically, **real-time session features**: what this viewer watched and skipped in the last minute. In short video, watch time and completion are the strongest signals because every impression produces them, whereas likes are sparse.

**Cold start and the feedback loop.** A new video has no history. It is given a small initial audience chosen by its content embedding, and its measured performance decides whether it is shown more widely, a step-by-step expansion. A new user has no history either, so the first session relies on popular and diverse content and adapts quickly from the first few swipes. Because the system trains on its own output, it can amplify whatever it already shows; exploration traffic and diversity rules are the counterweight, and logged exploration data is also what allows unbiased evaluation of new models.

**Engagement event pipeline.** Events are the fuel. Clients emit impressions, watch durations, interactions and negative feedback. They are written to a durable log and consumed twice. A **streaming path** updates counters, recent-history lists and sometimes embeddings in the feature store within seconds to minutes, so the next request sees them. A **batch path** joins events with the features that were used at serving time to make training examples, and models are retrained or updated continuously. Features must be computed the same way for training and for serving; logging the served features is the simplest way to avoid a mismatch.

**Serving budget and degradation.** A feed request has a strict latency budget, a few hundred milliseconds in total, split among recall, feature fetch, ranking and re-ranking. Each stage has a deadline and a fallback: if a recall source is slow it is skipped; if ranking times out, a lighter model or the recall score orders the batch; if personalisation is down entirely, a cached popular feed for the region is served. A request returns a small batch, so the system can react to behaviour quickly while keeping request volume manageable.

**The mobile client.** The client holds a short queue of upcoming items and keeps it topped up, requesting a new batch when a few remain. It prefetches the first segment of the next two or three clips, more on Wi-Fi and fewer on a metered or weak connection or in data-saver mode, and cancels prefetches the user swipes past. Only a few player instances exist and are recycled as the user scrolls, which bounds memory and decoder use. Events are queued locally and sent in batches, flushed when the app goes to the background, and retried with the same ids. On launch the app can show a batch fetched at the end of the last session so the first clip plays without waiting for the network.
Same idea at four depths

blocks.title: Beginner
blocks.text: Uploaded clips are converted into several sizes. For each viewer the system quickly gathers a few thousand possible clips, scores them carefully, and sends a short list. The app loads the start of the next clips early and reports what you watched so later picks improve.

blocks.title: Intermediate
blocks.text: Resumable upload feeds a parallel transcoding pipeline that writes a rendition ladder to object storage behind a CDN. A feed request runs candidate generation from several sources, a multi-task ranker over fresh features, and rule-based re-ranking. The client prefetches first segments and batches engagement events into a stream that updates a feature store.

blocks.title: Advanced
blocks.text: Decisions to defend: recall sources and their quotas, approximate nearest-neighbour index refresh for new videos, which predicted outcomes enter the final score and with what weights, how real-time the features must be, exploration budget for cold start, and per-stage deadlines with fallbacks. Prefetch depth trades start-up time against wasted bytes.

blocks.title: Expert
blocks.text: The hard problems are closing the loop in near real time at very large embedding-table scale, training-serving consistency, measuring long-term satisfaction instead of short-term watch time, creator-side fairness and cold start, integrity (spam, engagement bait, harmful content) inside the ranking objective, and the cost of video bytes where most downloaded data is from clips abandoned within seconds.
Functional requirements

items: Record, edit and upload a short video with caption and sound.
Process the video into playable versions and publish it after safety checks.
Serve an endless personalised feed with instant playback on swipe.
Like, comment, share, follow and mark "not interested".
Give new videos and new users a reasonable first experience.
Remove a video quickly from distribution when required.

blocks.text: Non-functional requirements

items: Swipe-to-first-frame is near instant in the common case.
Feed response within a few hundred milliseconds.
Uploaded video is viewable within about a minute.
Recent behaviour influences recommendations within minutes.
Feed remains available, in degraded form, when ranking or features fail.
Engagement events are not lost and are not double-counted.

blocks.text: Capacity estimate (assumptions, arithmetic shown)

items: Illustrative assumption: 500M daily viewers x 150 videos viewed per day = 75 billion views per day; 75B / 86,400 s = ~870,000 views per second average.
Illustrative assumption: batches of 10 items. 75B / 10 = 7.5 billion feed requests per day = ~87,000 per second average.
Illustrative assumption: 2,000 candidates ranked per request. 87,000 x 2,000 = ~174M model scorings per second, which is why ranking runs on accelerators with batched inference.
Illustrative assumption: 20M uploads per day x 30 MB original = 600 TB of originals per day; a ladder of 5 renditions totalling 40 MB adds 800 TB per day.
Illustrative assumption: an average view downloads 3 MB including wasted prefetch. 870,000 x 3 MB = ~2.6 TB per second, about 21 Tbps average CDN egress.
Illustrative assumption: 5 events per view at 200 bytes. 75B x 5 x 200 B = 75 TB of raw event data per day, ~4.3M events per second average.
Illustrative assumption: 1 billion video embeddings x 64 dimensions x 4 bytes = 256 GB per index copy before compression.

blocks.text: APIs

rows: POST
`/v1/uploads`
Starts a resumable upload session. Returns a session id and chunk size.
PUT
`/v1/uploads/{sessionId}?offset={bytes}`
Uploads one chunk at the given offset. Idempotent for the same offset and content.
GET
`/v1/uploads/{sessionId}`
Returns the confirmed offset so the client can resume.
POST
`/v1/videos`
Body: upload session id, caption, sound id, visibility. Header: Idempotency-Key. Creates the video in a processing state.
GET
`/v1/feed?cursor={token}&count={n}`
Returns an ordered batch of videos with rendition URLs, cover image, first-segment hints and a new cursor.
POST
`/v1/events/batch`
Body: list of engagement events with unique ids and client timestamps. Safe to retry.
POST
`/v1/videos/{videoId}/feedback`
Body: like, unlike, share or not_interested. Applied idempotently.

blocks.text: Data model

rows: video
video_id (key), creator_id, caption, sound_id, duration_ms, state, moderation_status, created_at
Sharded key-value or relational store
rendition
video_id, profile (key), codec, width, height, bitrate, segment_urls, first_segment_bytes
Metadata store; bytes in object storage behind the CDN
video_embedding
video_id (key), vector, model_version, updated_at
Approximate nearest-neighbour index, sharded
user_features
user_id (key), embedding, recent_video_ids, recent_skips, counters, updated_at
Low-latency feature store
video_features
video_id (key), impressions, avg_watch_ratio, like_rate, share_rate by time window
Low-latency feature store, updated by stream jobs
engagement_event

Durable log, then columnar warehouse

request_id, user_id, video_id, position, scores, feature_snapshot_ref
Columnar store for training and evaluation

blocks.text: Low-level design

items: Upload resume: server stores `session_id -> confirmed_offset`; a chunk is accepted only if its offset equals the confirmed offset, otherwise the server replies with the current offset.
Transcode fan-out: one job per ladder rung plus cover and moderation; the video becomes PUBLISHED when the minimum rung and moderation complete; other rungs attach later.
Recall merge: each source returns ids with a source score; merge with per-source quotas, de-duplicate, drop ids in the seen set (client-supplied ids plus a per-user probabilistic filter).
Final score: `w1 x p(finish) + w2 x expected_watch_seconds + w3 x p(like) + w4 x p(share) - w5 x p(quick_skip)`; weights are configuration.
Re-rank: greedy selection that penalises a candidate sharing creator, sound or topic with the previous k selected items.
Client queue: keep at least 3 unplayed items; when fewer remain, request the next batch; prefetch first segments for the next `N` where `N` depends on connection type.
Event batching: flush every few seconds or 20 events, and on app background; the server deduplicates by `event_id` and joins to `served_log` by `request_id`.

blocks.text: Security

items: Automated and human moderation gates distribution; removal purges the video from candidate indexes and invalidates CDN URLs.
Playback URLs are signed and short-lived to limit hotlinking and scraping.
Treat engagement events as untrusted: detect bots and fake engagement before events influence ranking or creator payouts.
Watch history is sensitive personal data: restrict access, allow users to clear it and honour deletion in features and training sets.
Apply stricter defaults and content rules for accounts of minors.
Rate-limit uploads and interactions per account and device to slow spam.

blocks.text: Trade-offs

rows: Two-stage recall then rank
Makes a huge corpus tractable; each stage is optimised for its own goal.
A good video missed by recall can never be ranked; two systems to keep consistent.
Any corpus too large to score fully per request.
Real-time feature updates
The feed reacts within a session; new videos get signal quickly.
Stream processing at very high volume is costly and harder to keep correct.
Short sessions with many items, where the last few swipes are highly informative.
Aggressive prefetch (three or more clips)
Swipes almost always start from local data.
Many prefetched bytes are never watched; costs user data and CDN egress.
Wi-Fi or unmetered connections.
Conservative prefetch (first segment of one clip)
Low waste of data and battery.
Fast swiping outruns the buffer and shows a spinner.
Metered, slow or data-saver conditions.
Optimise for watch time
Dense signal available on every impression; strongly predictive of engagement.
Can favour content that holds attention without leaving users satisfied.
As one objective among several, balanced with explicit and negative feedback.
High exploration share
New creators and topics surface; better data for training and evaluation.
Lower short-term engagement on the explored slots.
A small fixed share of impressions, larger for new users and new videos.

blocks.text: Failure scenarios

rows: Upload breaks at 90% on a mobile network
Without resumption the creator must start again and may give up.
Chunked upload with a persisted session id; the client asks for the confirmed offset and continues.
Transcoding backlog during a peak
New posts stay in "processing" for a long time.
Autoscale workers on queue depth, publish a single quick rendition first and add the rest of the ladder afterwards.
Ranking service times out
The feed request would fail and the viewer sees nothing new.
Per-stage deadlines; fall back to a lightweight model or recall ordering, and finally to a cached regional popular feed.
Feature store is stale or unavailable
Recommendations ignore recent behaviour or the ranker lacks inputs.
Serve with default or last known features, mark the request as degraded, and exclude it from training data.
Event pipeline lags
Already-seen videos repeat and new videos gain no signal.
The client sends the ids it has seen with each request for server-side de-duplication; monitor consumer lag and scale the stream jobs.
A harmful video passes automated checks and starts to spread
Wide distribution before review.
Stepwise audience expansion with checks at each step, fast removal from candidate indexes and CDN, and human review triggered by reports and velocity.
Viewer swipes faster than prefetch on a weak connection
Clips stall at the start.
Start at the lowest rendition, shorten the first segment, show the cover image immediately and adapt prefetch depth to measured throughput.
