blocks.text: Interview questions

blocks.title: Design the feed request path with a 300 ms budget.
blocks.text: The feed service calls several recall sources in parallel with a deadline of a few tens of milliseconds and merges a few thousand ids. It filters seen and ineligible items, fetches features in batched calls, and sends candidates to the ranker with its own deadline. Re-ranking applies diversity and policy, and the response returns about ten items with playback metadata. Each stage has a fallback so the request always returns.

blocks.title: How do you get a video from upload to viewable in under a minute?
blocks.text: Resumable chunked upload so failures do not restart. On completion, fan the file out to parallel encoders for each rung of the ladder; because clips are short, all rungs finish quickly. Publish as soon as one playable rendition and the cover exist and automated checks pass, then add the remaining rungs. Write to object storage behind the CDN and index the video for recall with its content embedding.

blocks.title: How does behaviour in the current session affect the next batch?
blocks.text: Client events go to a stream. Stream jobs update a per-user recent-history list and counters in a low-latency feature store within seconds. The next feed request reads those features, and recall can also use the last watched videos as seeds for similar items. Returning small batches means the system gets several chances to adapt within one session.

blocks.title: How would you design prefetch on the client?
blocks.text: Maintain a queue of upcoming items. Prefetch the first segment of the next N clips at a starting bitrate, where N depends on connection type, measured throughput and data-saver setting. Cancel prefetches for skipped items, cap the disk cache, and reuse a small pool of players. Fetch the next batch when the queue is nearly empty, and keep one batch across launches for an instant first clip.

blocks.title: How do you stop the recommender from showing only one kind of content?
blocks.text: Use several recall sources with quotas, reserve a share of impressions for exploration, add diversity constraints in re-ranking such as limits per creator and topic within a window, include negative feedback in the objective, and evaluate with longer-term measures like return visits instead of only watch time in the session.
Takeaways

items: Upload is resumable; transcoding is a parallel ladder; the first seconds of every clip are what matter most.
Recommendation is a funnel: cheap candidate generation over the whole corpus, expensive ranking over a few thousand, then rule-based re-ranking.
Watch duration and completion are the densest signals; real-time session features make the feed adapt within minutes.
New videos and new users need deliberate exploration, which also keeps the system from only reinforcing itself.
Engagement events feed both a fast streaming path for features and a batch path for training.
Prefetch on the client removes the network from the swipe; depth is tuned to connection and data cost.
Every serving stage has a deadline and a fallback so the feed never returns empty.

quiz.q: Why is recommendation split into candidate generation and ranking?
options: Because two teams need separate services
Scoring every video with an accurate model for each request is too expensive, so a cheap stage first narrows the set
quiz.why: Recall trades precision for speed over the whole corpus; ranking spends compute only on a few thousand items.

quiz.q: Which signal is densest for training a short-video ranker?
options: Watch duration and completion, because every impression produces them
quiz.why: Explicit actions are rare; how long each clip was watched is available for every view.

quiz.q: What makes a swipe feel instant?
options: The first segment of the next clips was already downloaded before the swipe
Sending the video over the event stream
quiz.why: Prefetch takes the network off the critical path at the moment of the swipe.

quiz.q: How is a brand-new video with no engagement history handled?
options: It is shown to everyone immediately
It is shown to a small audience chosen from its content, and distribution widens if it performs well
It waits a week for batch training
quiz.why: Exploration traffic gathers the first signals, and stepwise expansion limits the cost of poor content.

quiz.q: Ranking is unavailable. What should the feed service do?
options: Return an error to the app
Return a degraded feed from a simpler ordering or a cached popular list
quiz.why: An imperfect feed is better than an empty screen; each stage has a deadline and a fallback.

questions.q: Explain the client-server model and why most systems are built this way.
questions.a: A client sends a request and a server listens, does the work and returns a response. The server owns shared data and business rules, while clients are many, untrusted and replaceable. This separation lets you update logic in one place, secure data centrally and scale the server side independently of the clients. Communication usually follows request-response over a network protocol such as HTTP. Servers are normally long-running processes that handle many clients concurrently.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Centralising logic and data gives one source of truth and a single place to enforce security and rollouts. Clients stay thin and many different client types can reuse the same server.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Internet → Server → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Central server is simple to reason about but is a single point of failure unless replicated
Thick clients reduce server load but make updates and security harder
Every request pays network latency compared with local computation

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does peer-to-peer differ and when would you choose it?
How would you scale the server tier when clients grow 100x?
Where should validation live, client, server or both?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Trusting client-side validation as the only check
Treating the server as one machine instead of a replicated tier
Ignoring that the network between them is unreliable

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Names responsibilities of each side
Mentions trust boundary and central source of truth
Connects model to scaling and failure
Uses clear request-response vocabulary

questions.q: What happens when you type a URL into a browser and press Enter? Focus on the DNS step.
questions.a: The browser first checks its own cache and the OS cache for the IP of the hostname. On a miss it asks a recursive resolver, which walks the hierarchy: root servers point to the TLD servers, which point to the authoritative name server for the domain, which returns the IP record. The resolver caches the answer for its TTL and returns it. The client then opens a TCP connection, does a TLS handshake for https, sends the HTTP request and renders the response.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Humans use names but networks route by IP, so a distributed, cached lookup system translates between them. Caching at every layer keeps the hierarchy from being hit on each request.

points.title: Flow
items: Browser → OS cache → Recursive resolver → Root / TLD → Authoritative DNS

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Caching speeds lookups but delays propagation of changes
Recursive resolver adds a hop but offloads work from clients
DNS is a hard dependency: if it fails the site looks down

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do A, CNAME and NS records differ?
How can DNS be used for basic load balancing?
What changes if the resolver is far from the user?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Skipping caches and saying every request hits root servers
Confusing the resolver with the authoritative server
Forgetting TCP and TLS happen after DNS

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Describes cache then resolver then hierarchy
Distinguishes recursive and authoritative roles
Mentions TTL
Continues the chain to TCP/TLS/HTTP

questions.q: How does DNS TTL affect failover and migrations, and how would you pick a value?
questions.a: TTL tells resolvers how long they may cache a record. A long TTL reduces query load and lookup latency but means clients keep using an old IP after you change it. A short TTL lets you redirect traffic quickly during failover or migration but increases query volume and exposes you more to resolver outages. A common practice is to lower the TTL ahead of a planned migration, switch the record, then raise it again. Note that some resolvers and clients ignore or extend TTLs, so DNS alone is not instant failover.

points.title: Reasoning
items: TTL is the knob that trades change speed against query cost and resilience. Planned changes can be prepared for, unplanned failures need a faster mechanism than DNS alone.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Recursive resolver → Authoritative DNS → Load balancer → Origin

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Short TTL gives fast cutover but more DNS traffic and latency
Long TTL is cheap and fast but slow to change
Health-checked DNS failover adds complexity and still depends on client caching

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you do a zero-downtime migration to a new IP?
Why might clients still hit the old IP after TTL expiry?
How does anycast reduce reliance on DNS failover?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming changes propagate instantly everywhere
Setting TTL very low permanently without thinking about load
Using DNS as the only failover layer for critical services

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains the speed vs load trade-off
Describes lowering TTL before planned change
Acknowledges resolvers may not obey TTL
Suggests complementary failover mechanisms

questions.q: What is the difference between HTTP and HTTPS and why should everything use HTTPS?
questions.a: HTTP sends data in plain text so anyone on the path can read or modify it. HTTPS is HTTP carried inside a TLS session, which provides encryption, integrity and server authentication through a certificate issued by a trusted authority. This prevents eavesdropping, tampering and impersonation. It also is required for modern browser features and avoids warnings. The cost is a handshake and some CPU, both small on modern hardware and reduced by session resumption.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Networks between client and server are untrusted, so confidentiality, integrity and authenticity must be added at the transport layer. The overhead is small compared with the risk.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → TLS session → Reverse proxy → Service

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Extra handshake latency on new connections
Certificate issuance and renewal must be managed
Terminating TLS at the edge simplifies services but leaves internal traffic plain unless re-encrypted

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where would you terminate TLS and why?
What does a certificate actually prove?
What is HSTS?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying HTTPS hides which domain you connect to in all cases
Thinking HTTPS protects against a compromised server
Forgetting certificate expiry as an operational risk

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Names confidentiality, integrity and authentication
Explains role of certificates
Mentions TLS as the mechanism
Notes the cost is small

questions.q: Walk through a TLS handshake at a high level and explain how session resumption helps.
questions.a: The client sends supported versions and cipher suites; the server replies with its choice and its certificate. The client validates the certificate chain and hostname. Both sides perform a key exchange, typically ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, to derive shared session keys without sending them. After that all application data is encrypted with symmetric keys, which are fast. Session resumption lets a returning client reuse previously negotiated secrets via tickets or IDs, skipping part of the handshake and saving round trips. TLS 1.3 reduces the full handshake to one round trip.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Asymmetric crypto authenticates and agrees on keys, and symmetric crypto then protects the bulk data cheaply. Resumption amortises the expensive part across connections.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → ClientHello → Server cert → Key exchange → Encrypted data

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Forward secrecy costs a little CPU but limits damage from key leaks
Resumption tickets improve latency but need careful key rotation
Termination at a proxy centralises certs but needs trust in the proxy

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is forward secrecy?
What changes with TLS 1.3?
How would mutual TLS between services work?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying the certificate is used to encrypt all traffic
Confusing TLS with the HTTP layer
Ignoring certificate validation steps

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Orders hello, certificate, key exchange, encrypted traffic
Distinguishes asymmetric and symmetric roles
Explains resumption benefit
Mentions validation of chain and hostname

questions.q: Compare TCP and UDP. When would you pick each?
questions.a: TCP is connection oriented and gives reliable, ordered delivery with retransmission, flow control and congestion control. UDP is connectionless, sends independent datagrams and gives no delivery or ordering guarantees but has low overhead and no head-of-line blocking at the transport layer. Use TCP for web, APIs, databases and file transfer where correctness matters. Use UDP for real-time media, gaming, DNS and protocols that build their own reliability, such as QUIC. The choice depends on whether late data is worse than lost data.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Reliability costs latency and state. Applications where stale data is useless prefer UDP, while most business traffic needs the guarantees TCP provides.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Transport (TCP or UDP) → Network → Server

points.title: Trade-offs
items: TCP reliability adds handshake and retransmission delay
UDP is fast but the application must handle loss and ordering
TCP suffers head-of-line blocking on a lost packet

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is DNS typically UDP?
What is QUIC and why is it built on UDP?
How does TCP congestion control work at a high level?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying UDP is always faster in practice regardless of loss handling
Claiming UDP cannot be made reliable
Forgetting TCP connection setup cost

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Contrasts reliability, ordering and overhead
Gives suitable use cases for each
Mentions application-level reliability over UDP
Frames choice around loss vs latency

questions.q: What problems did HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 address compared with HTTP/1.1?
questions.a: HTTP/1.1 needed multiple connections for parallelism because only one request could be in flight per connection in practice, causing head-of-line blocking at the HTTP level. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection, compresses headers and uses binary framing, but a lost TCP packet still stalls all streams. HTTP/3 runs over QUIC on UDP, where streams are independent so loss on one does not block others, and it integrates TLS and speeds connection setup and migration. Semantics such as methods and status codes stay the same.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Each version removes a bottleneck of the previous one while keeping the application semantics unchanged.

points.title: Flow
items: Browser → HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 → CDN / proxy → Origin

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Multiplexing reduces connections but TCP loss still hurts HTTP/2
QUIC avoids that but is handled in user space and may be blocked by some networks
Fallback to older versions is required for compatibility

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why did domain sharding become an anti-pattern?
What is connection migration in QUIC?
Does HTTP/2 make server push a good idea?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying HTTP/2 removes all head-of-line blocking
Thinking HTTP/3 changes the API semantics
Ignoring that clients negotiate the version

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Names HTTP-level vs TCP-level head-of-line blocking
Mentions multiplexing and header compression
Explains QUIC over UDP
Notes backward compatibility

questions.q: What makes an API RESTful? Describe the key constraints and conventions.
questions.a: REST models the system as resources identified by URLs, manipulated through a uniform interface using HTTP methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates partially, DELETE removes. Requests are stateless, so each carries everything needed and the server keeps no session between calls. Responses use status codes and can be cacheable. Representations such as JSON describe the resource. In practice teams follow resource naming, correct status codes and idempotent semantics rather than the full hypermedia constraint.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A uniform, stateless interface lets any client and intermediary understand and cache requests and lets servers scale horizontally.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → HTTP request → API → Resource store

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Simple and cache friendly but can need many round trips for related data
Fixed response shapes cause over- or under-fetching
Statelessness pushes session data to the client or a shared store

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which methods are safe and which are idempotent?
How do you version a REST API?
How would you model an action that is not CRUD?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting verbs in URLs like /getUser
Returning 200 for every error
Using GET for operations with side effects

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Resources and methods used correctly
Statelessness explained
Status codes and idempotency mentioned
Pragmatic about hypermedia

questions.q: Compare REST and GraphQL. When would you choose GraphQL?
questions.a: REST exposes many fixed endpoints, each returning a defined shape, and benefits from simple HTTP caching and tooling. GraphQL exposes a typed schema and a single endpoint where the client specifies exactly the fields and nested relations it wants, avoiding over-fetching and multiple round trips. It suits diverse clients, such as mobile and web, with different data needs and fast-evolving frontends. The costs are harder HTTP caching, the N+1 problem in resolvers needing batching, query complexity and rate limiting concerns, and more server-side machinery. Many systems use REST for simple services and GraphQL as an aggregation layer.

points.title: Reasoning
items: GraphQL moves shaping of responses to the client at the price of server complexity, so it pays off when client needs vary a lot.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → GraphQL gateway → Resolvers → Services → Databases

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Flexible queries vs harder caching and cost control
Single endpoint simplifies clients but hides expensive queries
Strong typing helps tooling but needs schema governance

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you prevent expensive or abusive queries?
What is the N+1 problem and how does batching fix it?
How would you do authorization per field?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Claiming GraphQL is always faster
Ignoring depth and complexity limits
Forgetting that errors often return HTTP 200

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains over/under-fetching
Names caching and N+1 costs
Chooses based on client diversity
Mentions limits and governance

questions.q: Where does gRPC fit in compared with REST, and what are its trade-offs?
questions.a: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers for compact binary messages and HTTP/2 for multiplexed streams, with generated client and server code from a contract file. It supports unary calls and client, server and bidirectional streaming, deadlines and strong typing. It is a good fit for internal service-to-service communication where performance and a strict contract matter. Drawbacks are weaker browser support without a proxy layer, harder manual debugging because payloads are binary, and less natural HTTP caching. Public APIs usually remain REST or GraphQL for broad compatibility.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Binary encoding plus a shared schema gives efficiency and type safety internally, while public consumers value human-readable, widely supported formats.

points.title: Flow
items: Service A → gRPC stub → HTTP/2 → Service B

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Efficient and typed but less human-friendly
Streaming support but needs careful backpressure handling
Schema evolution must follow compatibility rules

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you evolve a protobuf schema safely?
How do deadlines propagate across calls?
How would you expose a gRPC service to browsers?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using gRPC for public browser APIs without a gateway
Reusing or renumbering protobuf field tags
Not setting deadlines on calls

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Mentions protobuf and HTTP/2
Names streaming and contracts
Identifies internal vs public fit
Lists operational downsides

questions.q: Compare polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets for real-time updates.
questions.a: Polling repeatedly asks the server for updates, which is simple but wasteful and adds delay up to the interval. Long polling holds a request open until data exists, lowering delay at the cost of many held connections. Server-Sent Events keep a single HTTP connection open for one-way server-to-client pushes with automatic reconnection. WebSockets upgrade a connection to a full-duplex channel for two-way low-latency messaging. Choose SSE for feeds and notifications, WebSockets for chat or collaboration, and polling when updates are rare or infrastructure is limited.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The right choice depends on message direction, frequency and infrastructure support, and persistent connections raise scaling and load balancer concerns.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Load balancer → Connection server → Message broker → Backend services

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Persistent connections give low latency but consume server resources
SSE is simple and one-way, WebSockets are flexible but need more handling
Polling is easy to scale but wasteful

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you scale WebSocket servers to millions of connections?
How do you handle reconnects and missed messages?
How does a load balancer treat long-lived connections?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using WebSockets when one-way push is enough
Not handling reconnection and message replay
Storing connection state only in one node memory

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Compares direction and latency
Mentions connection cost
Gives matching use cases
Considers reconnect handling

questions.q: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous communication between services?
questions.a: In synchronous communication the caller sends a request and waits for the response, such as an HTTP or gRPC call. It is simple and gives immediate results but couples availability and latency of caller and callee. In asynchronous communication the caller hands off a message or event through a queue or broker and continues, and the work is processed later. This decouples services, smooths traffic spikes and allows retries, but results are eventually consistent and flows are harder to trace. Use sync for queries needing an immediate answer and async for background work and fan-out.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Sync trades coupling for simplicity, while async trades immediacy for resilience and throughput.

points.title: Flow
items: Producer → Queue / broker → Consumer → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Sync is simple but failures cascade
Async absorbs bursts but adds eventual consistency
Async needs idempotent consumers and dead-letter handling

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you give the user feedback for an async operation?
What delivery guarantees do queues provide?
How do you prevent duplicate processing?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Making every call async by default
Chaining many sync calls in a request path
Ignoring duplicates with at-least-once delivery

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines both clearly
Explains coupling and failure impact
Chooses by use case
Mentions idempotency or retries

questions.q: Explain latency versus throughput and how they relate.
questions.a: Latency is the time one request takes from start to finish, usually measured in percentiles such as p50 and p99. Throughput is how many requests or bytes a system completes per unit time. They are related but not the same: adding parallelism can raise throughput without lowering per-request latency, and batching can raise throughput while increasing latency. As utilisation approaches capacity, queues build and latency rises sharply. Good designs report tail latency rather than averages and size capacity with headroom.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Users feel latency while capacity planning depends on throughput, and the two interact through queueing under load.

points.title: Flow
items: Clients → Load balancer → Service → Queue → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Batching improves throughput but adds delay
Running hot uses hardware efficiently but tail latency explodes
Caching lowers latency and increases effective throughput

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why do percentiles matter more than averages?
How does Little law relate concurrency, throughput and latency?
How would you find the bottleneck?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using average latency to judge user experience
Assuming more servers always reduce latency
Confusing bandwidth with throughput of requests

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines both with units
Mentions percentiles
Explains the trade-off
Mentions headroom or queueing

questions.q: What does availability mean, and how do the nines translate to downtime?
questions.a: Availability is the fraction of time a system correctly serves requests, often expressed as nines. 99.9 percent allows roughly 8.8 hours of downtime a year, 99.99 percent about 53 minutes and 99.999 percent about 5 minutes. Overall availability of serial dependencies is the product of each, so it is lower than any single component, while redundant parallel components raise it. Improve it with redundancy, health checks, failover, graceful degradation and fast recovery. Each extra nine costs disproportionately more, so the target should follow the business need.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Availability is arithmetic over dependencies, so chains of services reduce it and redundancy increases it, with sharply rising cost per nine.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Load balancer → Service replicas → Primary DB → Standby DB

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Redundancy raises availability but costs money and complexity
Strong consistency can lower availability during partitions
Faster failover needs more automation and testing

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do SLO, SLA and SLI differ?
How do you compute availability of two services in series?
What is graceful degradation?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Promising 100 percent availability
Ignoring dependency chains when computing the number
Counting only full outages, not partial failures

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Converts nines to downtime
Explains serial vs parallel composition
Lists techniques to improve it
Ties target to business need

questions.q: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
questions.a: Vertical scaling means giving one machine more CPU, memory or disk. It is simple, needs no code change and keeps data in one place, but it has a hardware ceiling, costs rise steeply and it remains a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer and spreads the work. It scales further and improves fault tolerance but requires stateless services or partitioned state, and brings distributed-system complexity. Most systems scale vertically first and design for horizontal scale as they grow.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Vertical is the cheapest first step but bounded, while horizontal removes the ceiling at the price of coordination complexity.

points.title: Flow
items: Clients → Load balancer → App server 1..N → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Vertical is simple but capped and risky
Horizontal scales and tolerates failure but needs stateless design
Stateful stores are hard to scale horizontally without sharding or replication

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What blocks horizontal scaling of the database?
How do you keep sessions working across servers?
When is vertical scaling still the right call?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming adding servers fixes a database bottleneck
Ignoring that horizontal scaling needs stateless services
Overbuilding for scale before it is needed

Mentions statelessness requirement
Identifies the data tier as hard

questions.q: What is the difference between stateless and stateful services, and why prefer stateless?
questions.a: A stateless service keeps no per-client data between requests, so any instance can handle any request. State such as sessions lives in a shared store like a database or cache, or in a signed token held by the client. A stateful service keeps data in its own memory or disk and requests must reach the right instance. Stateless instances can be added, removed and replaced freely, which makes autoscaling and failover easy. Stateful components still exist, usually isolated in databases, caches and brokers that handle replication and partitioning explicitly.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Pushing state to dedicated stores keeps the application tier interchangeable and simple to scale.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Load balancer → Stateless app instances → Session store → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Shared session store adds a network hop and a dependency
Signed tokens avoid lookups but are hard to revoke
Sticky sessions are easy but hurt balancing and failover

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you handle login sessions statelessly?
When are sticky sessions acceptable?
How do you scale a stateful database?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Storing sessions in local memory behind a load balancer
Believing stateless means no state exists anywhere
Writing local files that other instances need

points.title: What a good answer shows

Explains where state moves
Links to scaling and failover
Mentions session handling options

questions.q: What is a reverse proxy and what does it do for a backend system?
questions.a: A reverse proxy sits in front of backend servers and receives client requests on their behalf. It can terminate TLS, route by host or path, compress and cache responses, buffer slow clients, add headers and enforce basic limits. Clients see one address and never contact the origin servers directly, which hides topology and adds a protective layer. Load balancers and API gateways are specialised reverse proxies. The proxy itself must be made redundant so it does not become a single point of failure.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A single front door centralises cross-cutting concerns and shields the origins, but it becomes critical infrastructure.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Reverse proxy → App server A → App server B → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Centralises TLS and caching but adds a hop
Hides backends but needs redundancy itself
Misconfiguration can affect all traffic at once

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does a reverse proxy differ from a forward proxy?
How would you run the proxy tier highly available?
What headers preserve the real client IP?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Confusing forward and reverse proxies
Trusting client-supplied forwarded headers blindly
Leaving the proxy as a single instance

questions.q: Compare Layer 4 and Layer 7 load balancing. When do you use each?
questions.a: A Layer 4 balancer works on TCP or UDP connections using IP and port, forwarding packets without reading application data. It is fast, simple and protocol agnostic. A Layer 7 balancer understands HTTP, so it can route by path, host, header or cookie, terminate TLS, rewrite requests, apply rate limits and do canary routing. It needs more CPU and buffers requests. Use L4 for raw throughput, non-HTTP protocols or as an outer tier, and L7 where content-aware routing and observability are needed. Many architectures chain both.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The more of the request the balancer inspects, the more routing power it has and the more it costs per request.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → L4 load balancer → L7 proxy → Service pool → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: L4 is faster but blind to content
L7 is flexible but heavier and a larger attack surface
Terminating TLS at L7 simplifies services but concentrates keys

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you do canary releases at the balancer?
How does a balancer handle long-lived WebSockets?
What is connection draining?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming L7 is always better
Forgetting L4 cannot route by URL path
Ignoring connection draining during deploys

Names routing capabilities
Mentions cost trade-off
Describes layered deployment

questions.q: Describe common load balancing algorithms and how health checks fit in.
questions.a: Round robin hands requests to servers in turn, and weighted variants account for different capacities. Least connections sends traffic to the server with the fewest active connections, which suits uneven request cost. Hash-based methods such as IP hash or consistent hashing keep a given client or key on the same server, helping caches and affinity. Random with two choices picks the less loaded of two random servers and works well at scale. Health checks probe servers periodically and remove unhealthy ones from rotation, then add them back after they recover.

points.title: Reasoning
items: No algorithm fits every workload, and without health checks even a good algorithm keeps sending traffic to dead nodes.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Load balancer → Health check → Server pool

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Round robin is simple but ignores load differences
Least connections adapts but needs state tracking
Hashing aids locality but can create hot spots

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is consistent hashing and why use it here?
How do you avoid a thundering herd when a node returns?
Active vs passive health checks?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using round robin for very uneven request costs
Health checks that only test the port, not real readiness
Removing nodes too aggressively on a single failed probe

questions.q: What is an API gateway and which responsibilities belong there?
questions.a: An API gateway is the single entry point for clients to a set of backend services. It handles cross-cutting concerns such as routing, authentication, authorization checks, rate limiting, request validation, TLS termination, response transformation and logging or metrics. It can also aggregate several backend calls into one response for a client. Business logic should stay in services, not in the gateway. The gateway must be horizontally scaled and monitored because every request passes through it.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Centralising generic concerns avoids duplicating them in every service, but putting domain logic there creates a bottleneck and a coupling point.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → API gateway → Auth service → Microservice A → Microservice B

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Central policy and simpler clients vs an extra hop and potential bottleneck
Aggregation reduces client round trips but couples gateway to services
One shared gateway team can slow independent releases

questions.q: What is a CDN and how does it improve performance?
questions.a: A content delivery network is a set of edge servers distributed geographically that cache content close to users. A request is routed, usually by DNS or anycast, to a nearby edge. On a cache hit the edge responds directly, cutting latency and origin load, and on a miss it fetches from the origin and stores the result according to cache headers. CDNs are ideal for static assets, images and video, and can also terminate TLS and absorb traffic spikes and some attacks. Content freshness is controlled with TTLs, versioned URLs and purge requests.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Serving content from near the user reduces round-trip time, and caching shields the origin from repeated requests.

points.title: Flow
items: User → DNS / anycast → Edge cache → Origin shield → Origin

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Lower latency and origin load vs stale content risk
Purging is eventually applied across edges
Personalised or private content is hard to cache safely

questions.q: Why use connection pooling, and how do you size a pool?
questions.a: Opening a database connection involves network setup, authentication and server-side resources, so doing it per request is slow and does not scale. A pool keeps a bounded set of open connections that requests borrow and return. This caps concurrent load on the database, which handles a limited number of active queries efficiently. Size the pool from the database capacity and the application instance count, not from request volume, and keep the total across all instances below the server limit. Add timeouts for acquiring a connection, and release connections promptly, including on errors.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Reuse removes setup cost and a bounded pool protects the database from overload. Too large a pool simply moves queueing into the database.

items: App instance → Connection pool → Pooler / proxy → Database

Large pool increases contention and memory use
External poolers add a hop but share connections across many instances

questions.q: How do you approach a high-level design interview question step by step?
questions.a: Start by clarifying requirements and scope, separating functional from non-functional needs, and stating assumptions. Estimate scale such as users, requests per second and storage to guide choices. Define the core APIs and data model, then sketch a simple end-to-end architecture that works. After that deep-dive on bottlenecks: scaling the data tier, caching, queues, consistency and failure handling. Throughout, explain trade-offs and keep checking the design against the stated requirements.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A structured approach avoids jumping to technology and ensures each component is justified by a requirement or number.

points.title: Flow
items: Requirements → Estimation → API and data model → Architecture → Deep dives

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Spending too long on estimates leaves less time for design
Starting simple is clear but must evolve to meet scale
Depth on one area means less coverage of others

points.title: Follow-ups

How do you handle ambiguous requirements?
How would you evolve the design for 10x scale?

points.title: Common mistakes

Ignoring failure modes and data growth

questions.q: What is the difference between functional and non-functional requirements? Give examples.
questions.a: Functional requirements describe what the system does, for example users can place an order or search products. Non-functional requirements describe qualities of how it does it, such as availability, latency, consistency, durability, scalability, security and cost. Non-functional requirements usually drive the architecture, since a feature built for ten users and for ten million looks very different. Make them measurable, such as p99 latency under 300 ms or 99.9 percent availability. Agree on them early because they trade off against each other.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Features say what to build, while quality targets decide which architecture can meet them.

points.title: Flow
items: Requirements → Design constraints → Architecture choices → Validation

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Higher consistency can cost availability and latency
Higher availability costs redundancy
Tighter latency targets cost caching and capacity

points.title: Follow-ups

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Listing only features and no quality targets

Assuming all NFRs can be maximised together

questions.q: Show how you would do a back-of-the-envelope capacity estimate for a service with 10 million daily active users.
questions.a: State assumptions first: say each user makes 20 requests a day, so 10M x 20 = 200M requests, and dividing by 86,400 seconds gives about 2,300 requests per second on average. Apply a peak factor such as 3x to get roughly 7,000 requests per second to design for. For storage, if each user generates 1 KB of new data a day, that is 10 GB a day, about 3.6 TB a year before replication. Multiply by the replication factor and add headroom. All numbers are assumptions, and their purpose is to find the order of magnitude and the bottleneck, not to be exact.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Rough arithmetic shows whether a single database or cache suffices or whether partitioning is needed, so it guides the architecture.

points.title: Flow
items: DAU → Requests per second → Bandwidth → Storage → Server count

points.title: Trade-offs

questions.q: What is idempotency and how do you make a payment-style API safe to retry?
questions.a: An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition, POST is not. For a payment API, clients send a unique idempotency key with each logical request. The server stores the key with the result, and if the same key arrives again it returns the stored result instead of charging twice. The check and the write should be atomic, for example with a unique constraint on the key. Keys expire after a retention window and the key should be tied to the request payload to detect misuse.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Networks cause timeouts after the server already acted, so clients must retry, and the server must make that safe.

items: Client → API → Idempotency store → Payment service → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Extra storage and a lookup per request
Key retention window trades memory against safety
Concurrent duplicates need locking or a unique constraint

questions.q: Compare offset and cursor pagination. Which would you use for a large, frequently changing feed?
questions.a: Offset pagination uses page and size, which is simple and allows jumping to a page, but the database must scan and skip rows, getting slower deeper in, and results shift when rows are inserted or deleted between requests. Cursor pagination returns an opaque token that encodes the last seen sort key, and the next query selects rows after it using an index. It stays fast regardless of depth and is stable under inserts. For a large, changing feed, use cursor pagination with a unique, ordered key such as time plus id. The trade-off is that arbitrary page jumps are not supported.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Seeking by an indexed key is constant cost, while skipping rows grows linearly with the offset and gives inconsistent pages.

items: Client → API → Cursor decode → Indexed query → Database

Cursor is fast and stable but cannot jump to a page

questions.q: Explain the SOLID principles with a short example for each.
questions.a: Single responsibility means a class has one reason to change, such as separating invoice calculation from invoice printing. Open-closed means code is open to extension but closed to modification, for example adding a new payment method by adding a class, not editing a long if chain. Liskov substitution means subtypes must be usable wherever the base type is expected without breaking behavior. Interface segregation prefers small, focused interfaces over one large one. Dependency inversion means high-level code depends on abstractions, so a service depends on a repository interface rather than a concrete database class.

points.title: Reasoning

questions.q: What is the Strategy pattern? Show where it fits in a system like a pricing or payment module.
questions.a: Strategy defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface and lets the caller choose one at runtime. For example a PricingStrategy interface with implementations for regular price, member discount and promotional price. The checkout code depends only on the interface and receives the chosen strategy, so adding a new rule means adding a class, not editing conditionals. It follows open-closed and dependency inversion and makes each algorithm easy to unit test. Selection can be done by a factory or configuration.

questions.q: Explain the Observer pattern and how it relates to event-driven design.
questions.a: Observer lets a subject notify many subscribed observers when its state changes, without knowing their concrete types. For example an order object publishes an OrderPlaced event and email, inventory and analytics listeners react independently. It decouples the producer from consumers and makes adding a new reaction easy. Within one process it is a pattern of callbacks or listeners, and across services the same idea becomes publish-subscribe through a message broker. Care is needed with ordering, error handling in listeners and memory leaks from forgotten subscriptions.

questions.q: When would you use a Factory pattern, and how does it differ from just calling a constructor?
questions.a: A factory encapsulates object creation so callers get an instance of an interface without knowing the concrete class. Use it when the type depends on input or configuration, when construction is complex, or when you want to swap implementations. For example a NotificationFactory returns an email, SMS or push sender based on a channel value. This keeps creation logic in one place and supports open-closed by registering new types. A direct constructor is fine when there is a single concrete type and no variation.

questions.q: What is the Repository pattern and why use it?
questions.a: A repository presents a collection-like interface for loading and saving aggregates, such as findById and save, hiding how data is stored. The domain and application layers depend on the repository abstraction, while an implementation talks to SQL, a document store or an in-memory fake. This keeps persistence details out of business logic and makes unit testing easy with fakes. Typically there is one repository per aggregate root, not per table. Avoid leaking query-builder or ORM types through the interface.

questions.q: How would you model an order lifecycle with a state machine, and why?
questions.a: Define explicit states such as Created, Paid, Packed, Shipped, Delivered and Cancelled, and the allowed transitions between them, for example Paid to Packed but not Delivered to Created. questions.q: What is an aggregate in domain-driven design and how does it shape transaction boundaries?
questions.a: An aggregate is a cluster of related objects treated as one consistency unit, with a single aggregate root as the only entry point. The root enforces invariants, for example an Order ensures the total equals the sum of its line items. External code references other aggregates by id, not by object. A transaction should modify one aggregate at a time, so the aggregate boundary is the transactional boundary. Consistency between aggregates is eventual and achieved through domain events. Keep aggregates small to reduce contention.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Aligning transactions with aggregate boundaries keeps invariants enforceable locally and avoids large locks and distributed transactions.

points.title: Flow
items: Command → Aggregate root → Entities → Repository → Domain events

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Small aggregates reduce contention but need eventual consistency across them
Large aggregates give strong consistency but cause conflicts
Cross-aggregate rules need sagas or events

questions.q: How do race conditions happen in a service, such as overselling the last item, and how do you prevent them?
questions.a: Two requests read stock as 1, both decide to sell and both write, so the item is sold twice. This is a check-then-act race on shared state. Prevent it by making the check and update atomic: a conditional update such as UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = ? AND qty > 0 and checking the affected row count. Alternatives are row locks with SELECT FOR UPDATE, optimistic locking with a version column and retry, or serialising access through a queue per item. In-memory locks only work within one process, so multi-instance services need database-level or distributed coordination.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The fix is to remove the gap between reading and writing, using the database as the arbiter of the shared state.

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Atomic conditional update is simple and scales well
Pessimistic locks are safe but reduce concurrency
Optimistic retries suit low contention but waste work under high contention

questions.q: Where should transaction boundaries sit in a layered service, and what goes wrong when they are drawn badly?
questions.a: Put the transaction boundary at the application or use-case layer, so one business operation commits or rolls back as a unit, while repositories simply take part in it. Keep transactions short: do not hold one open while calling slow external services or waiting on users, because that holds locks and exhausts connections. Do the external call outside, or use an outbox so the message is stored in the same transaction and published after commit. Badly drawn boundaries cause partial updates when each repository commits separately, or long lock waits and deadlocks when a transaction is too wide.

questions.q: How do you choose between SQL and NoSQL databases?
questions.a: Relational databases offer structured schemas, joins, strong transactions and a powerful query language, and suit data with relationships and consistency needs such as orders and payments. NoSQL covers several models: key-value for fast lookups, document for flexible nested records, wide-column for huge write-heavy datasets and graph for relationships. They often give easier horizontal scaling and flexible schemas but weaker joins and sometimes weaker transactions. Choose based on access patterns, consistency needs, data shape and scale, not on fashion. Many systems use both, each for what it does best.

NoSQL scales out easily but pushes joins and integrity to the application

questions.q: What is a database index and how does it speed up queries?
questions.a: An index is an extra data structure, commonly a B-tree, that stores column values in sorted order with pointers to rows. Instead of scanning the whole table, the database can search the index in logarithmic time and jump to the matching rows. Indexes help filters, joins, sorting and uniqueness checks. The cost is extra storage and slower writes because every insert, update or delete must maintain the index. Add indexes for columns used in frequent, selective queries and verify with the query plan.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Trading write cost and space for much faster reads is worthwhile when the read patterns justify it.

questions.q: How do composite indexes work, and how would you design one for a query that filters by user and sorts by time?
questions.a: A composite index sorts rows by the first column, then by the second within it, and so on. For a query filtering user_id equals a value and ordering by created_at, an index on (user_id, created_at) lets the database find the user range and read rows already in time order, avoiding a separate sort. Column order matters: it follows the leftmost-prefix rule, so the index serves queries on user_id alone or user_id plus created_at, but not created_at alone. Put equality columns first, then range or sort columns. Adding selected columns can make it covering, avoiding table lookups.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Matching the index order to the query pattern lets the database both filter and sort from the index.

questions.q: What does ACID stand for? Explain each property.
questions.a: Atomicity means a transaction either fully applies or not at all, so partial changes are rolled back on failure. Consistency means a transaction moves the database from one valid state to another, respecting constraints and rules. Isolation means concurrent transactions do not see each other in-flight changes in ways that break correctness, to a degree set by the isolation level. Durability means once committed, data survives crashes, usually via a write-ahead log flushed to disk. Together they let applications such as banking rely on safe updates.

points.title: Reasoning
items: ACID packages the guarantees needed for correct multi-step updates, at some cost in performance and scalability.

questions.q: Describe the common transaction isolation levels and the anomalies each prevents.
questions.a: Read uncommitted allows dirty reads of uncommitted data and is rarely used. Read committed prevents dirty reads, but a row read twice can change, which is a non-repeatable read. Repeatable read keeps a stable view of rows already read, though phantom rows may appear in some implementations. Serializable gives results as if transactions ran one at a time, preventing all these anomalies at the highest cost. Behavior differs by database, for example snapshot-based repeatable read can still allow write skew. Pick the lowest level that protects your invariants and handle retries on serialisation failures.

items: Higher isolation buys correctness with less concurrency, so the level should match the anomalies the business cannot tolerate.

questions.q: Compare optimistic and pessimistic locking. When do you pick each?
questions.a: Pessimistic locking takes a lock on the data before changing it, for example SELECT FOR UPDATE, so others wait. It is safe under high contention but reduces concurrency and risks deadlocks and long waits. Optimistic locking does not lock; each row has a version number, and an update succeeds only if the version is unchanged, otherwise the caller retries or reports a conflict. It performs well when conflicts are rare and avoids holding locks across user think time. Use pessimistic for hot rows where conflicts are common, and optimistic for mostly independent updates.

questions.q: What is database replication and why do we use it?
questions.a: Replication copies data from one database node to others. In a common primary-replica setup all writes go to the primary, which ships changes to replicas, and reads can be served from replicas. This increases read capacity, provides redundancy so a replica can be promoted if the primary fails, and can place copies near users or support backups and analytics. Replication improves availability and read scale but does not by itself scale writes. Replicas may lag behind the primary, so reads from them can be stale.

questions.q: Compare synchronous and asynchronous replication and explain how replica lag affects the application.
questions.a: With synchronous replication the primary waits for at least one replica to confirm before acknowledging a commit, so no acknowledged write is lost on primary failure, but write latency rises and an unavailable replica can stall writes. With asynchronous replication the primary acknowledges immediately and ships changes later, giving lower latency and better write availability, but a failure can lose recent writes and replicas lag. Lag causes anomalies such as a user not seeing their own update. Mitigate by reading from the primary right after a write, tracking a position token, or routing a user to the primary for a short window. Semi-synchronous setups are a middle ground.

questions.q: What is sharding, and when do you need it?
questions.a: Sharding splits a dataset across multiple database nodes by a shard key, so each node holds only part of the data and handles part of the traffic. It scales both storage and write throughput beyond what one machine can handle. You usually need it only after simpler steps are exhausted: better indexes, caching, read replicas and a larger machine. Sharding adds complexity: queries spanning shards are harder, cross-shard transactions are costly, and rebalancing data is operationally heavy. Routing is done by the application, a proxy or the database itself.

questions.q: How do you choose a shard key, and what makes a bad one?
questions.a: A good shard key has high cardinality, spreads reads and writes evenly, and matches the most common query so most requests hit a single shard. For example user_id often works for user-centric data because a user data lives together. A bad key creates hot shards or scatter-gather queries: a monotonically increasing key like a timestamp sends all new writes to one shard, and a low-cardinality key like country limits distribution. Hashing the key evens out load but loses range scans. Also consider how you will rebalance, for example with many virtual buckets mapped to nodes.

questions.q: Explain the CAP theorem in practical terms.
questions.a: CAP says that when a network partition happens, a distributed data store must choose between consistency, meaning every read sees the latest write, and availability, meaning every request gets a non-error response. Partitions cannot be ruled out in real networks, so the real choice is during a partition. A CP system refuses or delays some requests to stay consistent, while an AP system keeps serving but may return stale or divergent data that is reconciled later. When there is no partition, the trade-off shifts to latency versus consistency. Different parts of one product can make different choices, such as strict consistency for payments and eventual for a feed.

questions.q: How do health checks and failover work for a replicated service, and what pitfalls exist?
questions.a: A load balancer or orchestrator probes each instance, using a liveness check to decide whether to restart it and a readiness check to decide whether to route traffic to it. Instances that fail several consecutive probes are removed from rotation and returned after passing again. For stateful components such as a database primary, failover means detecting failure, promoting a replica and redirecting clients, ideally with a fencing mechanism so the old primary cannot accept writes. Pitfalls include checks that are too shallow or too deep, flapping from aggressive thresholds, and cascading failure when a shared dependency check marks every instance unhealthy at once.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Automated detection and rerouting keeps traffic away from bad instances, but the checks themselves must be tuned and designed to avoid making failures worse.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Load balancer → Health probe → Healthy instances → Standby

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Fast detection reduces downtime but risks false positives
Deep checks catch more problems but can fail due to dependencies
Automatic failover is quick but needs split-brain protection

Including a downstream dependency check that takes all instances down together
No fencing during primary failover

questions.q: How would you design rate limiting for an API, and which algorithm would you use?
questions.a: Decide the key to limit by, such as user, API key or IP, and the limits per window. A token bucket is a common choice: tokens refill at a steady rate up to a capacity, each request consumes one, and bursts are allowed up to the bucket size. Alternatives are fixed window, which is simple but allows boundary bursts, and sliding window, which is smoother but costs more. In a multi-instance gateway the counters must be shared, typically in a fast store such as Redis with atomic operations, or approximated locally for speed. On exceeding the limit return HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Rate limiting protects capacity and fairness, and token bucket balances burst tolerance with simple state.

questions.q: Explain the cache-aside pattern and the main risks of caching in front of a database.
questions.a: In cache-aside the application first reads the cache, and on a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL and returns it. On writes it updates the database and then invalidates or updates the cache. This keeps the cache simple and tolerant of cache failure, since the database remains the source of truth. Risks include stale data between update and invalidation, a stampede when a popular key expires and many requests hit the database together, and cold-start load after a cache flush. Mitigate with sensible TTLs, request coalescing or locks on refill, jittered expiries and warming.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The pattern trades some freshness for large read savings, and the risks come from concurrent access to expiring entries.

points.title: Flow
items: App → Cache → Miss path → Database → Cache fill

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Big read speedup vs staleness
Invalidate-on-write is simple but has race windows
Write-through keeps cache fresher but couples writes to the cache

questions.q: How should a service handle timeouts and retries when calling another service?
questions.a: Always set a timeout on remote calls so a slow dependency cannot hold threads and connections indefinitely, and keep it shorter than the caller own deadline. Retry only operations that are idempotent or protected by idempotency keys, and only on transient errors such as timeouts or 503, not on client errors. Use exponential backoff with jitter and a small cap on attempts so retries do not synchronise and amplify load. Add a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing dependency for a period, and consider a retry budget. Retries at several layers multiply, so decide where they belong.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Unbounded waiting and naive retries turn a partial slowdown into a cascading outage, so both must be bounded and safe.

questions.q: What is dependency injection and how does it help with design and testing?
questions.a: Dependency injection means a class receives the collaborators it needs from outside, usually through its constructor, instead of creating them itself. For example an OrderService receives a PaymentGateway interface, so production passes the real client and tests pass a fake. This implements dependency inversion, reduces coupling and makes behavior configurable without code changes. A DI container can wire objects automatically, but plain constructor injection with a single composition root is often enough. Avoid hidden globals and service locators, which hide dependencies.

questions.q: Explain the cache-aside pattern and when you would choose it over write-through.
questions.a: In cache-aside the application checks the cache first, and on a miss it reads the database and then populates the cache. Writes go to the database and the cached entry is deleted or updated. It is simple, tolerates a cache outage because the database is still the source of truth, and only caches data that is actually read. Write-through instead writes to cache and database together on every write, which keeps the cache warm and fresh but caches data that may never be read and adds write latency. Choose cache-aside for read-heavy workloads with uneven access patterns.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Cache-aside keeps the database authoritative and the cache optional, so failures degrade performance rather than correctness.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → App Service → Cache → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: First read after a miss is slower because it pays for the database hit and the cache fill.
Stale data is possible between a database write and cache invalidation.

points.title: Follow-ups

questions.q: Compare write-through and write-behind caching. When is write-behind dangerous?
questions.a: Write-through writes synchronously to the cache and the backing store, so the store is always current and a cache loss does not lose data, at the cost of write latency. Write-behind acknowledges after writing to the cache and flushes to the store asynchronously, often batched, which gives low write latency and lets you coalesce repeated writes to the same key. The danger is durability: if the cache node dies before the flush, acknowledged writes are lost. It also makes the database lag the cache, so other readers of the database see stale data and ordering across keys can be violated. Use it only for data where bounded loss is acceptable or where the buffer is itself durable, such as a replicated log.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The core difference is when the write is acknowledged relative to durable storage, which decides the loss window.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Service → Cache → Write Queue → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Write-behind raises throughput and cuts latency but introduces a data loss window.
Write-through is safer but couples write latency to the slowest store.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you make write-behind durable?
How do you handle flush failures and retries without reordering writes?

points.title: Common mistakes

Ignoring that other consumers read the database directly and see stale values.

questions.q: How do you invalidate cached data, and why is it called one of the hard problems?
questions.a: Common strategies are TTL expiry, explicit delete on write, event-driven invalidation from change events, and versioned keys where a version bump makes old entries unreachable. TTL is simplest but allows bounded staleness; explicit delete is fresher but requires every writer to know every cache key that depends on the data. Event-driven invalidation from a change stream decouples writers from caches but adds lag and a new failure path. It is hard because derived and aggregated entries depend on many sources, because invalidation messages can be lost or reordered, and because a delete racing with a read-fill can re-insert stale data.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Invalidation is a distributed consistency problem between the cache and its source, with races on both sides.

points.title: Flow
items: Writer → Database → Change Event → Invalidator → Cache

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Short TTLs improve freshness but raise database load.

questions.q: A hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. How do you prevent a cache stampede?
questions.a: First coalesce: allow only one request per key to rebuild, using a short-lived lock or an in-process single-flight, while others wait briefly or serve the stale value. Second, serve stale-while-revalidate: keep a soft TTL and a longer hard TTL so expired data is returned while one background refresh runs. Third, add jitter to TTLs so many keys do not expire together, and proactively refresh very hot keys before expiry. For failures, negative-cache misses for a short time and protect the database with rate limiting and circuit breakers. The lock itself needs its own timeout so a crashed rebuilder does not block everyone.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A stampede is many concurrent rebuilds of the same value, so the fix is to make rebuilds single and to avoid synchronized expiry.

points.title: Flow
items: Clients → App Service → Single-flight Lock → Cache → Database

points.title: Trade-offs

questions.q: Which eviction policy would you pick for a Redis cache and why?
questions.a: Eviction runs when memory reaches the configured limit. LRU evicts the least recently used key and suits workloads with temporal locality, while LFU keeps frequently used keys and handles scan-like traffic better because one-time reads do not displace popular items. Redis offers approximated LRU and LFU, with variants that consider only keys that have a TTL, plus random and no-eviction. For a general cache I would choose an allkeys policy, often LFU or LRU, so memory pressure never causes write errors. I would avoid no-eviction for a cache because writes would start failing once memory is full.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The right policy follows the access pattern: recency favours LRU, long-term popularity favours LFU.

points.title: Flow
items: App → Redis → Eviction Policy → Memory Limit

points.title: Trade-offs
items: LFU resists scans but adapts slowly when popularity shifts.
Volatile policies protect keys without TTL but can run out of evictable keys.

questions.q: How does Redis Cluster shard data, and what limitations does that create for application design?
questions.a: Redis Cluster splits the key space into 16384 hash slots, computed from a CRC16 of the key, and assigns slot ranges to primary nodes, each with replicas for failover. Clients are redirected to the owning node and usually cache the slot map. Multi-key operations, transactions and Lua scripts must touch keys in the same slot, so you use hash tags in braces to co-locate related keys. Resharding moves slots between nodes online but a hot key still lives on one node, so sharding does not fix skew. Replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent acknowledged writes.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Slot-based sharding gives horizontal scale but constrains multi-key operations and does not remove hot-key or async replication limits.

items: Client → Slot Map → Primary Node → Replica → Failover

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Hash tags enable multi-key operations but can concentrate load on one slot.
Asynchronous replication keeps writes fast but allows loss on failover.

questions.q: How would you implement a distributed lock with Redis, and what are its limits?
questions.a: Acquire with a single atomic command that sets the key only if absent, with an expiry and a unique random value as the owner token. Release with a small script that deletes the key only if the stored value still matches the token, so you never release someone else lock. The expiry prevents a crashed holder from blocking forever, but if work outlasts the TTL two clients can hold the lock. Failover with asynchronous replication can also lose the lock. So use locks for efficiency, such as avoiding duplicate work, and use fencing tokens or database constraints when correctness depends on mutual exclusion.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A TTL-based lock is a lease, so it cannot guarantee exclusivity under pauses or failover without extra checks.

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Short leases recover quickly but risk expiry during slow work.

questions.q: Design a distributed rate limiter for an API used by many instances. Which algorithm and where does state live?
questions.a: Token bucket is a good default: each key has a bucket that refills at a steady rate and allows bursts up to capacity. A sliding window counter gives smoother enforcement of a strict limit at slightly higher cost. State must be shared, so keep counters in Redis and make the check-and-decrement atomic with a script or atomic commands, keyed by user, API key or IP. questions.q: Explain brokers, topics, partitions and consumer groups in Kafka.
questions.a: A broker is a server that stores partition data and serves clients. A topic is a named stream split into partitions, each an ordered append-only log; partitions are the unit of parallelism and are spread across brokers. Producers choose the partition, usually by hashing a key. A consumer group is a set of consumers that share a topic: each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, so adding consumers up to the partition count increases throughput. Different groups read the same topic independently, each tracking its own offsets.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Partitions give both scale and ordering boundaries, and consumer groups map partitions to workers.

points.title: Flow
items: Producer → Topic Partitions → Broker Cluster → Consumer Group → Consumers

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More partitions raise parallelism but add metadata, file handles and rebalance cost.

questions.q: How does Kafka replication work and what configuration gives you durability without losing availability?
questions.a: Each partition has a leader and follower replicas; producers and consumers talk to the leader, and followers fetch from it. The in-sync replica set contains replicas that are caught up, and a write is committed once all in-sync replicas have it. For durability set a replication factor of at least three, producer acks to all, and min.insync.replicas to two, so a write needs at least two copies and the system tolerates one broker loss. If in-sync replicas drop below the minimum, producers get errors, trading availability for safety. Disabling unclean leader election avoids promoting a stale replica, which would lose committed data.

items: Durability comes from requiring multiple in-sync copies before acknowledging, and availability depends on how many failures that quorum tolerates.

questions.q: How do consumer offsets work, and when should a consumer commit them?
questions.a: An offset is the position of a record within a partition. A consumer group stores the next offset to read per partition, in an internal Kafka topic. If you commit before processing, a crash can skip records, giving at-most-once. If you commit after processing, a crash causes reprocessing, giving at-least-once, which is the usual safe default when consumers are idempotent. Auto-commit on a timer can commit offsets for records not yet processed, so for important work commit manually after the side effect succeeds. Retention and offset resets decide what happens when no valid offset exists.

items: Broker Partition → Consumer → Process Record → Commit Offset → Offsets Topic

questions.q: Consumer lag is growing steadily on a topic. How do you diagnose and fix it?
questions.a: Lag is the gap between the latest offset and the committed offset, so first check whether the cause is slow consumers, too little parallelism, a hot partition, or frequent rebalances. Compare per-partition lag: one partition lagging suggests key skew or a poison record, while all partitions suggest insufficient throughput. Fix by speeding up processing, such as batching, async IO and removing slow downstream calls, then scale consumers up to the partition count, and increase partitions if needed with awareness of key mapping. Tune fetch and poll settings so processing finishes within the poll interval, otherwise the consumer is kicked out and rebalances. Alert on lag trend and time lag, not just a static number.

questions.q: How do you design retry topics and a dead letter queue for failing messages?
questions.a: Distinguish transient failures, such as a downstream timeout, from permanent ones, such as a malformed payload. For transient failures, publish the message to a retry topic with a delay tier, for example short then longer intervals, so the main partition keeps moving instead of blocking on one bad record. After a bounded number of attempts, send the message to a dead letter topic with the error, original topic, partition, offset and attempt count in headers. Permanent failures can go straight to the dead letter topic. Someone must monitor and replay the dead letter topic after a fix, and consumers must be idempotent because retries cause duplicates.

items: Separating retries from the main flow prevents one bad record from blocking a partition while still not losing the message.

questions.q: What delivery guarantees does Kafka offer, and how do you achieve effectively exactly-once processing?
questions.a: By default Kafka gives at-least-once delivery. Idempotent producers prevent duplicates from producer retries within a partition, and transactions let a producer write to multiple partitions and commit consumed offsets atomically, so a consume-transform-produce pipeline inside Kafka can be exactly-once when consumers read with read committed isolation. Once the result leaves Kafka, such as a write to a database or an HTTP call, Kafka cannot make that effect exactly-once. There you combine at-least-once delivery with an idempotent consumer that deduplicates using a message id or a natural key. So exactly-once is end-to-end only when every step is transactional or idempotent.

questions.q: How do you design an idempotent consumer?
questions.a: Assume every message may be delivered more than once and make processing the same message twice produce the same result. Give each message a unique id or use a natural business key, and record processed ids in the same transaction as the business change, so either both happen or neither. Alternatively use naturally idempotent operations such as upserts or set-to-value rather than increments. Use a unique constraint on the dedup key so a concurrent duplicate fails safely. Expire dedup records after a window longer than the maximum redelivery or retention horizon.
