questions.q: Explain event sourcing and CQRS, and when the added complexity is justified.
questions.a: Event sourcing stores state as an append-only sequence of events, and current state is derived by replaying them, often with snapshots to speed up rebuilds. This gives a full audit trail, the ability to rebuild read models and to answer temporal questions. CQRS separates the write model, which validates commands and emits events, from one or more read models optimized for queries and updated asynchronously from those events. Together they let reads scale independently and take shapes the write side would not. The cost is eventual consistency between write and read sides, event schema evolution, and harder debugging, so use them where audit, complex domain history or very different read shapes justify it, not for plain CRUD.

points.title: Reasoning
items: They trade simplicity for auditability and independent read scaling, which only pays off for certain domains.

points.title: Flow
items: Command → Aggregate → Event Store → Projector → Read Model → Query API

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Read models are eventually consistent with the write side.
Events are immutable, so schema changes need versioning and upcasting.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you fix a bad event that was already stored?
How do you rebuild a read model without downtime?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Applying event sourcing to every service by default.
Letting consumers read the event store internals instead of published event contracts.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines both patterns and how they combine.
States eventual consistency and schema evolution costs.
Gives criteria for when not to use them.

questions.q: What is the transactional outbox pattern and what problem does it solve?
questions.a: A service often must update its database and publish an event, but writing to both is a dual write that can leave them inconsistent if one fails. With the outbox pattern, the service writes the business change and an outbox row in the same local database transaction. A separate relay, either a poller or a change data capture reader, reads outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, then marks them sent. Delivery is at-least-once because the relay can crash after publishing and before marking, so consumers must be idempotent. This guarantees an event is published if and only if the state change committed.

points.title: Reasoning
items: It turns an unreliable dual write into one atomic local transaction plus a reliable asynchronous relay.

points.title: Flow
items: Service → DB (Entity + Outbox) → Relay / CDC → Message Broker → Consumers

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Adds a relay component and outbox table to operate and clean up.
Publishing is delayed slightly compared with direct publish.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Polling versus CDC for the relay: which and why?
How do you preserve event order per aggregate?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Publishing to the broker inside the database transaction and assuming atomicity.
Never deleting outbox rows so the table grows unbounded.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains the dual write problem.
Describes atomic outbox write and relay.
Notes at-least-once and idempotent consumers.

questions.q: Design a saga for an order that spans payment, inventory and shipping services. Compare orchestration and choreography.
questions.a: A saga replaces a distributed transaction with a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo it if a later step fails. In orchestration a central coordinator tells each service what to do, tracks state and triggers compensations, which makes the flow explicit and easier to monitor but concentrates logic in one place. In choreography services react to each other events with no central controller, which is loosely coupled but makes the overall flow hard to see and cyclic dependencies easy to create. Steps and compensations must be idempotent and retried, and the order should put hard-to-reverse steps last. Compensation is semantic, such as refund or release stock, and intermediate states are visible, so you design for that.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Sagas give eventual consistency across services without distributed locks, at the cost of explicit compensation logic.

points.title: Flow
items: Order Service → Saga Orchestrator → Payment → Inventory → Shipping

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Orchestration is clearer but the coordinator becomes a critical component.
Choreography avoids a coordinator but flow tracing and change are harder.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if a compensation itself fails?
How do you stop users seeing half-finished states?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming compensations always succeed and are instant.
Using two-phase commit across services and blocking on slow participants.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines local transactions with compensations.
Compares orchestration and choreography fairly.
Requires idempotent steps and handles compensation failure.

questions.q: When would you choose Kafka, RabbitMQ, or a plain REST call for communication between services?
questions.a: REST or gRPC fits request-response where the caller needs an immediate answer and can tolerate coupling to the callee availability. RabbitMQ is a traditional broker built for work queues and flexible routing, where messages are delivered to a consumer, acknowledged and removed, and it suits task distribution and per-message routing. Kafka is a distributed log that retains events for a configured time, supports replay and many independent consumer groups, and handles very high throughput, so it fits event streaming, audit and data pipelines. Pick by need: synchronous answer, task queue semantics, or durable replayable event stream. Often a system uses more than one.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The choice follows from whether you need an immediate response, queue semantics, or a retained replayable log.

points.title: Flow
items: Producer → REST / RabbitMQ / Kafka → Consumer

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Synchronous REST is simple but couples availability and latency of services.
Kafka offers replay and scale but has more operational weight than a simple queue.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you add reliability to a REST call between services?
Can Kafka act as a work queue, and what are the limits?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using Kafka for simple low-volume task queues that need per-message routing.
Making long chains of synchronous calls and inheriting every dependency failure.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Matches each technology to a communication style.
Mentions replay and retention for Kafka.
Notes coupling in synchronous calls.

questions.q: When should you use WebSockets versus server-sent events versus polling for real-time updates, and how do you scale them?
questions.a: Polling is simplest and works through any proxy but wastes requests and adds latency. Server-sent events give a one-way server to client stream over HTTP with automatic reconnect, which suits notifications and live feeds. WebSockets are full-duplex over one long-lived connection, best for chat or collaborative features needing client to server messages too. Because connections are stateful, scaling needs a load balancer that supports long-lived connections, a connection gateway tier, and a pub/sub backbone so a message published anywhere reaches the node holding the user connection. Plan for reconnect storms with backoff and jitter, heartbeat checks, and per-connection backpressure.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The protocol follows directionality and latency needs, and scaling stateful connections requires a fan-out layer behind them.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Load Balancer → WebSocket Gateway → Pub/Sub → Backend Service

points.title: Trade-offs
items: WebSockets are flexible but stateful and harder to load balance and deploy without dropping connections.
SSE is simpler but one-directional and limited in some environments.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you deploy a new gateway version without disconnecting everyone at once?
How do you handle a slow client that cannot keep up?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Keeping per-user state only in one gateway node memory.
Reconnecting all clients immediately after a failure, causing a storm.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Chooses protocol by directionality and needs.
Designs fan-out with pub/sub.
Addresses reconnect storms and backpressure.

questions.q: Monolith, modular monolith or microservices: how do you decide for a new product?
questions.a: A monolith is one deployable unit, which is simple to build, test, deploy and debug but can become tangled as it grows. A modular monolith keeps one deployable but enforces strong module boundaries and separate data ownership, giving most of the design benefit with little operational cost. Microservices split into independently deployed services, which allows team autonomy and independent scaling but adds network failure, distributed data consistency and heavy operational needs. For a new product with a small team and unclear domain boundaries, start with a modular monolith and extract services when there is a concrete reason, such as independent scaling, team ownership or different release cadence.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Boundaries are cheap to move inside one codebase and expensive to move across services, so defer the split until the domain is understood.

points.title: Flow
items: Clients → Single Deployable → Modules → Shared Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Microservices add independent deploys but also network calls, tracing and consistency work.
A modular monolith has weaker runtime isolation: one bug can take everything down.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep module boundaries from eroding?
What signals tell you a module should be extracted?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Splitting into many services before the domain boundaries are clear.
Calling a distributed monolith with a shared database microservices.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Recommends based on team size and domain clarity.
Names concrete extraction triggers.

questions.q: Why is database per service important, and how do you handle queries and transactions that span services?
questions.a: Giving each service its own datastore keeps it independently deployable and lets it change its schema and technology without breaking others. Other services access the data only through its API or events, never by reading its tables. Cross-service transactions are replaced with sagas and eventual consistency. Cross-service queries use API composition, where a gateway or aggregator calls several services and joins in memory, or a CQRS read model built from published events into a dedicated query store. Accept that joins and strong consistency across boundaries are gone, and design the domain so related data that must be consistent lives in one service.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Shared tables couple services at the schema level, which defeats independent deployment.

points.title: Flow
items: API Gateway → Order Service → Order DB → Event Bus → Query Read Model

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Autonomy increases but cross-service reporting and consistency get harder.
Duplicated read data speeds queries but must be kept in sync.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you migrate a shared database toward per-service ownership?
How do you do reporting across services?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Letting services read each other tables for convenience.
Expecting ACID transactions across services.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Offers sagas, API composition and read models.

questions.q: What is service discovery and how do client-side and server-side discovery differ?
questions.a: Service instances come and go with scaling and failures, so callers need a way to find current healthy addresses. A registry holds the instances, which register themselves or are registered by the platform, and health checks remove bad ones. With client-side discovery the caller queries the registry and picks an instance, doing its own load balancing. With server-side discovery the caller sends to a stable name, such as a load balancer or a Kubernetes Service, and the platform routes to a healthy instance. Server-side discovery keeps clients simple and language agnostic, while client-side gives more control but puts logic in every client.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Dynamic addresses require an indirection layer that tracks healthy instances.

points.title: Flow
items: Caller → Registry / DNS → Load Balancer → Service Instances

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Client-side discovery avoids an extra hop but needs a client library per language.
Server-side discovery adds a hop and a component that must be highly available.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does Kubernetes handle this natively?
How do you avoid routing to an instance that is shutting down?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Hardcoding instance addresses or caching DNS results too long.
Skipping health checks so dead instances stay in rotation.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Contrasts client-side and server-side models.
Connects to platform features like Kubernetes Services.

questions.q: What is a Backend for Frontend and how does it differ from a general API gateway?
questions.a: A Backend for Frontend is a thin service owned by a specific client experience, such as web or mobile, that aggregates and shapes data from many backend services for that client. It trims payloads, combines calls to reduce round trips, and absorbs client-specific changes so core services stay generic. A general API gateway is a shared edge component handling cross-cutting concerns like routing, authentication, rate limiting and TLS for all clients. They can coexist: the gateway at the edge and BFFs behind it. Keep business rules out of the BFF, otherwise logic duplicates across clients.

points.title: Reasoning
items: BFFs give each client an API tuned to its needs without bloating shared services.

points.title: Flow
items: Mobile App → API Gateway → Mobile BFF → Catalog Service → Order Service

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Each BFF is more code and a deployable to own, but clients move independently.
Aggregation in the BFF reduces round trips but can become a latency bottleneck.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Who should own the BFF: the client team or the backend team?
How do you avoid duplicating logic across BFFs?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting domain business rules in the BFF.
Creating one giant shared BFF that serves every client the same way.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines BFF as client-specific aggregation.
Distinguishes it from the gateway.
Names ownership and logic duplication risks.

questions.q: How do you make service-to-service calls resilient to a slow or failing dependency?
questions.a: Set explicit timeouts on every remote call so threads are not held forever. Retry only idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter, and cap total retries so you do not amplify load on a struggling service. Use a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing dependency for a period and fails fast, then probes for recovery. Isolate resources with bulkheads, such as separate pools per dependency, so one slow service cannot exhaust all threads. Provide fallbacks or degraded responses where the product allows, and apply load shedding when overloaded.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Without limits, a slow dependency consumes resources upstream and failures cascade.

points.title: Flow
items: Caller → Timeout + Retry → Circuit Breaker → Bulkhead Pool → Dependency

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Retries improve success on transient errors but can cause retry storms.
Fallbacks keep the product usable but may show stale or reduced data.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do retries at several layers multiply load?
How do you decide the timeout value?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Retrying non-idempotent writes without idempotency keys.
Using default or infinite timeouts.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Mentions timeouts, retries with backoff, breakers and bulkheads.
Understands retry amplification.
Considers idempotency and fallbacks.

questions.q: How would you migrate a monolith to services incrementally without a big-bang rewrite?
questions.a: Use the strangler approach: place a routing layer in front of the monolith and move one capability at a time to a new service, redirecting only that traffic. Choose seams along business capabilities with low coupling, and start with something valuable but not critical. Handle data carefully: first introduce an API boundary inside the monolith, then move the data with dual writes or change data capture, verify with shadow reads, and switch ownership. Keep each step reversible with feature flags and routing rules. Invest in observability and automated tests first, so you can compare behaviour and detect regressions.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Incremental extraction limits risk because each step is small and reversible, while the monolith keeps serving the rest.

points.title: Flow
items: Clients → Routing Layer → Monolith → New Service → Migrated Data Store

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Running both systems costs extra complexity during the transition.
Data migration is the riskiest step and slows the process.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep data in sync while both systems are live?
How do you decide extraction order?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Extracting the service but continuing to share the monolith database.
Rewriting everything at once with no incremental rollout.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Handles data migration explicitly.
Keeps steps reversible and measured.

questions.q: Explain pods, deployments, services and ingress and how a request reaches a pod.
questions.a: A pod is the smallest deployable unit, one or more containers sharing network and storage, and it is ephemeral. A Deployment declares the desired number of replicas and manages ReplicaSets, replacing failed pods and performing rolling updates. A Service gives a set of pods a stable virtual address and load balances across the pods matched by its label selector. An Ingress defines HTTP routing rules, such as host and path, and an ingress controller implements them at the cluster edge. A request arrives at the load balancer, the ingress controller applies routing rules, forwards to a Service, which picks a ready pod.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Each object adds a layer of indirection so pods can be replaced without clients noticing.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Load Balancer → Ingress Controller → Service → Pods

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More abstraction layers give flexibility but add hops and debugging surface.
Ingress consolidates entry points but the controller becomes a critical component.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is the difference between ClusterIP, NodePort and LoadBalancer services?
How does a Service know which pods are ready?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Addressing pods by IP, which changes on restart.
Running bare pods with no controller so nothing restarts them elsewhere.

Traces the request path end to end.
Understands label selectors and readiness.

questions.q: How do liveness, readiness and startup probes differ, and how can misconfigured probes cause outages?
questions.a: A readiness probe decides whether a pod receives traffic; failing it removes the pod from Service endpoints without restarting it. A liveness probe decides whether the container is stuck and should be restarted. A startup probe delays the other probes until a slow-starting app is up. Outages happen when liveness checks a shared dependency such as the database: a database blip makes all pods restart together and amplifies the incident. Too-aggressive thresholds or timeouts restart healthy but loaded pods, and readiness that never passes during startup keeps a rollout stuck. Keep liveness simple and local, and make readiness reflect ability to serve.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Liveness drives restarts and readiness drives traffic, so mixing their purposes turns dependency problems into restart loops.

points.title: Flow
items: Kubelet → Probe Check → Container → Endpoints → Service Traffic

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Strict probes detect failure fast but risk false positives under load.
Lenient probes avoid flapping but slow failure detection.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle graceful shutdown so in-flight requests finish?
What does a startup probe solve that a long initial delay does not?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Pointing liveness at downstream dependencies.
Using the same endpoint and settings for liveness and readiness.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Gives the distinct purpose of each probe.
Describes a realistic failure caused by bad probes.
Mentions graceful shutdown with readiness.

questions.q: How does a rolling deployment work in Kubernetes and how do you roll back?
questions.a: A Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually scales it up while scaling the old one down, controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable, so capacity stays available. New pods must pass readiness before old ones are removed, which makes readiness probes essential. If the new version is bad, you can roll back with the rollout undo command, which scales the previous ReplicaSet back up from the stored revision history. A progress deadline marks a stuck rollout as failed. For safer changes combine this with canary or blue-green strategies and automated checks, since rolling update alone exposes real users gradually but not selectively.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Gradual replacement with readiness gating keeps the service available while the revision history makes rollback fast.

points.title: Flow
items: Deployment → New ReplicaSet → Readiness Gate → Old ReplicaSet → Service

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Higher maxSurge speeds rollouts but needs spare capacity.
Both versions run at once, so changes must be backward compatible.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do database schema changes fit into a rolling deploy?
How do you detect a bad rollout automatically?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Skipping readiness probes so traffic hits pods that are not ready.
Shipping a breaking API or schema change that old and new pods cannot share.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains ReplicaSets, surge and unavailable settings.
Describes rollback mechanism.
Notes version coexistence requirements.

questions.q: How do resource requests and limits affect scheduling and stability, and how does the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler use them?
questions.a: Requests are what the scheduler reserves when placing a pod, and limits are the cap enforced at runtime. Exceeding a CPU limit causes throttling, while exceeding a memory limit gets the container killed with an out-of-memory error. Pods with requests equal to limits get the highest quality of service class and are evicted last under node pressure. The HPA scales replicas based on metrics such as CPU utilization measured relative to the request, so a missing or wrong request makes utilization meaningless. Set requests from observed usage, tune limits carefully, and give the HPA stabilization windows to avoid flapping.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Requests drive placement and autoscaling math, and limits drive runtime enforcement.

points.title: Flow
items: Metrics Server → HPA → Deployment → Scheduler → Nodes

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Low requests pack nodes densely but risk contention and eviction.
Tight CPU limits cause throttling and latency even when the node has spare CPU.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When would you scale on a custom metric such as queue depth?
What happens when the cluster has no capacity for new pods?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Omitting requests so the HPA and scheduler cannot work properly.
Setting memory limits too low and causing repeated out-of-memory kills.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Separates requests from limits and their effects.
Explains HPA utilization relative to requests.
Mentions QoS and stabilization.

questions.q: How should you manage configuration and secrets for containers running in Kubernetes?
questions.a: Build one image and inject environment-specific configuration at runtime through ConfigMaps and environment variables or mounted files, so the same artifact is promoted across environments. Secrets hold sensitive values, but by default they are only base64 encoded, so enable encryption at rest and restrict access with RBAC. Prefer syncing from an external secrets manager and rotating values, and avoid baking secrets into images or committing them to source control. Mounted files can be updated without redeploys in some cases, while environment variables need a restart. Limit which service accounts can read which secrets.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Separating config from the image keeps builds reproducible, and treating secrets specially limits exposure.

points.title: Flow
items: Secrets Manager → External Secrets Sync → K8s Secret → Pod → Application

points.title: Trade-offs
items: External secret managers improve rotation and audit but add a dependency.
Mounted files allow live updates but need the app to reload them.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you rotate a database password without downtime?
Who can read Secrets in a namespace and how do you restrict it?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Believing base64 encoding protects a Secret.
Putting credentials in the container image or in plain manifests in a repository.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Keeps config out of images.
Knows Secret weaknesses and mitigations.
Mentions rotation and access control.

questions.q: Design a deployment so a stateless API stays available during node failures and cluster upgrades.
questions.a: Run multiple replicas spread across nodes and zones using topology spread constraints or anti-affinity, so one node or zone loss leaves capacity. Add a PodDisruptionBudget so voluntary disruptions like node drains never remove too many pods at once. Use readiness probes and a preStop delay with graceful termination so pods drain in-flight requests before stopping. Set realistic requests so the scheduler places replacements quickly, and enable autoscaling with headroom for failover load. Keep the app stateless and externalize sessions and state so any pod can serve any request.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Availability comes from redundancy across failure domains plus controls over how disruptions are applied.

points.title: Flow
items: Load Balancer → Ingress → Service → Pods (Multi-Zone) → PDB + Drain

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Zone spreading costs cross-zone traffic and capacity headroom.
A strict PDB protects availability but can block node drains and upgrades.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you handle a stateful workload differently?
What if a PDB prevents a node from ever draining?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running all replicas on the same node or zone.
Ignoring termination grace and dropping in-flight requests on every deploy.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses spread, PDB and graceful termination.
Plans capacity headroom.
Keeps the service stateless.

questions.q: Why containerize with Docker, and what makes a good production image?
questions.a: Containers package an application with its dependencies so it runs the same on a laptop, in CI and in production, and they share the host kernel so they start fast and use fewer resources than virtual machines. A good image is small, using a minimal base and multi-stage builds that keep build tools out of the final image. It runs as a non-root user, pins versions, is rebuilt regularly to pick up security patches, and is scanned for vulnerabilities. Layers should be ordered so rarely changing steps cache well. Images should be immutable and tagged by version or digest rather than a floating latest tag.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Consistency and fast startup are the benefits, and small, minimal, immutable images reduce attack surface and deploy time.

points.title: Flow
items: Source → CI Build → Image Registry → Vulnerability Scan → Cluster Pull

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Minimal images are secure and small but harder to debug without shell tools.
Shared kernel gives density but weaker isolation than virtual machines.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you debug a distroless container in production?
Why avoid the latest tag in production?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running the process as root with a large base image full of tools.
Deploying the mutable latest tag so rollbacks are unclear.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Lists concrete image hygiene practices.
Understands immutability and tagging.

questions.q: Describe a CI/CD pipeline for a backend service and what each stage guards against.
questions.a: On each commit CI builds the code, runs unit tests and static checks such as linting and dependency vulnerability scans, so broken or risky changes are caught early. Next it builds an immutable artifact or container image once, tags it, and pushes it to a registry. Integration and contract tests run against that same artifact in a test environment. CD then promotes the identical artifact through staging to production, using a controlled rollout with health checks and automated rollback. Build once and promote ensures what you tested is what you ship, and configuration is injected per environment.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Each stage catches a class of defect cheaply before it reaches users, and promoting one artifact removes build drift.

points.title: Flow
items: Commit → Build + Test → Image Registry → Staging → Production Rollout

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More automated gates raise confidence but slow feedback if tests are slow.
Full automation to production needs strong tests and monitoring to be safe.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep the pipeline fast as the test suite grows?
How do you handle database migrations in the pipeline?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Rebuilding the artifact per environment so production differs from what was tested.
Having no automated rollback or health verification after deploy.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Builds once and promotes.
Includes verification and rollback.

questions.q: Compare blue-green and canary deployments. How do you choose and what makes each hard?
questions.a: Blue-green runs two full environments: you deploy to the idle one, test it, then switch all traffic at once and keep the old one for instant rollback. It gives fast, clean cutover and rollback but doubles capacity during the switch and exposes all users at once. Canary sends a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watches metrics such as errors and latency against the baseline, and increases gradually or aborts. It limits blast radius and uses real traffic but needs good observability, traffic splitting and a way to compare. Both struggle with shared state: database schema changes must be backward compatible so old and new versions work against the same data.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Blue-green optimizes for instant switch and rollback, while canary optimizes for limiting risk with real-traffic evidence.

points.title: Flow
items: Router → Stable Version → New Version → Metrics Analysis → Promote or Rollback

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Blue-green needs duplicate capacity but has simple semantics.
Canary needs reliable metrics and traffic control, and a small sample may miss rare errors.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What metrics would automatically abort a canary?
How do you handle schema migrations with either strategy?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Promoting a canary without enough traffic or time to see problems.
Making a breaking database change that the old version cannot handle during rollback.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Contrasts blast radius, cost and rollback.
Raises backward-compatible data changes.

questions.q: How do feature flags support safer releases, and what risks do they introduce?
questions.a: Feature flags separate deploying code from releasing a feature, so unfinished or risky code ships dark and is enabled gradually for internal users, a percentage of traffic, or a segment. If a problem appears you disable the flag without redeploying, which is a fast kill switch. They enable trunk-based development and experiments. The risks are flag debt, where old flags clutter code and create untested combinations, and the flag service becoming a dependency. Mitigate with defaults that fail safe if the service is unreachable, an ownership and expiry process for removing flags, and tests for both states.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Decoupling release from deploy reduces risk but adds configuration state that must be managed.

points.title: Flow
items: Code Deploy → Flag Service → Application → Segment Rules → Users

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Fast rollback and gradual rollout versus code complexity and flag cleanup.
Runtime flag lookups add a dependency and slight latency.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What should the default be if the flag service is down?
How do you make sure flags are cleaned up?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Never removing old flags.
Putting security or permission decisions solely in a client-visible flag.

questions.q: How would you roll out a database schema change with zero downtime alongside a service deploy?
questions.a: Use the expand and contract pattern across several releases. First, expand: add new columns or tables in a backward-compatible way, with nullable columns or defaults, and deploy code that writes both old and new shapes while still reading the old. Then backfill existing data in small batches to avoid long locks. Next switch reads to the new shape, verify, and finally contract by removing old columns after no running version needs them. Never combine a breaking schema change with the code that needs it in one step, because rolling deploys and rollbacks mean old and new code run against the same schema.

points.title: Reasoning
items: During a rollout both versions coexist, so every intermediate schema must work for both.

points.title: Flow
items: Migration Step → Schema (Expanded) → Dual-Write Service → Backfill Job → Contract Migration

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Multiple releases are slower but each step is safe and reversible.
Dual writes add temporary complexity and risk of divergence.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you backfill a huge table without blocking traffic?
How do you roll back after the contract step?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Renaming or dropping a column in the same release that stops using it.
Running a long blocking migration on a hot table during peak traffic.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Describes expand, migrate, contract phases.
Recognizes version coexistence.
Covers batched backfill and rollback.

questions.q: What are the three pillars of observability and how do they complement each other?
questions.a: Metrics are numeric time series, cheap to store and good for dashboards, trends and alerting on aggregate behaviour. Logs are discrete event records with detail about what happened, good for debugging a specific case but costly at volume. Traces follow a single request across services as spans, showing where time was spent and which dependency failed. A typical investigation starts from a metric alert, narrows to a service or endpoint, uses traces to find the slow or failing hop, then reads logs for details. Correlating them through a shared trace id and consistent labels makes this fast.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Each signal answers a different question, and they are most useful when linked together.

points.title: Flow
items: Service → Metrics → Logs → Traces → Dashboards and Alerts

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Rich logs and high-cardinality metrics are powerful but expensive to store and query.
Tracing needs context propagation and often sampling to control cost.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why can high-cardinality labels hurt a metrics system?
How do you correlate a log line with a trace?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Logging everything unstructured and relying on grep.
Having dashboards but no trace context across services.

questions.q: Explain SLI, SLO and error budget, and how you would define them for a checkout API.
questions.a: An SLI is a measured indicator of user-visible quality, such as the fraction of checkout requests that succeed or complete under a latency threshold. An SLO is the target for that indicator over a window, for example a stated percentage of successful requests over thirty days. The error budget is the allowed unreliability, one minus the SLO, which can be spent on deploys and experiments. When the budget is being burned too fast, the team slows risky releases and prioritizes reliability work. For checkout I would measure availability at the load balancer or gateway from the user perspective and a latency SLI on a high percentile, and pick targets from user needs and what is achievable rather than aiming for perfect.

points.title: Reasoning
items: SLOs turn reliability into a measurable target and the error budget turns it into a decision-making tool.

points.title: Flow
items: User Requests → SLI Measurement → SLO Target → Error Budget → Release Policy

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Stricter SLOs cost more and slow feature delivery.
Looser SLOs allow velocity but risk user dissatisfaction.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why measure at the edge rather than inside each service?
What do you do when the error budget is exhausted?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Choosing SLIs based on infrastructure metrics like CPU rather than user experience.
Setting 100 percent targets, which leaves no room for change.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines SLI, SLO and budget correctly.
Uses user-centred indicators.
Links budget to release decisions.

questions.q: How do you design good alerts that avoid alert fatigue?
questions.a: Alert on symptoms users feel, such as error rate or latency against the SLO, rather than every internal cause like high CPU. Each alert should be actionable, urgent enough to page someone, and link to a runbook and dashboard. Use burn-rate alerts on the error budget with multiple windows, so fast burns page quickly and slow burns create tickets. Add durations and thresholds to avoid flapping, group and deduplicate related alerts, and route by severity and ownership. Review alerts regularly and delete or fix those that fire without needing action.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Noisy alerts get ignored, so alerts must be few, meaningful and tied to user impact.

points.title: Flow
items: Metrics → Alert Rules → Alertmanager → On-call Pager → Runbook

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Sensitive alerts catch issues early but increase false positives.
Cause-based alerts help diagnosis but belong on dashboards, not pages.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What is the difference between paging and ticketing alerts?
How do you test that an alert actually fires?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Paging on resource thresholds that do not affect users.
Alerts with no owner or runbook.

Mentions burn rate or duration thresholds.

questions.q: How does distributed tracing work and how do you control its cost?
questions.a: A trace represents one request, made of spans for each operation, each with a start, duration and parent. A trace id and parent span id are propagated across process boundaries in headers, such as the W3C traceparent header, and through message headers for async work. Each service records spans and exports them to a collector, which stores them for querying. Capturing every trace is expensive, so use sampling: head sampling decides at the start and is cheap but may miss rare failures, while tail sampling decides after the trace completes and can keep errors and slow traces. Also limit span attributes and watch cardinality.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Propagating context ties spans across services, and sampling balances visibility against storage and overhead.

points.title: Flow
items: Service A → Context Propagation → Service B → Collector → Trace Store

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Tail sampling keeps interesting traces but needs buffering and more resources.
Aggressive head sampling is cheap but can miss rare problems.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep trace context through a Kafka hop?
How do you make logs searchable by trace id?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Dropping the trace headers in one service, which breaks the trace.
Recording sensitive data in span attributes.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains spans, ids and propagation.
Covers sampling strategies and tradeoffs.
Mentions async context propagation.

questions.q: What makes logs useful in a distributed system?
questions.a: Emit structured logs, typically JSON, with consistent fields such as timestamp, level, service, version, request id and trace id, so they can be filtered and aggregated. Propagate a correlation id across services so one request can be followed everywhere. Log at appropriate levels, include enough context to understand the event, and avoid logging secrets and personal data. Ship logs from stdout through an agent to a central store, since local files vanish with ephemeral containers. Control volume with sampling and retention policies because logs are among the most expensive signals to store.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Centralized, structured, correlated logs let you reconstruct what happened across many short-lived instances.

points.title: Flow
items: Service → Stdout → Log Agent → Central Log Store → Search UI

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Verbose logs help debugging but increase cost and noise.
Structured logs need discipline across teams but search far better.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you handle logging of personal data?
How do you debug when a log line is missing?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Logging secrets, tokens or full payloads.
Free-text logs with no correlation id.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Recommends structured logs with correlation ids.
Centralizes logs from ephemeral instances.
Considers privacy and cost.

questions.q: Latency for a service doubled after a deploy. Walk through how you investigate using observability data.
questions.a: First confirm scope and timing from metrics: which endpoints, percentiles and regions changed, and whether it lines up with the deploy marker. Compare against the previous version using canary or version labels, and check saturation signals like CPU, memory, garbage collection, connection pools and queue depth. Use traces to see which span grew, for example a new downstream call or slower query, and read logs for the slow requests for details. If evidence points to the release, roll back first to restore service, then root-cause in a safe environment. Finally, add a regression test or alert and record the finding in a post-incident review.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A structured narrowing from aggregate metrics to traces to logs finds the cause faster than guessing, and mitigation comes before full diagnosis.

points.title: Flow
items: Alert → Metrics Dashboard → Trace Analysis → Logs → Rollback / Fix

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Rolling back immediately restores service but can hide the cause if you do not capture evidence first.
Deep investigation in production risks further impact.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you tell a code regression from a dependency slowdown?
Why look at percentiles rather than averages?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Looking only at average latency.
Investigating at length while users are still affected instead of mitigating.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Follows a systematic metrics to traces to logs path.
Correlates with deploy events and saturation.

questions.q: Which metrics would you collect for a service, and what is the cardinality problem?
questions.a: Use the RED method for request-driven services: rate, errors and duration, and the USE method for resources: utilization, saturation and errors. Add business and dependency metrics such as queue depth, cache hit rate and downstream call latency. Record latency as histograms so you can compute percentiles across instances, since averaging per-instance percentiles is incorrect. Cardinality is the number of unique label combinations; labels like user id or full URL create huge numbers of series that exhaust memory and slow queries. Keep labels bounded, such as route template and status class, and put unbounded detail in logs or traces.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Standard method sets cover health, and bounding labels keeps the metrics system stable.

points.title: Flow
items: Application → Metrics Endpoint → Scraper → Time Series DB → Dashboards

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More labels give finer slicing but multiply stored series.
Histograms cost more than gauges but allow correct percentiles.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you choose histogram bucket boundaries?
Why average of percentiles is wrong?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Adding user id or request id as a metric label.
Alerting on average latency that hides tail behaviour.

Explains histograms and percentiles.

questions.q: Explain the OAuth2 authorization code flow and why PKCE is used.
questions.a: The client redirects the user to the authorization server, where the user authenticates and consents. The server redirects back to the client with a short-lived authorization code, which the client exchanges at the token endpoint for an access token, and optionally a refresh token. The code travels through the browser but tokens do not, and for confidential clients the exchange includes a client secret. PKCE adds a random code verifier whose hash, the challenge, is sent in the first request, and the verifier is sent at exchange. This stops an attacker who intercepts the code from redeeming it, which matters for public clients like mobile and single-page apps that cannot keep a secret.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The code flow keeps tokens off the front channel, and PKCE binds the code to the client that started the flow.

points.title: Flow
items: User → Client App → Authorization Server → Token Endpoint → Resource API

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Short-lived access tokens limit exposure but require refresh handling.
Public clients cannot hold secrets, so rely on PKCE and redirect URI checks.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Why is the implicit flow discouraged?
What is the difference between OAuth2 and OpenID Connect?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Confusing authorization with authentication.
Skipping redirect URI validation or the state parameter.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Explains PKCE purpose.
Distinguishes OAuth2 from OpenID Connect.

questions.q: Compare JWTs and server-side sessions. How do you handle revocation?
questions.a: A session stores state on the server, keyed by an opaque id in a cookie, so it is easily revoked and can change instantly, but needs a shared store when scaled out. A JWT is a signed token carrying claims, verified locally without a lookup, which suits stateless services and cross-service calls. Its weakness is revocation: a valid token stays valid until it expires. Mitigate with short access token lifetimes, refresh tokens that are rotated and revocable server-side, and a denylist for urgent cases. Always verify signature, algorithm, issuer, audience and expiry, and keep sensitive data out of the payload since it is only signed, not encrypted.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The tradeoff is stateless verification versus immediate revocability.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → API Gateway → Token Verification → Session / Revocation Store → Service

points.title: Trade-offs
items: JWTs remove lookups but make revocation and permission changes lag.
Sessions are easy to control but need shared storage and sticky handling or a cache.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where should the browser store tokens: cookie or local storage?
How does refresh token rotation detect theft?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Accepting tokens without checking audience, issuer and algorithm.
Putting secrets or personal data into the JWT payload.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Offers a realistic revocation strategy.
Lists validation checks.

questions.q: What is CSRF, how does it work and how do you defend against it?
questions.a: Cross-site request forgery tricks a logged-in user browser into sending an unwanted request to a site where the browser automatically attaches cookies. The server cannot tell the request was not intentional. Defenses include SameSite cookie attributes, which limit cross-site cookie sending, anti-CSRF tokens that must accompany state-changing requests, and checking Origin or Referer headers. Use proper HTTP methods so GET never changes state. APIs that authenticate with an explicit header token instead of cookies are not exposed to CSRF in the same way, though they have other concerns like token storage.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The attack relies on automatic credential attachment, so defenses either block that attachment or require a secret the attacker cannot know.

points.title: Flow
items: Malicious Site → User Browser → Cookie Attached → Target Server → Token Check

points.title: Trade-offs
items: SameSite is easy but not sufficient alone for every browser and flow.
Anti-CSRF tokens add server state or signing complexity.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does CSRF differ from XSS?
Does CORS prevent CSRF?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Changing state with GET requests.
Assuming CORS configuration alone prevents CSRF.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains automatic cookie attachment.
Lists layered defenses.
Distinguishes it from XSS.

questions.q: What is the difference between TLS and mTLS, and where would you use mutual TLS?
questions.a: TLS encrypts traffic and authenticates the server to the client using a certificate, protecting against eavesdropping and tampering. In mutual TLS the client also presents a certificate, so both sides are authenticated cryptographically. It is common for service-to-service traffic inside a cluster, where a service mesh or sidecar can issue short-lived workload certificates and rotate them automatically, giving encryption and strong service identity without application code. It also works for sensitive partner or device APIs. The operational cost is certificate issuance, rotation, revocation and trust distribution, so automation through a private certificate authority is essential.

points.title: Reasoning
items: mTLS adds client identity to transport security, which supports zero-trust between services.

points.title: Flow
items: Service A → Sidecar Proxy → mTLS Channel → Sidecar Proxy → Service B

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Strong identity and encryption versus certificate management overhead.
Mesh sidecars add latency and resource use but remove per-app work.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you rotate certificates without downtime?
Does mTLS replace authorization checks?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Believing mTLS alone handles authorization.
Using long-lived certificates with manual rotation.

points.title: What a good answer shows

Gives realistic use cases.
Addresses certificate lifecycle.

questions.q: How should an application store and handle secrets such as database passwords and API keys?
questions.a: Never commit secrets to source control or bake them into images. Store them in a dedicated secrets manager that provides encryption, access control, audit logs and rotation, and deliver them to workloads at runtime by identity rather than a shared password. Give each service least privilege access to only the secrets it needs. Rotate regularly and support rotation without downtime, for example by allowing two valid credentials briefly. Prefer short-lived, dynamically issued credentials where possible, and make sure logs and error messages never print them.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Centralized, audited, least-privilege secret handling limits the damage of any single leak.

points.title: Flow
items: Workload Identity → Secrets Manager → Runtime Injection → Application → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: A secrets manager adds a dependency that must be highly available.
Short-lived credentials are safer but need renewal logic.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you do if a secret leaks into a repository?
How do you bootstrap trust for the first secret?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Keeping secrets in environment files committed to a repository.
One shared credential used by every service with no rotation.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses a managed secret store with identity-based access.
Applies least privilege and rotation.
Knows how to respond to a leak.

questions.q: Design authorization for a multi-tenant API. How do you compare RBAC and attribute-based access control, and where do you enforce it?
questions.a: Authentication proves who the caller is, while authorization decides what they may do, and it must be checked on every request, server-side. RBAC assigns permissions to roles and roles to users, which is simple to reason about and audit but can explode into many roles. ABAC evaluates attributes of the user, resource and context, such as tenant, owner and time, which is more flexible for fine-grained rules but harder to test and explain. In a multi-tenant system always scope data access by tenant id derived from the verified identity, never from a client-supplied field. Enforce at the service holding the data, optionally with a central policy engine for consistency, and deny by default.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Correct isolation depends on enforcing checks at the resource and deriving tenant context from trusted identity.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → API Gateway → Authn Token → Policy Decision → Service + Tenant-Scoped Data

points.title: Trade-offs
items: RBAC is easy to manage but coarse; ABAC is expressive but complex.
Central policy gives consistency but adds latency and a dependency.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you prevent insecure direct object reference bugs?
How would you test that tenants cannot see each other data?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Relying on the gateway alone and skipping checks inside services.
Trusting a tenant id supplied in the request body.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Separates authentication from authorization.
Compares RBAC and ABAC.
Enforces tenant scoping server-side with deny by default.

questions.q: How do you protect a public API from abuse using rate limiting and related controls?
questions.a: Apply rate limits at the edge or gateway per API key, user and IP, with stricter limits on sensitive endpoints like login and password reset. Return 429 with a Retry-After header and use burst-friendly algorithms such as token bucket. Add authentication, request size limits, timeouts and input validation so single requests cannot consume excessive resources. For credential stuffing, add progressive delays, lockouts or challenges and monitor for distributed patterns. Combine this with a web application firewall or bot detection for volumetric and automated abuse, and alert on unusual spikes.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Abuse takes many forms, so layered controls at the edge protect both availability and accounts.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → CDN / WAF → API Gateway → Rate Limiter → Backend

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Tight limits stop abuse but can block legitimate bursts or shared networks.
Per-IP limits are simple but weak against distributed attackers.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you avoid blocking many users behind one corporate IP?
How would you protect the login endpoint specifically?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Limiting only at the application after the expensive work has already started.
Using one global limit for all endpoints regardless of cost.

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Places limits at the edge by identity and endpoint.
Uses proper 429 semantics.
Adds layered controls beyond rate limits.

questions.q: How would you secure service-to-service communication in a microservices platform end to end?
questions.a: Encrypt all internal traffic with TLS and prefer mutual TLS so each workload has a verifiable identity, with certificates issued and rotated automatically. Authenticate end-user context separately by propagating a validated token, and have each service check authorization rather than trusting the network. Restrict which services may talk to which using network policies and mesh authorization rules, following least privilege. Keep secrets in a secrets manager and give workloads short-lived credentials. Log and audit access, scan images and dependencies, and treat the internal network as untrusted, a zero-trust posture.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Defense in depth combines workload identity, encryption, authorization and network restriction so no single control failure exposes everything.

points.title: Flow
items: Service A → mTLS Sidecar → Network Policy → Service B → Authorization Check

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Mesh-based security centralizes policy but adds operational and latency cost.
Per-service authorization is precise but needs consistent libraries and testing.

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you propagate end-user identity safely between services?
How do you handle certificate expiry incidents?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Trusting any request that originates from inside the cluster.
Passing the original user token to every downstream service without audience checks.

questions.q: Explain CAP and PACELC. How do they change the way you pick a datastore for a payments ledger versus a product catalog?
questions.a: CAP says that during a network partition a system must choose between consistency (every read sees the latest write) and availability (every request gets a non-error answer). Partitions are not optional in a real network, so the real choice is CP or AP when a partition happens. PACELC adds the normal case: Else, when there is no partition, you still trade Latency against Consistency, because synchronous replication costs round trips. A payments ledger should be CP and pay the latency: reject or delay writes rather than risk double spend or a lost entry. A product catalog can be AP with eventual consistency: a slightly stale price or description is acceptable and reads stay fast and available. In practice you pick per use case, and often per operation within one system (for example strong reads for balance, cached reads for browsing).

points.title: Reasoning
items: CAP only describes behavior during a partition; PACELC is more useful day to day because latency versus consistency applies on every request. The right answer is driven by the cost of a wrong or stale answer for that data.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → API → Quorum Write → Replicas → Read Path

points.title: Trade-offs
items: CP gives correctness but returns errors or timeouts during a partition
AP stays available but needs conflict resolution and tolerates stale reads
Synchronous replication lowers data-loss risk but raises write latency

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Can one system offer both strong and eventual reads? How?
Where does a single-leader relational database sit in CAP?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Saying pick any two of three, as if partitions could be avoided
Treating CAP consistency as the same thing as ACID consistency
Choosing one global consistency level for all data instead of per use case

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: States that the partition tolerance is not a free choice
Uses PACELC to describe the no-partition tradeoff
Maps consistency level to the business cost of a wrong answer

questions.q: What is the difference between strong, causal, read-your-writes and eventual consistency, and when would you accept each?
questions.a: Strong (linearizable) consistency makes every read return the most recent committed write as if there were one copy of the data. Causal consistency preserves cause and effect: if B was written after reading A, nobody sees B without A. Read-your-writes guarantees a client sees its own updates even if other clients may lag. Eventual consistency only promises that replicas converge if writes stop. Use strong for balances, inventory decrement and uniqueness checks, read-your-writes for profile edits and carts so users never see their own change vanish, causal for comment threads and chat, and eventual for counters, feeds and analytics. Implement read-your-writes with sticky routing to the leader for a short window, or by passing a version or timestamp token that replicas must have reached.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Weaker models are cheaper and faster, so the skill is matching each model to the user-visible harm of staleness. Session guarantees give a good user experience without paying for full linearizability.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Router → Leader → Async Replica → Version Token

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Stronger guarantees cost latency and availability
Session guarantees need routing or token plumbing
Eventual consistency pushes conflict handling into the application

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you implement read-your-writes with read replicas?
What anomalies can a user see under eventual consistency?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using eventual consistency for uniqueness or stock decrement
Assuming replica lag is bounded without measuring or enforcing it
Confusing read-your-writes with linearizability

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines each model precisely with an example
Gives a concrete mechanism for session guarantees
Chooses by business impact, not by technology preference

questions.q: Compare single-leader, multi-leader and leaderless replication. Which would you pick for a user-profile store and which for a collaborative editing backend?
questions.a: Single-leader sends all writes to one node and streams the log to followers; it is simple, gives a clear ordering, and failover needs leader election. Multi-leader accepts writes in several places (often one per region), which gives local write latency and regional independence but creates write conflicts that need a resolution policy such as last-write-wins, merge functions or CRDTs. Leaderless replication (Dynamo style) writes to W of N replicas and reads from R, with quorum overlap when R plus W is greater than N, plus read repair and anti-entropy to converge. For a user-profile store, single-leader with read replicas is usually right: low conflict rate, simple reasoning, strong reads from the leader where needed. For collaborative editing, concurrent edits are the norm, so use multi-leader or CRDT or operational transform style merging rather than last-write-wins. Monitor replication lag and define what happens to in-flight writes on failover.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The decision is mostly about how often concurrent conflicting writes happen and whether you can merge them safely. Operational simplicity favors single-leader unless geography or conflict-free merging justifies more.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Leader → Replication Log → Followers → Failover Manager

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Single-leader is simple but write scaling and cross-region write latency are limited
Multi-leader improves local writes but needs conflict resolution
Quorums tune consistency but do not give linearizability by themselves

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What can go wrong if an old leader comes back after failover?
How does last-write-wins lose data with clock skew?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using last-write-wins everywhere and ignoring silent data loss
Ignoring replication lag when reading from followers
Picking multi-leader for a workload that has almost no conflicts

questions.q: Walk through how Raft reaches consensus and what guarantees you rely on when building a metadata service on top of it.
questions.a: Raft elects a single leader per term using randomized election timeouts and majority votes. The leader appends client commands to its log, replicates them to followers, and marks an entry committed once a majority has stored it; committed entries are applied to the state machine in order. A new leader must have the most up-to-date log among a majority, which prevents committed entries from being lost. Safety holds with up to f failures in a cluster of 2f plus 1 nodes, and progress needs a majority reachable. For a metadata service you rely on linearizable writes through the leader, ordered application, and durable committed state; reads need care, either going through the leader with a read index or lease, or accepting stale follower reads. Keep the cluster small (three or five), place members across failure domains, and use snapshots and log compaction to bound recovery time.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The staff-level point is knowing what consensus buys (ordered, durable, linearizable log) and what it costs (majority latency, small clusters, leader as a throughput bottleneck). Reads and membership changes are where designs usually go wrong.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Leader → Log Replication → Majority Ack → State Machine

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Majority commit adds a network round trip to every write
Larger clusters tolerate more failures but slow commits
Follower reads scale but may be stale

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you serve linearizable reads without writing to the log?
What happens during a partition that isolates the leader?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting a high-throughput data path through consensus instead of only metadata
Using an even number of nodes or spreading across too few failure domains
Assuming follower reads are linearizable

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains terms, majority commit and log up-to-date rule
Identifies read-path and membership-change pitfalls
Scopes consensus to small, critical metadata

questions.q: How do you design leader election for a set of workers, and how do you protect against two nodes both believing they are leader?
questions.a: Use a coordination service with consensus (for example an etcd or ZooKeeper style store) and acquire a lease or ephemeral lock keyed by the role. The holder renews the lease with heartbeats; if it stops renewing, the lease expires and another node can take over. The danger is split brain: a paused or partitioned old leader may still act after its lease expired. Protect with fencing tokens, a monotonically increasing number issued with each lease, and make downstream resources reject writes carrying an older token. Keep the lease TTL longer than expected pauses but short enough for acceptable failover, and have the leader stop work when it cannot renew. Prefer making leader-only work idempotent so a brief overlap is harmless.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Timing based locks cannot be trusted alone because of process pauses and clock drift. A fencing token moves the safety check to the resource that actually matters.

points.title: Flow
items: Candidate → Lease Store → Leader → Fencing Token → Protected Resource

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Short TTL gives fast failover but more false leader changes
Long TTL is stable but slows recovery
External coordination adds a dependency that must itself be highly available

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens if the coordination service is unavailable?
Why is wall-clock time unsafe for lease correctness?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Relying on a lock with TTL and no fencing
Implementing election with a single database row and no failure analysis
Doing non-idempotent work as leader

Plans for coordination service failure

questions.q: Compare two-phase commit and the Saga pattern. When is each appropriate, and how do you handle failures in a Saga?
questions.a: Two-phase commit has a coordinator ask all participants to prepare, then commit if all vote yes. It gives atomicity across resources but holds locks during the protocol, blocks if the coordinator fails at the wrong moment, and couples availability of every participant. A Saga breaks the work into local transactions, each with a compensating action (cancel, refund, release), coordinated either by choreography via events or orchestration via a central workflow. Sagas give availability and autonomy but only eventual consistency: intermediate states are visible, so you design for them (pending states, semantic locks). Handle failure by retrying idempotent steps, running compensations in reverse for completed steps, and persisting saga state so a crashed orchestrator resumes. Use 2PC inside a single database or a tightly controlled small set of resources; use Sagas across services and across company boundaries.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Microservices rarely can hold cross-service locks, so most systems accept intermediate states in exchange for availability. The design effort moves into compensation, idempotency and visibility of in-between states.

points.title: Flow
items: Orchestrator → Step 1 Service → Step 2 Service → Step 3 Service → Compensation Path

points.title: Trade-offs
items: 2PC is atomic but blocking and availability-coupled
Sagas scale and stay available but expose intermediate state
Orchestration is easier to reason about; choreography has less central coupling but is harder to trace

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if a compensation itself fails?
How do you make saga steps idempotent?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming compensations always succeed
Forgetting to persist saga state
Using 2PC across services owned by different teams

points.title: What a good answer shows

Describes compensations and idempotency
Chooses based on coupling and failure domains

questions.q: How do timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and bulkheads fit together, and how can retries make an outage worse?
questions.a: Timeouts bound how long a caller waits so a slow dependency cannot hold threads forever; set them from the dependency latency distribution and the caller overall deadline. Retries recover from transient errors but must be limited, use exponential backoff with jitter, apply only to idempotent operations or those with idempotency keys, and respect a retry budget. A circuit breaker watches the error or latency rate and opens to fail fast, then half-opens to probe recovery, which protects the dependency and the caller. Bulkheads isolate resources, such as separate thread or connection pools per dependency, so one failing downstream cannot exhaust capacity for others. Retries amplify load: if three layers each retry three times, one request becomes up to 27, creating a retry storm against an already struggling service. Propagate deadlines and retry at one layer only.

points.title: Reasoning
items: These patterns are layered defenses and each one can backfire if used alone. Unbounded or synchronized retries are a classic cause of cascading failure.

points.title: Flow
items: Caller → Timeout → Retry with Backoff → Circuit Breaker → Bulkhead Pool → Dependency

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Aggressive timeouts fail fast but can cut off slow successful requests
Circuit breakers protect systems but can reject valid traffic when tuned badly
Bulkheads cost spare capacity

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you choose a retry budget?
What fallback would you return when the breaker is open?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Retrying non-idempotent calls without a key
Using fixed-interval retries from many clients at once
Retrying at every layer of the stack

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains retry amplification
Mentions jitter, budgets and deadlines
Describes isolation per dependency

questions.q: What is backpressure and how would you apply it in a pipeline where a fast producer feeds a slow consumer?
questions.a: Backpressure is a signal from a slower stage to upstream stages to slow down or stop, so queues do not grow without bound and exhaust memory or add unbounded latency. Options are bounded queues with blocking or rejecting producers, pull-based consumption where the consumer asks for work, credit or window based flow control, and load shedding that drops or degrades low-priority work. In HTTP systems, return 429 or 503 with Retry-After and let clients back off. With a message broker, cap consumer prefetch, scale consumers on queue lag, and set queue length and message TTL limits. Decide per workload whether dropping, delaying or failing is acceptable, and expose queue depth and age as primary alerts. The goal is controlled degradation instead of collapse.

points.title: Reasoning
items: An unbounded buffer hides overload until it fails catastrophically and adds latency before it does. Bounded buffers and explicit overload responses make failure predictable.

points.title: Flow
items: Producer → Bounded Queue → Consumer → Lag Signal → Autoscaler

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Blocking producers keeps data but pushes latency upstream
Dropping protects the system but loses work
Autoscaling helps only if downstream dependencies can also scale

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you decide what to shed first?
How does a dead-letter queue relate to backpressure?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using an unbounded in-memory queue
Scaling consumers without checking the database they write to
Alerting on CPU instead of queue age

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Names bounded queues and pull or credit based flow control
Distinguishes shed, delay and fail
Monitors lag and age

questions.q: Compare fixed window, sliding window, token bucket and leaky bucket rate limiting, and explain how you would make it work across many servers.
questions.a: Fixed window counts requests per interval and is cheap but allows a burst of double the limit at window boundaries. Sliding window log is accurate but stores per-request timestamps; sliding window counter approximates it using the current and previous window weights. Token bucket refills tokens at a steady rate up to a capacity, allowing controlled bursts, and is the common default. Leaky bucket smooths output to a constant rate, good for protecting a downstream. For many servers, keep counters in a shared fast store such as Redis keyed by client and rule, using atomic operations or a Lua script so check and update are one step. To reduce latency and load, use local token pre-allocation or approximate counting with periodic sync. Decide fail-open versus fail-closed when the limiter store is down, and return 429 with Retry-After and rate headers.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Algorithm choice depends on whether bursts are acceptable and how exact the limit needs to be. Distribution adds atomicity, latency and failure-mode decisions.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Gateway → Limiter Check → Shared Counter Store → Service

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Exact global limits cost a network hop per request
Local approximate limits are fast but may overshoot
Fail-open protects availability but risks overload

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you rate limit per user, per IP and per API key together?
How do you handle a hot key in the limiter store?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Read then write counters without atomicity
Ignoring clock and boundary effects of fixed windows
Having no policy for limiter outage
