Defines failure mode and client signaling

questions.q: How do you define and design for RPO and RTO, and how do you choose between backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby and active-active?
questions.a: RPO is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time; RTO is how long you can be down. Start from business impact per service, since not everything needs the same tier. Backup and restore is cheapest with the highest RTO and RPO; pilot light keeps data replicated and a minimal core ready to scale up; warm standby runs a scaled-down full stack that can take traffic quickly; active-active serves from multiple regions and has near-zero RTO but the hardest data consistency. Replication method sets RPO: asynchronous replication gives a small but nonzero RPO, synchronous gives zero but adds latency. Automate failover and rehearse it with game days, since untested DR is a hope, not a plan. Also cover data corruption and human error with point-in-time recovery and immutable backups, because replication copies mistakes too.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The tier should be set by the cost of downtime versus the cost of redundancy, per service. Many DR failures come from untested runbooks and from replicating bad data.

points.title: Flow
items: Primary Region → Replication → Standby Region → Failover Automation → Traffic Switch

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Lower RTO and RPO cost more infrastructure and complexity
Synchronous replication reduces data loss but increases latency
Automatic failover is fast but can trigger on false positives

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you prevent failback from causing a second outage?
How do you test DR without risking production?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Setting one RTO and RPO for the whole company
Never restoring a backup to prove it works
Forgetting dependencies like DNS, secrets and third parties

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Derives targets from business impact
Maps tiers to cost and consistency
Includes testing and corruption recovery

questions.q: You need to serve users from multiple regions with low latency and survive a region loss. Compare active-passive and active-active, and explain how data would be handled.
questions.a: Active-passive serves all writes from one region and replicates to others; it is simpler, with strong consistency at the primary and failover when it dies, but remote users pay latency for writes and failover has RPO exposure with async replication. Active-active serves traffic from every region, so users hit the nearest one and a region loss only shifts traffic, but data placement becomes the central problem. Options are to partition data by home region (each user or tenant owned by one region, with others forwarding or reading replicas), use a globally consistent database that pays cross-region commit latency, or use multi-leader with conflict resolution for data that tolerates it. Route with latency-based DNS or anycast and health checks, keep per-region capacity able to absorb a failed neighbor, and keep global control-plane dependencies minimal. Start with read-local, write-to-home and move to broader active-active only where the product needs it.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Stateless tiers are easy to run in many regions; state is the hard part. Home-region ownership avoids most conflicts without global coordination.

points.title: Flow
items: Global DNS → Regional Edge → Regional Services → Home Region DB → Cross-Region Replication

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Active-active improves latency and availability but raises data and operational complexity
Global strong consistency adds cross-region latency to writes
Spare capacity per region costs money but makes failover safe

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a user who travels to another region?
What do you do about global unique constraints such as usernames?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Going active-active without a data ownership model
Not sizing remaining regions for failover load
Hidden single-region dependencies such as a global auth database

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Addresses data placement explicitly
Plans capacity for region loss
Finds shared dependencies that break independence

questions.q: Describe how you do capacity planning for a new service from product estimates, showing the arithmetic.
questions.a: Start with assumptions and label them as assumptions: for example 5M daily active users, 10 requests per user per day gives 50M requests per day, divided by 86,400 seconds is about 580 requests per second average. Apply a peak factor, say 3 to 5 times for daily and event peaks, giving roughly 1,700 to 2,900 rps peak. Estimate payload sizes to get bandwidth and storage: 1 KB per record times 5M new records per day is about 5 GB per day, so about 1.8 TB per year before replication and indexes. Divide peak rps by measured per-instance throughput from a load test, then add headroom for failures and deploys (for example N plus 1 or N plus 2 per zone). Size databases by read and write rates and working set versus memory, not just disk. Revisit with real traffic and load test results, and set autoscaling and alerts on saturation signals.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Numbers are only credible when assumptions are explicit and the derivation is visible. Measured per-node throughput replaces guesses as soon as a load test exists.

points.title: Flow
items: Traffic Estimate → Peak Factor → Per-Node Throughput → Headroom → Fleet Size

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More headroom lowers risk but raises cost
Planning for rare peaks versus using autoscaling and load shedding
Over-precise estimates create false confidence

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does the estimate change for a read-heavy versus write-heavy service?
How do you validate the estimate before launch?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using average rps instead of peak
Ignoring replication, index and overhead in storage
Presenting guesses as measured facts

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Shows arithmetic with stated assumptions
Uses peak factors and headroom
Plans validation with load tests

questions.q: A single key or partition is receiving a disproportionate share of traffic (hot key). How do you detect and mitigate it?
questions.a: Detect with per-key or per-partition request and latency metrics, top-k sketches, and alerts on skew between partitions. Mitigations depend on read versus write. For hot reads, add a local in-process cache with short TTL, a replicated cache tier, or replicate the hot item across several keys and read from a random copy. For hot writes, split the key into N sub-keys (for example counter shards) and aggregate on read or asynchronously, or batch and coalesce writes before hitting the store. Revisit the partition key so load spreads, for example add a salt or composite key, while accepting that range queries get harder. Use request coalescing to collapse identical concurrent requests, and rate limit abusive callers. Plan for celebrity or flash-sale cases explicitly instead of treating them as rare.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Hashing spreads keys, not load, so skewed popularity defeats it. The fix is to make the hot item itself divisible or cacheable.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Local Cache → Replicated Cache → Key Salt Router → Sharded Store

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Replicating a hot key adds invalidation complexity
Sharded counters make reads costlier
Local caches are fast but can serve stale data

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep a salted key queryable?
How would you prevent a cache stampede on a hot item expiry?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Adding more nodes while the load stays on one partition
Using a low-cardinality partition key such as country
Not monitoring skew

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Distinguishes hot read from hot write fixes
Mentions key splitting or replication
Detects with per-key metrics

questions.q: Your p50 latency is fine but p99 is terrible. How do you reason about and reduce tail latency in a fan-out architecture?
questions.a: In fan-out, a request waits for the slowest of many calls, so even a rare slow response becomes common: if each of 100 calls has a 1 percent chance of being slow, about 63 percent of requests hit at least one slow call. First measure with distributed tracing and percentile histograms, per dependency, not averages. Common causes are queueing from high utilization, garbage collection pauses, noisy neighbors, cold caches, lock contention and retries. Mitigations include running below high utilization, hedged requests (send a second request after a small delay and take the first answer, only for idempotent reads), request timeouts with partial results or fallbacks, reducing fan-out through caching or pre-aggregation, and isolating slow paths with bulkheads and priority queues. Set latency SLOs on percentiles and treat tail regressions as incidents.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Tail latency is driven by queueing and fan-out math rather than average speed. Fixes reduce the number of calls on the critical path or cap the impact of the slowest one.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Aggregator → Fan-out Calls → Hedged Request → Partial Result

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Hedging reduces tail but adds load
Partial results improve latency but reduce completeness
Lower utilization costs more hardware

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you size hedging delay?
How does autoscaling interact with tail latency?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Optimizing the average and ignoring percentiles
Hedging non-idempotent operations
Averaging percentiles across hosts

points.title: What a good answer shows

Lists concrete mitigations with costs
Uses tracing and histograms to locate causes

questions.q: How do you choose a sharding strategy, and how would you handle resharding without downtime?
questions.a: Pick the shard key from the dominant access pattern so most queries hit one shard, with high cardinality and even distribution. Hash sharding spreads load evenly but makes range scans expensive; range sharding supports range queries but risks hotspots on monotonic keys; directory or lookup based sharding is flexible but the lookup becomes a dependency. Use consistent hashing or many virtual shards (logical partitions mapped to physical nodes) so rebalancing moves small pieces instead of reshuffling everything. To reshard online, create the new topology, dual write or replicate changes, backfill historical data, verify with checksums or shadow reads, then cut over reads and finally writes, keeping rollback possible. Cross-shard queries and transactions should be avoided or handled with scatter-gather and Sagas. Plan the number of logical shards up front, since splitting them later is cheaper than changing the key.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The shard key is the hardest decision to undo. Logical partitions decouple data layout from physical machines so growth is incremental.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Router → Shard Map → Logical Shards → Physical Nodes

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Hash gives even load but poor range queries
Many logical shards add metadata and overhead
Cross-shard joins and transactions are costly

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a tenant that outgrows one shard?
How would you do global secondary indexes?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Choosing a monotonically increasing key as the only shard key
Mapping hash modulo node count so adding a node moves nearly all data
Having no verification step before cutover

questions.q: Explain how you would separate read and write paths (for example with CQRS or read replicas) for a read-heavy system, and what consistency problems appear.
questions.a: Keep a write path that validates and commits changes to the source of truth, and build read paths optimized for queries: read replicas, denormalized tables, search indexes or caches populated from change events. Changes flow through a log or change data capture stream so read models can be rebuilt and scaled independently. CQRS goes further and uses different models for commands and queries. The consequence is replication or projection lag, so a user may not see their own write immediately. Mitigate with read-your-writes routing, returning the written data in the response, or version tokens. Monitor lag, make projections idempotent and rebuildable, and keep the write model authoritative. Use it where read and write shapes or scale differ sharply; for simple CRUD the extra moving parts are not worth it.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Separation lets each side scale and be shaped for its job at the cost of eventual consistency and more components. It should be adopted for a measured read-write asymmetry.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Command API → Primary Store → Change Stream → Read Models → Query API

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Faster, cheaper reads versus stale reads and added complexity
Rebuildable projections add operational work
Denormalization duplicates data that must be kept in sync

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you rebuild a read model from scratch?
How do you deal with out-of-order events?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Applying CQRS to a simple CRUD service
Letting the read model become the source of truth by accident
Ignoring replication lag in user flows

Justifies when not to use it

questions.q: Design a URL shortener that handles 100M new URLs per month and a much higher redirect rate.
questions.a: Requirements: create short link, redirect with low latency, optional custom alias and expiry, high availability for redirects; reads far outnumber writes. 100M per month is about 38 writes per second on average (100M / 2.6M seconds), and a 100 to 1 read ratio implies a few thousand redirects per second, with peak higher. Core components: API service, ID generator, key-value store, cache, CDN or edge for redirects, and an async analytics pipeline. Data model: short_code as primary key mapping to long_url, created_at, expiry, owner. Generate codes using a base62 encoding of a unique counter or ID (range allocation per node avoids a single bottleneck) rather than hashing and resolving collisions, or use random codes with a uniqueness check. The hard problem is serving redirects fast and reliably: cache hot codes, use a read-optimized key-value store partitioned by code, return 301 or 302 deliberately (302 allows analytics and changes), and record clicks asynchronously so the redirect path never depends on analytics.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The system is a read-dominated key-value lookup, so the design is about ID generation without collisions and a very short, cache-friendly redirect path.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → CDN/Edge → Redirect Service → Cache → KV Store → Analytics Queue

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Counter-based IDs are collision-free but guessable unless obfuscated
301 reduces load but hides repeat clicks and makes link changes hard
Strong global uniqueness versus per-node ID ranges

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you prevent abuse and malicious URLs?
How do you expire and reclaim short codes?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Hashing the URL and truncating without handling collisions
Putting analytics writes on the redirect critical path
Using a relational join-heavy schema for a key lookup

questions.q: Design a rate limiting service used by many internal and public APIs.
questions.a: Requirements: enforce limits per user, API key, IP and endpoint, low added latency (single digit milliseconds), accurate enough, configurable rules, and graceful behavior when it fails. Components: rule configuration store with a cache on each node, limiter library or sidecar at the gateway, shared counter store (such as Redis) and a metrics pipeline. Data model: key built from rule id plus identity plus window, with token count and last refill time, updated atomically with a script. Rules are versioned and pushed to gateways so changes do not need deploys. The hard problem is correctness at scale with low latency: use token bucket with atomic updates, shard counters by key, allow slight overshoot with local pre-fetched token batches if needed, and decide fail-open or fail-closed per rule (open for general APIs, closed for abuse-prone endpoints). Return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers, and give operators dashboards to see who is being throttled.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The service sits on every request path, so latency and failure behavior matter as much as the counting algorithm. Atomic updates and a defined failure mode are the key correctness points.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Gateway → Limiter Library → Counter Store → Rules Config → Upstream API

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Central accuracy versus local speed
Fail-open availability versus fail-closed protection
Fine-grained rules increase key cardinality and memory

points.title: Follow-ups

How do you roll out a new limit safely?

items: Non-atomic read-modify-write on counters
No dry-run or shadow mode for new rules
Making the limiter a single point of failure

questions.q: Design a notification system that sends push, SMS and email at scale, with user preferences and no duplicates.
questions.a: Requirements: multiple channels, transactional and marketing types, user preferences and quiet hours, at-least-once delivery without visible duplicates, rate limits per provider, and delivery tracking. Components: notification API, preference and template services, a queue per channel and priority, channel workers calling providers (push gateways, SMS, email), and a status store with webhook receivers for delivery callbacks. Data model: notification (id, user, type, payload, idempotency key), per-channel delivery attempts with status, and user preferences per type and channel. Flow: producer calls API with an idempotency key, the service checks preferences, renders template, enqueues; workers send with retries and backoff, record result, and fall back to another channel when appropriate. The hard problem is reliable delivery without duplicates or floods: idempotency keys, deduplication windows, priority queues so OTPs are not stuck behind a campaign, per-provider rate limits, and a dead-letter queue for permanent failures.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Providers are slow, rate limited and unreliable, so queues, idempotency and prioritization matter more than the send call itself.

points.title: Flow
items: Producer → Notification API → Preferences + Templates → Channel Queues → Workers → Provider

points.title: Trade-offs
items: At-least-once delivery means dedup logic is required
Separate queues cost more but isolate priority and channel failures
Fallback channels improve reach but can annoy users

Sending synchronously from the calling service

questions.q: Design a chat and messaging app supporting 1:1 and group chats, online presence, message history and multi-device sync.
questions.a: Requirements: low-latency delivery, ordering within a conversation, offline delivery, group chats, history, read receipts, multi-device. Components: persistent connection gateways (WebSocket) that map user and device to a gateway node via a presence registry, a chat service, a message store, push notification service for offline users, and a media service with object storage. Data model: messages partitioned by conversation id and ordered by a per-conversation sequence or time-sortable id; a per-user inbox or sync cursor to fetch what a device missed. Send path: client sends with a client-generated id, server assigns sequence, persists, then fans out to online recipients through their gateways and enqueues push for offline ones. The hard problems are ordering, delivery guarantees and group fan-out: use at-least-once delivery with client ack and dedupe by message id, per-conversation ordering via a single writer or sequencer, and for large groups fan out on read or via a queue rather than per-message writes to every member. Handle presence with heartbeats and TTL, and reconnect storms with backoff.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The core challenges are stateful connections, ordering per conversation and reliable offline sync. Sequence numbers and per-device cursors make delivery recoverable.

Per-conversation single writer gives ordering but limits hot-conversation throughput
End-to-end encryption limits server-side features such as search

How would you handle a group with a million members?

No ack and dedupe so reconnects cause duplicates or loss
Storing presence in a durable database with per-heartbeat writes

questions.q: Design a social news feed. How do you handle users who follow millions of accounts or are followed by millions?
questions.a: Requirements: low-latency personalized feed, new posts visible quickly, follow graph, ranking, and scale to celebrity accounts. Components: post service, social graph service, feed generation service, feed cache per user, ranking service and a media CDN. Data model: posts by id and author, follow edges in both directions, and a precomputed feed list of post ids per user. Fan-out on write pushes a new post id to each follower feed, making reads cheap but expensive for authors with huge follower counts; fan-out on read builds the feed at request time by merging recent posts from followed accounts, cheap to write but slow to read. The hybrid is the usual answer: fan-out on write for normal authors, and for celebrity authors merge their posts at read time. Rank a candidate set using lightweight signals, hydrate post bodies from a cache, paginate with cursors, and accept eventual consistency in feed content.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The follower distribution is extremely skewed, so a single strategy fails at one end. A hybrid bounds both write amplification and read cost.

items: Client → Feed API → Feed Cache → Ranker → Post Store → Fan-out Workers

Fan-out on read keeps writes cheap but slows reads
Ranking quality versus latency budget

How would you backfill a new user feed?

questions.q: Design an on-demand video streaming service, focusing on upload, transcoding and playback.
questions.a: Requirements: upload large videos, play smoothly on varied networks and devices, fast start, global reach, cost control. Components: upload service with resumable chunked uploads to object storage, a transcoding pipeline that produces multiple resolutions and bitrates in segmented formats, a metadata service, a CDN for delivery and a player using adaptive bitrate streaming. Data model: video metadata (id, owner, status, renditions, manifest location) in a database, media segments and manifests in object storage. Upload triggers a job queue; workers split the video, transcode in parallel per segment or rendition, generate thumbnails and manifests, then mark the video ready. Playback fetches a manifest and the player picks segments by measured bandwidth, switching quality as conditions change. The hard problem is delivery cost and latency: serve popular content from CDN edge caches, tier or expire cold content, pre-position expected hits, and make transcoding idempotent and retry-safe so a failed worker only repeats a segment.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Bandwidth and storage dominate cost, and the CDN absorbs most traffic. Adaptive bitrate plus segment-level parallel transcoding handle device variety and processing time.

points.title: Flow
items: Uploader → Object Storage → Transcode Queue → Transcode Workers → CDN → Adaptive Player

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More renditions improve compatibility but increase storage and compute
Pre-transcoding all formats versus on-demand for rarely watched videos
Longer segments reduce overhead but slow quality adaptation

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you reduce time to first frame?
How would you protect content with DRM or signed URLs?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Serving video bytes through application servers
One monolithic transcoding job per video with no checkpointing
No resumable upload for large files

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Separates upload, processing and delivery paths
Explains adaptive bitrate
Reasons about CDN and storage cost

questions.q: Design the driver-rider matching and location tracking for a ride-hailing service.
questions.a: Requirements: ingest frequent driver location updates, find nearby available drivers fast, match without double-assigning a driver, track the trip, and handle surges. Components: location ingestion gateway, a geospatial index of available drivers, matching service, trip service, and a pricing service. Data model: driver state (id, location, status, last update) kept in an in-memory geospatial structure partitioned by geohash or similar cell, and durable trip records in a database. Drivers send updates every few seconds into a stream; the index is updated with TTLs so stale drivers drop out. On a request, query nearby cells, rank candidates by ETA and fairness, then offer to the best driver. The hard problem is atomic assignment under concurrency: use a conditional state transition (available to offered to assigned) with a short offer timeout and re-offer, so one driver cannot accept two rides and one rider is not matched twice. Partition by city or region so hot cities scale independently.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Location data is high-volume and short-lived, so it belongs in memory with TTL; the correctness-critical part is the driver and trip state machine.

points.title: Flow
items: Driver App → Location Gateway → Geo Index → Matching Service → Trip Service → Rider App

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Frequent updates improve accuracy but raise ingest cost
Matching the nearest driver versus global batch optimization
In-memory index is fast but needs rebuild after failure

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a dense city cell with thousands of drivers?
What happens if the matching service crashes mid-offer?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Writing every location ping to the main relational database
Computing nearest driver by scanning all drivers
No state machine or timeout for offers

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses a spatial index with partitioning
Guarantees single assignment atomically
Separates ephemeral location from durable trips

questions.q: Design a food delivery platform covering restaurant discovery, ordering, courier dispatch and live status.
questions.a: Requirements: browse nearby restaurants with menus and availability, place and pay for an order, restaurant acceptance, courier assignment, and real-time status. Components: catalog and search service, menu and availability service, cart and order service, payment service, dispatch service, location tracking, and notification service. Data model: restaurants and menus in a read-optimized store with a search index, orders with an explicit state machine (placed, accepted, preparing, ready, picked up, delivered, cancelled) and event history. Order flow: validate cart and price, authorize payment, create the order, notify the restaurant, and on acceptance start dispatch. The hard problem is coordinating three parties with unreliable timing: make state transitions explicit and idempotent, use timeouts (restaurant does not accept, courier not found) with compensation such as cancel and refund, and estimate delivery time from preparation time plus travel using live data. Keep browse paths cached and eventually consistent, while the order path is strongly consistent.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The order is a long-running workflow involving humans with unpredictable response times, so an explicit state machine with timeouts and compensation is the center of the design.

points.title: Flow
items: Customer App → Order Service → Payment → Restaurant App → Dispatch → Courier App

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Assigning couriers early reduces wait but wastes courier time if prep is slow
Cached menus are fast but may show unavailable items
Strong order consistency versus latency on browse

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle an item going out of stock after checkout?
How do you estimate delivery time and keep it honest?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: No timeout for restaurant acceptance
Treating browse and order paths with the same consistency needs
Ignoring cancellation and refund flows

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Models orders as a state machine
Handles multi-party timeouts and compensation
Separates read-heavy discovery from transactional ordering

questions.q: Design the cart and checkout for a grocery quick-commerce app with local store inventory, slots and time-bound promotions.
questions.a: Requirements: fast cart updates, accurate store-level availability, delivery slot selection, promotions and pricing, and a reliable checkout that does not oversell. Components: cart service, catalog and pricing service, store inventory service, promotion engine, slot service, checkout orchestrator and order service. Data model: cart keyed by user with items, quantities and a pricing snapshot version; inventory per store and SKU with available and reserved counts; slot capacity per store and window. Cart operations stay cheap and tolerate stale availability, showing soft warnings. At checkout the orchestrator revalidates prices and promotions, atomically reserves inventory and a slot with a short expiry, creates the order and starts payment; on failure or timeout the reservations are released. The hard problem is consistency at the moment of commitment: browse and cart are eventually consistent and cached, while reserve-and-order is strongly consistent per store-SKU, idempotent via a checkout key, and every price shown must be reconciled before charging.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Accuracy is only required at the commit step, so the system tolerates staleness earlier to stay fast. Reservations with expiry prevent overselling without holding locks across user think time.

points.title: Flow
items: App → Cart Service → Pricing + Promo → Checkout Orchestrator → Inventory + Slot Reserve → Order Service

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Reserving at add-to-cart avoids surprises but locks stock for abandoned carts
Recomputing price at checkout may differ from what the user saw
Per-store inventory accuracy depends on store-side stock updates

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a promotion that expires mid-checkout?
What happens when store stock counts are wrong?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Trusting client-sent prices
Holding database locks during payment
Reserving without an expiry

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Distinguishes soft cart state from hard commit
Uses expiring reservations and idempotency
Revalidates price and availability server-side

questions.q: Payment succeeded but order creation failed. How do you design the order-with-payment flow so this cannot leave a customer charged without an order?
questions.a: Requirements: never lose a captured payment, never create duplicate orders, and recover automatically. Persist an order intent first (status pending payment) with an idempotency key before calling the payment provider, so every later step has a durable anchor. Pass the same key to the provider, and treat the provider webhook or status query as the source of truth for payment outcome rather than the client redirect. When a payment confirmation arrives, an idempotent handler moves the existing order to confirmed; if order creation downstream fails, retry through a queue from the durable intent. A reconciliation job periodically finds payments marked succeeded with no confirmed order and either completes the order or issues a refund after a defined time, and finds orders pending too long to cancel or query the provider. Use the outbox pattern so the state change and the event to fulfilment are committed together. Alert on reconciliation backlog, and give support tools to view the full timeline.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The two systems cannot share a transaction, so the design assumes partial failure and makes it repairable. Durable intent, idempotency and reconciliation turn a dangerous gap into a bounded, self-healing state.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Order Intent → Payment Provider → Webhook Handler → Order Confirm Queue → Reconciliation Job

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Creating the order before payment adds pending orders to clean up
Auto-refund is safe but may disappoint users compared to completing the order
Reconciliation adds latency to recovery but catches every gap

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if the webhook is delivered twice or never?
How do you handle the user retrying the payment button?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Trusting the browser redirect as proof of payment
Creating the order only after payment with no retry path
No reconciliation for missed webhooks

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses durable intent plus idempotency keys
Treats provider status as source of truth
Includes reconciliation and outbox

questions.q: For live order tracking, compare polling, WebSocket and push notifications. What would you use and how does it scale?
questions.a: Polling is simplest and works through any proxy but wastes requests and adds latency equal to the interval; long polling reduces waste. WebSocket (or server-sent events for one-way updates) gives low latency but needs stateful connections, a connection gateway, and reconnect handling. Push notifications reach users when the app is closed but are not guaranteed or instant and suit milestone events only. A good design combines them: the app fetches current order state by API on open, subscribes over WebSocket or SSE while the screen is visible, and relies on push for key milestones in the background. Status changes are published to a topic keyed by order id, gateway nodes subscribe for connected users, and every update carries a version so clients ignore stale ones and fetch state after a reconnect. Courier location is high-frequency and ephemeral, so throttle updates and do not persist every point. Use polling with backoff as the fallback.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Each mechanism has a distinct role: pull for correctness, stream for live view, push for background. Versioned state plus a snapshot fetch on reconnect removes most consistency problems.

points.title: Flow
items: Order Service → Event Bus → Tracking Gateway → WebSocket/SSE → App → Push Fallback

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Streaming gives freshness but costs connection state
Polling is robust but heavier on servers at scale
Push is reliable for reach but not for latency

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you scale 1M concurrent connections?
How do you avoid missing an update during reconnect?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Short fixed-interval polling from every client
No snapshot fetch after reconnect
Persisting every location ping as a business event

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Compares mechanisms with a clear recommendation
Handles reconnect and ordering
Considers scale of connections

questions.q: Design search with autocomplete suggestions for an e-commerce site.
questions.a: Requirements: suggestions within roughly 100 ms of each keystroke, relevant results, typo tolerance, freshness for new products, and high availability. Components: an indexing pipeline fed by catalog change events, a search engine with an inverted index for full queries, a separate suggestion service backed by a prefix structure (trie or edge n-gram index) with popularity scores, and query logging for ranking. Data model: product documents with searchable fields and facets; suggestion entries as phrase, score and category, rebuilt periodically from query logs and catalog. For autocomplete, serve the top-k completions for a prefix from memory or a cache, blend popular queries with product names, and personalize lightly. The hard problem is latency and relevance together: debounce on the client, cache popular prefixes at the edge, precompute top-k per prefix node, and filter blocked or out-of-stock items. Full search uses analyzers, synonyms, fuzzy matching and a ranking function combining text relevance with sales and availability signals.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Autocomplete is a latency-critical prefix lookup that is best separated from full search. Precomputing top-k per prefix trades storage for speed.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Edge Cache → Suggest Service → Prefix Index → Search Engine → Indexing Pipeline

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Precomputed suggestions are fast but can lag trends
Fuzzy matching improves recall but costs latency
Personalization improves relevance but reduces cacheability

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep out-of-stock items out of suggestions?
How do you handle a trending query spike?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running a full wildcard query on every keystroke
No debounce or request cancellation on the client
Using the primary database for search

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Separates suggest from full search
Explains prefix structure and top-k precomputation
Covers indexing freshness and ranking signals

questions.q: Design a ticket booking system with seat selection and locking, expecting a very popular event to sell out in minutes.
questions.a: Requirements: never sell the same seat twice, hold seats briefly during payment, survive a surge, and be fair. Components: event and seat inventory service, a hold service, booking and payment service, a virtual waiting room and a notification service. Data model: seat rows with status (available, held, sold), hold owner and hold expiry; bookings referencing seats. Selecting a seat performs an atomic conditional update from available to held with an expiry (compare-and-set or a row lock), returning failure if someone else got it; payment success converts held to sold; a sweeper or TTL releases expired holds. The hard problem is the surge: place users in a waiting room queue and admit them at a rate the backend can serve, keep seat availability reads cached and approximate while the hold itself is strongly consistent, and partition inventory by event so one event does not take down others. Make booking idempotent, and show clear feedback when a seat is lost.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Correctness lives in one atomic transition per seat, and the surge is handled by admission control rather than by making the database faster. Expiring holds prevent abandoned sessions from blocking inventory.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → Waiting Room → Seat Service → Hold with TTL → Payment → Booking Store

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Longer holds help users pay but reduce inventory turnover
A waiting room adds friction but protects the system
Cached availability may show seats that are gone

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if payment completes after the hold expired?
How do you stop bots from grabbing seats?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Check-then-update without atomicity
Holding seats without an expiry
Letting all users hit the seat service at once

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses atomic hold with expiry
Designs admission control for surges
Handles the payment-after-expiry edge

questions.q: Design a payment gateway that merchants call to charge cards, with high correctness requirements.
questions.a: Requirements: authorize, capture, refund and void; never double charge; durable and auditable; high availability; strict security boundaries. Components: public API with idempotency keys, a payment service owning the state machine, a ledger, connectors to card networks or acquirers, a tokenization vault isolated from the rest of the system, a webhook dispatcher, and a reconciliation service. Data model: payments with explicit states (created, authorized, captured, failed, refunded), an append-only double-entry ledger, and an idempotency table keyed by merchant and key. Every state transition is persisted before and after the external call, so a crash leaves a recoverable record; unknown outcomes (timeouts) are resolved by querying the acquirer, never by blindly retrying a charge. The hard problem is exactly-once effect over an unreliable network: idempotency keys on the API, deterministic request ids toward acquirers, outbox for webhooks to merchants, and daily reconciliation against settlement files to catch discrepancies. Keep card data in a minimal, audited scope.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Money movement demands an auditable state machine and a ledger that is never edited, only appended. Unknown outcomes must be resolved by asking the other side, not by guessing.

points.title: Flow
items: Merchant API → Idempotency Layer → Payment State Machine → Acquirer Connector → Ledger → Webhook + Reconciliation

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Strong consistency and audit trails cost throughput and latency
Multiple acquirers improve availability but increase integration complexity
Isolating card data reduces risk but adds hops

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a timeout after sending an authorization?
How would you fail over between acquirers safely?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Retrying charge calls without idempotency
Updating balances in place instead of an append-only ledger
Logging sensitive card data

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explicit state machine with idempotency
Handles unknown outcomes and reconciliation
Separates sensitive data scope

questions.q: Design a live streaming platform where a broadcaster streams to hundreds of thousands of viewers with low delay and live chat.
questions.a: Requirements: ingest a live stream, deliver with a few seconds of delay or less, scale to many viewers, adaptive quality, live chat, and recording for replay. Components: ingest servers accepting the broadcaster stream, a real-time transcoder producing multiple renditions, a packager creating short segments and manifests, a CDN for fan-out, a chat service and a recording pipeline to object storage. Data model: stream metadata and state, chat messages in a time-ordered store, and segments with rolling manifests. Unlike on-demand video, transcoding and packaging run continuously, so the pipeline must be low latency and redundant. The hard problem is the latency versus scale tradeoff: shorter segments and low-latency chunked delivery reduce delay but cut cache efficiency and raise request rates; use CDN origin shielding so a viral stream does not overload the origin. Chat needs fan-out via WebSocket gateways with rate limiting and sampling for huge rooms, and ingest needs redundancy so a single encoder failure does not end the stream.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Live content cannot be pre-processed, so every stage is real-time and delay compounds across stages. The CDN carries viewer scale while the origin and transcoders are protected.

points.title: Flow
items: Broadcaster → Ingest → Live Transcoder → Packager → Origin Shield + CDN → Viewer Player

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Lower latency reduces cache efficiency and resilience to network jitter
More renditions improve playback but increase real-time compute
Showing every chat message is impractical in huge rooms

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle ingest failure mid-stream?
How do you keep chat usable with 500,000 viewers?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Serving viewers directly from the transcoder
Treating live like on-demand with batch transcoding
No origin shielding for a viral stream

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Describes the real-time pipeline stages
Explains latency versus scale tradeoff
Protects the origin with CDN layers

questions.q: Design a distributed cache cluster. How do you partition, replicate, evict and keep it consistent with the database?
questions.a: Requirements: sub-millisecond to low-millisecond reads, horizontal scaling, high hit rate, tolerance for node loss. Components: cache nodes holding data in memory, a client library or proxy that routes by key using consistent hashing, optional replicas per partition, and a metrics and admin plane. Data model: key to value with TTL and metadata, evicted using LRU or LFU when memory is full. Partition with consistent hashing and virtual nodes so adding or removing nodes moves a small fraction of keys; replicate hot or critical partitions to survive node failure, accepting that a cache can also simply refill from the source. Use cache-aside: read from cache, on miss load from the database and populate; on writes update the database then invalidate (or update) the cache. The hard problems are invalidation and stampedes: set TTLs as a safety net, use request coalescing or locks so a hot key expiry does not send thousands of requests to the database, add jitter to TTLs, and avoid caching errors.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A cache is a performance layer, not a source of truth, so the design focuses on routing, refill behavior and bounded staleness. Most production incidents come from stampedes and invalidation races.

points.title: Flow
items: App → Cache Client → Consistent Hash Ring → Cache Nodes → Database

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Write-through keeps cache fresh but adds write latency
Cache-aside is simple but allows stale reads and races
Replication improves availability but costs memory

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you avoid a thundering herd after a node restart?
What race can occur between a read refill and an invalidation?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Hash modulo node count so scaling remaps most keys
No TTL, relying only on explicit invalidation
Treating the cache as durable

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses consistent hashing and eviction policy
Explains cache-aside and invalidation
Addresses stampede and node failure

questions.q: Design a distributed job scheduler that runs millions of delayed and recurring jobs reliably.
questions.a: Requirements: run jobs at or after a time, recurring schedules, at-least-once execution, retries, priorities, observability, and horizontal scale. Components: scheduling API, a job store partitioned by time and tenant, a trigger service that finds due jobs, a queue to dispatch to workers, worker fleet and a status and retry manager. Data model: job (id, schedule or run_at, payload, status, attempts, next_run_time, lease owner and expiry) with an index on next_run_time per partition. Triggers poll the due range per partition, claim jobs with a lease using a conditional update, and enqueue them; workers execute and ack, and a lease timeout returns unacked jobs for retry. The hard problem is running each job at least once without a single bottleneck and without duplicates causing damage: partition the time index so many triggers work in parallel, make execution idempotent with a job-run id, use leases to detect dead workers, and apply exponential backoff with a retry limit and dead-letter handling. For recurring jobs, compute the next run when the current one starts or ends, deciding explicitly how to handle missed runs.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The scheduler is a time-indexed store plus a lease-based claim mechanism. Duplicates are unavoidable under failure, so jobs must be idempotent and the platform must make that easy.

points.title: Flow
items: Scheduler API → Job Store → Trigger Service → Dispatch Queue → Workers → Retry + DLQ

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Polling is simple but adds latency; timer wheels are precise but need memory and recovery
At-least-once is safe for most jobs but requires idempotency
Long leases reduce duplicates but slow dead-worker recovery

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a job that runs longer than its lease?
What should happen to missed runs after downtime?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: One global scanner for all jobs
Assuming exactly-once execution
No limit on retries or visibility for stuck jobs

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Partitions due-job discovery
Uses leases and idempotency
Defines retry, DLQ and missed-run policy

questions.q: Design a metrics and monitoring system that ingests millions of data points per second and supports dashboards and alerting.
questions.a: Requirements: high write throughput, fast range queries and aggregations, retention tiers, alerting with low delay, and protection from label explosion. Components: agents or SDKs that batch and send metrics, ingestion gateways, a stream or queue for buffering, a time-series store sharded by series and time, a query engine with downsampling, and an alert evaluator. Data model: series identified by metric name plus label set, with points of timestamp and value stored in compressed time-ordered blocks. Writes are append-only and batched; data is rolled up into coarser resolutions as it ages to cut cost. The hard problems are cardinality and query cost: every unique label combination is a new series, so enforce limits on label cardinality and avoid unbounded values like user ids. Alert evaluation runs on a schedule against recent data with duplicate-suppression and a path that stays up even when dashboards are overloaded. Use replication for durability and isolate tenants so one noisy team cannot degrade others.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Time-series workloads are append-heavy and read by time range, so storage is organized by series and time with compression and rollups. Cardinality is the main scalability risk and must be policed.

points.title: Flow
items: Agents → Ingest Gateway → Buffer Stream → Time-Series Store → Query Engine → Alert Evaluator

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Downsampling saves storage but loses fine detail
Push versus pull collection affects discovery and firewalling
Strict cardinality limits protect the system but constrain users

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you make alerting more reliable than the dashboards?
How do you query across months of data quickly?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using high-cardinality labels such as request id
Storing raw points forever at full resolution
Alerting through the same overloaded query path

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains series model and compression
Addresses cardinality and rollups
Isolates alerting path and tenants

questions.q: Design inventory reservation for an e-commerce platform so that stock is never oversold but carts and checkouts stay fast.
questions.a: Requirements: accurate available-to-sell counts, no overselling under concurrency, short holds during checkout, release on failure or timeout, and fast reads on product pages. Components: inventory service as the owner of counts, reservation records with TTL, order service, a stream of inventory events, and cached availability for browsing. Data model: per SKU and location, on_hand, reserved and available (on_hand minus reserved), and reservation rows (id, order, sku, qty, expires_at, status). Reserve with an atomic conditional update that decrements available only if enough remains; confirm converts the reservation into a committed deduction after payment, and a sweeper releases expired reservations. The hard problem is contention on popular SKUs and correct release: shard counts for hot items into buckets, make reserve and release idempotent by reservation id, and reconcile periodically against physical counts. Product pages read cached, slightly stale availability, with the strict check happening at reservation time.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The correctness boundary is a single atomic decrement per SKU, and everything else tolerates staleness. Expiring reservations ensure abandoned checkouts do not permanently remove stock.

points.title: Flow
items: Order Service → Reserve API → Inventory Store → Reservation TTL → Commit on Payment → Availability Cache

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Reserving earlier prevents disappointment but ties up stock
Sharded counters reduce contention but complicate exact totals
Allowing slight overselling with backorders can be a business choice

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle returns and cancellations?
What if the reservation sweeper is down?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Read stock then write without atomic condition
Reservations with no expiry
Making product page reads hit the strict inventory path

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses atomic conditional decrement
Handles expiry and idempotent release
Separates browse reads from commit path

questions.q: Design a flash sale where 1 million users compete for 10,000 units at a fixed start time.
questions.a: Requirements: protect the system from a sudden spike, never oversell, be fair, and fail gracefully for those who miss out. Components: CDN-served static sale page, a virtual waiting room or token-based admission, a rate-limited purchase API, an in-memory stock counter, an async order pipeline and payment flow. Data model: a pre-loaded stock counter in a fast store, reservation or order intents, and final orders in the database. Strategy: serve everything static from the edge, let users into a queue with random or first-come ordering, and admit only a controlled number into the purchase path. Decrement stock atomically in memory (for example a script that checks and decrements), return success only if the decrement worked, and push the order to a queue for durable creation; unpaid reservations expire and stock is returned. The hard problem is the thundering herd on one counter and bot traffic: shard the counter across buckets, enforce per-user limits, use captchas or proof of work, and reject early and cheaply once sold out with a cached sold-out flag.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Most requests must be rejected at the cheapest possible layer, so admission control and an in-memory atomic counter shield the database. The durable order pipeline runs asynchronously at its own pace.

points.title: Flow
items: CDN → Waiting Room → Purchase API → Atomic Stock Counter → Order Queue → Order DB

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Fairness via queue versus raw speed
In-memory counter is fast but needs durable reconciliation
Asynchronous order creation gives instant answers but delayed confirmation

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if the in-memory counter node crashes?
How do you stop bots and duplicate accounts?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Sending the full spike to the relational database
No early sold-out short circuit
Allowing unlimited quantity per user

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses admission control and edge caching
Atomic stock with durable reconciliation
Plans for bots and failure recovery

questions.q: You own a large monolith and the org wants microservices. How do you decide whether and how to migrate?
questions.a: First clarify the problem: slow delivery, scaling hot spots, team contention, reliability or technology limits. If a modular monolith with better boundaries, build times and deploy tooling would fix it, do that, since microservices add network failure, distributed data and operational overhead. If you proceed, extract incrementally using the strangler pattern: put a routing layer in front, carve out a bounded context with clear data ownership, move it behind an API, and route traffic gradually with the ability to roll back. Prioritize modules by business value and independence: those with different scaling or change rates, or owned by a dedicated team. Treat shared database tables as the hardest part: define ownership, use change events or anti-corruption layers during transition, and avoid distributed transactions by redesigning flows as Sagas. Invest early in observability, CI/CD, contract testing and on-call before splitting, and measure outcomes such as lead time and incident rate, not number of services.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Microservices are an organizational and operational tradeoff, not an upgrade. The migration succeeds when it is incremental, reversible and driven by a specific problem.

points.title: Flow
items: Monolith → Routing Layer → Extracted Service → Own Data Store → Event Sync → Observability

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Team autonomy and independent scaling versus distributed-system complexity
Big-bang rewrite risk versus long period of dual maintenance
Shared database speed versus clear ownership

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you decide service boundaries?
When would you merge services back together?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Splitting by technical layer instead of business capability
Keeping a shared database across services
Starting the migration with no observability or deployment automation

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Starts from the problem and alternatives
Plans incremental, reversible extraction
Handles data ownership and success metrics

questions.q: How do you decide between building a component in-house and buying or adopting a managed service or open-source product?
questions.a: Start with whether the capability is a differentiator for the business: build what is core and differentiating, buy or adopt what is commodity. Compare total cost of ownership, not license price: engineering time to build, operate, secure and upgrade, on-call load, hiring, and the opportunity cost of what the team would not build instead. Evaluate fit against hard requirements (scale, latency, compliance, data residency), vendor risk (lock-in, pricing changes, roadmap, support, exit path) and integration effort. Run a time-boxed proof of concept against the real workload, and define an exit strategy such as keeping a thin abstraction at the boundary where switching would be plausible. Write down the decision, the assumptions, and the triggers that would make you revisit it, for example cost crossing a threshold or a requirement the vendor cannot meet. Be honest that building usually costs more over time than the initial estimate suggests.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The right answer depends on strategic value and long-term operating cost. Documenting assumptions and revisit triggers makes the decision reversible instead of dogmatic.

points.title: Flow
items: Requirements → Core vs Commodity → TCO + Risk → Proof of Concept → Decision Record → Revisit Triggers

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Building gives control but permanent maintenance cost
Buying speeds delivery but adds lock-in and cost growth
Open source is flexible but you own operations and upgrades

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you reduce lock-in without over-engineering?
When does it make sense to replace a vendor with an in-house system?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Building because the technology is interesting

questions.q: How would you roll out a major change (for example a new storage backend or service version) across multiple regions safely?
questions.a: Treat regions as blast-radius boundaries and roll out progressively: dev and staging, then a small canary in one low-risk region, then wider regions in waves, with automated health gates between steps based on SLO signals (error rate, latency, saturation) and business metrics. Use feature flags to separate deploy from release, so code ships dark and exposure ramps by percentage or cohort and can be turned off without a redeploy. For data changes use expand and contract: add the new structure, dual write, backfill, verify with shadow reads and comparisons, shift reads, then retire the old path later. Keep rollbacks cheap and tested, and avoid changes that cannot be rolled back without a plan for how to roll forward. Avoid rolling out to all regions at once even when it looks safe, and avoid changing code and data format in the same step. Communicate with a runbook, an owner on call for each wave, and clear abort criteria.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The aim is to find problems when they affect a small share of users. Progressive exposure with automated gates and fast rollback limits blast radius.

points.title: Flow
items: Staging → Canary Region → Health Gate → Wave Rollout → Feature Flag Ramp → Rollback Path

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Slower rollouts reduce risk but delay value
Dual writing allows safe migration but adds temporary complexity
Feature flags add code paths that need cleanup

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What would make you stop a rollout?
How do you handle a change that cannot be rolled back?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Deploying to all regions simultaneously
Health gates based only on host metrics, not user impact
Never cleaning up flags and old code paths

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses progressive delivery with automated gates
Separates deploy from release
Plans reversible data migration

questions.q: During a major incident you must choose between rolling back, a forward fix, or degrading features. How do you decide, and what do you do afterward?
questions.a: First priority is to stop user harm, not to find the root cause. If a recent change correlates with the impact and rollback is safe and tested, roll back, because it is the fastest known-good state. A forward fix is justified when rollback is impossible or riskier (for example an irreversible data migration), and only when the fix is small and understood. Degrading features or shedding load is the right move when the cause is overload or a failing dependency: disable non-critical features, serve cached or static content, and protect the core user journey. Assign an incident commander, a communications lead and investigators so decisions are not made in a crowd; communicate status on a regular cadence. Capture timeline and evidence while it is fresh. Afterwards run a blameless review focused on contributing factors and system gaps, and track concrete actions such as detection, rollout safeguards and runbooks with owners and dates.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Mitigation comes before diagnosis. The safest action is usually the one with the best-known outcome and the smallest blast radius.

points.title: Flow
items: Detect → Declare + Roles → Mitigate → Communicate → Resolve → Blameless Review

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Rollback is fast but may discard fixes or be impossible after migrations
Forward fix may be cleaner but risks making things worse
Degradation protects the core but reduces functionality

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you decide when to declare an incident?
How do you keep postmortem actions from being ignored?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Debugging root cause while users are still impacted
No single incident commander
Postmortems that assign blame or produce no owned actions

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Prioritizes mitigation over diagnosis
Chooses by risk and reversibility
Describes roles, communication and follow-up

questions.q: Leadership asks you to cut infrastructure cost by 30 percent without hurting reliability. How do you approach it?
questions.a: Begin with data: break down spend by service, team and resource type, and find the biggest line items and waste, such as idle or oversized instances, unused storage, excessive log and metric retention, cross-zone and egress traffic, and non-production environments running all day. Take the safe wins first: rightsizing, autoscaling, scheduled shutdown of non-production, storage tiering and lifecycle policies, commitment discounts for steady baseline, and cache or compression to cut data transfer. Then examine architecture-level changes with explicit reliability impact, such as reducing redundancy for low-tier services, consolidating clusters, or changing replication factors, using service tiers and SLOs to decide where reliability headroom can be traded. Measure reliability before and after with the same SLIs, and set guardrails so savings that burn error budget are reverted. Make cost visible through tagging and per-team reporting so savings persist, and be clear that some reliability investments are worth more than the saving.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Cost and reliability are tradeoffs per service tier, and SLOs provide the language to make them explicit. Waste removal comes first because it does not trade reliability at all.

points.title: Flow
items: Cost Breakdown → Waste Removal → Rightsizing + Commitments → Tier-Based Tradeoffs → SLO Guardrails → Cost Reporting

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Less redundancy saves money but raises outage risk
Commitment discounts lower unit cost but reduce flexibility
Aggressive rightsizing leaves less headroom for spikes

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which services would you not touch and why?
How do you stop costs creeping back?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Cutting redundancy first without measuring impact
Optimizing small items while ignoring the largest
No ownership or reporting so costs return

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Starts from measurement
Orders actions by risk
Uses SLOs to bound reliability tradeoffs

questions.q: How do you deprecate a widely used API without breaking consumers or stalling the roadmap?
questions.a: Define why and for whom: understand consumers through usage metrics and logs (who calls it, how often, which fields) so you know the real blast radius. Provide a replacement first with a migration guide, tooling or an adapter, because deprecation without an alternative just creates anger. Announce a timeline with clear stages: deprecation notice with headers and documentation, warnings in responses and dashboards, brownouts (short planned failures) to flush out unknown callers, and finally removal. Contact top consumers directly and offer help; for external consumers keep the timeline long and honor commitments. Track the remaining traffic per consumer and make the sunset date a decision with named owners, allowing a time-boxed exception process. Keep the old path minimal and frozen, versioned, and make removal reversible for a short period by keeping the code behind a flag. Do not extend the date repeatedly without a reason, since that teaches consumers to ignore it.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Deprecation is a migration project with a communications component. Usage data, a ready replacement and staged enforcement turn a surprise break into a managed change.

points.title: Flow
items: Usage Analysis → Replacement API → Deprecation Notice → Brownouts → Consumer Migration → Removal

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Long timelines protect consumers but prolong maintenance
Brownouts find hidden callers but cause controlled breakage
Adapters ease migration but extend the life of old behavior

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a consumer who will not migrate?
How do you version APIs to make future deprecations easier?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Announcing removal without a replacement
No visibility into who is still calling
Repeatedly moving the date so it is never taken seriously

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses usage data to find consumers
Provides staged enforcement and migration help
Holds the timeline with an exception process

questions.q: How do you set meaningful SLIs, SLOs and error budgets for a service, and how do you use them to make decisions?
questions.a: Start from user journeys: choose a few SLIs that reflect what users feel, such as the proportion of successful requests, latency at a percentile for key endpoints, and freshness or correctness where relevant, measured at the edge or client rather than only inside the service. Set SLOs from user expectations, historical performance and cost, not from aspiration; 99.9 percent allows about 43 minutes of downtime in a 30-day month, and each extra nine costs far more. The error budget is one minus the SLO; when budget remains, ship features and take risks, and when it is burning fast, slow releases and prioritize reliability work. Alert on budget burn rate over multiple windows rather than on raw thresholds so alerts are tied to user impact. Review SLOs periodically with product, keep them few, and differentiate tiers so critical paths get tighter targets than internal tools. Dependencies count: your SLO cannot exceed the combined reliability of what you depend on without fallbacks.

points.title: Reasoning
items: SLOs convert reliability into an explicit, shared tradeoff with product velocity. Good SLIs reflect user experience and burn-rate alerts focus attention on real impact.

points.title: Flow
items: User Journey → SLI → SLO Target → Error Budget → Burn-Rate Alert → Release Policy

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Tighter SLOs improve reliability but slow delivery and raise cost
Client-side measurement is truthful but harder to collect
Too many SLOs dilute attention

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you do when the error budget is exhausted?
How do you set an SLO for a service with unreliable dependencies?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using server CPU or uptime as the SLI
Setting 100 percent targets
Alerting on every blip instead of burn rate

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Chooses user-centric SLIs
Links error budget to decisions
Understands dependency limits and cost per nine

questions.q: How do you implement idempotency for a write API such as create-payment or create-order, and what edge cases matter?
questions.a: The client sends a unique idempotency key with each logical operation, reusing the same key on retries. The server stores the key with a request fingerprint and the result in a table with a unique constraint on the key (scoped per client), and the check and the business write happen in the same transaction so a crash cannot leave one without the other. On a duplicate key with the same fingerprint, return the stored response; with a different fingerprint, reject as a conflict. For requests still in progress, return a conflict or wait, using a status column to mark in-flight versus completed. Expire keys after a window that covers realistic retry periods. When the operation calls an external system, pass a derived idempotency key downstream so retries do not repeat the side effect. Natural idempotency (PUT of full state, unique business keys) is better where possible than bolting on keys.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Networks make retries inevitable, so safe retries must be designed in. The atomicity between the key record and the write is what makes the guarantee real.

points.title: Flow
items: Client → API → Idempotency Table → Business Transaction → Stored Response

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Keys add storage and a lookup on every write
Long retention is safer but costs more
Wait-or-reject choice for in-flight duplicates affects latency

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if the same key is reused with a different body?
How do you make an event consumer idempotent?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Checking the key and writing in separate non-atomic steps
Generating a new key on each retry
Not passing a derived key to downstream providers

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains key plus atomic storage
Handles in-flight and mismatched duplicates
Extends idempotency to downstream calls

questions.q: What is the dual-write problem and how does the transactional outbox pattern solve it?
questions.a: A service that updates its database and then publishes an event to a broker cannot make both atomic: if it crashes between them, the database changes but no event is sent, or the reverse, leaving downstream systems inconsistent. The outbox pattern writes the business change and an event row to an outbox table in the same local database transaction. A separate relay, either a poller or change data capture tailing the database log, reads unpublished outbox rows and publishes them to the broker, marking them sent. Delivery is at-least-once, since the relay may publish and crash before marking, so consumers must be idempotent or deduplicate by event id. Keep ordering per aggregate by partitioning on the entity key, clean up old rows, and monitor outbox lag. It avoids distributed transactions while keeping state and events consistent.

points.title: Reasoning
items: It converts an impossible cross-system atomic write into one local transaction plus reliable asynchronous delivery. The price is duplicates and slight delay, both handled by idempotent consumers.

points.title: Flow
items: Service → DB Transaction → Outbox Table → Relay / CDC → Broker → Idempotent Consumer

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Extra table and relay to operate
Polling is simple but adds latency; CDC is faster but adds infrastructure
At-least-once delivery requires consumer deduplication

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep event order per entity?
How is this different from publishing inside the transaction?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Publishing to the broker inside the database transaction and assuming atomicity
Consumers that are not idempotent
Never pruning the outbox table

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains the failure window clearly
Describes relay and at-least-once semantics
Includes idempotent consumers and ordering

questions.q: Explain consistent hashing and how it is used for load balancing and partitioning, including virtual nodes and what it does not solve.
questions.a: Consistent hashing maps both keys and nodes onto a hash ring; a key belongs to the first node clockwise from its position. When a node is added or removed only the keys in its adjacent range move, roughly 1 over N of the data, unlike modulo hashing where nearly everything remaps. Virtual nodes place each physical node at many points on the ring, which evens out load, and lets you weight stronger machines more. For replication, store a key on the next several distinct nodes along the ring. It is used for cache clusters, partitioned databases and sticky load balancing. It does not solve hot keys, because one popular key still lands on one node, and it does not remove the need to move data when membership changes. Membership and ring state must be propagated consistently to clients or routers.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Its value is minimal data movement on membership change. It spreads keys, not load, so skew still needs separate handling.

points.title: Flow
items: Key → Hash Function → Hash Ring → Virtual Nodes → Physical Node

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Virtual nodes improve balance but increase routing metadata
Client-side routing is fast but needs ring updates
Simple ring does not account for node capacity unless weighted

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you handle a hot key on the ring?
How do clients learn about ring changes safely?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using few or no virtual nodes so load is uneven
Assuming it fixes hot keys
Using hash modulo and calling it consistent hashing

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains minimal remapping
Uses virtual nodes and replication along the ring
States limitations

questions.q: What delivery guarantees do message queues offer (at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once), and how do you get correct results in practice?
questions.a: At-most-once sends without retry, so messages can be lost; at-least-once retries until acknowledged, so messages can be duplicated; exactly-once delivery across a network is not generally achievable, but exactly-once effect is. The practical recipe is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing: each message carries a unique id and the consumer records processed ids or uses natural idempotency such as upserts, in the same transaction as its side effect. Acknowledge only after the work is durably done, and handle poison messages with a retry limit and a dead-letter queue. Some brokers offer transactional or exactly-once processing within their own ecosystem (consume, process and produce atomically), which helps stream pipelines but does not extend to external side effects like emails or payments. Ordering is usually guaranteed per partition only, so partition by the entity that needs ordering.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Since duplicates are inevitable under failure, correctness comes from idempotent consumers rather than from trusting the transport. Broker-level exactly-once is limited to its own boundary.

points.title: Flow
items: Producer → Broker → Consumer → Idempotency Store → Side Effect → Dead-Letter Queue

points.title: Trade-offs
items: At-least-once is safe but needs deduplication
Dedup stores cost memory and lookups
Strict global ordering limits parallelism

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a poison message?
How do you keep ordering while scaling consumers?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Claiming exactly-once delivery with no qualification
Acknowledging before processing completes
No dead-letter handling

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Distinguishes delivery from effect
Uses idempotency keys and ack discipline
Handles ordering and poison messages

questions.q: How would you implement a distributed lock, and why can a simple Redis-based lock be unsafe for correctness?
questions.a: A lock is a lease on a key with an owner token and a TTL so a crashed holder eventually releases it. A simple implementation sets the key only if absent with an expiry, and releases it by deleting only if the stored token matches. The safety problem is that the holder may be paused (garbage collection, scheduling, network delay) past the TTL, another client acquires the lock, and then the first client resumes and still acts, so two clients operate at once. Failover of a single-node store can also lose the lock. For efficiency uses such as avoiding duplicate work, this is acceptable. For correctness, use a consensus-backed store and fencing tokens: each acquisition returns an increasing number, and the protected resource rejects operations with a lower token than it has seen. Better still, avoid locks by using optimistic concurrency (version checks) or conditional writes at the datastore.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Expiring locks cannot guarantee mutual exclusion alone because time and pauses are unreliable. The protected resource must enforce ordering, which is what fencing does.

points.title: Flow
items: Client A → Lock Service → Fencing Token → Protected Resource → Client B

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Simple locks are fast but only safe for efficiency
Consensus-based locks are safer but slower
Optimistic concurrency avoids lock service but causes retries on conflict

points.title: Follow-ups
items: When is a lock only an optimization and not a correctness tool?
How would you implement the same guarantee with a conditional database update?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Releasing a lock without checking the owner token
Assuming TTL guarantees exclusion
Using a lock where a version check would do

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains pause and expiry hazard
Mentions fencing tokens
Offers optimistic concurrency as an alternative

questions.q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it? Cover invalidation strategy as well.
questions.a: A cache stampede happens when a popular key expires or is evicted and many concurrent requests all miss and hit the database to rebuild it, potentially overloading it.
