Prevention options include request coalescing (single flight) so one request rebuilds while others wait, a short-lived lock or lease on rebuild, serving stale data while refreshing in the background (stale-while-revalidate), early probabilistic refresh before expiry, and randomized TTL jitter so keys do not expire together. For cold starts, warm the cache before taking traffic and protect the database with rate limiting or a concurrency cap. For invalidation, the common approach is cache-aside: update the database and then delete the key, with TTLs as a backstop; be aware of the race where a slow reader repopulates an old value after the delete, which short TTLs, versioned keys or event-driven invalidation can limit. Negative caching with a short TTL protects against repeated misses for non-existent keys.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Caches fail loudly at the moment of expiry under load, so rebuild must be controlled. Invalidation races are rarely eliminated, only bounded by TTL and versioning.

points.title: Flow
items: Request → Cache Miss → Single-Flight Lock → Database → Cache Refill

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Serving stale data keeps latency low but shows old values
Locks prevent stampede but add waiting
Short TTLs bound staleness but raise database load

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you warm a cache before a launch?
How would you cache a not-found result safely?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Identical TTLs on keys loaded at the same time
No protection when a whole cache node is lost
Invalidating by update-then-set in a racy order

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Names multiple stampede defenses
Understands invalidation races
Protects the database as the last line

questions.q: How do you design for graceful degradation and load shedding so that a traffic spike or dependency failure does not take down the whole product?
questions.a: Classify features and requests by criticality, such as checkout and login versus recommendations and badges, and define what degraded looks like for each. Add admission control at the edge: concurrency limits and queue timeouts per service, priority-based load shedding that rejects low-priority or low-value requests first, and clear 429 or 503 responses with Retry-After. Use fallbacks for non-critical dependencies (cached or default content, hiding a widget) with circuit breakers so slow dependencies fail fast, and bulkheads so one tenant or feature cannot exhaust shared resources. Feature flags and kill switches let operators disable expensive features instantly. Prefer shedding early and cheaply, before work has consumed resources, and keep the shedding path itself lightweight. Test it with load tests and game days, since degradation paths that are never exercised usually fail. Alert on shed rate and degraded-mode usage so teams know when users are affected.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Overload kills unprepared systems by spreading failure everywhere, whereas a prioritized design sacrifices the least valuable work to preserve the core. It needs to be built and rehearsed in advance.

points.title: Flow
items: Edge → Admission Control → Priority Queue → Core Services → Fallbacks → Kill Switches

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Shedding preserves the core but disappoints some users
Fallback content may be stale or generic
Priority rules need maintenance as the product changes

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you decide request priority without trusting the client?
How would you test degradation modes safely?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating all requests as equally important
Letting queues grow instead of rejecting early
Fallbacks that have never been exercised

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines criticality tiers
Combines shedding, fallbacks and isolation
Plans testing and observability of degraded modes

questions.q: How do you perform a zero-downtime database schema change or data migration on a large production table?
questions.a: Use the expand and contract approach in small, individually reversible steps. Expand: add the new column or table in a backward compatible way (nullable, no heavy locking, using online schema change tooling for large tables). Deploy application code that writes to both old and new structures, then backfill existing rows in throttled batches that watch replication lag and load. Verify correctness by comparing old and new data and by shadow reading. Switch reads to the new structure behind a flag, observe, and keep the ability to switch back. Only after a stable period contract: stop writing the old structure, then drop it in a later release. Never combine a destructive change with the code release that depends on it, and make sure old and new application versions can run simultaneously during rollout. Rehearse on production-like data volumes, schedule low traffic windows for risky steps, and have a documented rollback at each stage.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Large tables and rolling deploys mean old and new code overlap, so every step must be compatible with both. Small reversible steps turn a risky cutover into routine work.

points.title: Flow
items: Expand Schema → Dual Write → Throttled Backfill → Verify → Switch Reads → Contract

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More steps and releases but much lower risk
Dual writes add temporary complexity and load
Online schema tools take longer but avoid long locks

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a backfill that is too slow?
What if you discover bad data after switching reads?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running a blocking ALTER on a huge table at peak
Dropping the old column in the same release
Backfilling without throttling and lag checks

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Describes expand, migrate, contract
Ensures old and new code compatibility
Includes verification and rollback

questions.q: Design a distributed unique ID generator for many services that produces roughly time-sortable 64-bit IDs.
questions.a: Requirements: globally unique IDs, high throughput without a central bottleneck, roughly sortable by creation time, compact, and tolerant of node failure. A common design composes the ID from a timestamp in milliseconds since a custom epoch, a machine or worker id, and a per-millisecond sequence number, packed into 64 bits. Each node generates IDs locally with no coordination, so it scales linearly and has no network hop. Worker ids are assigned at startup through a coordination service or a lease, ensuring no two live nodes share one. The hard problems are clock behavior and uniqueness: if the clock moves backward, wait until it catches up or refuse to issue IDs rather than risk duplicates, and handle sequence exhaustion within a millisecond by waiting for the next one. Sorting is only approximate across nodes because of clock skew, so do not rely on strict global ordering. Alternatives are UUIDs (no coordination, larger, poor index locality unless time-ordered variants are used) and ID range allocation from a central service.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Embedding time, worker identity and a sequence gives uniqueness without coordination per ID. The risks are duplicate worker ids and clock regressions, both of which must be handled explicitly.

points.title: Flow
items: Service → ID Library → Timestamp + Worker + Sequence → Worker Lease → Datastore

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Time-sortable IDs help index locality but leak creation time
Local generation scales but depends on clocks
Central allocation is simple but adds a dependency and hop

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you do if the system clock goes backward?
How do you assign worker ids in an autoscaled environment?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming IDs are strictly ordered across nodes
Reusing worker ids across live nodes
Ignoring clock regression

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Shows bit layout and reasoning
Handles clock and worker id edge cases
Compares alternatives such as UUID and range allocation

questions.q: How would you layer a mobile client, and what is each layer allowed to know about?
questions.a: Split the client into a presentation layer, a domain layer and a data layer, with dependencies pointing inward only. Presentation renders state and forwards user intent; it never talks to the network or the database directly. The domain layer holds business rules and use cases expressed in plain models, with no knowledge of transport or storage formats. The data layer owns remote APIs, the local database, caches and the mapping between wire objects and domain models. Each layer exposes a small interface, so a screen can be tested with a fake use case and a use case with a fake repository. The value is not the number of layers but the rule that **wire formats and storage schemas never leak into the UI**.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Mobile apps outlive any single backend contract or UI redesign, so isolating change is the goal. Inward-only dependencies let the API, the database and the UI evolve independently and make each piece testable without a device.

points.title: Flow
items: Screen → State Holder → Use Case → Repository → Local DB → Remote API

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More layers mean more mapping code and indirection for simple screens
Strict boundaries slow the first feature but speed up every later change
A thin domain layer is fine for CRUD screens; forcing use cases everywhere adds ceremony

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Where does input validation live, and why?
How do you stop a shared model object from coupling every layer?
When would you skip the domain layer for a feature?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Passing API response objects straight into the UI
Letting the presentation layer decide caching or retry policy
Describing a pattern name without stating the dependency rule

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: States the direction of dependencies explicitly
Assigns networking, storage and mapping to the data layer
Explains how each layer is tested in isolation
Acknowledges when the layering is overkill

questions.q: What is the repository pattern on a mobile client, and why is it described as a single source of truth?
questions.a: A repository is the one component that answers the question "what is the current data for X" for the rest of the app. It hides whether data came from memory, the local database or the network, and it decides when to refresh. In the single-source-of-truth form, the UI observes the **local store** only; network responses are written into the store, and the store emits the change to observers. This means every screen showing the same entity updates together and the app works when offline with whatever was last stored. The repository also owns freshness policy such as time-to-live, stale-while-revalidate and forced refresh. Writes go through it too, so optimistic updates and rollback happen in one place.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Without one owner of data, two screens fetch the same entity separately and disagree. Routing reads through the local store turns consistency between screens into a storage property rather than something each screen has to remember.

points.title: Flow
items: Screen → Repository → Local Store → Remote API → Local Store → Observers

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Observing the store adds a write and a read on every fetch, costing some latency
Persisting everything increases disk use and requires schema migrations
A pure pass-through repository is simpler but loses offline reads and cross-screen consistency

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does the repository decide data is stale?
How do you show a loading or error state when the UI only observes the store?
What should not be persisted at all?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Returning network data to the caller and separately writing it to disk, creating two truths
Putting cache policy in screens instead of the repository
Caching sensitive data without thinking about encryption or logout cleanup

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains that the UI reads from the local store, not from responses
Names a freshness policy and who owns it
Covers how writes and optimistic updates flow
Mentions cleanup on logout or account switch

questions.q: A mobile codebase has grown to many teams and slow builds. How do you modularize it, and what rules govern dependencies between modules?
questions.a: Split by **feature** first, not by technical layer, so a team owns a vertical slice such as checkout or search. Under the features sit shared core modules: networking, storage, design system, analytics and auth, each exposing a narrow public interface. Features must not depend on each other directly; they depend on small contract modules that hold interfaces and navigation routes, and the app shell wires implementations together at startup. This keeps the dependency graph shallow and acyclic, which is what allows incremental and parallel builds. Enforce the rules with build tooling rather than convention, because a single convenient import eventually reconnects everything. Measure success by build time for a one-line change and by how many modules a typical change touches.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Build time and team independence both depend on the shape of the dependency graph. Feature-to-feature edges are the main cause of rebuild cascades and merge conflicts, so they are the thing to forbid.

points.title: Flow
items: App Shell → Feature Module → Feature Contract → Core Modules → Platform SDK

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Contract modules add boilerplate and indirection for navigation
Too many tiny modules slow project sync and raise configuration cost
Shared core modules become bottlenecks if their ownership is unclear

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does feature A open a screen owned by feature B?
How do you keep a shared models module from becoming a dumping ground?
How would you support dynamic or on-demand delivery of a feature?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Modularizing by layer only, so every change touches every module
Allowing direct feature-to-feature imports
Having no automated check for dependency rules

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Proposes feature-first modules over shared core modules
Describes how features communicate without depending on each other
States an enforcement mechanism
Defines a measurable outcome such as incremental build time

questions.q: What does offline-first mean for a mobile app, and how is it different from simply caching responses?
questions.a: Offline-first means the app treats the **local database as the primary data source** and the network as a background synchronization channel. Reads always come from local storage, so screens render instantly and identically whether or not there is connectivity. Writes are applied locally first and recorded for later upload, so the user can keep working. Response caching, by contrast, only helps reads that were already fetched and usually blocks or fails writes when offline. Offline-first therefore requires a sync engine, a way to track pending changes, and a plan for conflicts. It also requires honest UI: the user should be able to see what is still pending.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Mobile connectivity is intermittent by default, so designing for the offline case makes the online case fast as a side effect. The cost is that the client becomes a small distributed-systems node with its own state to reconcile.

points.title: Flow
items: User Action → Local DB → UI Update → Sync Engine → Server → Local DB

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Much better perceived speed and resilience, at the cost of a sync engine to build and maintain
Local writes may later be rejected, so the UI needs a way to surface that
Storing more data locally increases disk use and the security surface

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which features should stay online-only, and why?
How do you show the user that a change has not synced yet?
What happens to local data when the user logs out?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Calling an HTTP cache offline-first
Ignoring writes and only discussing reads
Not mentioning conflicts or pending-state UI

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: States that reads and writes hit local storage first
Distinguishes this from response caching
Names sync, pending tracking and conflict handling as requirements
Mentions user-visible pending or failed state

questions.q: Design a client-side write queue (outbox) so that user actions made offline are reliably delivered later.
questions.a: Persist every mutation as a row in a durable outbox table in the same local transaction that applies the optimistic change, so the two can never disagree. Each entry carries a client-generated operation id, the entity id, the operation type, a payload, a creation time and an attempt count. A single worker drains the queue in order per entity, sending the operation id as an **idempotency key** so a retry after a lost response does not apply twice. On success it removes the entry and reconciles the local row with the server version; on a retryable failure it backs off; on a permanent rejection it rolls back the optimistic change and tells the user. Operations on different entities can run in parallel, but those on the same entity must stay ordered. Coalesce redundant entries, for example several edits to the same field, before sending.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The app can be killed at any moment, so intent must be on disk before the UI claims success. Ordering plus idempotency gives effectively-once application over an at-least-once transport.

points.title: Flow
items: User Action → Local Transaction → Outbox Table → Sync Worker → API with Idempotency Key → Reconcile Local Row

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Strict global ordering is simple but one stuck operation blocks everything; per-entity ordering is more complex but resilient
Coalescing saves data and requests but loses intermediate history
Storing operations rather than final state enables merging but makes the queue larger

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle an operation that depends on a server id not yet assigned?
What do you do with a poison entry that always fails?
How is the queue handled on logout?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Keeping the queue in memory only
Writing the optimistic change and the outbox entry in separate transactions
Retrying forever without distinguishing permanent from transient errors

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Queue is durable and written atomically with the local change
Uses client-generated ids for idempotent retries
Defines ordering guarantees
Handles permanent rejection with rollback and user feedback
Addresses dependent operations or temporary ids

questions.q: Two devices edit the same record while offline. How do you detect and resolve the conflict?
questions.a: Detection needs a version on every record: the client sends the base version it edited, and the server rejects or flags the write if the stored version has moved on. Resolution strategy depends on the data. **Last-write-wins** using a server-assigned order is acceptable for low-value fields but silently discards work, and device clocks should never be the arbiter. **Field-level merge** resolves most real conflicts because two users rarely change the same field. For sets and counters, send operations such as add item or increment rather than final state so they commute. For rich collaborative content use a CRDT or operational transform, accepting the metadata overhead. When automatic merge is unsafe, keep both versions and ask the user, which should be rare if the model is designed well.

points.title: Reasoning
items: There is no universal winner; the correct policy follows from the meaning of the data and the cost of lost work. Modelling changes as intent rather than snapshots removes most conflicts before a policy is even needed.

points.title: Flow
items: Device A Edit → Outbox with Base Version → Server Version Check → Merge Policy → Resolved Record → Delta to Devices

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Last-write-wins is trivial but loses data without telling anyone
Operation-based sync merges well but needs ordered or commutative operations
CRDTs converge automatically but add storage and complexity, and tombstones accumulate
Asking the user is always correct but is poor experience if frequent

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle a delete on one device and an edit on another?
Why is device time a poor basis for ordering?
How do you garbage-collect tombstones?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Relying on device clocks for ordering
Applying one policy to every data type
Forgetting deletes, which need tombstones to propagate

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Describes version-based conflict detection
Chooses different policies for different data shapes
Addresses delete versus edit
Avoids trusting client clocks
Explains what the user sees when merge is not possible

questions.q: Design delta sync so a client that has been offline for days can catch up without downloading everything.
questions.a: Give each sync scope a monotonically increasing **server change sequence** and have the client store the last sequence it fully applied as a cursor. The client asks for changes after its cursor; the server returns a page of upserts and tombstones plus a new cursor and a flag saying whether more remain. The client applies each page in a single local transaction together with the cursor update, so a crash mid-sync never leaves partial state. Deletes must be represented as tombstones retained for a bounded window. If the cursor is older than that window, or the server signals a schema or scope change, the server replies with a reset and the client performs a full resync into fresh tables before swapping. Prefer opaque server-issued cursors over timestamps, since timestamps miss rows committed out of order.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Bandwidth and battery make full refresh unacceptable for anything large, and a transactional cursor gives a simple correctness argument. The reset path is what keeps tombstone storage bounded.

points.title: Flow
items: Client Cursor → Changes API → Change Log → Page of Upserts and Tombstones → Local Transaction → New Cursor

points.title: Trade-offs
items: A change log costs server storage and write amplification
Longer tombstone retention reduces full resyncs but grows storage
Per-scope cursors are precise but multiply bookkeeping; one global cursor is simple but over-fetches

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does the client handle changes arriving for entities it has pending local edits on?
What if access to some data is revoked while the client is offline?
How do you combine delta sync with a push or socket nudge?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using updated-at timestamps as the cursor and missing late commits
Updating the cursor outside the transaction that applies the data
Having no full-resync path

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Uses a server-issued monotonic cursor
Applies pages and cursor atomically
Represents deletes as tombstones with bounded retention
Defines a full resync fallback
Considers interaction with pending local writes

questions.q: When should a mobile client retry a failed request, and how should it space the retries?
questions.a: Retry only failures that are likely transient: connection errors, timeouts, and server responses that signal overload or temporary unavailability. Do not retry client errors such as validation or authorization failures, since the same request will fail the same way. Space attempts with **exponential backoff plus random jitter** so that many devices recovering from the same outage do not hit the server in lockstep. Cap both the delay and the number of attempts, and honor any retry-after hint from the server. Safe reads can be retried freely, but writes must be idempotent before they are retried. For user-initiated actions, stop quickly and show a retry affordance instead of spinning indefinitely.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Retries turn a transient failure into success, but uncoordinated retries from a large install base can amplify an outage. Jitter and caps are what make retrying safe at fleet scale.

points.title: Flow
items: Request → Failure Classifier → Backoff with Jitter → Retry → Give Up and Surface Error

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More retries improve success rate but drain battery and delay the error message
Aggressive retry helps one user and hurts the backend during incidents
Background work can retry for hours; foreground work should fail fast

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What makes a write safe to retry?
How should retry policy differ for background sync versus a button tap?
What is a retry budget?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Retrying every error including client errors
Fixed-interval retries with no jitter
Retrying non-idempotent writes blindly

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Classifies retryable versus non-retryable failures
Uses exponential backoff with jitter and caps
Ties write retries to idempotency
Distinguishes foreground from background policy

questions.q: A user taps Pay, the request times out, and the app retries. How do you guarantee they are not charged twice?
questions.a: The client generates a unique **idempotency key** when the user initiates the action, persists it with the pending operation, and sends it on every attempt for that same intent. The server stores the key with the outcome in the same transaction as the side effect, and on a repeat returns the stored result rather than executing again. A timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure, so the client must retry with the same key or query the operation status; it must never mint a new key for the same tap. The key must survive process death, which is why it lives on disk. The server should also reject a reused key whose payload differs, and keep keys long enough to cover the longest realistic retry window. The UI disables the button, but that is a courtesy, not the guarantee.

points.title: Reasoning
items: On mobile, lost responses are common, so at-least-once delivery is the only achievable transport guarantee. Idempotency on the server converts that into effectively-once side effects.

points.title: Flow
items: Tap → Persist Operation and Key → API Request → Idempotency Store → Side Effect → Stored Result

points.title: Trade-offs
items: The server must store keys and results, which costs storage and a lookup per write
Short key retention saves space but risks duplicates for long-offline clients
A status endpoint adds API surface but avoids blind retries

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if the first attempt is still in progress when the retry arrives?
How long should keys be retained?
How does this interact with an offline write queue?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Generating a new key on each retry
Treating a timeout as a definite failure
Relying on a disabled button as the only protection

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Key is created per user intent and persisted before sending
Server stores key and result atomically with the effect
Timeout handled as unknown outcome
Covers concurrent duplicate and payload mismatch

questions.q: How do you design the networking layer of an app whose users are often on slow or flaky connections?
questions.a: Assume every request can stall, fail midway or succeed without the response arriving. Set explicit connect and read timeouts tuned per request class rather than one global default, and make requests cancellable when the screen that needed them goes away. Prioritize: content for the visible screen goes before prefetch, analytics and background sync, with a bound on concurrent connections. Reduce round trips with batching, compression, connection reuse and by letting the server return everything a screen needs in one response. Treat the OS reachability signal as a hint only; the real test is whether a request succeeds, since a device can be connected to a network with no usable path. Finally, degrade gracefully: show cached content with a staleness indicator, queue writes, and adapt payload size such as image quality to measured throughput.

points.title: Reasoning
items: On poor networks latency is dominated by round trips and stalls rather than payload bytes. A design that orders, bounds and cancels work keeps the visible experience responsive when capacity is scarce.

points.title: Flow
items: Screen Request → Priority Queue → HTTP Client → Timeout and Retry Policy → Response Cache → UI

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Short timeouts fail fast but abort requests that would have succeeded on slow links
Batching saves round trips but couples unrelated requests to one failure
Adaptive quality saves data but adds logic and inconsistent visuals

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you measure network quality on the client?
Which requests should be cancelled on navigation and which should not?
How do you test this before release?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Trusting the reachability flag to decide whether to attempt a request
One timeout value for all request types
Letting background traffic compete equally with the visible screen

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Per-class timeouts and cancellation
Request prioritization with bounded concurrency
Reduces round trips
Treats reachability as a hint
Describes graceful degradation with cached data

questions.q: Compare polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events, WebSockets and push notifications for getting updates to a mobile app.
questions.a: **Polling** asks on a timer; it is simple and works everywhere but wastes requests and adds latency up to the interval. **Long polling** holds the request open until there is data, cutting latency while staying plain HTTP. **Server-Sent Events** keep one HTTP response open as a server-to-client stream, good for one-way feeds with built-in reconnection semantics. **WebSockets** give a full-duplex connection, suited to chat or collaborative features where the client also sends frequently. All four only work while the app process is running and connected, which on mobile mostly means the foreground. **Push notifications** go through the OS vendor service and are the only way to reach an app that is suspended or killed, but delivery is best effort and not ordered. A typical design uses a socket or stream in the foreground and push to wake or notify otherwise.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The decision is driven by direction of traffic, required latency and, uniquely on mobile, whether the app is alive. No in-app connection survives backgrounding reliably, so push is complementary rather than an alternative.

points.title: Flow
items: Server Event → Foreground: Socket or Stream → Background: Push Service → OS → App → Fetch Fresh State

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Persistent connections give low latency but cost battery and server connection state
Polling is cheap to build but expensive at scale and slow to react
Push reaches a dead app but can be delayed, collapsed or dropped

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens to a WebSocket when the app goes to the background?
When is plain polling the right answer?
How do you avoid missing events during a reconnect?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming a socket stays connected in the background
Treating push as a reliable ordered message channel
Choosing WebSockets for a feed that only flows one way and updates rarely

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Describes each option and its direction of traffic
Separates foreground transport from background wake-up
States that push is best effort
Matches a transport to a concrete use case

questions.q: What delivery guarantees do APNs and FCM actually provide, and how should that shape your design?
questions.a: Both are **best-effort** relays: they accept a message, try to deliver it when the device is reachable, and give no guarantee of delivery, ordering or timing. If the device is offline the service stores messages for a limited time governed by an expiry you set, and may keep only the most recent one for a given collapse identifier. Priority matters: lower-priority messages can be deferred to save battery, and the OS power-saving modes can delay delivery further. The user can disable notifications, and device tokens change or become invalid, so the server must refresh tokens on launch and prune ones the provider rejects. Therefore treat a push as a **hint that something changed**, not as the data itself: keep the source of truth on the server and have the app fetch current state when it wakes or opens. Never encode state transitions as a sequence of pushes that must all arrive.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Designing as if push were a queue leads to stuck or wrong UI when one message is dropped or reordered. Treating it as a nudge toward a pull makes correctness independent of delivery.

points.title: Flow
items: Backend Event → Push Provider → Device OS → Notification or Wake → App Fetch → Server State

points.title: Trade-offs
items: High priority improves timeliness but is subject to provider and OS policing if overused
Collapsing saves the user from a pile of stale alerts but hides intermediate events
Rich payloads save a fetch but are size-limited and may be stale by the time they show

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep device tokens fresh and remove dead ones?
How would you measure real delivery rate?
What goes in the payload versus fetched after open?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming every push arrives and arrives in order
Storing a device token once and never updating it
Putting sensitive data in the payload

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: States best effort, no ordering, bounded storage
Mentions expiry, collapse and priority
Covers token lifecycle and invalidation
Designs push as a hint followed by a fetch

questions.q: You want an order-status surface on the lock screen that starts and updates even when the app is not running. How do you design it?
questions.a: Use the platform live-update surface: on iOS a Live Activity, on Android an ongoing notification style, each driven remotely by push. There are two token kinds to manage. A **push-to-start** token, on OS versions that support it, lets the server create the surface without the app running; once created, the system issues a **per-activity update token** that the app or its extension must report to the server for subsequent updates and the final end event. The server maps order id to these tokens and sends a compact state payload on each real status change, with a stale date so the surface does not show outdated data forever. Updates are budgeted by the OS, so send only meaningful transitions and use elevated priority sparingly. Because the exact capabilities and limits vary by OS version, the design must fall back to starting the surface from the foreground app, and to ordinary notifications where the feature is absent or disabled.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The surface is rendered by the system from a small state object, so the backend effectively owns the UI state machine. Token lifecycle and update budget, not rendering, are the hard parts.

points.title: Flow
items: Order Event → Live Update Service → Token Store → Push Provider → OS Surface → Update Token back to Server

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Remote start works without the app but depends on OS version and user settings
Frequent updates feel live but risk throttling; coarse updates are safe but less informative
Putting more in the payload avoids fetches the surface cannot make, but payload size is limited

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens if the update token never reaches your server?
How do you end the surface if the final push is lost?
How do you keep in-app tracking and the lock-screen surface consistent?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Assuming one device token serves alerts, start and updates
Streaming every location tick as an update
No stale date or end-of-life handling, leaving a frozen surface

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Distinguishes start token from per-activity update token
Server owns state and sends only meaningful transitions
Handles update budget and priority
Defines stale and end behavior when pushes are lost
Has a fallback for unsupported OS versions

questions.q: Can you rely on silent (background) push to keep app data fresh? What are the limits?
questions.a: No. A silent push asks the OS to wake the app briefly to do background work, but the system decides whether and when to honor it. Delivery is throttled based on factors such as frequency, battery state, power-saving mode and how the user uses the app, and the precise budgets are not published and vary by OS version. On iOS an app the user has force-quit is generally not woken by silent push until it is launched again; on Android, manufacturer battery optimizations can also suppress delivery. When the app is woken it gets only a short execution window, so the work must be small and must finish cleanly. Use silent push as an **opportunistic optimization** that makes the next launch fresher, and always run the same sync on foreground so correctness never depends on it. Anything the user must see should be a visible notification.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Background execution is a privilege the OS rations to protect battery, so any design with a hard dependency on it will fail for some share of users. Making foreground sync the guaranteed path keeps the feature correct.

points.title: Flow
items: Server Change → Silent Push → OS Scheduler → Brief App Wake → Delta Sync → Local DB

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Opportunistic freshness improves launch experience but is unpredictable to measure
Sending more silent pushes can reduce, not increase, how many are honored
Visible notifications are more reliable but interrupt the user

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you measure how often silent pushes actually run?
What scheduled background mechanisms complement silent push?
How do you keep the wake-up work within its time window?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Building a feature that is only correct if silent push arrives
Quoting exact delivery quotas as facts
Doing heavy sync or large downloads in the wake window

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: States that delivery is throttled and not guaranteed
Mentions force-quit and power-saving effects
Keeps wake-up work short
Makes foreground sync the correctness path

questions.q: How should a mobile list API paginate: offset or cursor? Why does it matter more on mobile?
questions.a: Prefer **cursor pagination**: the server returns items plus an opaque cursor pointing after the last item, and the client sends it back for the next page. With offset pagination, when new items are inserted at the top between requests, the next page shifts and the user sees duplicates or skips rows; cursors anchored on a stable sort key avoid that. Cursors are also cheaper for the database on deep pages. It matters more on mobile because infinite scroll sessions are long, requests are slow and can be retried, and the list is usually persisted locally and merged across refreshes. The response should include whether more pages exist, and items need stable ids so the client can de-duplicate. Offset is acceptable for small, static lists or when the UI needs jump-to-page.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Feeds change while the user scrolls, so pagination must be stable under concurrent inserts. A cursor on an immutable ordering key gives that stability and makes retries harmless.

points.title: Flow
items: List Screen → Repository → Page Request with Cursor → API → Indexed Query → Items and Next Cursor

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Cursors are stable and fast but cannot jump to an arbitrary page
Offset is simple and supports page numbers but drifts under inserts and slows on deep pages
Opaque cursors let the server change strategy later but are harder to debug

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What sort key do you use when two items share a timestamp?
How do you handle pull-to-refresh on a partially loaded list?
What page size would you choose and why?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Using offset on a frequently changing feed
Exposing cursor internals that the client then depends on
No stable item ids for de-duplication

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains the duplicate and skip problem with offset
Describes an opaque cursor on a stable key
Mentions client de-duplication by id
Notes when offset is acceptable

questions.q: What is a Backend for Frontend, and when is it worth introducing one for mobile?
questions.a: A Backend for Frontend is a thin server-side layer owned alongside the mobile client that exposes endpoints shaped for mobile screens. It aggregates calls to several domain services, trims payloads to the fields the screen renders, and hides internal service boundaries. This matters on mobile because each round trip is expensive, and because **shipped binaries cannot be changed**: moving orchestration to the server lets you fix or reshape it without an app release. The BFF is also a natural place for response shaping per app version, auth token translation and consistent error formats. It should not hold business rules; those stay in domain services, or the BFF becomes a second monolith. It is worth it when screens need data from many services or when mobile and web needs diverge; for one simple backend it is extra hops and ownership for little gain.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The client is the hardest tier to update, so logic that changes often should live where it can be redeployed quickly. A BFF trades a small amount of server complexity for fewer round trips and release independence.

points.title: Flow
items: Mobile Screen → BFF Endpoint → Parallel Service Calls → Aggregate and Trim → Single Response

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Fewer round trips and smaller payloads, at the cost of another deployable to own
Per-client BFFs fit each client well but duplicate logic across them
Aggregation makes one slow dependency delay the whole screen unless partial responses are designed

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How does the BFF respond when one downstream service is down?
Who owns the BFF, the mobile team or a platform team?
How does a BFF compare with a client-specified query API?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Putting domain business logic in the BFF
One generic BFF for all clients that satisfies none
Ignoring partial failure of aggregated calls

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines the BFF as screen-shaped aggregation owned with the client
Connects the value to round trips and unpatchable binaries
Keeps business rules out of it
Addresses partial failure
States when not to build one

questions.q: App versions from two years ago are still in use. How do you evolve an API without breaking them?
questions.a: Assume every released binary is permanent and make changes **additive by default**: add fields and endpoints, never remove or change the meaning of existing ones. Clients must be written tolerantly, ignoring unknown fields and handling unknown enum values with a safe default, since that is what lets the server add things later. Send app version and platform on every request so the server can branch or shape responses for specific versions when needed. For a genuinely breaking change, introduce a new endpoint or version and run both until old usage falls below a threshold visible in metrics. Pair this with a minimum supported version and a forced-upgrade mechanism so there is a deliberate way to retire the oldest clients. Finally, protect the contract with tests that replay requests from old released versions against new server builds.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The server deploys in minutes while clients upgrade over months, so the server carries the compatibility burden. Additive evolution plus tolerant readers keeps most changes free; explicit versioning and sunsets handle the rest.

points.title: Flow
items: Old and New App Versions → Version Header → API Gateway → Compatibility Shaping → Service → Usage Metrics by Version

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Additive-only keeps clients working but accumulates deprecated fields
Per-version branching on the server is flexible but becomes hard to test
Forcing upgrades removes legacy cost but loses users on old devices

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you add a new value to an enum that old clients switch over?
How do you decide when to drop support for a version?
How would server-driven UI change this picture?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Renaming or repurposing a field in place
Strict client parsing that crashes on unknown values
No telemetry on which versions call which endpoints

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Additive changes and tolerant readers
Explicit handling of unknown enum values
Version signal on requests and server-side shaping
Deprecation driven by usage metrics
Contract tests against old clients

questions.q: What is server-driven UI, when would you use it, and what are its limits?
questions.a: In server-driven UI the server returns a description of the screen, a tree of known component types with their data, layout hints and actions, and the client renders it using natively built components. It lets a team change layout, ordering and content without shipping a release, and keeps platforms consistent. The contract is a **component schema**: the client advertises which components and schema version it supports, and the server composes only from that set, with a defined fallback for anything unknown. It fits content-heavy, frequently changing surfaces such as home pages, promotions and onboarding. It fits poorly for highly interactive or animation-heavy screens, or ones needing complex local state and offline behavior. The costs are a harder debugging story, a need for strong schema governance, and the fact that new component types still require a release.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The technique moves composition from the slowest-to-change tier to the fastest. It only works if the component vocabulary is stable and versioned, because every old client must still render something sensible.

points.title: Flow
items: Client Capabilities → Layout Service → Component Tree Response → Component Registry → Native Renderer → Action Handler

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Faster iteration and experimentation versus weaker type safety and harder debugging
A rich schema is powerful but approaches building a browser
Server composition needs the network, so offline support needs cached layouts

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What does the client do when it receives a component it does not know?
How do you version the component schema?
How do you test a server layout against old app versions?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Sending raw styling for everything and losing design-system consistency
No fallback for unknown components
Driving complex stateful flows entirely from the server

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Describes the component tree and native renderer model
Explains capability negotiation and unknown-component fallback
Identifies suitable and unsuitable screens
Addresses offline and caching of layouts
Notes governance and testing cost

questions.q: Design a forced-upgrade mechanism for a mobile app.
questions.a: Have the app send its version and platform to a lightweight config endpoint at launch and on return to foreground, and have the server answer with a **minimum supported version** and a **recommended version**. Below the minimum, the app shows a blocking screen with a link to the store; below recommended, it shows a dismissible prompt. Also enforce it at the API: requests from versions under the minimum receive a specific upgrade-required error, so even a stale cached config cannot let an unsafe client continue. Thresholds should be configurable per platform and optionally per OS version, because a device may be unable to install the newest build. The blocking screen must be extremely simple and depend on almost nothing, since it has to work in very old builds. Use the hard block rarely, for security or data-corruption issues, and only after the new version is fully available in the store.

points.title: Reasoning
items: This is the only lever for retiring binaries you cannot patch, so it must be shipped early and be nearly impossible to break. Server-side enforcement is what makes it trustworthy.

points.title: Flow
items: App Launch → Version Check Endpoint → Min and Recommended Versions → Soft Prompt or Hard Block → Store Page → API Enforcement

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Hard blocks protect integrity but lock out users who cannot update
Checking only at launch misses long-lived sessions; checking often adds requests
In-app update flows are smoother but platform-specific

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you do for devices whose OS cannot run the new version?
What if the config endpoint itself is unreachable?
How do you avoid blocking users before the store rollout completes?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Client-only enforcement with no API-side check
A block screen that depends on components that may be broken
Raising the minimum before the new build is fully rolled out

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Separates soft and hard thresholds
Enforces at the API as well as in the client
Handles devices that cannot upgrade
Defines behavior when the check fails
Coordinates with store rollout

questions.q: Where should a mobile app store access and refresh tokens?
questions.a: Store them in the platform secure storage: the Keychain on iOS and a Keystore-backed encrypted store on Android. These keep secrets encrypted with keys tied to the device, and can restrict access to when the device is unlocked. Do not put tokens in plain preferences, files, logs, crash reports or analytics. The **access token** should be short-lived and can be held in memory during a session; the **refresh token** is long-lived and is the one that most needs secure storage. Choose an accessibility level that matches whether background work needs the token while the device is locked, and exclude tokens from device backups unless migration is intended. On logout, delete them locally and revoke them on the server.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The client is an untrusted environment, so the goal is to limit what a stolen backup, another app or casual inspection can obtain. Short lifetimes bound the damage if a token leaks anyway.

points.title: Flow
items: Login → Auth Server → Tokens → Secure Storage → In-Memory Access Token → API Requests

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Stricter accessibility is safer but can break background refresh while locked
Requiring biometrics to read a token is strong but adds friction
Short access-token lifetime limits exposure but increases refresh traffic

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What should happen to tokens when the app is reinstalled or restored to a new device?
How does a compromised or rooted device change the picture?
How do you stop tokens appearing in logs?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Storing tokens in plain preferences or a local database unencrypted
Logging authorization headers
One long-lived token with no refresh or revocation

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Names platform secure storage
Distinguishes access and refresh token handling
Mentions accessibility and backup considerations
Covers logout and server-side revocation

questions.q: Explain refresh token rotation and how the client should handle many requests failing with an expired token at once.
questions.a: With rotation, each use of a refresh token returns a new access token and a **new refresh token**, and the old one is invalidated. If an already-used refresh token is presented again, the server treats it as possible theft and revokes the whole token family, forcing re-login. On the client, an expired access token often surfaces on several concurrent requests, so the refresh must be **single-flight**: the first failure triggers one refresh, the others wait, and all are replayed with the new token. Without that, parallel refreshes race, one wins, and the losers present a stale token and trigger the theft response. Persist the new refresh token before using the new access token, because a crash between the two would strand the user. Allow a small server-side grace for a retried refresh whose response was lost, and send the user to login only on a definite invalid-token response, not on a network error.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Rotation makes a leaked refresh token short-lived and its reuse detectable. The client side is a concurrency problem, and getting it wrong shows up as random logouts.

points.title: Flow
items: API Call → Expired Token Response → Single-Flight Refresh → Auth Server → Persist New Tokens → Replay Queued Requests

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Rotation adds reuse detection but makes lost responses risky without a grace window
A grace window fixes flaky networks but slightly widens the replay opportunity
Proactive refresh before expiry reduces failures but depends on a sane device clock

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do multiple processes or app extensions share the refresh safely?
What if the refresh response is lost in transit?
How do you avoid logging the user out during a server outage?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Each failing request starting its own refresh
Logging out on any refresh failure including timeouts
Using the new access token before the new refresh token is saved

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains rotation and reuse detection
Describes single-flight refresh and request replay
Handles lost refresh response
Separates network failure from invalid credentials
Considers extensions or multi-process access

questions.q: Would you implement certificate pinning in a mobile app? How do you do it without risking an outage?
questions.a: Pinning makes the app trust only specific keys for your hosts, so a mis-issued certificate or a user-installed root cannot be used to intercept traffic. It is worth it for apps handling money, health or credentials, and less clearly so elsewhere, because the main risk is self-inflicted: if the server key changes and shipped apps do not have a matching pin, those apps cannot connect at all. To manage this, pin **public keys rather than leaf certificates**, and always ship at least one **backup pin** for a key held offline that is not yet deployed. Plan rotation so new pins are in released binaries long before the server switches. Decide deliberately whether to include a remotely updatable pin set or an expiry after which pinning relaxes, since each trades some security for recoverability. Monitor pin failures by version, and remember pinning raises the bar against interception but does not stop a determined attacker on a device they control.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The benefit is defense against a compromised trust store; the cost is an availability risk tied to client release cycles. A sound answer weighs both and builds the recovery path first.

points.title: Flow
items: App → TLS Handshake → Chain Validation → Pin Check → Backup Pin → API

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Stronger interception resistance versus the risk of locking out every installed client
Pinning an intermediate or root is more forgiving but protects less
Remote pin updates aid recovery but become a target themselves

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you rotate a pinned key safely?
How do third-party SDKs and content delivery hosts fit in?
How do debugging and corporate proxies work with pinning?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Pinning a single leaf certificate with no backup
No rotation plan that accounts for old app versions
Claiming pinning makes reverse engineering impossible

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: States the threat pinning addresses
Pins public keys with a backup pin
Describes rotation across release cycles
Has monitoring and a recovery strategy
Is honest about limits on a compromised device

questions.q: How do you gain confidence that an API request comes from your genuine, unmodified app on a real device?
questions.a: Use the platform attestation services, App Attest on iOS and Play Integrity on Android. The server issues a one-time **challenge**, the app asks the platform to produce a signed statement bound to that challenge, and the server verifies it and reads the verdict about app and device integrity. On iOS the flow also establishes a hardware-backed key so later requests can carry assertions signed by it. The decision must be made **on the server**; any check evaluated in the client can be patched out. Treat the result as a risk signal that feeds a policy, combined with rate limits, account history and behavior, rather than a single gate, because the services have quotas, can be unavailable, and are not supported on every device. Apply it to sensitive actions such as login, payment or promotion redemption instead of every call.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Embedded secrets can always be extracted, so identity of the app has to be asserted by something the attacker does not control. Attestation raises the cost of automation and tampering but is probabilistic, which is why it feeds risk scoring.

points.title: Flow
items: App → Server Challenge → Platform Attestation → Signed Token → Server Verification → Risk Policy

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Blocking on failure stops abuse but also blocks legitimate users on unsupported or unusual devices
Attesting every request is strongest but adds latency and hits quotas
A hard dependency on the vendor service turns their outage into yours

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you do when the attestation service is unavailable?
How do you prevent replay of an attestation token?
How do you roll this out without blocking good users?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Evaluating the verdict in the client
No server-issued nonce, allowing replay
Treating attestation as absolute proof

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Names the platform mechanisms accurately
Uses a server challenge and server-side verification
Treats the verdict as a risk signal with fallbacks
Scopes attestation to sensitive operations
Plans a monitor-then-enforce rollout

questions.q: How do you design deep linking so it is both reliable and safe?
questions.a: Use domain-verified links, Universal Links on iOS and App Links on Android, where the OS confirms through a file hosted on your domain that your app may handle those URLs. Custom URL schemes can be claimed by any app, so they must never carry secrets such as auth codes without additional protection. Route every incoming link through **one central router** that parses it, validates parameters against an allowlist of destinations, and treats all values as untrusted input. A link should only navigate; it must not perform a state-changing action without user confirmation, and it must not let an external caller open arbitrary internal screens or load arbitrary URLs in an in-app web view. If the destination needs authentication, hold the link, send the user through login, then resume. Each link should also resolve on the web for users without the app, and deferred deep linking after install should carry only non-sensitive context.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A deep link is an external entry point into the app, so it deserves the same validation as an API endpoint. Central routing gives one place to enforce it and to keep behavior consistent across sources.

points.title: Flow
items: Link Tap → OS Domain Verification → App Link Router → Validate and Allowlist → Auth Gate → Destination Screen

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Verified links are safe but depend on correct domain configuration and can fall back to the browser
A strict allowlist is safe but needs updating for each new destination
Deferred linking improves onboarding but relies on matching that may be imprecise

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What happens to a link opened while the user is logged out?
How do you handle a link to a screen that does not exist in an older app version?
How would you protect an authorization redirect that uses a custom scheme?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Passing tokens through custom URL schemes unprotected
Links that trigger actions without confirmation
Scattered link handling with no central validation

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Prefers domain-verified links and explains why
Central router with validation and allowlist
No state change without confirmation
Handles logged-out and unsupported-version cases
Provides a web fallback

questions.q: What is a phased rollout of a mobile release, and what do you watch while it is in progress?
questions.a: A phased rollout makes a new version available to a small percentage of users first and increases that share over days. The purpose is to find crashes and regressions on real devices while the affected population is small. Watch crash-free users and sessions against the previous version, hangs or unresponsive events, startup time, and the business metrics for core flows such as login and checkout, along with error rates on the APIs the new version calls. Define the thresholds that would pause the rollout **before** starting. Note that pausing stops further exposure but does not remove the build from devices that already installed it, so the real fix is a new version or a remote switch. Phased delivery usually governs automatic updates, and a user may still be able to fetch the new version manually.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A mobile release cannot be withdrawn from devices, so limiting exposure is the main risk control at the binary level. Agreeing on stop conditions ahead of time removes debate during an incident.

points.title: Flow
items: Build → Store Review → Small Percentage → Health Metrics → Pause or Expand → Full Rollout

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Slower rollout reduces blast radius but delays features and fixes
Small early cohorts may not include the device types that fail
Pausing limits new exposure but leaves existing installs affected

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you do for users already on a bad build?
How does this differ from a feature flag rollout?
How would you speed up a critical fix?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Believing a pause rolls users back
Looking only at crash rate and ignoring business metrics
Deciding thresholds after a problem appears

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains staged exposure and its purpose
Names stability and business metrics compared to baseline
States that installed builds cannot be recalled
Mentions predefined pause criteria

questions.q: How do feature flags and remote config fit into a mobile release strategy, and what are the risks?
questions.a: They separate **shipping code from releasing behavior**. Code for a new feature ships dark in the binary, and a server-controlled flag turns it on for a percentage, a cohort or a platform version, with the ability to turn it off quickly; this is the closest thing mobile has to rollback. Remote config generalizes that to tunable values such as timeouts or thresholds. Every flag needs a safe compiled-in default, because the first launch and offline launches run before any fetch succeeds. Decide when values take effect: applying mid-session can change the UI under the user, so most apps fetch in the background and activate on next launch, with a faster path for kill switches. The risks are flag debt, an exploding number of untested combinations, and config itself becoming an unreviewed way to change production. Treat config changes like deploys, with validation, gradual rollout and an audit trail, and remove flags once a feature is fully released.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Binary rollout is slow and one-directional, so runtime control is what makes fast, reversible change possible. That power needs the same discipline as code deployment because a bad config reaches users faster than a bad build.

points.title: Flow
items: Flag Service → Targeting Rules → Client Fetch → Local Cache with Defaults → Activation Point → Feature Code Path

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Fast reversibility versus more code paths to test and maintain
Activating on next launch is stable but slows reaction; live activation is fast but can disrupt sessions
Client-side evaluation works offline but exposes rules; server-side evaluation hides rules but needs the network

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you make a kill switch take effect faster than normal config?
How do you keep experiment assignment consistent across sessions?
How do you clean up stale flags?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: No sensible default when the fetch has not completed
Changing config for everyone at once with no validation
Leaving flags in the code permanently

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Separates deployment from release
Defines defaults and offline behavior
Chooses an activation policy and justifies it
Treats config as a governed production change
Addresses flag cleanup

questions.q: A mobile binary cannot be rolled back once installed. How does that change the way you engineer and operate releases across an organization?
questions.a: Treat every release as permanent and move reversibility elsewhere. First, ship risky changes behind **remote kill switches** and keep the previous code path until the new one is proven, so recovery is a config change. Second, make data changes roll-forward safe: local schema migrations must be tested from every still-supported version, must be resumable, and a new version must not write data that the previous server contract or a downgraded read path cannot tolerate. Third, keep the server backward compatible with all live versions so that a server rollback is always possible independently of the client. Fourth, reduce exposure with internal dogfood, beta channels and phased rollout tied to automated health gates. Fifth, keep a fast lane: a release train short enough that a fix can go out quickly, an understanding of expedited store review, and a forced-upgrade lever for the worst cases. Finally, define ownership, with a release owner, clear stop conditions and a post-release review of anything that needed a hotfix.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Since the artifact is irreversible, safety has to come from runtime control, compatibility and limited exposure. At staff level this is a system of process and tooling rather than a single technique.

points.title: Flow
items: Flagged Code → Dogfood and Beta → Phased Rollout → Health Gates → Kill Switch → Hotfix Train

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Keeping old code paths costs binary size and maintenance but buys recovery time
Frequent small releases lower risk per release but raise process overhead
Strict gates catch regressions but can block releases on noisy metrics

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you recover from a bad local database migration already in users hands?
What cannot be protected by a flag?
How do you make the kill switch itself reliable?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Planning to pull the release as a recovery step
Irreversible data migrations shipped with no flag and no tested recovery
Coupling a server change to a client version so neither can be rolled back alone

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Moves reversibility to flags and server control
Addresses data and migration safety explicitly
Keeps client and server independently deployable
Uses staged exposure with automated gates
Covers hotfix path and ownership

questions.q: App cold start has become slow. How do you approach measuring and fixing it?
questions.a: Define the metric first: time from process start to first frame, and time to a **usable** first screen with real content, measured in production as percentiles segmented by device class and OS version. Then break startup into phases, process and library load, app initialization, first screen construction and first data, and attribute time to each with tracing. The usual cause is eager initialization: SDKs, dependency graphs, database opens and config fetches all running before the first frame. The fix is to classify every startup task as required before first frame, required before interaction, or deferrable, and to run only the first group synchronously. Render the first screen from **cached data** instead of waiting for the network, and keep disk and network work off the main thread. Lock in the gains with a startup budget, a regression test in CI on a low-end device, and an owner for every initializer.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Startup regresses through many small additions rather than one bug, so the durable fix is governance of what may run at launch. Measuring to usable content prevents optimizing a blank first frame.

points.title: Flow
items: Process Start → Critical Init → First Frame → Cached Content → Deferred Init → Network Refresh

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Deferring initialization speeds launch but can make the first use of a feature slower
Rendering cached content is fast but may briefly show stale data
Preloading in the background helps warm starts but uses memory and battery

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you measure startup reliably in production?
How do you stop a third-party SDK from adding launch time?
What differs between cold, warm and hot starts?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Optimizing on a high-end device only
Measuring first frame while the screen is still an empty skeleton
Fixing once with no budget or regression guard

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Defines a user-meaningful startup metric with percentiles
Breaks startup into phases and attributes cost
Classifies and defers initialization work
Uses cached data for first render
Adds a budget and regression detection

questions.q: Design the image loading pipeline for a mobile app with image-heavy lists.
questions.a: A request flows through a **memory cache** of decoded bitmaps, then a **disk cache** of encoded bytes, then the network. The client asks for an image sized for the view and screen density, using a URL scheme that lets a resizing service or CDN return the right dimensions and a modern compressed format, since downloading a large original for a thumbnail wastes data, memory and decode time. Decoding and resizing happen off the main thread, and the image is downsampled to the target size while decoding. Identical in-flight requests are de-duplicated, and a request is cancelled when its list cell is recycled. Show a placeholder, ideally a tiny blurred preview or dominant color delivered with the list data, to avoid layout jumps. Both caches are bounded and evicted least-recently-used, and the memory cache is trimmed on OS memory warnings.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Images dominate bytes, memory and jank in most apps. Doing the sizing on the server side and bounding each cache tier addresses all three at once.

points.title: Flow
items: List Cell → Memory Cache → Disk Cache → CDN Resizer → Background Decode → Display

points.title: Trade-offs
items: A larger memory cache scrolls smoothly but raises the chance of the app being killed in the background
Many size variants improve fit but lower CDN cache hit rate
Better compression formats save data but cost decode time and need capability negotiation

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you invalidate a cached image that changed on the server?
How would you adapt quality on a slow or metered network?
How do you prefetch without wasting data?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Loading full-resolution images into small views
Decoding on the main thread
Not cancelling requests for recycled cells, causing wrong images and wasted work

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Describes memory, disk and network tiers
Requests correctly sized images from the server or CDN
Decodes off the main thread with downsampling
Handles cancellation and de-duplication
Bounds caches and responds to memory pressure

questions.q: How do you design an app to stay within memory limits and survive being killed by the OS?
questions.a: Start from the constraint: the OS gives each app a memory budget that varies by device and OS version, terminates foreground apps that exceed it, and reclaims background apps under pressure without notice. Design therefore has two parts, staying low and recovering well. To stay low, bound every cache by size, keep large objects such as decoded images and media buffers sized to what is displayed, page long lists rather than holding whole datasets, and stream large files instead of loading them. React to memory-pressure signals by dropping caches and anything rebuildable. To recover well, assume process death at any time: persist essential UI state such as navigation position, scroll and form drafts, keep the source of truth on disk, and restore so the user returns to the same place. Measure peak memory, out-of-memory terminations and background kill rate in the field per device class, and watch for leaks with automated checks.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Out-of-memory kills do not look like crashes to the user; they look like the app losing its place. Treating termination as normal and state restoration as a feature is what makes the app feel reliable.

points.title: Flow
items: Screen State → Bounded Caches → Memory Pressure Signal → Cache Trim → Persisted State → Restore on Relaunch

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Larger caches improve speed but raise kill probability
Persisting more state improves restoration but costs writes and migration effort
Aggressive trimming saves memory but causes reloads and jank

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you detect out-of-memory terminations when there is no crash report?
What state should be persisted versus rebuilt?
How do you find a leak that only appears after long sessions?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Unbounded in-memory caches
Assuming the process lives as long as the user session
Testing only on devices with large memory

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: States that budgets vary and background kills are normal
Bounds caches and large allocations
Handles memory-pressure callbacks
Designs state restoration after process death
Names field metrics for memory health

questions.q: How do you design an app to be frugal with battery and mobile data?
questions.a: The main battery costs are the radio, location, CPU wakeups and the screen, so the design goal is to do less, less often, and together. **Batch network work**: each wake of the cellular radio carries a tail cost after the transfer, so many small scattered requests are worse than one combined burst. Hand deferrable work to the OS scheduler with constraints such as unmetered network or charging, instead of running timers. Replace polling with push or with a connection only while the screen needing it is visible, and pick the lowest location accuracy and update rate that serves the feature. For data, request right-sized images, use compression and delta sync, cache with validators so unchanged responses cost almost nothing, and respect the system low-data and battery-saver modes by pausing prefetch and autoplay. Measure with field metrics per version: background network bytes, wakeups, location time and any OS-reported excessive-usage signals.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Energy use is driven by how often hardware is woken more than by how much work is done per wake. Letting the OS coalesce work across apps is the single most effective lever.

points.title: Flow
items: Work Request → Classify Urgent or Deferrable → OS Scheduler with Constraints → Batched Network Burst → Cache and Delta → Usage Metrics

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Batching saves energy but delays freshness
Prefetching improves speed but wastes data when the content is never viewed
High location accuracy improves features but is one of the largest drains

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you attribute battery drain to a specific feature?
What should change when the user enables data saver?
How does a persistent connection affect battery?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Timers that poll in the background
Ignoring low-data and power-saving modes
Requesting best-accuracy continuous location by default

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Identifies radio, location and wakeups as main costs
Batches and defers work through the OS scheduler
Reduces bytes with sizing, compression and deltas
Honors system data and battery modes
Defines field metrics

questions.q: How should a mobile app collect and upload analytics events without hurting the user experience or losing data?
questions.a: Events are appended to a **persistent local queue** rather than sent one by one. Each event gets a client-generated unique id, a device timestamp and a session identifier. An uploader flushes in batches when a count or age threshold is reached, when the app moves to the background, and opportunistically when other network activity is already happening. A batch is deleted locally only after the server acknowledges it, which makes delivery at-least-once, and the server de-duplicates by event id. The queue is bounded in size and age with a defined drop policy so a long offline period cannot fill the disk. Batches are compressed, uploads back off on failure, and the server records its own receive time so device clock errors can be corrected. Analytics work always runs off the main thread and at lower priority than user-facing requests.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Per-event uploads waste battery and are lost when the app is killed. A durable queue with acknowledged batches gives reliable delivery at low cost, with de-duplication handling the inevitable retries.

points.title: Flow
items: Event → Persistent Queue → Batch Trigger → Compressed Upload → Ingest API Ack → Delete Batch

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Larger batches save battery but delay data and lose more if the queue is dropped
At-least-once delivery needs server de-duplication
A bounded queue protects disk but drops data for long-offline users

points.title: Follow-ups
items: Which events should bypass batching?
How do you handle wrong device clocks?
How do you honor a user withdrawing analytics consent?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Sending one request per event
Keeping the queue in memory only
Deleting events before the server acknowledges them

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Durable queue with batching triggers
Acknowledge-then-delete with idempotent event ids
Bounded queue with a drop policy
Handles clock skew using server receive time
Keeps work off the main thread and low priority

questions.q: Design the client side of a chat application.
questions.a: The local database is the source of truth: conversations and messages are stored locally and the UI observes them.
