Sending writes the message locally with a **client-generated id** and a pending status, places it in an outbox, and the transport delivers it; the server acknowledgement supplies a server id and a per-conversation sequence number, and the row moves to sent. In the foreground a WebSocket carries messages, acknowledgements, receipts and typing signals; when it reconnects, the client runs a **gap sync** per conversation from its last seen sequence, because nothing can be assumed about what was missed. In the background, push notifications alert the user and the app syncs on open. Ordering in the UI uses server sequence, with pending messages shown at the end. History is paged backward on demand, media is uploaded separately through resumable uploads with the message referencing the result, and thumbnails are cached. Delivery and read receipts are small idempotent updates, and unread counts are derived from sequence positions rather than incremented blindly.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Chat combines every mobile problem: offline writes, unreliable transport, ordering and multi-device state. Local-first storage plus server-assigned sequence numbers gives a simple model in which reconnect is just another delta sync.

points.title: Flow
items: Compose → Local DB and Outbox → WebSocket → Chat Server Ack with Sequence → Gap Sync on Reconnect → Push when Backgrounded

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Server sequence gives a total order but pending messages may reorder once acknowledged
Storing full history locally enables search and offline but grows storage
End-to-end encryption improves privacy but complicates search, multi-device and push previews

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you prevent a retried send from appearing twice?
How do you keep unread counts consistent across two devices?
How does the design change for very large group conversations?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Treating the socket as reliable and skipping gap sync
Ordering by device timestamp
Relying on push to deliver message content

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Local store as source of truth with outbox
Client ids for de-duplication and server sequence for ordering
Reconnect gap sync
Clear foreground socket and background push roles
Covers media, pagination and receipts

questions.q: Design a grocery cart that works offline and syncs across a user's devices.
questions.a: The cart lives in the local database and every change is applied there first. Changes are recorded as **operations**, add item, set quantity, remove item, in an outbox, rather than uploading the whole cart, so edits from two devices merge instead of overwriting each other. The server applies operations idempotently using client operation ids and returns the authoritative cart with a version. Merge rules are explicit: quantity changes on the same item resolve by latest server-ordered write or by summing deltas, and removal is a tombstone so an item does not reappear from a stale device. Price, stock and offers are **server truth**: the client shows cached values clearly marked as possibly out of date, and the server revalidates the cart on sync and again at checkout, returning adjustments such as unavailable items or changed prices for the user to accept. Checkout itself is online-only. A guest cart is merged into the account cart on login using the same operation model.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Cart contents are user intent and can be merged; prices and stock are facts only the server knows. Separating the two tells you what may be optimistic and what must be confirmed before money moves.

points.title: Flow
items: Add to Cart → Local Cart and Outbox → Cart Sync API → Server Merge and Revalidation → Authoritative Cart → Checkout Validation

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Operation sync merges well but needs careful tombstone handling
Showing cached prices keeps the app usable offline but risks surprise at checkout
Summing quantity deltas preserves both edits but can double an intended single change

points.title: Follow-ups
items: An item goes out of stock while the user is offline. What do they see?
How do you merge a guest cart with an existing account cart?
How do you keep the cart badge correct on every screen?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Uploading the whole cart and letting the last device win
Trusting client-side prices at checkout
No tombstones, so removed items come back

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Local-first cart with operation-based sync
Idempotent operations and explicit merge rules
Server-authoritative price and stock with revalidation
Clear user handling of adjustments
Covers guest-to-account merge

questions.q: Design an infinite-scrolling image feed that feels instant, including prefetching.
questions.a: The feed API returns cursor-paged items containing ids, image URLs or a URL template, dimensions and a tiny placeholder such as a dominant color, so cells can be laid out at final size before any image arrives. Items are stored locally so the feed opens instantly from the last session and then refreshes. Prefetch runs at two levels: the **next page of metadata** is requested when the user is a few screens from the end, and **images for the next few items** in the scroll direction are fetched ahead of display. Prefetch requests are lower priority than visible ones and are cancelled when direction or velocity changes. The amount of prefetch adapts to conditions: generous on unmetered fast networks, minimal or off on metered, slow or low-data mode. Images go through a bounded memory and disk cache with sizes matched to the view. Only a window of items stays materialized in memory, and scroll position is preserved across process death.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Perceived speed comes from never showing an empty cell, which needs known dimensions, local persistence and work done slightly ahead of the user. Prefetch is speculative, so it must be cheap to cancel and sensitive to network cost.

points.title: Flow
items: Scroll Position → Page Prefetch → Feed API → Local Feed Store → Image Prefetch Queue → Image Cache

points.title: Trade-offs
items: More prefetch means smoother scrolling but wasted data when the user stops
Persisting the feed gives instant open but may show stale ranking first
A large in-memory window avoids reloads but increases memory pressure

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you insert new items at the top without moving what the user is reading?
How do you measure whether prefetch is paying off?
How would video items change the design?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: No image dimensions in the response, causing layout jumps
Prefetch at the same priority as visible content
Ignoring metered or low-data conditions

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Cursor pagination with dimensions and placeholders
Separate metadata and image prefetch
Prioritization and cancellation of speculative work
Network-aware prefetch policy
Bounded memory and persisted position

questions.q: Design a live order tracking screen showing status and estimated arrival.
questions.a: Model the order as a **server-owned state machine** and have the client render whatever state it last received; the client never infers transitions. On opening, the screen fetches a full snapshot with status, estimate, a version number and a server timestamp, then subscribes to updates over a stream or socket scoped to that order, falling back to polling with backoff if the stream fails. Every update carries the version, and the client ignores anything older than what it holds, which makes duplicates and reordering harmless. On reconnect or return to foreground it refetches the snapshot instead of trusting that no update was missed. When the app is not in the foreground, key transitions arrive as push notifications and, where the OS supports it, a lock-screen live update. The screen shows data age and a clear degraded state when updates stop, counts down the estimate locally between updates, and stops all subscriptions once the order reaches a terminal state.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The user needs a trustworthy status more than a fast one, so correctness comes from snapshot plus versioned updates, not from the stream being perfect. Showing staleness honestly avoids a frozen screen that looks live.

points.title: Flow
items: Open Screen → Snapshot API → Order Stream → Version Check → Render State → Push when Backgrounded

points.title: Trade-offs
items: A stream gives low latency but costs battery; polling is simple but slower
Frequent estimate updates feel live but can make the number jitter
Push covers background but may arrive late or not at all

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep the in-app screen and lock-screen surface consistent?
What do you show if no update has arrived for a long time?
How does adding a courier map change the transport choice?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Advancing state on the client with timers
Applying updates without a version check
Leaving the connection open after the order completes

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Server-owned state machine with versioned snapshots
Stream with polling fallback and refetch on resume
Idempotent, order-tolerant update handling
Background coverage with push or live surface
Staleness indication and terminal cleanup

questions.q: Design a file uploader that continues when the app is backgrounded and resumes after failures.
questions.a: Persist an upload record with file reference, server upload id, state and progress before starting, so the job survives process death. Copy or secure access to the file so it remains readable later. Hand the transfer to the **OS background transfer facility**, a background upload session on iOS and a scheduled worker or foreground service on Android, because an app cannot rely on running its own code while suspended, and the rules vary by OS version. Make the upload **resumable**: the client creates an upload session on the server, sends the file in chunks or ranges, and after any interruption asks the server how many bytes it has and continues from there. Chunks go directly to object storage through pre-authorized URLs where possible, and a final commit call with an idempotency key and checksum makes the file visible. Apply constraints such as unmetered network for large files, retry with backoff, and reflect state in the UI from the persisted record, including a notification on completion or permanent failure.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Large uploads outlast the app's foreground time, so the transfer must be owned by the system and the protocol must tolerate being cut at any byte. Persisted state plus server-side offset query makes resumption deterministic.

points.title: Flow
items: Pick File → Persist Upload Record → Create Upload Session → OS Background Transfer → Chunks to Object Storage → Commit with Checksum

points.title: Trade-offs
items: OS-managed transfers survive suspension but give less control over timing and progress
Smaller chunks lose less on failure but add request overhead
Direct-to-storage upload offloads your servers but needs careful scoping of upload credentials

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What if the source file is edited or deleted mid-upload?
How do you clean up abandoned partial uploads?
How do you handle credentials expiring during a long upload?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Running the upload in app code and assuming it continues in the background
Restarting from zero after every failure
Keeping progress only in memory

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Durable upload record created before transfer
Uses OS background transfer mechanisms
Resumable protocol with server offset query
Idempotent commit with integrity check
Handles constraints, expiry and cleanup

questions.q: Design a mobile video player with adaptive bitrate streaming.
questions.a: Video is encoded into several renditions at different bitrates and resolutions, cut into short segments, and described by a manifest, typically HLS or DASH, served from a CDN. The player downloads the manifest, picks a rendition, and fetches segments into a buffer ahead of the playhead. The **adaptation algorithm** chooses the rendition for each next segment using measured throughput and current buffer level: step down quickly when the buffer is draining to avoid stalls, and step up cautiously to avoid oscillation. Start with a conservative rendition and a small initial buffer for fast time-to-first-frame, then build up. Cap the rendition by screen size, device decode capability, metered-network or data-saver settings and thermal state. Handle lifecycle: release decoders when backgrounded, support audio-only or picture-in-picture where appropriate, and resume from the saved position. Instrument quality of experience, startup time, rebuffer ratio, average bitrate, switch count and playback failures, since those metrics are how the algorithm is tuned. Protected content adds a license request step and offline downloads add storage management.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Mobile bandwidth changes second to second, so one fixed quality either stalls or wastes data. The design is a control loop balancing startup speed, stalls and visual quality, and it can only be tuned with field measurements.

points.title: Flow
items: Manifest → ABR Controller → Segment Fetch from CDN → Buffer → Decoder → QoE Metrics

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Larger buffers reduce stalls but waste data when the user leaves early
Aggressive upswitching improves quality but risks rebuffering
Shorter segments adapt faster but increase request overhead
Preloading the next video speeds swipes but spends data speculatively

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How would you design preloading for a vertical swipe feed of videos?
How does the design change for low-latency live streams?
How do you decide the bitrate ladder?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Choosing quality by connection type instead of measured throughput and buffer
Ignoring device capability and screen size when picking a rendition
No quality-of-experience telemetry

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Explains renditions, segments and manifest
Describes throughput- and buffer-based adaptation with hysteresis
Optimizes startup separately from steady state
Applies device, data and thermal caps
Defines QoE metrics
Covers lifecycle and resume

questions.q: Design the rider-side map that tracks a driver's position in real time.
questions.a: Two clients are involved. The driver app samples location at a rate adapted to speed and state, filters out low-accuracy fixes, batches points when the network drops, and uploads each with a timestamp and sequence number. A location service keeps the latest position per trip and fans it out to subscribed riders. The rider app, while the screen is visible, holds a stream or socket subscription for that trip and receives position, heading, a route polyline and an updated arrival estimate. Updates arrive every few seconds at best, so the client **interpolates**: it animates the marker smoothly from the previous point to the new one along the route rather than jumping, and may project slightly forward, correcting gently when the next fix arrives. Out-of-order or stale points are dropped by sequence and timestamp, and the marker is shown as stale if updates stop. The route geometry is sent once and updated only on reroute, map tiles are cached, and when the app is backgrounded the subscription closes and push or a lock-screen live update carries the milestones.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Raw location is sparse, noisy and delayed, so a good experience depends on client-side smoothing as much as on transport. Scoping the connection to screen visibility keeps battery cost acceptable on both devices.

points.title: Flow
items: Driver GPS → Location Ingest → Trip Fan-out → Rider Stream → Interpolation → Map Marker

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Higher sampling rate looks smoother but drains the driver's battery and data
Forward projection hides latency but can show the car somewhere it is not
Snapping to the route looks clean but is wrong when the driver deviates

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle the driver going through a tunnel?
How would you reduce battery use on the driver device?
How does the server scale fan-out for many concurrent trips?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Moving the marker only when a new point arrives, producing jumps
Keeping the stream open in the background
Trusting every GPS fix without accuracy filtering

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Covers both driver upload and rider subscription paths
Adaptive sampling and batching on the driver
Interpolation and stale-point handling on the rider
Subscription tied to screen visibility with background fallback
Addresses gaps, reroutes and stale indication

questions.q: Design an in-app notification inbox with unread counts that stay correct across devices.
questions.a: The inbox is a **server-stored list**, independent of push; a push notification is only an alert that a new item exists, so the inbox is complete even when pushes are dropped or disabled. The client keeps a local copy, loads it with cursor pagination, and stays current with delta sync on launch, on foreground and when a push arrives. Each item has a stable id, type, payload, created time and read state. Marking read is an idempotent operation applied locally at once and queued for upload; a mark-all-read is expressed as "read up to this point" rather than as a list of ids. The unread count is **computed by the server** and returned with each sync, with the client adjusting optimistically in between, because counting independently on each device drifts. The app icon badge is set from that count, and a push can carry the new count so the badge updates while the app is closed. Tapping an item routes through the central deep-link router, and items have a retention period after which they expire.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Treating push and inbox as separate systems removes the dependence on best-effort delivery. A server-derived count is the only version that agrees across devices.

points.title: Flow
items: Notification Event → Inbox Store → Push Alert → Client Delta Sync → Local Inbox → Read-State Sync and Badge

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Server-side count is consistent but needs a round trip to be exact
Local persistence gives instant open but needs sync and expiry handling
Carrying the badge count in push keeps it fresh but can be wrong if a push is missed

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you keep the badge right when the app has not been opened for days?
How do you handle a notification whose target no longer exists?
How would you add categories and per-category preferences?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Building the inbox from received pushes
Incrementing unread counts locally on each device
Mark-all-read implemented as thousands of individual updates

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Inbox stored on the server, separate from push delivery
Delta sync with local persistence and pagination
Idempotent read-state operations including a watermark for mark-all
Server-derived unread count and badge
Deep-link routing and retention

questions.q: Design a mobile analytics SDK that other app teams will embed.
questions.a: As a guest in someone else's app, the SDK's first requirement is to do no harm: tiny public API, near-zero startup cost with lazy initialization, all work off the main thread, bounded memory and disk, and no crash may escape it. Internally, events pass through enrichment, adding session, device and app context, then into a durable bounded queue, and an uploader sends compressed batches with backoff, deleting only on acknowledgement, with unique event ids so the server can de-duplicate. Sessions are derived from foreground and background transitions with an inactivity timeout. Behavior such as batch size, flush interval, sampling rate and a global **kill switch** comes from remote configuration, because the SDK's code is frozen inside every host release. Privacy is built in: consent gating before anything is collected or sent, a way to reset identifiers and delete queued data, no collection of sensitive fields by default, and compliance with platform tracking rules. Provide a stable, versioned event schema, backward-compatible ingestion for old SDK versions, and a debug mode that lets integrators see and validate what is sent.

points.title: Reasoning
items: An SDK inherits the constraints of every app that embeds it and cannot be patched once shipped, so safety, remote control and compatibility matter more than features. Trust from host teams is the product.

points.title: Flow
items: Track Call → Enrichment → Durable Queue → Batch Uploader → Ingest API → Remote Config and Kill Switch

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Rich automatic capture is convenient but raises privacy risk and overhead
Sampling cuts cost but complicates exact counts
A minimal API is stable but pushes work onto integrators

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you guarantee the SDK never crashes the host app?
How do you evolve the event schema without breaking old SDK versions?
How would you measure and publish the SDK's own overhead?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Heavy synchronous initialization at app launch
No remote way to throttle or disable the SDK
Treating consent and data deletion as an afterthought

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: States host-app safety constraints explicitly
Durable, bounded, acknowledged batching pipeline
Remote configuration including a kill switch
Consent, identifier reset and data minimization
Versioned schema and backward-compatible ingestion
Integrator tooling for validation

questions.q: Design a feature-flag SDK for mobile apps.
questions.a: Flag reads must be **synchronous, local and never fail**, since they sit on hot paths including startup. The SDK therefore evaluates against an in-memory snapshot loaded from disk, with compiled-in defaults when nothing is cached. A background fetch retrieves updates, sending the user and device context, and uses a version or validator so an unchanged config costs almost nothing. Choose where rules are evaluated: server-side evaluation returns only the resolved values for this user, keeping targeting rules private and payloads small, while client-side evaluation works offline for context changes but ships the rules. New values are staged and **activated at a defined boundary**, usually next launch, so a flag does not change mid-session; kill switches get a faster path such as activation on next foreground or a push-triggered refresh. Percentage rollouts use deterministic hashing of a stable identifier so assignment is sticky, and each first evaluation logs an exposure event for experiment analysis. Add typed accessors, local overrides for testing, change listeners, staleness telemetry, and handling for identity change on login and logout so one user never sees another user's flags.

points.title: Reasoning
items: The SDK controls behavior of code that is already shipped, so its own failure modes matter most: it must return a sane answer with no network and must not flip behavior at unpredictable times. Consistency and safe defaults outrank freshness.

points.title: Flow
items: Flag Read → In-Memory Snapshot → Disk Cache and Defaults → Background Fetch → Staged Values → Activation and Exposure Log

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Server-side evaluation hides rules but needs a fetch when context changes
Launch-time activation is stable but slows propagation
Blocking startup on a fresh fetch gives correct first-launch values but hurts launch time and fails offline

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you handle the very first launch before any fetch completes?
How do you keep experiment assignment stable when a user logs in?
How quickly can a kill switch reach users, and what limits it?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Network call on the read path
Flags changing value mid-session without an activation model
No exposure logging, making experiments unanalyzable

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Local synchronous evaluation with defaults
Explicit fetch, cache and activation model
Reasoned choice between client- and server-side evaluation
Sticky bucketing and exposure events
Identity change handling and a fast kill-switch path
Testing overrides and staleness telemetry

questions.q: Your app has years of locally stored user data. How do you evolve the local database schema safely across releases?
questions.a: Users skip versions, so a migration must work from **any** still-supported schema version to the current one, not just from the previous release; keep every schema version and test the full chain plus direct jumps in CI with realistic data sizes. Run migrations in a transaction so an interruption leaves the old schema intact, and make long migrations resumable and off the main thread behind a progress state, since a slow blocking migration at launch looks like a hang and may get the app terminated. Classify stored data: anything that is a cache of server state can be dropped and refetched, which is the cheapest and safest migration; only unsynced user data such as outbox entries and drafts truly needs transforming. Prefer additive changes, and for risky restructures use expand-then-contract across two releases. Because the binary cannot be rolled back, have a recovery path: detect a failed or corrupt database, preserve unsynced data if possible, rebuild from the server, and report it. Track migration duration and failure rate by version in the field.

points.title: Reasoning
items: A broken migration is among the worst mobile failures, because it hits at launch, repeats on every start and cannot be undone by a rollback. Minimizing what must be migrated and rehearsing every path is the realistic defense.

points.title: Flow
items: App Launch → Schema Version Check → Migration Chain → Transactional Apply → Verify → Fallback Rebuild from Server

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Dropping and refetching caches is safe but costs data and a slower first launch after update
Supporting very old schema versions is user-friendly but multiplies test paths
Background migration keeps launch responsive but the app must run against a partially migrated store

points.title: Follow-ups
items: What do you do with outbox entries written in an old format?
How do you handle a user who restores a backup from an older version?
How do you test migrations against production-scale data?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Testing only the previous-version-to-current path
Long migrations on the main thread at launch
No recovery plan when a migration fails in the field

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Handles upgrades from any supported version
Transactional, resumable, off-main-thread migrations
Separates rebuildable cache from irreplaceable local data
Defines a failure recovery path
Has CI coverage and field telemetry

questions.q: The backend has a major outage and then recovers. How should a large fleet of mobile clients behave so they do not make it worse?
questions.a: The danger is synchronized behavior: every client retrying at once during the outage, then every client refreshing at once on recovery. Client retries use exponential backoff with jitter and a **retry budget** so retries are a bounded fraction of normal traffic. A client-side circuit breaker per host or endpoint class stops sending after repeated failures and probes occasionally. The server can shed load explicitly with overload responses and retry-after hints, and the client must honor them. Requests carry a priority so that under stress the client drops prefetch, analytics and background sync first and keeps user-initiated actions. Anything periodic, config fetches, token refreshes, sync timers, needs jitter so the fleet is not aligned to the clock, and mass push notifications should be spread out because they cause a wave of app opens. During the outage the app serves cached data, queues writes and tells the user plainly. A remote control plane, served from infrastructure independent of the main backend, lets operators lower request rates or disable features. Rehearse this with fault injection before it is needed.

points.title: Reasoning
items: Millions of independent clients behave like one large distributed system that you can no longer redeploy during the incident. Load-shedding behavior therefore has to be designed and shipped in advance, with remote knobs to adjust it.

points.title: Flow
items: Request → Priority and Retry Budget → Circuit Breaker → API Gateway Load Shedding → Cached Fallback → Remote Throttle Config

points.title: Trade-offs
items: Conservative retries protect the backend but slow recovery for individual users
Circuit breakers reduce load but can hold off after the service is healthy
A separate control plane adds infrastructure but is the only lever when the main one is down

points.title: Follow-ups
items: How do you avoid a stampede when a cached config expires for everyone at the same moment?
How do you test client outage behavior before release?
What should the user see during the outage?

points.title: Common mistakes
items: Immediate or fixed-interval retries across the fleet
Timers and expiries aligned to the same wall-clock moment
Remote controls hosted on the same system that is failing

points.title: What a good answer shows
items: Identifies synchronized retry and recovery stampede as the core risk
Backoff with jitter, retry budget and circuit breaking
Honors server load-shedding signals
Prioritizes user-initiated traffic over background work
Independent remote control plane and jittered periodic work
Mentions rehearsal through fault injection
